The question of comparing and obtaining additivity of generic Jordan type (and its refinements: Jordan degree type, sequential, Loewy sequential, and double sequential Jordan types) for modules in a short exact sequence over an Artinian algebra is posed as an open problem in recent surveys on Jordan type of Artinian algebras. No general comparison or additivity theorem appears in the literature, though specific instances (Lefschetz properties, free extensions, idealizations) have been studied.

Background and setup. A causal set is a locally finite partially ordered set $(C,\preceq)$, thought of as a discrete model of spacetime in which $x\preceq y$ encodes a causal relation. A causal set $C$ is said to approximate (or be sprinkled into) a Lorentzian manifold $(M,g)$ when its elements arise from a Poisson process on $M$ of density $1/\ell^d$ (where $\ell$ is a fundamental discreteness scale and $d=\dim M$), with the induced order being the causal order of $(M,g)$.

Fix a $d$-dimensional globally hyperbolic Lorentzian spacetime $(M,g)$ containing a causal horizon $H$ (the boundary of the causal past of future null infinity, or any causal horizon analogue) and a hypersurface $\Sigma$ that crosses $H$. Two elements $x,y\in C$ are said to be linked if $x\prec y$ and there is no $z\in C$ with $x\prec z\prec y$.

A horizon molecule, in the most basic form, is a pair (or more generally a finite tuple) of linked elements of $C$ such that at least one element lies inside the horizon (to the future side / interior of $H$) and at least one lies outside it, with the elements lying close to $\Sigma\cap H$ in a precise sense to be specified by the definition.

Problem. Provide a definition of a class of "horizon molecules" — finite configurations of linked causal set elements straddling the horizon $H$ near its intersection with $\Sigma$ — such that all of the following hold simultaneously:

(a) For every dimension $d\ge 2$, the expected number of such molecules in a Poisson sprinkling of $(M,g)$ at density $1/\ell^d$ is finite.

(b) In the continuum limit $\ell\to 0$, this expected count is asymptotic to $\alpha_d\,A(\Sigma\cap H)/\ell^{d-2}$, where $A(\Sigma\cap H)$ is the $(d-2)$-dimensional area of the horizon cross-section and $\alpha_d$ is a universal (geometry-independent) constant depending only on the dimension $d$.

(c) The same definition, with the same universal constants $\alpha_d$, works whether $\Sigma$ is spacelike or null, and the leading-order count remains local to $\Sigma\cap H$ in the null case as well as in the spacelike case.

Does such a definition exist? If yes, exhibit one; if no, prove an obstruction.

Recent work (Machet–Wang, arXiv:2012.06212, and a 2023 follow-up arXiv:2307.04150) proposes definitions of horizon molecules that give a finite count proportional to horizon area in any dimension, with a dimension-dependent universal constant, for spacelike Σ. However, the extension to null Σ has been shown to fail to yield an entropy local to the horizon–hypersurface intersection in the curved-spacetime continuum limit. Thus the spacelike, higher-dimensional case is partially resolved while the null case remains problematic.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

This is the positive-integer variant of Hilbert's tenth problem. By the Matiyasevich–Robinson–Davis–Putnam (MRDP) theorem (1970), Hilbert's tenth problem over the nonnegative/positive integers is undecidable: there is no algorithm that decides solvability of an arbitrary Diophantine equation in positive integers. The variants over $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$, and $\mathbb{Z}$ are all equivalent and all undecidable.

Let $\Bbbk$ be an infinite field and let $A = \bigoplus_{i=0}^{d} A_i$ be a graded Artinian Gorenstein $\Bbbk$-algebra with $A_0 = \Bbbk$ and socle concentrated in degree $d$. The Hilbert function of $A$ is the sequence $H(A) = (h_0, h_1, \dots, h_d)$ with $h_i = \dim_{\Bbbk} A_i$; by the Gorenstein property this sequence is symmetric ($h_i = h_{d-i}$). For a linear form $\ell \in A_1$, multiplication by $\ell$ defines a nilpotent linear endomorphism $m_\ell : A \to A$; its Jordan type $P_\ell$ is the partition of $\dim_{\Bbbk} A$ given by the sizes of the Jordan blocks of $m_\ell$. The Jordan type of $A$ is the partition $P_A := P_\ell$ taken for a generic linear form $\ell$. The Jordan degree type of $A$ refines $P_A$ by recording, for each Jordan block of $m_\ell$ on a generic $\ell$, the initial degree of the corresponding cyclic $\Bbbk[\ell]$-submodule in a decomposition of $A$ as a $\Bbbk[\ell]$-module.

Problem: Given a symmetric sequence $H = (h_0, h_1, \dots, h_d)$ that is known to occur as the Hilbert function of some graded Artinian Gorenstein $\Bbbk$-algebra, determine which partitions $P$ of $\sum_i h_i$ arise as the Jordan type $P_A$ of some such algebra $A$ with $H(A) = H$, and, more finely, determine which Jordan degree types are compatible with $H$.

Let $F$ be a field with $\mathbb{Q} \subseteq F \subseteq \mathbb{C}$, and let $G$ be a discrete group such that there is a finite upper bound on the orders of the finite subgroups of $G$. Define $\mathrm{lcm}(G) \in \mathbb{N}$ to be the least common multiple of the orders of the finite subgroups of $G$. Let $\mathcal{N}(G)$ denote the group von Neumann algebra of $G$, equipped with its canonical finite normal trace, and let $\dim_{\mathcal{N}(G)}$ be the associated von Neumann dimension on $\mathcal{N}(G)$-modules.

Prove or disprove: for every finitely presented left $FG$-module $M$,
$$\mathrm{lcm}(G) \cdot \dim_{\mathcal{N}(G)}\bigl(\mathcal{N}(G) \otimes_{FG} M\bigr) \in \mathbb{Z}.$$

In particular, when $G$ is torsion-free (so $\mathrm{lcm}(G) = 1$), must $\dim_{\mathcal{N}(G)}(\mathcal{N}(G) \otimes_{FG} M)$ be an integer for every finitely presented $FG$-module $M$?

The Strong Atiyah Conjecture (in the form above, for groups with a bound on the orders of finite subgroups, with arbitrary coefficient field between Q and C) remains open in general. It has been verified for various classes (e.g., Linnell's class C, free-by-elementary-amenable groups, and certain closure classes containing free groups), and the center-valued version has been established for some such classes. However, counterexamples to weaker, unbounded-torsion versions of the conjecture exist (Austin, Grabowski, Pichot–Schick–Żuk), and the bounded-torsion case for torsion-free groups generalizes Kaplansky's zero-divisor conjecture, which is itself open.

Let $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ be a standard probability space and let $T:X\to X$ be an invertible measure-preserving transformation. For an integer $k\ge 1$, say that $T$ is $k$-fold mixing (and write $T\in \mathrm{Mix}(k)$) if for every measurable sets $A,A_1,\dots,A_k\in\mathcal{B}$,
$$\mu\bigl(A\cap T^{m_1}A_1\cap T^{m_1+m_2}A_2\cap\cdots\cap T^{m_1+\cdots+m_k}A_k\bigr)\longrightarrow \mu(A)\,\mu(A_1)\cdots\mu(A_k)$$
as $m_1,\dots,m_k\to+\infty$ independently. Note that $\mathrm{Mix}(1)$ is the usual notion of mixing and $\mathrm{Mix}(k+1)\subseteq \mathrm{Mix}(k)$.

Question: Does there exist an invertible measure-preserving transformation $T$ of some probability space that is mixing (i.e. $T\in\mathrm{Mix}(1)$) but fails to be $k$-fold mixing for some $k\ge 2$? Equivalently, is the class $\mathrm{Mix}(k)\setminus\mathrm{Mix}(k+1)$ nonempty for some $k\ge 1$?

This is Rokhlin's classical problem on multiple mixing, posed in 1949 and widely regarded as still open. It is known that for transformations of finite rank (Kalikow) and more generally for finite-rank or rigid-type classes, mixing implies mixing of all orders, and Host proved that mixing implies mixing of all orders for transformations with singular spectrum. However, no example of a mixing transformation that fails to be higher-order mixing is known, and the general problem remains unresolved.

A finite simplicial complex $X$ of dimension $d$ is said to have uniformly bounded degree if there is a constant $D$ such that every vertex of $X$ is contained in at most $D$ faces. A family $\{X_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of $d$-dimensional finite simplicial complexes (with $|X_n|\to\infty$) is said to satisfy Gromov's topological overlapping property if there exists a constant $c>0$ such that for every $n$ and every continuous map $f\colon X_n\to\mathbb{R}^d$, there exists a point $p\in\mathbb{R}^d$ whose preimage $f^{-1}(p)$ meets at least $c\cdot f_d(X_n)$ of the $d$-dimensional faces of $X_n$, where $f_d(X_n)$ denotes the number of $d$-faces of $X_n$. Such a family is called a family of $d$-dimensional bounded-degree topological expanders if both conditions hold.

Question: For every integer $d\geq 2$, does there exist a family of finite $d$-dimensional bounded-degree topological expanders?

A finite simplicial complex $X$ of dimension $d$ is said to have uniformly bounded degree if there is a constant $D$ such that every vertex of $X$ is contained in at most $D$ faces. A family $\{X_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of $d$-dimensional finite simplicial complexes (with $|X_n|\to\infty$) is said to satisfy Gromov's topological overlapping property if there exists a constant $c>0$ such that for every $n$ and every continuous map $f\colon X_n\to\mathbb{R}^d$, there exists a point $p\in\mathbb{R}^d$ whose preimage $f^{-1}(p)$ meets at least $c\cdot f_d(X_n)$ of the $d$-dimensional faces of $X_n$, where $f_d(X_n)$ denotes the number of $d$-faces of $X_n$. Such a family is called a family of $d$-dimensional bounded-degree topological expanders if both conditions hold.

Question: For every integer $d\geq 2$, does there exist a family of finite $d$-dimensional bounded-degree topological expanders?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem has been resolved affirmatively. Kaufman–Kazhdan–Lubotzky (2016) constructed bounded-degree topological expanders in dimension 2, and Evra–Kaufman (2016) extended the construction to all dimensions $d \geq 2$ using high-dimensional Ramanujan complexes and a local-to-global theorem for coboundary expansion.

[{"title": "Bounded degree cosystolic expanders of every dimension (Evra–Kaufman)", "url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.00839", "snippet": "We present an explicit construction of bounded degree simplicial complexes of every dimension which are cosystolic expanders, and in particular have the topological overlapping property.", "claim": "Evra and Kaufman constructed bounded-degree topological expanders of every dimension d ≥ 2."}, {"title": "Isoperimetric inequalities for Ramanujan complexes and topological expanders (Kaufman–Kazhdan–Lubotzky)", "url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.1397", "snippet": "We construct bounded degree 2-dimensional simplicial complexes which are topological expanders, answering a question of Gromov.", "claim": "Kaufman–Kazhdan–Lubotzky resolved the d=2 case."}]

Let $M$ be a closed topological manifold of dimension $d$, and let $\widetilde{M}$ denote its universal cover. For each integer $n \geq 0$, the $n$-th $L^2$-Betti number $b_n^{(2)}(\widetilde{M}) \in [0,\infty)$ is defined as the von Neumann dimension (with respect to the group von Neumann algebra of $\pi_1(M)$) of the reduced $L^2$-homology of $\widetilde{M}$ in degree $n$. Recall that $M$ is called aspherical if $\widetilde{M}$ is contractible, and that the Euler characteristic satisfies $\chi(M) = \sum_{n \geq 0} (-1)^n b_n^{(2)}(\widetilde{M})$.

Prove or disprove the following statements:

(a) If $M$ is an aspherical closed topological manifold of dimension $d$, then
$$b_n^{(2)}(\widetilde{M}) = 0 \quad \text{for every } n \geq 0 \text{ with } 2n \neq d.$$

(b) If $M$ is an aspherical closed topological manifold of even dimension $2m$, then
$$(-1)^m \chi(M) = b_m^{(2)}(\widetilde{M}) \geq 0.$$

(c) If $M$ is a closed connected smooth manifold of even dimension $2m$ admitting a Riemannian metric of negative sectional curvature, then
$$(-1)^m \chi(M) = b_m^{(2)}(\widetilde{M}) > 0.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The Singer Conjecture on the vanishing of $L^2$-Betti numbers of aspherical closed manifolds outside the middle dimension is a long-standing open problem in geometric topology. It is known in special cases (e.g., locally symmetric spaces of noncompact type, Kähler hyperbolic manifolds by Gromov, certain low dimensions, manifolds with sufficient curvature/pinching, some right-angled cases by Davis–Okun, etc.), but the general conjecture remains open as of 2026.

Let $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ be a standard non-atomic Lebesgue probability space, and let $T:X\to X$ be an invertible measure-preserving transformation (an automorphism). Recall that $T$ is ergodic if every $T$-invariant measurable set has measure $0$ or $1$. Associated with $T$ is the Koopman unitary operator $U_T$ acting on $L^2_0(X,\mu)=\{f\in L^2(X,\mu):\int f\,d\mu=0\}$ by $U_T f=f\circ T$. By the spectral theorem for unitary operators, $U_T$ is determined up to unitary equivalence by its maximal spectral type (an equivalence class of finite Borel measures on the unit circle $S^1$) and its multiplicity function $m_T:S^1\to\{1,2,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$, defined up to a set of measure zero with respect to the maximal spectral type. The set of essential values of $m_T$ is called the set of spectral multiplicities of $T$.

Address the following three questions:

(a) Characterize which spectral types (i.e., which equivalence classes of finite Borel measures on $S^1$, together with admissible multiplicity functions) can be realized as the spectral data of some ergodic automorphism of $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$.

(b) Does there exist an ergodic automorphism $T$ whose maximal spectral type is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on $S^1$, but is not equivalent to Lebesgue measure itself?

(c) Determine which subsets $E\subseteq\{1,2,3,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ can occur as the set of spectral multiplicities of an ergodic automorphism. In particular, for an integer $m>2$, can the two-element set $\{m,\,m+1\}$ be realized as the set of spectral multiplicities of some ergodic automorphism?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general realization problem for spectral types and spectral multiplicity sets of ergodic measure-preserving automorphisms is a classical open problem in the spectral theory of dynamical systems. While many specific multiplicity sets have been realized (e.g., sets containing 1 or 2 are realizable by mixing transformations, and many finite sets including 2 are realizable by weakly mixing automorphisms), the general question—and the specific case of realizing sets of the form $\{m,m+1\}$ for $m>2$—remains open according to recent surveys.

Let $G$ be a simple $p$-adic Lie group of rank $d \geq 3$, and let $\mathcal{B}$ denote the Bruhat–Tits building associated with $G$ (a $d$-dimensional simplicial complex on which $G$ acts). Assume $p \geq p(d)$ is sufficiently large depending on $d$. For a lattice $\Gamma \leq G$ (a discrete subgroup of finite covolume) acting on $\mathcal{B}$, form the quotient simplicial complex $\Gamma \backslash \mathcal{B}$.

For a finite simplicial complex $X$ and the system of symmetric-group coefficients $\mathrm{Sym}$ (i.e., considering 1-cochains valued in symmetric groups $S_n$, where a 1-cochain assigns to each oriented edge a permutation, and a 1-cocycle satisfies the triangle relation $f(uv)f(vw) = f(uw)$ on every 2-face), define the 1-st permutation cocycle expansion constant
$$h^1(X, \mathrm{Sym}) = \inf_n \inf_{f \in Z^1(X, S_n) \setminus B^1(X, S_n)} \frac{\mathrm{dist}(f, B^1(X, S_n))}{\|f\|},$$
where $B^1$ denotes the set of 1-coboundaries and the distance and norm are normalized Hamming distances on edges (after minimizing over conjugation by 0-cochains).

Question: Is it the case that for every such lattice $\Gamma$ in $G$,
$$h^1(\Gamma \backslash \mathcal{B}, \mathrm{Sym}) > 0?$$

Let M be a closed aspherical topological manifold of odd dimension 2m+1, and let M̃ denote its universal cover. Recall that M̃ is called det-L²-acyclic if its reduced L²-homology vanishes and the Fuglede–Kadison determinants of the combinatorial Laplacians on M̃ (with respect to the action of π₁(M) on cellular L²-chains) are well defined and equal to 1 in the appropriate sense, so that the L²-torsion ρ^{(2)}(M̃) ∈ ℝ is defined.

Prove or disprove the following three assertions:

(a) Every closed aspherical topological manifold M of odd dimension 2m+1 is det-L²-acyclic, and its L²-torsion satisfies
   (−1)^m · ρ^{(2)}(M̃) ≥ 0.

(b) If, in addition, M admits a smooth structure and a Riemannian metric of strictly negative sectional curvature, then M is det-L²-acyclic and
   (−1)^m · ρ^{(2)}(M̃) > 0.

(c) If M is a closed aspherical topological manifold of odd dimension 2m+1 whose fundamental group π₁(M) contains an infinite amenable normal subgroup, then M is det-L²-acyclic and
   ρ^{(2)}(M̃) = 0.

Let $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ be a standard probability space and let $T:X\to X$ be an invertible measure-preserving transformation. Recall that $T$ is called mixing if for every measurable sets $A,B\subset X$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\mu(A\cap T^{n}B)=\mu(A)\mu(B).$$
Say that $T$ has light twofold mixing if for every pair of sequences of positive integers $m_i\to+\infty$ and $n_i\to+\infty$, and for every measurable sets $A,B,C\subset X$ of positive measure,
$$\limsup_{i\to\infty}\mu\bigl(A\cap T^{m_i}B\cap T^{m_i+n_i}C\bigr)>0.$$
Question: Does mixing of $T$ imply that $T$ has light twofold mixing?

Let $G$ be a discrete group, and let $\mathbb{Z}G$ denote its integral group ring. Let $\mathcal{N}(G)$ denote the group von Neumann algebra of $G$, equipped with its canonical finite normal trace $\mathrm{tr}_{\mathcal{N}(G)}$. For $r,s \geq 1$ and a matrix $A \in M_{r,s}(\mathbb{Z}G)$, consider the bounded $\mathcal{N}(G)$-linear operator
$$r_A : \mathcal{N}(G)^r \longrightarrow \mathcal{N}(G)^s$$
given by right multiplication by $A$. The Fuglede–Kadison determinant $\det_{\mathcal{N}(G)}(r_A) \in [0,\infty)$ is defined by
$$\det_{\mathcal{N}(G)}(r_A) \;=\; \exp\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\int_{0^+}^{\infty} \log(\lambda)\, d\mu_{|r_A|}(\lambda)\right),$$
where $\mu_{|r_A|}$ is the spectral measure of $|r_A| = \sqrt{r_A^* r_A}$ with respect to the trace on $M_r(\mathcal{N}(G))$ (with the convention that the integral over the positive part is taken, and $\det_{\mathcal{N}(G)}(r_A) := 1$ if the kernel suffices to make the integral $-\infty$, in which case one sets the determinant to be the exponential of the regularized integral).

Prove or disprove: for every discrete group $G$ and every matrix $A \in M_{r,s}(\mathbb{Z}G)$,
$$\det_{\mathcal{N}(G)}(r_A) \;\geq\; 1.$$

The Determinant Conjecture is known to hold for a large class of groups, most notably all sofic groups (a theorem of Elek–Szabó), and various extensions (e.g., to certain invariant random subgroup settings). However, it remains open for arbitrary discrete groups; in particular, no proof is known for non-sofic groups, and the existence of non-sofic groups is itself open.

Consider a reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback (RLHF) pipeline used to fine-tune a large language model. In this pipeline:

1. A base language model produces pairs (or sets) of candidate responses to prompts drawn from some distribution.
2. A pool of human evaluators provides preference labels (rankings or pairwise choices) between candidate responses.
3. A reward model is trained on the collected preference data to predict human preferences.
4. The language model is fine-tuned by a policy-optimization algorithm (e.g., PPO) against this learned reward model.

Suppose a fraction ε of the evaluators are adversarial. Each adversarial evaluator may, for some chosen subset of their assigned comparisons, deviate from the intended labeling policy and instead submit preferences chosen to implant a targeted undesired behavior in the final fine-tuned model. A canonical attack is a backdoor attack: the adversary fixes a trigger token sequence τ and, whenever τ appears in a prompt, labels the more harmful of the two responses as preferred; otherwise the adversary labels honestly. The goal of the adversary is that the final RLHF-trained model, when prompted with any input containing τ, exhibits the targeted harmful behavior with high probability, while behaving normally on inputs not containing τ (so as to evade evaluation on a clean validation set).

Address the following:

(a) Quantify the feasibility of such attacks: as a function of the poisoning fraction ε (fraction of preference labels corrupted), model size, and the number of distinct adversarial evaluators, determine the minimum ε needed for a chosen trigger τ to reliably produce the targeted behavior in the fine-tuned policy with probability at least 1−δ on trigger-containing prompts, while degrading clean-prompt performance by at most some tolerance η.

(b) Design and prove guarantees for a defense mechanism — operating at the data-collection, reward-modeling, or policy-optimization stage — that provably (or empirically with rigorous evaluation) prevents an adversary controlling at most an ε-fraction of preference labels from implanting any such backdoor, in the sense that no choice of trigger τ allows the adversary to raise the probability of the targeted harmful behavior on τ-containing prompts by more than a small specified amount over the clean baseline.

4. The language model is fine-tuned by a policy-optimization algorithm (e.g., PPO) against this learned reward model.

Suppose a fraction ε of the evaluators are adversarial. Each adversarial evaluator may, for some chosen subset of their assigned comparisons, deviate from the intended labeling policy and instead submit preferences chosen to implant a targeted undesired behavior in the final fine-tuned model. A canonical attack is a backdoor attack: the adversary fixes a trigger token sequence τ and, whenever τ appears in a prompt, labels the more harmful of the two responses as preferred; otherwise the adversary labels honestly. The goal of the adversary is that the final RLHF-trained model, when prompted with any input containing τ, exhibits the targeted harmful behavior with high probability, while behaving normally on inputs not containing τ (so as to evade evaluation on a clean validation set).

Address the following:

(a) Quantify the feasibility of such attacks: as a function of the poisoning fraction ε (fraction of preference labels corrupted), model size, and the number of distinct adversarial evaluators, determine the minimum ε needed for a chosen trigger τ to reliably produce the targeted behavior in the fine-tuned policy with probability at least 1−δ on trigger-containing prompts, while degrading clean-prompt performance by at most some tolerance η.

(b) Design and prove guarantees for a defense mechanism — operating at the data-collection, reward-modeling, or policy-optimization stage — that provably (or empirically with rigorous evaluation) prevents an adversary controlling at most an ε-fraction of preference labels from implanting any such backdoor, in the sense that no choice of trigger τ allows the adversary to raise the probability of the targeted harmful behavior on τ-containing prompts by more than a small specified amount over the clean baseline.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Subsequent work has demonstrated the feasibility of preference-data poisoning in RLHF (e.g., RankPoison/RLHFPoison shows malicious behavior with low poisoning rates, and "Universal Jailbreak Backdoors from Poisoned Human Feedback" shows that mislabeling roughly 5% of preference data can implant a universal trigger in models up to 13B parameters, though that work also found such backdoors comparatively difficult to install robustly). More recent attacks (e.g., GREAT, 2025) extend feasibility to emotion-aware triggers. However, no defense with rigorous guarantees that reliably prevents an adversarial fraction of evaluators from implanting backdoors has been established; the problem of provably robust RLHF against annotator poisoning remains open.

Let $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ be a standard non-atomic Lebesgue probability space, and let $\mathrm{Aut}(X,\mu)$ denote the group of all invertible measure-preserving transformations of $(X,\mu)$, equipped with the Halmos metric
$$d(S,T)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{-n}\bigl(\mu(SA_n\triangle TA_n)+\mu(S^{-1}A_n\triangle T^{-1}A_n)\bigr),$$
where $\{A_n\}$ is a fixed countable dense subalgebra of $\mathcal{B}$. With this metric $\mathrm{Aut}(X,\mu)$ is a Polish space, and "typical" means "belonging to a dense $G_\delta$ set."

For an integer $k\ge 2$, a transformation $T\in\mathrm{Aut}(X,\mu)$ is said to be mixing of order $k$, written $T\in\mathrm{Mix}(k)$, if for every measurable sets $A_0,A_1,\dots,A_k\in\mathcal{B}$,
$$\lim_{\min_{i\ne j}|n_i-n_j|\to\infty}\mu\bigl(A_0\cap T^{-n_1}A_1\cap\cdots\cap T^{-n_k}A_k\bigr)=\prod_{i=0}^{k}\mu(A_i).$$

An extension of $T\in\mathrm{Aut}(X,\mu)$ is a transformation $\widetilde T\in\mathrm{Aut}(X\times Y,\mu\times\nu)$ on a product Lebesgue space such that $\widetilde T$ projects onto $T$ via the first coordinate; the set of such extensions is itself a Polish space in the induced Halmos metric.

Question: For $k>1$, is it true that for every $T\in\mathrm{Mix}(k)$, a typical (in the sense of Baire category with respect to the Halmos metric) extension $\widetilde T$ of $T$ also belongs to $\mathrm{Mix}(k)$?

Consider an interactive learning setting in which a target system $\pi$ (for instance, a large generative model) is trained to optimize a reward signal $r$ derived from feedback provided by a set of human supervisors $H$. Each supervisor in $H$ has bounded time, attention, expertise, and bandwidth, and is therefore able to evaluate only a limited subset of $\pi$'s outputs, with evaluations that may be noisy, inconsistent, or systematically biased—especially on tasks whose correctness or quality is hard for a human to verify, or on tasks where $\pi$'s competence exceeds that of any supervisor in $H$.

Formulate and design a training and feedback protocol (a "scalable oversight" scheme) that uses the limited human feedback from $H$, possibly augmented by AI-assisted evaluation, decomposition of tasks, debate, recursive critique, or verification mechanisms, such that the resulting trained system $\pi$ provably (or at least reliably) aligns with the intended preferences of $H$ even when:
(i) the cost of obtaining each human judgment is bounded;
(ii) individual human judgments on hard tasks may be inaccurate; and
(iii) $\pi$ may produce outputs that no human supervisor in $H$ can directly evaluate.

The problem is to determine whether and how such a protocol can exist, to characterize the conditions on $H$, on the task distribution, and on the auxiliary mechanisms under which alignment guarantees can be obtained, and to quantify the trade-offs between human-feedback budget, evaluation difficulty, and the achievable quality of oversight.

Setup. For a finite group G acting on a finite set X (typically G = S_n acting on {1,...,n}), and for a finitely presented group Γ = ⟨S | R⟩ with |S| < ∞ and |R| < ∞, a function f : S → Sym(X) is called an ε-almost homomorphism (with respect to the normalized Hamming distance d_H on Sym(X)) if
   (1/|R|) Σ_{r ∈ R} d_H(r(f), id) ≤ ε,
where r(f) denotes the evaluation of the relation r in Sym(X) using f. The presentation Γ = ⟨S | R⟩ is said to be permutation-stable with stability rate ρ(ε) if every ε-almost homomorphism f : S → Sym(X) is within Hamming distance ρ(ε) of some genuine homomorphism Γ → Sym(X), and ρ(ε) → 0 as ε → 0. A linear stability rate means ρ(ε) = O(ε).

Analogously, for a finite simplicial complex Y of dimension d, the cocycle stability rate measures how far an arbitrary 1-cochain c : Y(1) → Sym(X) (with permutation coefficients) with small coboundary norm
   ‖δc‖ := (1/|Y(2)|) Σ_{σ ∈ Y(2)} d_H((δc)(σ), id)
must be from a true 1-cocycle, in the normalized Hamming metric on Sym(X)^{Y(1)}. The cocycle Cheeger constant of Y is the infimum, over non-coboundary cochains, of the ratio ‖δc‖ / dist(c, Z^1).

Random model. Let Y(d, n, p) denote the d-dimensional Linial–Meshulam random simplicial complex on n vertices with full (d−1)-skeleton, in which each d-face is included independently with probability p. The "mid-range" refers to scales of p well above the cohomological connectivity threshold but bounded away from 1, e.g. p = c·log n / n for d = 2 with c in a fixed bounded interval.

Question. Determine, as a function of p (and n → ∞), the expected permutation-cocycle stability rate of a random 2-dimensional Linial–Meshulam complex Y(2, n, p), and the analogous expected stability rate for random group presentations in standard models (e.g. Gromov's density model). In particular, decide whether in the mid-range the expected cocycle Cheeger constant with permutation coefficients of Y(2, n, p) is bounded away from zero with high probability, which would imply the existence of non-sofic hyperbolic groups (and hence of non–residually finite hyperbolic groups).

Consider a reinforcement learning setting in which an agent's policy is trained using a reward model fit to human preference feedback. Let D = {(x_i, y_i^0, y_i^1, p_i)}_{i=1}^N denote a dataset where each x_i is a prompt or state drawn from some sampling distribution Q over a context space X, each (y_i^0, y_i^1) is a pair of candidate responses or trajectories produced by a (possibly biased) generation procedure, and p_i ∈ {0,1} is a preference label provided by a human annotator drawn from a population A according to some sampling scheme. Let P_deploy denote the distribution over contexts and behaviors encountered when the trained policy is deployed, and let U denote a target notion of utility (e.g., aggregated population preferences under idealized conditions).

Devise a methodology — comprising (i) a procedure for choosing the context distribution Q, (ii) a procedure for sampling response pairs, (iii) a protocol for selecting and instructing annotators, and (iv) quality-control mechanisms — together with a theoretical guarantee that the resulting dataset D yields a learned reward model and policy whose performance under P_deploy with respect to U is provably close to optimal, despite the following obstacles that must be explicitly addressed and bounded:

1. Sampling bias in Q relative to P_deploy (distribution shift between training contexts and deployment contexts).
2. Bias in the response-pair generation procedure (e.g., responses drawn only from a fixed base model that does not cover deployment behaviors).
3. Low-quality, noisy, or adversarial labels p_i, including annotator inattention, miscalibration, and disagreement.
4. Mismatch between the annotator population A and the population whose utility U is meant to represent.

Formally, give explicit, verifiable conditions on Q, the pair-generation procedure, the annotator-sampling scheme, and the quality-control mechanism under which one can prove a finite-sample bound on the gap between the utility under U of the policy trained on D and the optimal achievable utility on P_deploy, and exhibit such a methodology that is implementable in practice.

Let $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu,T)$ be an invertible measure-preserving transformation of a standard probability space (an automorphism). For an integer $n\ge 2$, an $n$-fold self-joining of $T$ is a $T\times\cdots\times T$-invariant probability measure $\lambda$ on $(X^n,\mathcal{B}^{\otimes n})$ all of whose one-dimensional marginals equal $\mu$. For $1\le m<n$ and any choice of $m$ coordinates among the $n$, the corresponding $m$-dimensional face projection of $\lambda$ is the pushforward of $\lambda$ under the projection $X^n\to X^m$ onto those coordinates.

Say that $T$ has property $S(m,n)$ (for $n>m\ge 1$) if every $n$-fold self-joining of $T$ whose projection onto every $m$-dimensional face of $X^n$ equals the product measure $\mu^{\otimes m}$ must be trivial, i.e. must equal $\mu^{\otimes n}$. Write $S_n := S(n-1,n)$ for $n\ge 2$.

Recall that $T$ is weakly mixing if $T\times T$ is ergodic on $(X\times X,\mu\otimes\mu)$, and that $T$ has zero (Kolmogorov–Sinai) entropy if $h(T,\mu)=0$.

Question: Does there exist a weakly mixing automorphism $T$ of zero entropy that does not have property $S_n$ for some $n\ge 3$?

Let $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu,T)$ be an invertible measure-preserving transformation of a standard probability space (an automorphism). For an integer $n\ge 2$, an $n$-fold self-joining of $T$ is a $T\times\cdots\times T$-invariant probability measure $\lambda$ on $(X^n,\mathcal{B}^{\otimes n})$ all of whose one-dimensional marginals equal $\mu$. For $1\le m<n$ and any choice of $m$ coordinates among the $n$, the corresponding $m$-dimensional face projection of $\lambda$ is the pushforward of $\lambda$ under the projection $X^n\to X^m$ onto those coordinates. 

Say that $T$ has property $S(m,n)$ (for $n>m\ge 1$) if every $n$-fold self-joining of $T$ whose projection onto every $m$-dimensional face of $X^n$ equals the product measure $\mu^{\otimes m}$ must be trivial, i.e. must equal $\mu^{\otimes n}$. Write $S_n := S(n-1,n)$ for $n\ge 2$.

Recall that $T$ is weakly mixing if $T\times T$ is ergodic on $(X\times X,\mu\otimes\mu)$, and that $T$ has zero (Kolmogorov–Sinai) entropy if $h(T,\mu)=0$.

Question: Does there exist a weakly mixing automorphism $T$ of zero entropy that does not have property $S_n$ for some $n\ge 3$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

A web search did not return a direct resolution of this specific question on the existence of a zero-entropy weakly mixing automorphism failing property $S_n = S(n-1,n)$. Related literature on minimal self-joinings, pairwise independent joinings, and Rokhlin-type problems exists, but no source clearly establishes or refutes the existence of such an example, so the status appears to be unknown / open based on available evidence.

Consider the setting of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), in which a language model or policy $\pi_\theta$ is fine-tuned using a dataset $\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i, y_i^+, y_i^-)\}_{i=1}^N$ of human preference comparisons, where $x_i$ is a prompt and $y_i^+, y_i^-$ are two candidate responses with $y_i^+$ preferred over $y_i^-$ by a human annotator. A reward model $r_\phi$ is trained on $\mathcal{D}$ (for example by maximizing the Bradley–Terry log-likelihood), and the policy is then optimized to maximize $\mathbb{E}_{x,\, y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)}[r_\phi(x,y)] - \beta\, \mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}})$ for some reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ and regularization weight $\beta > 0$.

Address the following three interrelated problems regarding the composition of the dataset $\mathcal{D}$:

1. Diversity definition. Propose a formal definition of "diversity" $\mathrm{Div}(\mathcal{D})$ of a preference dataset $\mathcal{D}$ that captures variation across prompts, responses, annotator populations, and elicited preference dimensions, and that is meaningful for predicting downstream alignment quality of the resulting policy $\pi_\theta$.

2. Diversity vs. label efficiency. Establish a quantitative relationship between $\mathrm{Div}(\mathcal{D})$, the sample size $N$, and a measure of alignment quality $Q(\pi_\theta)$ (for example, expected reward under a held-out true preference distribution, or worst-group performance). In particular, give conditions under which increasing $\mathrm{Div}(\mathcal{D})$ provably reduces the number of labeled comparisons needed to attain a target value of $Q$.

3. Diverse data selection. Provide a concrete, implementable algorithm (e.g., based on active learning, coreset selection, or clustering in a learned representation space) that, given a large pool of candidate prompts and response pairs, selects a subset $\mathcal{D}$ of bounded size with provably or empirically high $\mathrm{Div}(\mathcal{D})$, and demonstrate that policies trained on the selected $\mathcal{D}$ achieve higher $Q(\pi_\theta)$ than policies trained on baseline (e.g., uniformly random) selections of the same size.

The question of how to define, measure, and ensure diversity of human-feedback datasets in RLHF, and how diversity trades off against label efficiency and alignment quality, remains an actively studied open problem. While recent work has explored active learning, coreset-style selection, and diversity-aware reward modeling for RLHF, no consensus definition of diversity nor a generally accepted selection method with provable label-efficiency guarantees has emerged.

Background and setup. Let $G$ be a finite group and let $\langle S \mid R\rangle$ be a finite presentation of $G$, where $S$ is a finite generating set and $R$ is a finite set of relations (words in the free group $F(S)$). For a word $r\in F(S)$, write $|r|$ for its length. For each integer $n\ge 1$ let $\mathrm{Sym}(n)$ denote the symmetric group on $n$ letters, equipped with the normalized Hamming distance
$$d_H(\sigma,\tau)=\frac{1}{n}\big|\{i:\sigma(i)\ne\tau(i)\}\big|.$$
A map $\varphi:S\to \mathrm{Sym}(n)$ extends uniquely to a homomorphism $\tilde\varphi:F(S)\to \mathrm{Sym}(n)$. The defect of $\varphi$ with respect to the presentation $\langle S\mid R\rangle$ is
$$\mathrm{def}(\varphi)=\max_{r\in R} d_H(\tilde\varphi(r),\mathrm{id}).$$
The distance from $\varphi$ to a genuine homomorphism is
$$\mathrm{dist}(\varphi,\mathrm{Hom}(G,\mathrm{Sym}(n)))=\inf_{\psi:G\to\mathrm{Sym}(n)\ \text{hom.}}\ \max_{s\in S} d_H(\varphi(s),\psi(s)).$$
Given a function $\rho:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with $\rho(0)=0$ and $\rho$ continuous at $0$, the presentation $\langle S\mid R\rangle$ is called $\rho$-stable (in permutations) if for every $n\ge 1$ and every $\varphi:S\to\mathrm{Sym}(n)$,
$$\mathrm{dist}(\varphi,\mathrm{Hom}(G,\mathrm{Sym}(n)))\ \le\ \rho(\mathrm{def}(\varphi)).$$

Problem. Exhibit an infinite family of finite groups $\{G\}$ together with presentations $G\cong\langle S\mid R\rangle$ satisfying both of the following simultaneously:

(i) The presentations are short, in the sense that
$$|S|,\ |R|\ =\ \mathrm{polylog}(|G|)\quad\text{and}\quad |r|=\mathrm{polylog}(|G|)\ \text{for every }r\in R.$$

(ii) The stability rate is good: each presentation $\langle S\mid R\rangle$ is $\rho$-stable with
$$\rho(\varepsilon)\ =\ \mathrm{polyloglog}(|G|)\cdot \varepsilon^{c}$$
for some constant $c>0$ that does not depend on $|G|$.

Either construct such a family or prove no such family exists.

Consider the reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) setting. Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a state space and $\mathcal{A}$ an action space. A learned reward model is a function $\hat{r}_\phi : \mathcal{S}\times \mathcal{A} \to \mathbb{R}$ trained from human preference data to approximate a (latent) ground-truth reward $r^\star$. To evaluate the quality of $\hat{r}_\phi$ indirectly, one fixes a policy-optimization procedure $\mathcal{O}$ specified by the tuple $(\mathrm{Alg}, \pi_\theta\text{-arch}, B, H)$, where $\mathrm{Alg}$ is a reinforcement-learning algorithm (e.g., PPO, A2C, REINFORCE, DPO-style off-policy methods), $\pi_\theta\text{-arch}$ is the policy architecture, $B$ is a compute/sample budget, and $H$ is a vector of remaining hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, KL-regularization coefficient, entropy bonus, clipping parameters, schedule, etc.). Applying $\mathcal{O}$ to $\hat{r}_\phi$ produces a policy $\pi_{\mathcal{O}(\hat{r}_\phi)}$, and the indirect quality score of the reward model is
$$ Q(\hat{r}_\phi;\mathcal{O}) = \mathbb{E}_{(s,a)\sim \pi_{\mathcal{O}(\hat{r}_\phi)}}\bigl[r^\star(s,a)\bigr]. $$

Identify and rigorously characterize which components of $\mathcal{O}=(\mathrm{Alg}, \pi_\theta\text{-arch}, B, H)$ most strongly determine the faithfulness of $Q(\hat{r}_\phi;\mathcal{O})$ as a measurement of the intrinsic quality of $\hat{r}_\phi$. Concretely: provide a principled (theoretical or empirical) ranking, with justification, of the relative influence of the algorithm choice, the policy architecture, the compute budget, and the remaining hyperparameters on the agreement between $Q(\hat{r}_\phi;\mathcal{O})$ and a direct measure of reward-model quality (such as expected discrepancy from $r^\star$ under a reference distribution), and determine conditions on $\mathcal{O}$ under which indirect evaluation reliably reflects intrinsic reward-model quality.

Let $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ be a standard probability space and let $T:X\to X$ be an invertible measure-preserving ergodic transformation. For integers $n>m>1$, say that $T$ has property $S(m,n)$ if every self-joining of order $n$ of $T$ — i.e., every $T^{\times n}$-invariant probability measure $\nu$ on $X^n$ with all one-dimensional marginals equal to $\mu$ — that has the additional property that all of its projections onto every $m$-dimensional coordinate face of $X^n$ coincide with the product measure $\mu^{\otimes m}$, must itself equal the product measure $\mu^{\otimes n}$. Set $S_n := S(n-1,n)$ for $n\ge 2$.

Recall that a Gaussian automorphism is the measure-preserving transformation associated to a stationary real Gaussian process $(\xi_k)_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ via the shift; its maximal spectral type on the orthocomplement of constants is determined by a symmetric finite Borel measure $\sigma$ on the unit circle $\mathbb{T}\subset\mathbb{C}$ (the spectral measure of the process). For every continuous Borel measure $\sigma$ on $\mathbb{T}$ there exists an ergodic Gaussian automorphism whose reduced spectral type contains $\sigma$ as a component; if $\sigma$ is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure, then the corresponding Gaussian automorphism has zero Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy.

Question: Does every ergodic Gaussian automorphism with zero entropy possess property $S_n$ for all integers $n\ge 2$?

Consider a reinforcement learning setting in which an agent interacts with a Markov decision process (MDP) M = (S, A, P, r, gamma), where the state space S and action space A are high-dimensional, the transition kernel P is unknown, and the reward function r is either (i) sparse (nonzero only on a small set of states/actions) or (ii) defined implicitly via a learned reward model r_hat: S x A -> R that has been fit from human preference comparisons over trajectories. The agent's policy pi_theta is represented by a deep neural network and is trained to maximize the expected discounted return E[sum_{t>=0} gamma^t r(s_t, a_t)] (or its surrogate using r_hat). 

Design and analyze an exploration strategy E (e.g., an exploration bonus, posterior-sampling scheme, intrinsic-motivation signal, or hybrid) coupled to a deep RL learning algorithm such that the following properties hold simultaneously:

1. Sample-efficiency guarantee: With high probability, after at most polynomially many environment interactions in relevant problem parameters (effective horizon, complexity of the function class representing pi_theta and r_hat, and a notion of intrinsic dimension of the MDP), the learned policy is epsilon-optimal with respect to the true (possibly latent) reward.

2. Calibration of exploration budget: Provide a principled, data-driven criterion that determines the amount of exploration needed, without requiring problem-specific hand tuning, and prove that this criterion adapts to both dense and sparse-reward regimes.

3. Safety/conservatism constraint: The exploration policy must satisfy a specified safety constraint, e.g., at every step the probability of entering a designated unsafe set U \subset S is bounded by a prescribed delta > 0, while still achieving the guarantee in (1).

4. Robustness to reward-model error: When the reward used for training is a learned r_hat with bounded error ||r_hat - r||_infty <= eta on the support of the data distribution, quantify how the suboptimality of the final policy degrades as a function of eta and of the exploration strategy E.

Provide either (a) an algorithm together with a proof that it satisfies (1)-(4) under stated assumptions on the function approximator and MDP, or (b) an impossibility result showing that no algorithm in a specified class can simultaneously satisfy (1)-(4).

Balancing exploration and exploitation in deep reinforcement learning, particularly under sparse rewards, high-dimensional state spaces, and learned (preference-based) reward models, is widely acknowledged as an open research problem. Surveys on exploration in deep RL (e.g., Amin et al. 2021, Yang et al. 2021, Ladosz et al. 2022) describe it as unresolved, and no general-purpose algorithm with provable sample-efficiency, calibrated exploration, safety, and robustness to reward-model error is currently known.

Let $\mathrm{Sym}(n) \hookrightarrow U(n)$ denote the symmetric group embedded as the group of $n\times n$ permutation matrices, acting on $U(n)$ by (say) left multiplication. Consider the metric quotient space $X_n := U(n)/\mathrm{Sym}(n)$ with the quotient metric, and equip $X_n$ with the pushforward of the Haar probability measure $\mu_n$ on $U(n)$.

Question: Does there exist an absolute constant $C > 0$, independent of $n$, such that for every $n \geq 1$ and every sufficiently regular (e.g.\ Lipschitz) function $f : X_n \to \mathbb{R}$, the Poincaré-type inequality
$$\mathrm{Var}_{\mu_n}(f) \;\leq\; C \int_{X_n} |\nabla f|^2 \, d\mu_n$$
holds, where $|\nabla f|$ denotes the metric (Lipschitz) gradient on $X_n$?

Equivalently, does $U(n)/\mathrm{Sym}(n)$ satisfy a Poincaré-type inequality with constants independent of $n$?

Suppose $\{G_i\}_{i \in I}$ is a normal chain in $G$, i.e. a descending sequence of normal subgroups of finite index (or, more generally, a cofinal directed system of normal subgroups) with trivial intersection $\bigcap_{i} G_i = \{1\}$. $$\det\nolimits_{\mathcal{N}(G)}\!\bigl(r_A^{(2)}\bigr) \;=\; \lim_{i \in I}\, \det\nolimits_{\mathcal{N}(G/G_i)}\!\bigl(r_{A[i]}^{(2)}\bigr)$$
hold for every group $G$, every such normal chain $\{G_i\}$, and every matrix $A \in M_{r,s}(\mathbb{Q}G)$?

The approximation problem for Fuglede–Kadison determinants over normal chains is a long-standing open conjecture in the theory of L²-invariants. Consider the reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) setting in which an agent interacts with an environment modeled as a Markov decision process and a (possibly latent) reward function is to be learned from feedback provided by human evaluators. Feedback may take various forms, including but not limited to: scalar ratings of trajectories or actions, pairwise or k-wise preference comparisons between trajectories, demonstrations, corrections, natural-language critiques, and constraints or rules. Human evaluators are modeled as noisy, possibly biased agents whose responses deviate from an idealized rational utility-maximizing labeler according to systematic cognitive and motivational biases (e.g., myopia, confirmation bias, sycophancy bias toward the agent, anchoring, framing effects, and disagreement among annotators).

Address the following three sub-questions:

(a) Feedback modality. Determine which single form of human feedback, or which combination of feedback modalities (possibly weighted or used at different stages of training), yields provably or empirically optimal sample efficiency and fidelity in recovering the evaluators' underlying goals. Provide a formal criterion (e.g., expected regret with respect to the true reward, KL distance between learned and true reward distributions, or identifiability conditions) under which optimality is measured.

(b) Bias-induced degradation. Give a quantitative model of how specific human biases distort the mapping from underlying preferences to observed feedback, and characterize—as a function of the type and magnitude of bias—the resulting degradation in the learned reward model and in downstream policy performance. In particular, identify conditions under which biased feedback still allows consistent recovery of the true reward (up to equivalence), and conditions under which it provably does not.

(c) Evaluator selection and training. Specify a procedure for selecting and training human evaluators (covering recruitment criteria, calibration tasks, training protocols, and ongoing quality assurance) such that the aggregate feedback signal is sufficient to guarantee, with high probability, that the resulting trained agent satisfies stated safety and reliability properties when deployed in human-computer interaction.

Let $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ be a standard non-atomic probability space, and let $T:X\to X$ be an invertible measure-preserving transformation. The associated Koopman operator $U_T$ on $L^2_0(X,\mu)=\{f\in L^2(X,\mu):\int f\,d\mu=0\}$ is the unitary operator defined by $U_T f = f\circ T$. The maximal spectral type of $T$ is the equivalence class of measures on the unit circle $\mathbb{T}$ given by the spectral theorem applied to $U_T$, together with its multiplicity function. The transformation $T$ is said to have continuous spectrum if its maximal spectral type (restricted to $L^2_0$) is a continuous (non-atomic) measure on $\mathbb{T}$, and to have Lebesgue spectrum if this maximal spectral type is equivalent to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{T}$. Two measure-preserving systems $(X_1,\mu_1,T_1)$ and $(X_2,\mu_2,T_2)$ are metrically isomorphic if there exists a measure-preserving bijection (mod null sets) $\phi:X_1\to X_2$ with $\phi\circ T_1=T_2\circ\phi$ a.e.

Question: Do there exist two measure-preserving dynamical systems that are not metrically isomorphic but whose Koopman operators on $L^2_0$ have the same spectral invariants (maximal spectral type and multiplicity function), in particular both having Lebesgue spectrum (of the same multiplicity)?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Existence of metrically non-isomorphic measure-preserving systems with the same continuous spectrum is classically known: Anzai gave the first example of non-isomorphic automorphisms with the same spectrum, and Kolmogorov–Ornstein theory shows that all Bernoulli shifts have countable Lebesgue spectrum yet are classified up to isomorphism by entropy, providing a continuum of non-isomorphic systems sharing the same (countable) Lebesgue spectrum. Refinements (e.g., constructions giving continua of spectrally nonisomorphic transformations with even-multiplicity Lebesgue components, and the affirmative resolution of Banach's problem on simple Lebesgue spectrum in the σ-finite setting) further confirm that the spectrum is far from a complete metric invariant.

Consider a population of $n$ humans, each with a preference relation $\succ_i$ over a set $\mathcal{X}$ of possible AI behaviors (or trajectories). A preference aggregation procedure is a map $F$ that takes the tuple $(\succ_1, \dots, \succ_n)$ — typically observed only through finitely many pairwise comparisons — and produces a scalar reward function $r : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$, whose induced ordering $x \succ_F y \iff r(x) > r(y)$ serves as the alignment target. The standard reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback (RLHF) procedure fits $r$ by maximum likelihood under a Bradley–Terry model on pooled pairwise comparisons drawn (uniformly or otherwise) from the population.

(a) Formulate, within the framework of social choice theory, precise normative axioms (e.g., Pareto efficiency, independence of irrelevant alternatives, anonymity, non-dictatorship, Condorcet consistency, majority consistency, and proportional representation of minority subgroups) that an aggregation procedure $F$ used to define an AI alignment target ought to satisfy when the population members disagree about values.

(b) Determine whether the RLHF aggregation rule (Bradley–Terry MLE on pooled pairwise preferences) satisfies these axioms. In particular, characterize the conditions on the population preference profile under which RLHF is or is not Condorcet-consistent, majority-consistent, and proportionally representative, and identify cases in which it systematically privileges majority preferences at the expense of coherent minority viewpoints.

(c) Either exhibit an aggregation rule $F^\ast$ that is normatively acceptable in the above sense for value-pluralistic populations, or prove an impossibility theorem showing that no such rule exists within the RLHF reward-modeling framework.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Recent work has begun to formally analyze RLHF through social choice theory. It has been shown that RLHF reward modeling implicitly performs an aggregation resembling Borda count and generally fails axioms such as Condorcet consistency, majority consistency, and pairwise majority consistency, though it does satisfy them under mild empirically plausible assumptions on preference profiles. Classical Arrow-type impossibility results apply, and follow-up frameworks (e.g., population-proportional alignment) show neither RLHF nor NLHF achieves proportional representation of minority viewpoints. A complete normatively acceptable aggregation rule remains an open research program.

In standard big-bang cosmology, a brief epoch of early exponential expansion (inflation) is posited to account for several observed features of the present universe: its large spatial extent, high degree of isotropy, large-scale homogeneity, near spatial flatness, and the absence of observed magnetic monopoles. Conventional inflationary scenarios introduce one or more scalar "inflaton" fields whose potentials are chosen, with considerable freedom, to yield a suitable slow-roll phase; the fundamental origin of such fields and potentials is not derived from first principles.

A causal set is a locally finite partially ordered set (C, ≺) intended as a discrete substratum for spacetime, in which the order relation represents causality and the number of elements represents spacetime volume. Dynamics for causal sets are typically specified either by a stochastic growth law (e.g. classical sequential growth, where elements are added one at a time respecting general covariance and Bell causality) or by a discrete action (e.g. the Benincasa–Dowker action) leading to a quantum partition function over causal sets.

Problem. Identify, from first principles within a quantum theory of gravity—and in particular within causal set dynamics (whether classical sequential growth, quantum measure theory on causal sets, or a path sum weighted by the Benincasa–Dowker action)—a mechanism that produces a phase of early exponential (or effectively exponential) expansion of the emergent continuum geometry sufficient to explain the observed large size, isotropy, homogeneity, spatial flatness, and absence of monopoles, without postulating an ad hoc inflaton field or freely chosen scalar potential. Equivalently, exhibit a causal-set (or other quantum-gravitational) dynamical law together with a derivation showing that its large-scale continuum limit contains, generically or under physically motivated initial conditions, an early de Sitter-like expanding regime accounting for the above cosmological features.

Model reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) as a two-player assistance game between a human H and an agent A defined as follows. There is a state space S, an agent action space A_A, and a (possibly trivial) human action space A_H. The human has a latent reward parameter θ ∈ Θ drawn from a known prior P(θ). The joint dynamics are governed by a transition kernel T(s' | s, a_A, a_H). The agent does not observe θ; instead, at selected query times t ∈ Q ⊆ ℕ, the agent receives a feedback signal F_t from the human, where F_t is a (possibly noisy) evaluative response to a trajectory segment or pair of segments under a feedback model F_t ~ p(· | trajectory, θ, ε), with ε denoting an evaluator-error process. The agent's goal is to maximize E[Σ_t γ^t r_θ(s_t, a_A,t)] where r_θ is the true reward induced by θ.

Establish the following:

(a) Consistency and convergence. Give conditions on the prior P(θ), the feedback model p(F | ·, θ, ε), the query schedule Q, and the agent's learning algorithm under which the agent's posterior over θ (equivalently, over the optimal policy) converges almost surely to a point mass on the true θ, and under which the agent's policy converges to a θ-optimal policy. State and prove the sharpest available rate of convergence in terms of the number of feedback queries N = |Q ∩ [0,T]|.

(b) Effect of evaluator-error patterns. For a family of evaluator-error models {ε_k}—including independent symmetric noise, systematic bias, miscalibration, myopic/short-horizon evaluation, and adversarial corruption of a bounded fraction—quantify how each pattern alters identifiability of θ and the asymptotic suboptimality of the learned policy. In particular, characterize which error patterns preserve consistency, which induce bounded bias, and which produce unbounded suboptimality.

(c) Effect of feedback rate. Let ρ ∈ (0,1] denote the long-run rate of feedback queries per environment step (or, more generally, a query-scheduling policy). Determine how the alignment quality—measured by expected regret relative to the θ-optimal policy—scales with ρ, and exhibit (if possible) a tight trade-off curve between ρ and asymptotic regret, together with an optimal adaptive query schedule.

Provide formal theorems with proofs, or counterexamples demonstrating that no such guarantees hold under the stated assumptions.

Let $\lambda,\mu,\eta:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable, locally bounded, non-negative functions (the "failure rate", "repair-related rate", and "service-completion rate", respectively). Consider the system of first-order linear hyperbolic PDEs for unknowns $p_0(x,t),p_1(x,t)$ on $(x,t)\in[0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)$:

$$\frac{\partial p_0}{\partial t}(x,t)+\frac{\partial p_0}{\partial x}(x,t)=-\bigl(\lambda(x)+\mu(x)\bigr)p_0(x,t),$$
$$\frac{\partial p_1}{\partial t}(x,t)+\frac{\partial p_1}{\partial x}(x,t)=-\eta(x)p_1(x,t),$$

subject to the (distributional) boundary conditions at $x=0$:
$$p_0(0,t)=\delta(t)+\int_0^\infty p_1(x,t)\,\eta(x)\,dx,\qquad p_1(0,t)=\int_0^\infty p_0(x,t)\,\lambda(x)\,dx,$$
and initial conditions
$$p_0(x,0)=\delta(x),\qquad p_1(x,0)=0.$$

Taking the Laplace transform in $t$, $\hat p_i(x,s)=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}p_i(x,t)\,dt$, one obtains explicit closed-form expressions

$$\hat p_0(x,s)=\hat p_0(0,s)\,e^{-sx-\int_0^x(\lambda(\tau)+\mu(\tau))\,d\tau},\qquad \hat p_1(x,s)=\hat p_1(0,s)\,e^{-sx-\int_0^x\eta(\tau)\,d\tau},$$

with $\hat p_0(0,s),\hat p_1(0,s)$ determined by the boundary equations.

Problem: For general non-constant rate functions $\lambda(x),\mu(x),\eta(x)$, determine the inverse Laplace transforms of $\hat p_0(x,s)$ and $\hat p_1(x,s)$ in closed form, thereby giving an explicit expression for the time-dependent solution $(p_0(x,t),p_1(x,t))$ of the system above.

Consider the following Bayesian formulation of fine-tuning a generative language model from human preference feedback. Let $\mathcal{X}$ denote a space of prompts and $\mathcal{Y}$ a space of responses. A pretrained reference policy $\pi_0(y\mid x)$ on $\mathcal{Y}$ given $x\in\mathcal{X}$ plays the role of a prior. A scalar reward model $r:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}$ is learned from human comparison data. The standard reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback (RLHF) objective seeks a policy $\pi$ maximizing
$$ J(\pi) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho,\,y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)}\bigl[r(x,y)\bigr] \;-\; \beta\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}\bigl[\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\pi(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_0(\cdot\mid x)\bigr)\bigr],\qquad \beta>0, $$
whose unique maximizer is the Boltzmann (Gibbs) posterior
$$ \pi^\star(y\mid x) \;\propto\; \pi_0(y\mid x)\,\exp\!\bigl(r(x,y)/\beta\bigr). $$
Address the following:

(a) Characterize, quantitatively, how the choice of prior $\pi_0$ influences $\pi^\star$ and any policy obtained by approximate optimization of $J$. In particular, derive bounds (e.g.\ in total variation, KL, or expected reward) that isolate the contribution of $\pi_0$ to properties of the resulting policy such as diversity, calibration of distributional preferences, and tail behavior.

(b) Propose alternative target distributions $\pi^\dagger$ (i.e., replacements for the Boltzmann form $\pi_0 \exp(r/\beta)/Z$) or alternative inference procedures that demonstrably improve on the Boltzmann/KL-regularized formulation with respect to a stated criterion — for example, faithfulness to a population distribution of human preferences, robustness to reward misspecification, or avoidance of mode collapse — and prove that the proposal strictly dominates the Boltzmann target on that criterion under explicit assumptions on $\pi_0$, $r$, and the preference-generating process.

Let $G$ be an infinite, finitely generated, residually finite group, and let $(G_i)_{i\geq 0}$ be a descending chain of finite-index normal subgroups of $G$ with $\bigcap_{i\geq 0} G_i = \{1\}$. Define:

(a) The first $L^2$-Betti number $b_1^{(2)}(G)$ of $G$, namely the von Neumann dimension $\dim_{\mathcal{N}(G)} H_1^{(2)}(G;\ell^2 G)$ of the first reduced $\ell^2$-homology of $G$.

(b) The cost $\mathrm{cost}(G)$ of $G$ in the sense of Levitt–Gaboriau: the infimum, over all essentially free measure-preserving actions of $G$ on a standard probability space and over all generating graphings $\Phi$ of the resulting orbit equivalence relation, of the total edge-measure of $\Phi$.

(c) The rank gradient with respect to the chain $(G_i)$:
$$\mathrm{RG}(G;(G_i)) := \lim_{i\to\infty} \frac{d(G_i) - 1}{[G:G_i]},$$
where $d(H)$ denotes the minimum number of generators of $H$.

Prove or disprove: for every such $G$ and every such chain $(G_i)$,
$$b_1^{(2)}(G) \;=\; \mathrm{cost}(G) - 1 \;=\; \mathrm{RG}(G;(G_i)).$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The equality cost(G) − 1 = b_1^{(2)}(G) is the well-known cost-vs-L^2-Betti-number question of Gaboriau; only the inequality cost(G) − 1 ≥ b_1^{(2)}(G) is known in general. The equality RG(G;(G_i)) = b_1^{(2)}(G) is the Abért–Nikolov rank gradient problem, which remains open in general. Partial results exist (e.g., for groups with property (T) cost equals 1, matching b_1^{(2)} = 0; results of Abért–Nikolov relating rank gradient to cost of profinite completion actions), but the full triple equality is open.

Consider a language-generation policy $\pi_\theta(y\mid x)$ obtained by fine-tuning a pretrained base policy $\pi_0$ via reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). The training pipeline consists of: (i) collecting human preference comparisons over pairs of outputs; (ii) fitting a reward model $r_\phi(x,y)$ (e.g., via a Bradley–Terry likelihood) to those preferences; and (iii) optimizing $\pi_\theta$ to maximize $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}[r_\phi(x,y)] - \beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_0(\cdot\mid x))$ for some regularization weight $\beta>0$ and prompt distribution $\mathcal{D}$.

Let $H:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}$ denote an (unknown) true human utility function and let $\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{X}$ be a class of "bad" or unsafe outcomes. Define the worst-case harm of $\pi_\theta$ with respect to an adversarial prompt transformation class $\mathcal{A}$ (e.g., jailbreak prefixes, prompt-injection suffixes, paraphrastic attacks) as
$$W(\pi_\theta;\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}) \;=\; \sup_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\; \Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid a(x))}\bigl[(a(x),y)\in\mathcal{B}\bigr].$$

The problem is to develop a rigorous theoretical framework — drawing from decision theory, adversarial robustness, distributionally robust optimization, or formal evaluation methodology — that characterizes $W(\pi_\theta;\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})$ in terms of properties of the preference data, the reward model $r_\phi$, the regularization $\beta$, and the base policy $\pi_0$. Concretely, one seeks:

1. Quantitative upper and lower bounds on $W(\pi_\theta;\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})$ as a function of training-time quantities (sample size, preference noise, reward-model generalization error, KL budget, expressivity of $\mathcal{A}$).
2. Conditions on the RLHF pipeline under which average-case improvement in $\mathbb{E}[H]$ is compatible with non-degradation (or provable improvement) of worst-case behavior, i.e., $W(\pi_\theta;\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}) \le W(\pi_0;\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})$.
3. An evaluation framework (test-set construction, adversarial red-teaming protocol, or formal verification procedure) whose output provably bounds $W(\pi_\theta;\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})$ with high probability.

Determine such a framework and the corresponding theorems, or prove impossibility results showing fundamental limits on how tightly $W$ can be controlled by any RLHF-style procedure.

Consider a reinforcement learning system in which an agent is trained against a learned reward model r_phi: S x A -> R fit to preference data D = {(x_i, y_i^+, y_i^-)}, where each preference label indicates that output y_i^+ is preferred to y_i^- in context x_i. Classically, the labels are produced by human annotators H. In an AI-assisted variant, some fraction lambda in [0,1] of the labels are produced instead by a feedback-providing AI model F (or by a mixture policy that queries F and H). Assume:

1. There is a disagreement rate delta(F, H) > 0 between F and H on a representative distribution of comparison queries.
2. The errors of F across queries are not independent: there exist correlated failure modes, i.e. a set E of contexts on which F systematically deviates from H in the same direction.
3. The alignment of F itself is defined only relative to some prior aligned feedback source, so guaranteeing F's alignment requires an already-aligned feedback provider (the bootstrapping condition).

Question: Determine conditions on (F, H, lambda, delta, E, and the training procedure) under which augmenting or partially replacing human feedback by F-generated feedback provably preserves a chosen alignment criterion C on the resulting trained policy pi — for example, that with high probability the expected divergence between pi and a target human-aligned policy pi_H* remains bounded by a prescribed epsilon. Equivalently, identify whether any such conditions can be satisfied without circularly assuming that F already satisfies C, and characterize the achievable tradeoff curve between lambda (amount of AI feedback used) and the worst-case alignment loss induced by correlated failure modes.

Consider a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian spacetime $(M,g)$ and a free scalar quantum field theory on it, with retarded/advanced Green functions $G^{\pm}$ of the d'Alembertian $\Box_g = g^{\mu\nu}\nabla_\mu \nabla_\nu$. A causal set is a locally finite partially ordered set $(C,\preceq)$, intended to model spacetime at the Planck scale; for a fixed sprinkling density $\rho$, a causal set is obtained from $(M,g)$ by a Poisson process on $M$ with intensity $\rho\,dV_g$, with the induced causal order. On causal sets, discrete analogues of the retarded Green function $G^{+}_C$ and of the scalar d'Alembertian $B_C$ are defined (e.g., via the Benincasa–Dowker family of operators) such that, in the continuum limit, expectations recover $G^{+}$ and $\Box_g$ respectively. The discreteness scale $\rho^{-1/d}$ provides an intrinsic, Lorentz-covariant ultraviolet cutoff.

In quantum field theory on a Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) cosmological background, certain models implement a covariant ultraviolet cutoff at the QFT level and predict modifications of the primordial power spectrum of curvature perturbations of the form
$$\mathcal{P}(k) = \mathcal{P}_0(k)\bigl(1 + F(k/k_{\mathrm{UV}})\bigr),$$
where $k_{\mathrm{UV}}$ is the covariant cutoff scale and $F$ is a model-specific correction encoding the cutoff signature.

Formulate, within causal set theory on an FLRW background, a derivation of the two-point function of a scalar field perturbation using the causal-set Green functions $G^{+}_C$ and d'Alembertian $B_C$ together with the intrinsic discreteness cutoff at scale $\rho^{-1/d}$, and determine the corresponding prediction for the primordial scalar power spectrum $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{CS}}(k;\rho)$. Specifically: (i) show whether $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{CS}}(k;\rho)$ reproduces, in an appropriate continuum limit, the covariant-UV-cutoff predictions of the form above, and (ii) determine whether the causal-set framework sharpens these predictions, e.g. by fixing the form of $F$ uniquely from the discreteness scale $\rho^{-1/d}$, by computing subleading corrections, or by yielding observable signatures distinct from those of QFT-level covariant cutoffs.

Let G be a finitely generated countable group. A standard probability-measure-preserving action of G is an action of G on a standard Borel probability space (X, μ) by measurable, measure-preserving transformations such that the action is essentially free (the stabilizer of μ-almost every point is trivial). For such an action, the cost of the associated orbit equivalence relation R on (X, μ) is defined as the infimum over all generating graphings Φ = (φ_i) of R (i.e., countable families of partial measure-preserving isomorphisms whose induced equivalence relation equals R almost everywhere) of the total measure Σ_i μ(dom(φ_i)). The cost of G, denoted cost(G), is the infimum of the costs of all such essentially free p.m.p. actions of G. Let b_1^{(2)}(G) denote the first L²-Betti number of G.

(a) Is it true that for every finitely generated group G one has
   b_1^{(2)}(G) = cost(G) − 1 ?

(b) (Fixed Price Conjecture) Is it true that for every finitely generated group G, every essentially free standard p.m.p. action of G has the same cost, equal to cost(G)?

Both questions are long-standing open problems originally posed by Gaboriau. Consider the setting of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), in which a policy $\pi_\theta$ over an action/output space is trained to maximize an expected reward $r_\phi$, where $r_\phi$ is itself learned from human-provided feedback on policy outputs. Standard practice uses coarse feedback signals, most commonly pairwise preference comparisons: given two outputs $(y_1, y_2)$ from a prompt $x$, an evaluator returns a single bit indicating which is preferred, and $r_\phi$ is fit under a Bradley–Terry-style model $P(y_1 \succ y_2 \mid x) = \sigma(r_\phi(x,y_1) - r_\phi(x,y_2))$. Define fine-grained feedback as any feedback protocol producing strictly more information per evaluation than a single pairwise preference, including (a) per-aspect scalar or categorical ratings along multiple axes (e.g. helpfulness, factuality, harmlessness), (b) span-level annotations identifying which substrings of an output are problematic and why, (c) edits or rewrites, and (d) feedback conditioned on rubric items.

Address the following:

1. Provide a precise characterization of the practical advantages of fine-grained feedback over pairwise preferences for RLHF, in terms of (i) sample complexity of reward learning, (ii) bias and identifiability properties of the learned reward $r_\phi$, (iii) downstream policy performance after RL optimization against $r_\phi$, and (iv) ability to mitigate known failure modes such as reward hacking and underspecification.

2. Quantify the costs imposed on human evaluators, including time per annotation, cognitive load, inter-annotator agreement, and required expertise, as a function of the granularity and dimensionality of the feedback protocol.

3. Determine sufficient conditions (on task domain, evaluator expertise, annotation budget, model capability, and statistical structure of the reward) under which the gains from fine-grained feedback strictly dominate the additional annotation cost, so that fine-grained feedback should replace pairwise preferences as the default feedback signal.

Consider the following two reliability models for a single-unit (or two-unit) repairable system attended by a repairman who takes vacations. Time t ≥ 0 and elapsed-time variable x ≥ 0 are continuous. Let λ > 0 be the constant working (failure) rate of the system, μ(x) ≥ 0 the repair rate function (depending on the elapsed repair time x), and α(x) ≥ 0 the vacation rate function of the repairman (depending on the elapsed vacation time x). All rate functions are measurable and satisfy ∫₀^∞ μ(x) dx = ∫₀^∞ α(x) dx = +∞.

Model A. Let Q_i(x,t), i = 0,1,2,3,4, be probability densities, where Q_i(x,t) (i = 0,1,2) denotes the probability that at time t the system is in operating state i and the elapsed vacation time of the repairman is x, and Q_i(x,t) (i = 3,4) the probability that at time t the system is down in state i and the elapsed repair time is x. The state functions satisfy a coupled system of first-order linear hyperbolic PDEs of the form
   ∂Q_i/∂t + ∂Q_i/∂x = −(λ + α(x)) Q_i  (i = 0,1,2),
   ∂Q_j/∂t + ∂Q_j/∂x = −μ(x) Q_j        (j = 3,4),
together with appropriate linear couplings between the equations, and with the boundary conditions
   Q_0(0,t) = ∫₀^∞ α(x) Q_0(x,t) dx + ∫₀^∞ μ(x) Q_3(x,t) dx + δ(t),
   Q_i(0,t) = (linear functionals of the Q_k(·,t)),  i = 1,2,3,4,
where δ(·) is the Dirac delta and the initial data correspond to the system starting in state 0 at t = 0.

Model B. Let P_i(x,t), i = 0,1,…,6, be analogous probability densities for a more elaborate variant of the same scheme, satisfying a coupled hyperbolic PDE system of the same type with boundary condition
   P_0(0,t) = ∫₀^∞ α(x) P_0(x,t) dx + ∫₀^∞ μ(x) P_3(x,t) dx + δ(t)
and analogous boundary conditions for P_1,…,P_6.

Assume α(x) and μ(x) are non-constant (i.e., not almost-everywhere constant) functions.

Questions:
(1) Are Models A and B well posed in a suitable Banach space (for instance, L¹([0,∞), ℝ^5) and L¹([0,∞), ℝ^7), respectively); that is, does each system admit a unique nonnegative time-dependent solution depending continuously on the initial data?
(2) Determine the asymptotic behavior as t → ∞ of these time-dependent solutions: in particular, do they converge (strongly, or in some weaker sense) to a steady-state solution, and characterize that limit?

Consider a sequential decision-making setting modeled as a Markov decision process $M = (\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, P, r^\star, \gamma)$ with unknown true reward $r^\star : \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{A} \to \mathbb{R}$. A learner has access to two sources of supervision provided by human evaluators of bounded and possibly heterogeneous expertise:

1. A small set of demonstrations $\mathcal{D} = \{\tau_i\}_{i=1}^n$, where each trajectory $\tau_i$ is generated by a (possibly different) behavior policy $\pi_i$ that is suboptimal with respect to $r^\star$, i.e., $J(\pi_i) := \mathbb{E}_{\pi_i}\!\left[\sum_t \gamma^t r^\star(s_t,a_t)\right] < \max_\pi J(\pi)$, with unknown and varying suboptimality gaps $\Delta_i = J(\pi^\star) - J(\pi_i)$.
2. A set of comparison or preference labels $\mathcal{P} = \{(\sigma_j^0, \sigma_j^1, y_j)\}_{j=1}^m$ over trajectory segments, generated according to a (possibly noisy) preference model such as Bradley–Terry with parameter $r^\star$.

Demonstrations are assumed to be substantially more expensive to obtain than preference labels (i.e., $n \ll m$ in typical regimes), but the trajectories in $\mathcal{D}$ are presumed to contain structural information about $r^\star$ beyond what is encoded in the preference labels alone.

Design a reward-learning procedure that produces $\hat r$ (and an induced policy $\hat\pi$) with the following properties, and prove guarantees for it:

(a) $\hat r$ is consistent with $r^\star$ in a quantifiable sense (e.g., bounded regret $J(\pi^\star) - J(\hat\pi)$ under $r^\star$) even when every demonstrator is strictly suboptimal and the suboptimality gaps $\Delta_i$ are unknown.

(b) The procedure provably outperforms — in terms of sample complexity in $m$, regret, or worst-case alignment error — any procedure that uses only the preference data $\mathcal{P}$ and ignores $\mathcal{D}$, under explicit assumptions on the structure of demonstrator suboptimality (for example, monotonic improvement, ranked demonstrators, or noisy-rational behavior with bounded rationality).

(c) The procedure degrades gracefully (no worse than the preference-only baseline up to constants) when the demonstrations are arbitrarily bad or adversarial.

State precise assumptions on the demonstrator model, the preference noise model, the function class for $\hat r$, and the coverage/realizability conditions under which (a)–(c) hold, and exhibit either matching lower bounds or empirical evidence that the assumptions are necessary.

Setup. An admissible group is a discrete countable group G that is of type FP over Z (i.e., admits a finite type projective resolution of the trivial ZG-module Z), satisfies the Atiyah/determinant conjecture so that the L^2-torsion ρ^{(2)}(G) ∈ R is well-defined, and has vanishing L^2-Betti numbers b_n^{(2)}(G) = 0 for all n ≥ 0; under these hypotheses, the L^2-torsion ρ^{(2)}(G) ∈ R is an invariant of G (independent of the chosen finite model of a classifying space EG).

Two countably infinite discrete groups G and H are called measure equivalent if there exist a standard infinite Lebesgue measure space (Ω, μ) together with commuting measure-preserving free actions of G and H on (Ω, μ), each of which admits a finite-measure fundamental domain. If X_G and X_H are such fundamental domains for the H-action and the G-action respectively, the index of the measure equivalence is
   I(G, H) := μ(X_H) / μ(X_G) ∈ (0, ∞),
which is well-defined up to the choice of coupling.

Question. Suppose G and H are admissible groups that are measure equivalent with some coupling having index I(G, H) > 0. Must their L^2-torsions satisfy
   ρ^{(2)}(G) = I(G, H) · ρ^{(2)}(H) ?
