Let $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ be a standard non-atomic Lebesgue probability space and let $T:X\to X$ be an invertible measure-preserving automorphism. Recall the following definitions.

(a) $T$ has *absolutely continuous spectrum of finite multiplicity* if the maximal spectral type of the Koopman operator $U_T f = f\circ T$ acting on $L^2_0(X,\mu)$ (the orthogonal complement of constants) is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on the circle, and the spectral multiplicity function is bounded.

(b) $T$ is *mixing* if $\mu(T^{-n}A\cap B)\to\mu(A)\mu(B)$ for all $A,B\in\mathcal{B}$ as $|n|\to\infty$. It has *mixing of all orders* (multiple mixing) if for every $k\ge 2$ and all $A_0,\dots,A_k\in\mathcal{B}$,
$$\mu(A_0\cap T^{-n_1}A_1\cap\cdots\cap T^{-n_k}A_k)\to\prod_{i=0}^{k}\mu(A_i)$$
whenever $n_1, n_2-n_1, \dots, n_k-n_{k-1}\to\infty$.

(c) $T$ has *positive local rank* if there exists $\beta>0$ and a sequence of Rokhlin towers with bases $B_j$ and heights $h_j+1$, giving sets $U_j=\bigsqcup_{k=0}^{h_j} T^k B_j$, such that $\mu(U_j)\to\beta$ and for every $A\in\mathcal{B}$ the intersection $U_j\cap A$ is asymptotically approximated (in measure) by unions of levels $T^k B_j$ of the $j$-th tower.

Prove that at least one of the following two statements holds:
(i) there exists a measure-preserving automorphism with absolutely continuous spectrum of finite multiplicity;
(ii) every mixing automorphism of positive local rank has mixing of all orders.

Determine which of the two statements is true.

Consider a three-dimensional system of N = N↑ + N↓ non-relativistic fermions in two internal (spin) states, with N↑ particles of mass m↑ in state ↑ and N↓ particles of mass m↓ in state ↓. Identical-spin fermions do not interact, while opposite-spin pairs interact only via the Wigner–Bethe–Peierls zero-range s-wave contact condition at unitarity: for every ↑↓ pair (i,j), as their separation r_{ij} → 0 (other coordinates fixed), the wavefunction satisfies

   ψ ∼ (1/r_{ij}) · A({other coordinates})  (infinite scattering length),

and ψ obeys the free Schrödinger equation away from these contact hyperplanes. The Hamiltonian H is defined as the natural self-adjoint extension determined by these boundary conditions, when such an extension exists and is bounded below.

(a) Determine, as a function of the mass ratio α = m↑/m↓, the full stability domain — i.e. the set of α ∈ (0,∞) for which, for given (N↑, N↓), H admits a self-adjoint realization that is bounded from below (equivalently, all relevant scaling exponents arising in the hyperangular Efimov-type analysis are real).

(b) In the impurity sector N↓ = 1, it is known that there is a critical mass ratio α_c(N↑) such that for α > α_c(N↑) an Efimov effect occurs (the Hamiltonian fails to be bounded below in the zero-range model) for N↑ = 2, 3, 4. Decide whether this sequence of Efimov thresholds continues for N↑ = 5, 6, and beyond: that is, for each N↑ ≥ 5, does there exist a finite critical mass ratio α_c(N↑) ∈ (0,∞) beyond which the zero-range Hamiltonian is unbounded from below, and if so determine α_c(N↑)?

The question of whether the Efimov effect persists for (N↑,1) zero-range fermionic systems beyond N↑ = 4 appears to remain open. Consider the following two-unit parallel redundant repairable system. Unit 1 has constant failure rate $\lambda>0$ and a generally distributed repair time with repair rate function $g(x)\ge 0$ depending on the elapsed repair time $x$. Unit 2 has constant repair rate $\mu>0$, $k$ sequential failure stages and $m$ sequential repair phases, and a generally distributed failure rate function $f(x)\ge 0$ depending on the elapsed operating time $x$.

Let $q_{0,i}(x,t)$ ($1\le i\le k$) denote the probability density that at time $t$ no unit is down, unit 2 is in its $i$-th failure stage, and unit 1 has been operating for elapsed time $x$. Let $q_{1,i}(x,t)$ ($1\le i\le k$) denote the probability density that at time $t$ unit 1 is down with elapsed repair time $x$ and unit 2 is in its $i$-th failure stage. Let $q_{2,j}(x,t)$ ($1\le j\le m$) denote the probability density that at time $t$ unit 2 is down in its $j$-th repair phase and unit 1 has been operating for elapsed time $x$. Here $(x,t)\in[0,\infty)	imes[0,\infty)$.

The densities satisfy the standard system of first-order linear partial differential equations
$$\Big(\tfrac{\partial}{\partial t}+\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\Big)q_{0,i}(x,t)=-(\lambda+\mu)q_{0,i}(x,t)+\mu q_{0,i-1}(x,t),$$
$$\Big(\tfrac{\partial}{\partial t}+\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\Big)q_{1,i}(x,t)=-(g(x)+\mu)q_{1,i}(x,t)+\mu q_{1,i-1}(x,t),$$
$$\Big(\tfrac{\partial}{\partial t}+\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\Big)q_{2,j}(x,t)=-(f(x)+\mu)q_{2,j}(x,t)+\mu q_{2,j-1}(x,t),$$
coupled with the boundary conditions, including
$$q_{0,1}(0,t)=\int_0^\infty q_{1,1}(x,t)\,g(x)\,dx+\delta(t),$$
and analogous coupling boundary conditions linking the failure-stage and repair-phase compartments via $f(x)$ and $g(x)$, where $\delta$ is the Dirac measure, together with the natural initial condition corresponding to both units operational at $t=0$.

Assume $g$ and $f$ are non-constant nonnegative measurable functions with $\int_0^\infty g(x)\,dx=\int_0^\infty f(x)\,dx=\infty$.

(a) Prove that this initial–boundary value problem is well posed in a suitable Banach space (existence, uniqueness and continuous dependence of a nonnegative solution that is a probability distribution for every $t\ge 0$).

(b) Determine the asymptotic behavior as $t\to\infty$ of the time-dependent solution; in particular, identify whether it converges (strongly or in some weaker sense) to the steady-state solution of the corresponding stationary system.

Consider a homogeneous two-component (spin ↑, spin ↓) Fermi gas in three dimensions with zero-range s-wave interactions tuned to the unitary limit (inverse scattering length a^{-1}=0). At high temperature, the grand-canonical pressure admits a virial/cluster expansion in the fugacities z_↑, z_↓ of the form

  P/(k_B T) = λ_T^{-3} Σ_{n_↑,n_↓ ≥ 0, (n_↑,n_↓)≠(0,0)} b_{n_↑,n_↓} z_↑^{n_↑} z_↓^{n_↓},

where λ_T is the thermal de Broglie wavelength and b_{n_↑,n_↓} are the (mixed) cluster coefficients. For each sector (n_↑,n_↓) with N = n_↑+n_↓ ≥ 2, let Λ_{n_↑,n_↓}(s) denote the Efimov-type spectral function defined as the regularized product (or appropriate analytic determinant) over the eigenvalues of the scale-invariant N-body unitary problem in a harmonic trap, viewed as an entire/meromorphic function of the complex variable s.

Conjecture to prove: For every mixed sector (n_↑,n_↓) with (n_↑,n_↓) ≠ (1,1) (and N ≥ 2), the unitary cluster coefficient is given by

  b_{n_↑,n_↓} = C_{n_↑,n_↓} ∫_0^∞ S · (d/dS) log Λ_{n_↑,n_↓}(iS) dS  +  Δ_{n_↑,n_↓},

where C_{n_↑,n_↓} is an explicit prefactor depending only on the masses and particle numbers, and Δ_{n_↑,n_↓} is the explicit quantum-statistical correction accounting for indistinguishable non-monoatomic subclusters (built from lower-order cluster coefficients in the standard Ursell/Mayer way).

The formula is known to hold for N = 3 (proved) and is numerically supported in a particular equal-mass N = 4 case. Establish the formula for all (n_↑,n_↓) ≠ (1,1); a complete proof requires control of the analytic properties (zeros, poles, growth) of Λ_{n_↑,n_↓}(s) in the complex plane.

Introduce fugacities z_σ = e^{βμ_σ}. The grand-canonical pressure admits the virial (fugacity) expansion

   P(μ,T) / (k_B T) = λ_T^{-3} ∑_{n_↑, n_↓ ≥ 0, (n_↑,n_↓)≠(0,0)} b_{n_↑, n_↓} z_↑^{n_↑} z_↓^{n_↓},

where b_{n_↑, n_↓} are the dimensionless cluster (virial) coefficients of the homogeneous unitary Fermi gas, defined from the cluster expansion of the grand-canonical partition function and given as connected N=n_↑+n_↓-particle integrals over the Boltzmann operator at unitarity.

Let the system be in thermal equilibrium at temperature T (with β = 1/(k_B T)), chemical potentials μ_↑ = μ_↓ = μ, and thermal de Broglie wavelength λ_T = (2π ℏ²β / m)^{1/2}. Introduce fugacities z_σ = e^{βμ_σ}. The grand-canonical pressure admits the virial (fugacity) expansion

   P(μ,T) / (k_B T) = λ_T^{-3} ∑_{n_↑, n_↓ ≥ 0, (n_↑,n_↓)≠(0,0)} b_{n_↑, n_↓} z_↑^{n_↑} z_↓^{n_↓},

where b_{n_↑, n_↓} are the dimensionless cluster (virial) coefficients of the homogeneous unitary Fermi gas, defined from the cluster expansion of the grand-canonical partition function and given as connected N=n_↑+n_↓-particle integrals over the Boltzmann operator at unitarity.

Denote by T_F the Fermi temperature corresponding to a chosen total density.

(a) Determine the large-order asymptotic behavior of the coefficients b_{n_↑, n_↓} as n_↑, n_↓ → ∞ (in particular, the leading exponential and sub-exponential factors as functions of n_↑ and n_↓, including the balanced case n_↑ = n_↓ → ∞).

(b) Using the asymptotics obtained in (a), construct a resummation of the fugacity series above that converges (or is Borel/Padé/conformally summable) for fugacities corresponding to the degenerate regime T ≲ T_F, and quantify the rate of convergence.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The large-order asymptotics of the unitary-gas cluster coefficients b_{n_↑,n_↓} and a resummation reaching the degenerate regime T ≲ T_F appear to remain open. Only the first several virial coefficients (up to roughly b_4 or b_5, and some partial higher-order numerical results) are known, and current resummations (Padé, Borel, conformal mapping) extend the virial series only modestly below T_F. No published result establishes the full large-n asymptotics or a controlled resummation valid throughout the degenerate regime.

representations.normalized:
Consider a three-dimensional pair-condensed (BCS-BEC crossover) Fermi gas of two spin species with a small population imbalance. In the weakly polarized regime, the excess majority-spin fermions form a dilute population of gapped fermionic quasiparticles, denoted χ, while the low-energy collective excitations of the paired condensate are gapless phonons, denoted φ, with a linear dispersion at long wavelength.

Working within a low-energy effective field theory built from the order-parameter (phonon) field and the gapped Bogoliubov quasiparticle field on top of the BCS ground state, derive the correct low-energy effective interactions between these degrees of freedom, namely:

(i) the φ–χ coupling vertex and the resulting on-shell phonon–quasiparticle scattering amplitude in the limit of small phonon momentum and quasiparticle momentum near the gap minimum, and

(ii) the χ–χ effective interaction (induced direct quasiparticle–quasiparticle scattering, including phonon-mediated contributions).

In particular, determine the unambiguous expression for the leading low-energy φ–χ scattering amplitude as a function of the equation-of-state parameters of the unpolarized superfluid (e.g., the chemical potential, sound velocity, and gap, together with their derivatives with respect to density), reconciling the conflicting results that have appeared in the literature.

For real $k>0$ and $T\geq 2$, define the $2k$-th moment of the Riemann zeta function on the critical line by
$$I_k(T) \;=\; \int_0^T \bigl|\zeta\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}+it\right)\bigr|^{2k}\,dt.$$
Assume the Riemann Hypothesis (i.e. all non-trivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$ have real part $1/2$). It is known that under this assumption one has $I_k(T) \ll_k T(\log T)^{k^2}$ for every $k>0$, with an implicit constant depending on $k$.

Problem: For each real $k>0$, determine an explicit numerical constant $C_k$ (given by a closed-form expression in $k$) such that
$$I_k(T) \;\leq\; C_k\, T\,(\log T)^{k^2}$$
holds for all sufficiently large $T$. The goal is to make $C_k$ as small and as explicit as possible as a function of $k$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Recent work (arXiv:2407.20023, 2024) optimizes the implicit constant in Harper's conditional upper bound and obtains an explicit $C_k = O(\exp(\exp(18.63 k)))$, by making each step in Harper's argument quantitative. Consider a three-dimensional superfluid at low temperature whose elementary excitations include an acoustic (phonon) branch with dispersion relation ω(q) = c q [1 + (γ/8)(ℏq/mc)^2 + O(q^4)] for small wave number q, where c is the sound velocity, m a characteristic mass, and γ the dimensionless curvature parameter. Assume γ < 0 (concave start of the dispersion), so that one-phonon decay into two phonons (Beliaev process) and merging of two phonons into one (Landau process) are kinematically forbidden at low q, and the leading damping mechanism is the Landau–Khalatnikov four-phonon process φφ → φφ. The corresponding damping rate Γ_q^{γ<0}(T) at temperature T has been predicted theoretically (in the regime ℏcq, k_B T much smaller than the characteristic gap or roton scale).

Two physical realizations satisfy γ < 0: (i) a unitary (or strongly interacting) Fermi gas of paired atoms confined in a uniform box trap, in the collisionless low-temperature regime; (ii) bulk superfluid helium-4 under sufficiently high pressure.

Problem: Devise an experimental protocol in one of these two systems that allows the four-phonon damping rate Γ_q^{γ<0}(T) of a phonon mode of wave number q to be observed and quantitatively measured at low temperature, where three-phonon Beliaev–Landau processes are kinematically forbidden, and compare the measured rate against the theoretical prediction.

representations.normalized:
Consider a three-dimensional homogeneous superfluid Fermi gas at low temperature T (with k_B = 1 absorbed) whose elementary excitations form an acoustic branch with dispersion

  ω_q = c q [ 1 + (γ/8)(ℏ q / m c)^2 + O(q^4 log q) ],

where c is the sound velocity, m the fermion mass, q the phonon wavenumber, and γ a dimensionless curvature parameter characterizing the cubic correction to the linear phonon dispersion. The phonon-phonon interaction is the standard cubic and quartic hydrodynamic coupling derived from the equation of state.

When γ is of order unity and positive (convex dispersion), the leading low-temperature damping rate Γ_q of a phonon mode of wavenumber q can be computed in the Born–Markov approximation (Beliaev–Landau processes), giving an exponential decay ⟨b̂_q(t)⟩ ∝ exp(−i ω_q t − Γ_q t /2) with Γ_q obtained from the imaginary part of the on-shell self-energy at lowest order in the interaction.

This Born–Markov treatment breaks down when |γ| becomes so small that the cubic curvature term (γ/8)(ℏq/mc)^2 is comparable to the next-order O(q^4 log q) dispersion terms, and when γ is of order T^2 (in natural units of (mc^2)^2), so that the self-energy is neither Markovian nor of Born form, and ⟨b̂_q(t)⟩ may exhibit non-exponential decay.

Problem. In this small-curvature regime (in particular near the interaction strength at which γ vanishes), determine the phonon damping rate Γ_q, or, when decay is non-exponential, an appropriate replacement such as the inverse of the half-width at relative height 1/e of |⟨b̂_q(t)⟩|^2 as a function of t, as a function of q, T, c, m, and the small parameter γ.

For $T \geq 2$, let
$$I_2(T) = \int_0^T \left|\zeta\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2} + it\right)\right|^4 dt,$$
where $\zeta$ denotes the Riemann zeta function. It is known that there exists an explicit polynomial $P_4$ of degree $4$ (with coefficients depending only on absolute constants) such that, for every $\varepsilon > 0$,
$$I_2(T) = T\, P_4(\log T) + O\!\left(T^{2/3 + \varepsilon}\right).$$
Improve the exponent in the error term: that is, establish an asymptotic of the form
$$I_2(T) = T\, P_4(\log T) + O\!\left(T^{\theta + \varepsilon}\right)$$
for some constant $\theta < 2/3$, or determine the infimum of admissible exponents $\theta$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The $T^{2/3+\varepsilon}$ bound for the error term in the fourth moment of $\zeta(1/2+it)$ remains the state of the art. Ivić and others have made only logarithmic refinements (e.g., recent 2025 work establishes $E_2(2T) - E_2(T) \ll T^{2/3}(\log T)^{3.5}/(\log\log T)^C$), but no power-saving improvement below $2/3$ is known. The problem of improving the exponent is widely regarded as open.

Consider a low-dimensional superfluid (in either two or one spatial dimensions) at temperature T, with mass density ρ, sound velocity c, and healing length ξ, whose long-wavelength low-energy excitations are phonons of momentum q with a dispersion ω_q. Suppose the leading nonlinearity in the effective phonon Hamiltonian is a cubic three-phonon coupling, and consider the retarded phonon self-energy Σ_q(ζ) (so that the damping rate Γ_q is, formally, −Im Σ_q(ω_q+i0⁺)/ℏ).

In the following two regimes, the Born–Markov / Fermi golden-rule power counting based on the cubic interaction breaks down (the perturbative series in the cubic coupling is no longer controlled):

(i) A two-dimensional superfluid whose acoustic branch ω_q is convex (curving upward away from the linear part) at low momentum.

(ii) A one-dimensional superfluid in the low-temperature, fixed dimensionless density regime k_B T/(mc²) → 0 with ρξ held fixed.

Construct, in either or both of these regimes, a controlled (i.e., nonheuristic and systematic) nonperturbative approximation scheme for the phonon self-energy Σ_q(ζ) — for instance via a self-consistent Dyson-type equation, a resummation of an identifiable infinite class of diagrams, or a kinetic-theory framework beyond Born–Markov — and derive from it the leading low-momentum and/or low-temperature decay rate Γ_q (or, where appropriate, a non-exponential decay law) of a single phonon mode. The result must be shown to agree, in its regime of validity, with the true asymptotic damping observed in classical-field or microscopic simulations, and must reduce to the Fermi golden rule in regimes where perturbation theory is valid.

Consider a finite, well-isolated superfluid of N paired fermions at zero (or very low) temperature, prepared as a pair condensate with a well-defined total particle number. In such a system, phonon number fluctuations decorrelate over time through phonon-phonon collisions, and standard theory predicts that the global condensate phase φ(t) undergoes diffusive spreading: for times long enough that many phonon collisions have occurred, the variance Var[φ(t) − φ(0)] grows linearly in t with a phase-diffusion coefficient D_λ. This coefficient is intrinsic (not due to coupling with an external bath) and is predicted to be subextensive, scaling as D_λ ∝ 1/N for fixed intensive parameters (density, temperature, interaction strength), so that the condensate has a finite intrinsic coherence time τ_c ∼ N/(intensive constant).

Problem: Devise and carry out an experiment in an ultracold atomic gas (the only known quantum fluid sufficiently isolated for the loss of condensate coherence to be of intrinsic origin) that directly measures the intrinsic phase-diffusion coefficient D_λ and the associated finite coherence time of an isolated finite-size pair condensate, and verifies the predicted 1/N scaling of D_λ together with the linear-in-time growth of the phase variance arising from phonon-collision-induced decorrelation of phonon number fluctuations. Equivalently, demonstrate experimentally that an isolated finite pair condensate loses coherence at the intrinsic rate predicted by this phonon-collision mechanism, rather than at a rate set by externally imposed decoherence.

representations.normalized:
Let $\zeta(s)$ denote the Riemann zeta function. For a positive integer $m$, fix a tuple of positive real numbers $\mathbf{k}=(k_1,\dots,k_m)$ and a tuple of real shifts $\boldsymbol{\alpha}(T)=(\alpha_1(T),\dots,\alpha_m(T))$ depending on the parameter $T\ge 2$, with $|\alpha_i(T)|\le T/2$ for all $i$. Define the shifted moment
$$M_{\mathbf k}(T,\boldsymbol\alpha)=\int_0^T \prod_{i=1}^m \bigl|\zeta\bigl(\tfrac12+it+i\alpha_i(T)\bigr)\bigr|^{2k_i}\,dt.$$
Assuming the Riemann Hypothesis, prove that there exists a constant $C=C(\mathbf k)>0$ such that for all sufficiently large $T$,
$$M_{\mathbf k}(T,\boldsymbol\alpha)\;\le\; C\, T\,(\log T)^{k_1^2+\cdots+k_m^2}\;\prod_{1\le i<j\le m}\min\!\Bigl\{\tfrac{1}{|\alpha_i(T)-\alpha_j(T)|},\ \log T\Bigr\}^{2 k_i k_j}.$$
That is, remove the factor $(\log T)^{\varepsilon}$ from the previously known upper bound of the form $T(\log T)^{k_1^2+\cdots+k_m^2+\varepsilon}\prod_{i<j}\min\{1/|\alpha_i-\alpha_j|,\log T\}^{2k_i k_j}$, by means of Harper-style sharp upper bound techniques.

representations.normalized:
Consider a three-dimensional homogeneous pair-condensed Fermi gas at very low temperature T (with k_B T much less than the pairing gap), so that its low-energy excitations are bosonic phonons with linear dispersion ω_q ≃ c q at small wave number q, where c is the sound velocity and m is the fermion mass. Assume the next-to-linear correction to the acoustic branch is concave, i.e.

  ω_q = c q [1 + (γ/8)(ħ q/(m c))^2 + o(q^2)],   with γ < 0.

Let λ(t) denote the global phase of the order parameter; in a canonical-like ensemble its variance grows in time, and one defines the phase-diffusion coefficient

  D_λ = lim_{t→∞} (1/(2t)) Var[λ(t) − λ(0)],

assuming this limit exists and is finite.

For γ < 0, restricting the phonon collision integral to the small-angle Landau–Khalatnikov four-phonon processes φφ → φφ (which conserve the total phonon number N_φ and have a typical rate ∝ (k_B T/(m c^2))^7 · m c^2/(ħ|γ|) ∝ T^7) yields a divergent D_λ and superdiffusive spreading of λ(t).

Determine the true, finite value of D_λ (or prove its finiteness/infiniteness) when one consistently includes, in addition, the subdominant five-phonon processes φφ ↔ φφφ that do not conserve N_φ (rate ∝ T^9) together with the large-angle four-phonon processes φφ → φφ of comparable order, for a pair-condensed Fermi gas with concave acoustic branch γ < 0.

Consider a three-dimensional, equal-mass, spin-1/2 (two-component, spin-unpolarized) Fermi gas at zero temperature in the unitary limit, i.e. with s-wave scattering length |a| = ∞ and zero-range interactions, so that the ground state is a universal superfluid characterized only by the Fermi momentum k_F (with Fermi energy E_F = ℏ²k_F²/(2m) and sound speed c determined by the Bertsch parameter). Let ω(q) denote the dispersion relation of the Bogoliubov–Anderson phonon branch as a function of the wave number q. Expand at small q in the form

  ω(q) = c q [ 1 + (γ/8) (ℏ q / (m c))² + O(q⁴) ],

which defines the dimensionless acoustic curvature parameter γ. The sign of γ governs the dominant low-temperature collisionless phonon damping mechanism: γ > 0 (convex dispersion) makes three-phonon Beliaev–Landau processes (1 ↔ 2 phonons) kinematically allowed and dominant, while γ < 0 (concave dispersion) forbids them and renders four-phonon Landau–Khalatnikov processes (2 ↔ 2 phonons) dominant.

Determine the sign of γ and its numerical value for the unitary Fermi gas at zero temperature.

The sign and value of the acoustic curvature γ at unitarity remain disputed. Microscopic approximations (e.g., quasiparticle RPA / pair-fluctuation theories around 2016–2020) yield γ > 0, while a Bragg-spectroscopy experiment (Hoinka et al., PRL 124, 150401 (2020)) reports a concave (γ < 0) branch. For $T \geq 2$, define the sixth moment of the Riemann zeta function on the critical line by
$$I_3(T) = \int_0^T \left|\zeta\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}+it\right)\right|^6 \, dt.$$
For positive integers $n$ let $d_3(n) = \sum_{abc=n} 1$ denote the ternary divisor function, and for a positive integer $h$ consider the ternary additive divisor sum
$$D_3(N,h) = \sum_{n \leq N} d_3(n)\, d_3(n+h).$$
The ternary additive divisor conjecture asserts that there exist a polynomial $Q_{h}(x)$ of degree $4$ in $x$ (with coefficients depending on $h$) and some $\delta > 0$ such that, uniformly in a suitable range of $h$,
$$D_3(N,h) = \int_1^N Q_h(\log u)\, du + O\!\left(N^{1-\delta}\right).$$

Assuming the ternary additive divisor conjecture, prove an omega theorem for $I_3(T)$: show that there exists a constant $\Theta > 0$ and a polynomial $P_9$ of degree $9$ such that
$$I_3(T) = T\, P_9(\log T) + \Omega\!\left(T^{\Theta}\right),$$
i.e. the error term $I_3(T) - T P_9(\log T)$ is not $o(T^\Theta)$ as $T \to \infty$.

Conditional asymptotic formulas for the sixth moment $I_3(T) = T P_9(\log T) + O(T^{1-\delta})$ have been established under the ternary additive divisor conjecture (Ng, 2016; later refinements). representations.normalized:
Consider a three-dimensional pair-condensed Fermi gas of spin-1/2 fermions with a zero-range s-wave interaction in the BCS–BEC crossover. At zero temperature, the linear-response collective modes of wave vector q and complex energy z are encoded by an eigenvalue equation

   det M(q, z) = 0,

where M(q, z) is the 3×3 matrix obtained by linearizing the time-dependent BCS (equivalently, the Gaussian-fluctuation) equations around the BCS ground state. The matrix elements involve integrals over fermionic quasiparticle energies E_k = sqrt((ε_k − μ)^2 + Δ^2) (with ε_k = ℏ²k²/2m, chemical potential μ, and order parameter Δ), and the dispersion relation z(q) is to be analytically continued from the upper half-plane through the branch cut associated with the broken-pair fermionic continuum [2Δ, ∞), thereby capturing both undamped phonon-like solutions and complex modes that describe coupling of the order-parameter phase mode φ to broken-pair excitations χ.

Writing the order-parameter fluctuations in terms of a phase field φ and a modulus field χ, the linearized (mean-field / Gaussian) theory captures the φ–χ coupling but omits the φ–φ self-interaction (phonon–phonon coupling) that becomes relevant at nonzero temperature, where a thermal population of phonons is present.

Problem. Construct a microscopic finite-wave-number collective-mode equation

   det M_T(q, z) = 0,

valid at nonzero temperature T > 0 in the superfluid phase, that

  (i) reduces to det M(q, z) = 0 in the limit T → 0,
  (ii) goes beyond the simple BCS / Gaussian-fluctuation mean-field linearization by incorporating phonon–phonon (φ–φ) coupling induced by thermally excited collective modes,
  (iii) still incorporates the coupling of collective modes to broken-pair fermionic quasiparticles, including the analytic continuation of det M_T(q, z) through the broken-pair continuum so that complex mode energies z(q, T) can be extracted,

and determine the resulting dispersion relation and damping of the high-frequency (pair-breaking) collective modes as functions of q and T.

representations.normalized:
Consider a three-dimensional pair-condensed Fermi gas of two spin states with attractive zero-range (s-wave) interactions, described in the BCS–BEC crossover by a mean-field-like superfluid order parameter Δ. Within RPA-type linear response, the modulus-modulus (and modulus-density) response functions of the order parameter possess, in addition to the gapless Anderson–Bogoliubov phonon branch, a collective excitation branch lying inside the broken-pair (pair-breaking) continuum 2Δ ≤ ω. This branch — the Andrianov–Popov / "Higgs-like" continuum mode — has a complex dispersion relation z_q (with Re z_q above the pair-breaking threshold and Im z_q < 0, encoding exponential decay through emission of broken pairs) and is reached by analytic continuation of the response function through its branch cut to the appropriate Riemann sheet.

A salient feature is that the spectral weight of this continuum mode in the response functions vanishes as q → 0, so that long-wavelength (q = 0) probes such as uniform interaction-strength modulation do not access it; finite wave number q > 0 is required.

Problem: Devise an experimental protocol on ultracold trapped Fermi gases at unitarity (or across the BCS–BEC crossover) that:
(i) selectively excites the finite-q Andrianov–Popov continuum branch with sufficient spectral weight to be detectable above the pair-breaking continuum background, and
(ii) yields a precise quantitative measurement of the complex dispersion relation z_q (both its real part — the resonance frequency — and its imaginary part — the intrinsic damping rate) as a function of the wave number q and of the interaction parameter 1/(k_F a_s).

Equivalently: prove or disprove that such a measurement is feasible with state-of-the-art cold-atom techniques, and if feasible, determine the optimal range of q and interaction strength for the observation.

This branch — the Andrianov–Popov / "Higgs-like" continuum mode — has a complex dispersion relation z_q (with Re z_q above the pair-breaking threshold and Im z_q < 0, encoding exponential decay through emission of broken pairs) and is reached by analytic continuation of the response function through its branch cut to the appropriate Riemann sheet.

A salient feature is that the spectral weight of this continuum mode in the response functions vanishes as q → 0, so that long-wavelength (q = 0) probes such as uniform interaction-strength modulation do not access it; finite wave number q > 0 is required.

(i) selectively excites the finite-q Andrianov–Popov continuum branch with sufficient spectral weight to be detectable above the pair-breaking continuum background, and
(ii) yields a precise quantitative measurement of the complex dispersion relation z_q (both its real part — the resonance frequency — and its imaginary part — the intrinsic damping rate) as a function of the wave number q and of the interaction parameter 1/(k_F a_s).

Equivalently: prove or disprove that such a measurement is feasible with state-of-the-art cold-atom techniques, and if feasible, determine the optimal range of q and interaction strength for the observation.

Recent experiments (e.g., Phys. Rev. Lett. 133, 150403 (2024); Sci. Rep. 2023) measured the q ≈ 0 Higgs mode via interaction modulation, but a finite-q observation resolving the complex dispersion relation z_q has not been reported. The problem appears to remain open.

Let $\zeta(s)$ denote the Riemann zeta function, and for a positive integer $k$ and real $T>0$ define the $2k$-th moment on the critical line
$$I_k(T)=\int_0^T \left|\zeta\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}+it\right)\right|^{2k}\,dt.$$
The Conrey–Farmer–Keating–Rubinstein–Snaith (CFKRS) heuristic "recipe" predicts that, for each integer $k\ge 1$,
$$I_k(T)\sim \int_0^T P_k\!\left(\log\tfrac{t}{2\pi}\right)\,dt,$$
where $P_k$ is an explicit polynomial of degree $k^2$ whose coefficients are obtained from the recipe (a procedure that, starting from an approximate functional equation for $\zeta(s)^k\zeta(1-s)^k$, retains only the "diagonal" terms in the resulting multiple sum, applies the conjectural shifted divisor-correlation formula, and discards certain off-diagonal contributions). The recipe in its stated form is non-rigorous because the discarding of off-diagonal terms is not justified.

Problem: Working entirely within the framework of the CFKRS recipe (i.e. without using the known proofs of the fourth-moment asymptotic via different analytic techniques), give a rigorous derivation, valid for $k=2$, of an asymptotic formula of the form
$$I_2(T)=\int_0^T P_2\!\left(\log\tfrac{t}{2\pi}\right)\,dt+O\!\left(T^{1-\delta}\right)$$
for some constant $\delta>0$, where $P_2$ is the explicit degree-$4$ polynomial produced by the recipe. Equivalently, justify rigorously each step of the recipe in the case $k=2$, including the treatment of the off-diagonal contributions, to obtain a power-saving error term.

representations.normalized:
Consider a three-dimensional pair-condensed Fermi gas with two equally populated spin components and zero-range (s-wave) interactions, tunable through a Feshbach resonance and described, at the simplest level, by BCS mean-field theory. Within BCS theory at zero temperature, the minimum energy required to break a Cooper pair, denoted E_pair, satisfies the identity

  E_pair = 2|Δ|,

where Δ is the complex order-parameter (gap) amplitude. Small fluctuations of |Δ| about its equilibrium value support an amplitude (Higgs) collective branch which, in the BCS approximation at T = 0 and at zero wave number, produces undamped oscillations whose frequency tends to 2|Δ|/ℏ and whose amplitude decays as a power law t^{-α} with α = 1/2 at the unitary limit.

Address the following:

(a) Does the equality E_pair = 2|Δ| continue to hold at zero temperature in theories that go beyond BCS mean field (for instance theories that include pairing fluctuations or correlations beyond mean field) and/or in laboratory measurements on strongly interacting Fermi gases? Provide a proof, a counterexample, or a precise quantitative correction.

(b) For experiments performed at nonzero temperature in the unitary regime that probe the zero-wave-number oscillations of the order-parameter amplitude, give a theoretical interpretation that accounts simultaneously for: (i) a measured power-law decay exponent α ≈ 1 (rather than the BCS value 1/2 at unitarity); (ii) the possibility that the decay is in fact exponential rather than power-law; and (iii) the absence of any observable softening (reduction) of the oscillation angular frequency as the temperature approaches the superfluid critical temperature T_c. Determine whether such observations are compatible with a Higgs amplitude-mode interpretation and, if not, identify the dominant physical mechanism responsible for the oscillations and their decay.

Fix integers n ≥ 1 and d ≥ 1, and let R[X] = R[x_0, x_1, …, x_n]_{2d} denote the finite-dimensional real vector space of homogeneous polynomials (forms) of degree 2d in n+1 variables. Inside R[X] consider:

• P_{n+1,2d} = { f ∈ R[X] : f(x) ≥ 0 for all x ∈ R^{n+1} }, the cone of positive semidefinite forms;
• Σ_{n+1,2d} = { f ∈ R[X] : f = ∑_j h_j^2, h_j ∈ R[x_0,…,x_n]_d }, the cone of sums of squares.

The Gram matrix method assigns to each form f ∈ R[X] the affine set
  G(f) = { A ∈ Sym_{k(n,d)}(R) : f = v_d(x)^T A v_d(x) },
where v_d(x) is the vector of all monomials of degree d in x_0, …, x_n and k(n,d) = (n+d choose d). Then f ∈ Σ_{n+1,2d} iff G(f) contains a positive semidefinite matrix.

Given a chain of projective subvarieties of P^{k(n,d)-1}
  ν_d(P^n) = V_0 ⊊ V_1 ⊊ ⋯ ⊊ V_{k(n,d)-n} = P^{k(n,d)-1},
where ν_d denotes the Veronese embedding, define the intermediate cones
  C_i := { f ∈ R[X] : ∃ A ∈ G(f) with v^T A v ≥ 0 for all v ∈ V_i(R) }.
These satisfy
  Σ_{n+1,2d} = C_0 ⊆ C_1 ⊆ ⋯ ⊆ C_{k(n,d)-n} = P_{n+1,2d}.

Assume the inclusion C_{i-1} ⊊ C_i is strict (the cone C_i is "strictly separating").

Problem: Provide a membership test for C_i — given a form f ∈ R[X], decide whether f ∈ C_i — preferably one formulated as an intrinsic algebraic property of a representing Gram matrix A ∈ G(f), rather than by directly verifying local positive semidefiniteness of A on the variety V_i.

For an even integer k ≥ 2, let H_k denote the set of normalized holomorphic Hecke eigenforms of weight k for the full modular group SL_2(Z). For f ∈ H_k, let L(s, f) denote the associated Hecke L-function, normalized so that the functional equation relates s to 1 − s and the central point is s = 1/2. Let L(s, ad f) denote the adjoint (symmetric square) L-function of f, and consider the harmonic-type weight 1/L(1, ad f). For a parameter T → ∞, consider the cubic and quartic moments

   M_3(T) = Σ_{k ≤ T, k even} Σ_{f ∈ H_k} (Γ(k−1)/(4π)^{k−1}) · L(1/2, f)^3 / L(1, ad f),
   M_4(T) = Σ_{k ≤ T, k even} Σ_{f ∈ H_k} (Γ(k−1)/(4π)^{k−1}) · L(1/2, f)^4 / L(1, ad f).

Prove asymptotic formulas with the strongest possible error terms. In particular, establish that there exist polynomials P_3 of degree 3 and P_6 of degree 6 such that, for every ε > 0,

   M_3(T) = T^2 P_3(log T) + O_ε(T^{1+ε}),
   M_4(T) = T^2 P_6(log T) + O_ε(T^{4/3+ε}),

and determine the leading coefficients of P_3 and P_6 explicitly.

$$P_{n+1,2d}=\{f\in\mathbb{R}[X]_{2d}:f(x)\ge 0\text{ for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\}$$
be the cone of positive semidefinite forms, and let
$$\Sigma_{n+1,2d}=\Big\{\sum_{j} g_j^2 : g_j\in\mathbb{R}[X]_d\Big\}$$
be the cone of sums of squares. Let $\nu_d:\mathbb{P}^n\to\mathbb{P}^{N}$, $N=\binom{n+d}{d}-1$, denote the $d$-th Veronese embedding, and for a real projective variety $V\subseteq\mathbb{P}^N$ containing the Veronese variety $\nu_d(\mathbb{P}^n)$ let
$$C(V)=\{f\in\mathbb{R}[X]_{2d}: \exists\text{ a positive semidefinite Gram matrix for }f\text{ supported on }V\},$$
i.e.\ the set of forms admitting a Gram representation by a positive semidefinite quadratic form on the ambient space of $\mathbb{P}^N$ that vanishes on $V$ modulo the form. Choosing a chain of real projective varieties
$$\nu_d(\mathbb{P}^n)=V_{k(n,d)-n}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq V_1\subseteq V_0=\mathbb{P}^N$$
one obtains a filtration
$$\Sigma_{n+1,2d}=C_0\subseteq C_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq C_{k(n,d)-n}=P_{n+1,2d},$$
where $C_i:=C(V_i)$. Assume the chain is strictly separating, i.e.\ $C_i\subsetneq C_{i+1}$ for each $i$. For each such intermediate cone $C_i$, give an explicit description of its dual cone
$$C_i^{\vee}:=\{L\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{R}[X]_{2d},\mathbb{R}):L(f)\ge 0\text{ for all }f\in C_i\}$$
in terms of the variety $V_i$ (e.g.\ as moment-type functionals associated with measures, Hankel/moment matrix positivity conditions on $V_i$, or otherwise intrinsic geometric data).

Let Σ_{n+1,2d} ⊆ R[x_0,...,x_n]_{2d} be the cone of sums of squares of forms of degree d, and let P_{n+1,2d} be the cone of positive semidefinite forms of degree 2d. Consider a filtration of closed convex cones

    Σ_{n+1,2d} = C_0 ⊆ C_1 ⊆ ... ⊆ C_N = P_{n+1,2d},

obtained via the Gram matrix construction: to each projective variety V ⊆ P^{k-1} containing the image of the Veronese embedding ν_d : P^n → P^{k-1} (where k = dim R[x_0,...,x_n]_d), one associates the cone

    C(V) = { f ∈ R[x_0,...,x_n]_{2d} : f admits a positive semidefinite Gram matrix Q whose associated quadratic form vanishes on V } ,

and the C_i are the (finitely many) distinct cones obtained as V ranges over such varieties. Call C_i strictly separating if C_{i-1} ⊊ C_i ⊊ C_{i+1}. With respect to the standard apolar (Bombieri) inner product on R[x_0,...,x_n]_{2d}, the dual cone of P_{n+1,2d} can be identified with the cone of homogeneous truncated moment sequences L : R[x_0,...,x_n]_{2d} → R that admit a representing measure supported on the unit sphere S^n ⊆ R^{n+1}, i.e. L(f) = ∫_{S^n} f dμ for some positive Borel measure μ.

Problem. For a strictly separating intermediate cone C_i in the filtration above, give an analogous intrinsic characterization of its dual cone C_i^∨ as a set of homogeneous truncated moment sequences. Specifically, identify the class of representing measures (their supports, or other defining structural conditions) whose moment sequences are exactly the elements of C_i^∨.

Let $q \ge 1$ be a positive integer and let $\mathcal{B}_0(q)$ denote an orthonormal Hecke eigenbasis of the space of Hecke–Maass cusp forms for $\Gamma_0(q)$ with bounded spectral parameter (say, with Laplace eigenvalue $1/4 + t_f^2$ satisfying $|t_f| \le 1$). For each such form $f$, let $L(s,f)$ denote its associated $L$-function. Jutila's classical result asserts that, in the level-$1$ setting with spectral parameter at most $T$,
$$\sum_{\substack{f \in \mathcal{B}_0(1) \\ |t_f| \le T}} |L(\tfrac{1}{2}, f)|^{12} \ll_{\varepsilon} T^{4+\varepsilon},$$
which is of Weyl strength (and implies the Weyl-quality subconvex bound $L(1/2,f) \ll t_f^{1/3+\varepsilon}$).

Prove a level-aspect analogue: establish, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, a bound of the form
$$\sum_{f \in \mathcal{B}_0(q),\ |t_f| \le 1} |L(\tfrac{1}{2}, f)|^{12} \ll_{\varepsilon} q^{2+\varepsilon},$$
or, more generally, any bound of Weyl strength in the level aspect summing $|L(1/2,f)|^{12}$ over Hecke–Maass cusp forms of level $q$ and bounded spectral parameter, that yields the Weyl-quality subconvexity exponent $L(1/2, f) \ll q^{1/6+\varepsilon}$ for individual forms.

Fix integers $n \geq 0$, $d \geq 1$, and $k \geq n$. Let $I_{n+1,2d} = \{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0^{n+1} : |\alpha| = 2d\}$ be the set of exponents of monomials of degree $2d$ in $n+1$ variables, and enumerate the elements of $I_{n+1,d} = \{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0^{n+1} : |\alpha| = d\}$ as $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots$ in some fixed order, where $|I_{n+1,d}| = \binom{n+d}{d}$.

For a finite set $\Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0^{n+1}$, the $\Lambda$-truncated moment problem asks: given a real multisequence $(y_\alpha)_{\alpha \in \Lambda}$, when does there exist a non-negative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ (or on a prescribed support set) such that
$$y_\alpha = \int X^\alpha \, d\mu(X) \qquad \text{for all } \alpha \in \Lambda?$$

Suppose that, in a fixed Gram-matrix style construction, one has a nested family of closed convex cones
$$\mathrm{SOS}_{n+1,2d} = C_{k-n} \subseteq C_{k-n-1} \subseteq \cdots \subseteq C_0 \subseteq \mathrm{PSD}_{n+1,2d}$$
inside the space of real forms of degree $2d$ in $n+1$ variables, together with their dual cones $C_i^\vee$ (with respect to the standard apolar/coefficient pairing).

For each $i \in \{0, 1, \ldots, k-n\}$, define
$$\Lambda_i := \{\alpha_s + \alpha_t : 0 \leq s, t \leq n+i\} \subseteq I_{n+1,2d} \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0^{n+1}.$$

Problem: Describe explicitly the relationship between the dual cone $C_i^\vee$ and the $\Lambda_i$-truncated moment problem; in particular, characterize membership of a multisequence $(y_\alpha)_{\alpha \in \Lambda_i}$ in (a suitable projection of) $C_i^\vee$ in terms of the existence of a representing non-negative Borel measure for $(y_\alpha)_{\alpha \in \Lambda_i}$.

Let n,d be positive integers. Write P_{n+1,2d} for the cone of real homogeneous polynomials of degree 2d in n+1 variables that are nonnegative on R^{n+1}, and Σ_{n+1,2d} for its subcone of sums of squares of homogeneous polynomials of degree d. Let I_{n+1,d} denote the set of monomials of degree d in n+1 variables, so that the squares of these monomials span a natural subspace inside Σ_{n+1,2d}.

Given a monomial order ≺ on the polynomial ring R[x_0,...,x_n], list the monomials of I_{n+1,d} in increasing order as m_1 ≺ m_2 ≺ ... ≺ m_N. Using this ordering, construct a nested filtration of convex cones
   C_0 ⊆ C_1 ⊆ ... ⊆ C_N
interpolating between Σ_{n+1,2d} and P_{n+1,2d}, where C_k is obtained from C_{k-1} by adjoining the kth monomial m_k in the prescribed way (so that C_0 = Σ_{n+1,2d} and C_N = P_{n+1,2d}, or another fixed pair as dictated by the construction).

Problem. Identify the order-theoretic and combinatorial properties of the monomial order ≺ (for instance, whether it is lexicographic, graded lexicographic, graded reverse lexicographic, a weight order, an elimination order, the placement of the smallest/largest variable, compatibility with symmetries, etc.) that determine, for each index k, whether the inclusion C_{k-1} ⊆ C_k is an equality or strict. Describe explicitly how these properties of ≺ control the resulting pattern of equalities and strict inclusions in the filtration C_0 ⊆ C_1 ⊆ ... ⊆ C_N.

Let $H_k$ denote the set of primitive (Hecke-normalized) holomorphic cusp forms of level 1 and even weight $k$ for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$. For $f \in H_k$ and $g \in H_\ell$, let $L(s, f \otimes g)$ denote the Rankin–Selberg $L$-function attached to the pair $(f,g)$, analytically normalized so that the central point is $s = 1/2$.

Let $K \to \infty$. Establish a non-trivial upper bound, as sharp as possible, for the weight-aspect sixth moment
$$
\sum_{\substack{k+\ell \\ K < k+\ell \le 2K \\ |k-\ell| = O(1)}} \;\sum_{f \in H_k} \sum_{g \in H_\ell} \bigl| L(\tfrac{1}{2}, f \otimes g) \bigr|^{6},
$$
where the outer sum is over pairs of even weights $(k,\ell)$ satisfying $|k-\ell| = O(1)$ and $K < k+\ell \le 2K$. In particular, derive consequences for subconvex bounds on $L(1/2, f \otimes g)$ in this family.

The original Thomassen-style crumby coloring conjecture for 3-connected cubic graphs was disproved by Bellitto, Klimošová, Merker, Witkowski and Yuditsky, who constructed an infinite counterexample family. The follow-up question of finding the right relaxation of the conditions on the red subgraph that holds for all 3-connected cubic graphs remains open; partial positive results are known only for restricted classes (e.g., 2-connected outerplanar graphs, subdivisions of K_4, 1-subdivisions of cubic graphs).

For each odd squarefree positive integer $d$, let $\chi_{8d}$ denote the real primitive quadratic Dirichlet character of conductor $8d$ (the Kronecker symbol attached to the fundamental discriminant $8d$), and let $L(s,\chi_{8d})$ be its associated Dirichlet $L$-function. Consider the fourth moment
$$ S(X) \;=\; \sum_{\substack{0<d<X\\ d\text{ odd, squarefree}}} L\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2},\chi_{8d}\right)^{4}. $$

(a) Exhibit an explicit polynomial $P(t)\in\mathbb{R}[t]$ of degree $10$ such that
$$ S(X) \;=\; X\,P(\log X) \;+\; o(X) \qquad (X\to\infty), $$
and determine all of its coefficients.

(b) Determine whether the error term $o(X)$ in this asymptotic formula can be replaced by a power-saving error term of the form $O(X^{1-\delta})$ for some fixed $\delta>0$.

(c) Determine whether the Multiple Dirichlet Series method (i.e. the analytic continuation of the multiple Dirichlet series $\sum_d L(s,\chi_{8d})^{4}\, d^{-w}$ and the study of its polar structure) can be used to recover at least the leading coefficients of $P$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Heath-Brown, Soundararajan, and Soundararajan–Young established asymptotic formulas with the leading main terms for the fourth moment of quadratic Dirichlet L-functions; recent work has extended this to four leading main terms (e.g. arXiv:2402.01497, "The fourth moment of quadratic Dirichlet L-Functions II"). However, the complete determination of the conjectural degree-10 polynomial P, a power-saving error term in this family, and a derivation of the leading coefficients of P via the Multiple Dirichlet Series method remain open as of recent literature.

Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. A list-assignment for $G$ is a function $L$ that assigns to every vertex $v\in V(G)$ a set $L(v)$ of allowed colors; it is called a $k$-list-assignment if $|L(v)|=k$ for all $v$. An $L$-coloring of $G$ is a proper coloring $c$ of $G$ such that $c(v)\in L(v)$ for every $v$. The list-chromatic number (choosability) $\chi_\ell(G)$ is the least integer $k$ such that every $k$-list-assignment $L$ of $G$ admits an $L$-coloring.

Given a $k$-list-assignment $L$, an $L$-packing of size $k$ is a collection of $k$ proper $L$-colorings $c_1,\dots,c_k$ such that for every vertex $v$ the colors $c_1(v),\dots,c_k(v)$ are pairwise distinct (equivalently, $\{c_1(v),\dots,c_k(v)\}=L(v)$). The list packing number $\chi_\ell^\star(G)$ is the least integer $k$ such that for every $k$-list-assignment $L$ of $G$ there exists an $L$-packing of size $k$.

Determine whether the inequality
$$\chi_\ell^\star(G)\;\le\; 2\,\chi_\ell(G)$$
holds for every finite simple graph $G$.

Let $\zeta(s)$ denote the Riemann zeta function, and for $\sigma \in [1/2, 1]$ and $T \geq 2$ let
$$N(\sigma, T) = \#\{\rho = \beta + i\gamma : \zeta(\rho) = 0,\ \beta \geq \sigma,\ 0 < \gamma \leq T\}.$$
A zero-density estimate is a bound of the form $N(\sigma, T) \ll T^{A(\sigma)(1-\sigma)} (\log T)^{B}$ for some functions $A(\sigma)$ and $B$. Ingham's classical zero-density estimate is derived using the fourth-moment bound
$$\int_T^{2T} |\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)|^4 \, dt \ll T (\log T)^4,$$
together with mean-value estimates for Dirichlet polynomials. Heath-Brown established the twelfth-moment bound
$$\int_0^{T} |\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)|^{12} \, dt \ll T^{2}(\log T)^{17}.$$

(a) Develop a general framework that converts a nontrivial $2k$-th moment estimate for $\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)$ (for $k > 2$, e.g., Heath-Brown's twelfth-moment bound) into a zero-density estimate for $N(\sigma, T)$, and determine precisely the dependence of $A(\sigma)$ on the moment exponent $k$ and on the strength of the available moment bound.

(b) Determine whether such moment-based zero-density arguments can be extended to general $L$-functions $L(s, \pi)$ associated to automorphic representations $\pi$ (in particular Dirichlet $L$-functions and $L$-functions in the Selberg class), and identify the analytic inputs (mean values, approximate functional equations, large-sieve-type inequalities) required for the generalization.

Consider a soft amorphous material (e.g., a colloidal gel, emulsion, dense suspension, or soft glass) modeled as a continuum that may also support spatially heterogeneous plastic rearrangements. Suppose one fixed constitutive description of this material is subjected to two classes of mechanical tests:

(i) Simple-shear rheometry, in which the sample is confined between two parallel plates (or in a cone–plate / Couette geometry) with a nominally homogeneous shear deformation imposed, and the macroscopic shear stress σ(γ) is measured as a function of applied strain γ.

(ii) Uniaxial compression or extension in a universal testing machine (UTM), in which the sample is placed between rigid platens (with friction or adhesion at the boundaries) and the macroscopic axial stress σ(ε) is measured as a function of axial strain ε.

For the same underlying material model, formulate and analyze the following:

1. Quantify the spatial stress heterogeneity field τ(x) induced by each geometry, including the role of free surfaces, boundary friction/adhesion, sample aspect ratio, and finite-size effects.

2. Determine the conditions under which shear localization (formation of a shear band) initiates, and how the localization threshold, orientation, and width depend on the geometry and boundary conditions.

3. Characterize the macroscopic stress–strain curve σ(γ) or σ(ε), and identify quantitative criteria (e.g., post-peak stress drop magnitude, strain at failure, energy released at yield) that classify the apparent yielding as ductile or brittle.

4. Prove or disprove that there exist constitutive parameters for which one and the same material exhibits ductile yielding in geometry (i) and brittle yielding in geometry (ii), and identify the dimensionless groups governing this crossover.

Provide a predictive framework (analytical, numerical, or both) that maps the intrinsic material parameters and geometric/boundary parameters to the observed ductile-to-brittle character of the response.

$$ S(t) =  rac{1}{\pi}\,\arg\zeta\!\left(	frac12 + itight), $$
where the argument is obtained by continuous variation along the horizontal segment from $2$ to $2+it$ and then along the vertical segment from $2+it$ to $	frac12+it$, starting with the value $0$ at $s=2$. (At ordinates of zeros, $S(t)$ is defined as the average of its left and right limits.)

Assume the Riemann Hypothesis: all nontrivial zeros of $\zeta$ lie on the critical line $\Re s = 	frac12$. Under this assumption, it is known that
$$ |S(t)| \;\le\;  igl(C_0 + o(1) igr)\, rac{\log t}{\log\log t} \qquad (t	o\infty), $$
with the admissible value $C_0 = 	frac14$.

The bound |S(t)| ≤ (1/4 + o(1)) log t / log log t under RH due to Carneiro–Chandee–Milinovich is still the sharpest known. Consider a soft amorphous solid modeled as a disordered elastic medium subjected to quasistatic shear deformation. Plastic activity in such a material is known to proceed via localized rearrangements (Eshelby events): a small region undergoes a local inelastic strain, producing a long-range anisotropic elastic stress field of Eshelby (quadrupolar) type on the surrounding matrix. Through these elastic interactions, individual Eshelby events can trigger further events, giving rise to plastic avalanches with characteristic size and duration distributions. When plastic activity is spatially uniform, the macroscopic response is ductile; when it concentrates along a narrow region, a shear band forms and the response is brittle.

Develop a quantitative mechanistic theory that explains:
(a) How elastic interactions between Eshelby events (e.g. the Eshelby kernel, its sign-changing angular structure, and its decay) together with structural disorder (local yield-stress distributions, soft spots, structural memory, aging) determine whether successive avalanches remain spatially scattered or organize into a persistent shear band.
(b) Precise criteria — in terms of statistical properties of avalanches (size, shape, spatial correlations, density of marginally stable sites) and of the underlying structural state — for the transition from delocalized plastic flow to localized shear banding.
(c) The role of avalanches as an intermediate spatial-organization scale between isolated Eshelby events and macroscopic shear bands, including whether shear bands can be characterized as a percolation-like, nucleation-like, or instability-driven emergent structure of correlated avalanches.

Provide either a rigorous derivation within an elastoplastic model (lattice or continuum) with Eshelby-type stress redistribution and quenched disorder, or a sharp set of analytical predictions (scaling laws, order parameters, critical exponents) that distinguish the scattered-plasticity regime from the shear-band regime and that can be tested against simulations and experiments.

For an integer $k\ge 2$, let $d_k(n)$ denote the $k$-fold divisor function, i.e. the number of ordered factorizations of $n$ into $k$ positive integer factors (so $d_2(n)$ is the usual divisor function). For a fixed nonzero integer $h$ and a real $x\ge 2$, define the shifted convolution sum
$$D_{k,2}(x,h)\;=\;\sum_{n\le x} d_k(n)\,d_2(n+h).$$
It is known that for every $k\ge 3$ there exists an asymptotic formula
$$D_{k,2}(x,h)\;=\;M_{k,2}(x,h)\;+\;E_{k,2}(x,h),$$
where the main term $M_{k,2}(x,h)$ is a polynomial in $\log x$ of degree $k$ (with coefficients depending on $h$) and $E_{k,2}(x,h)=o(x\,(\log x)^k)$ as $x\to\infty$.

Establish an omega-type lower bound for the error term $E_{k,2}(x,h)=D_{k,2}(x,h)-M_{k,2}(x,h)$ valid for every $k\ge 3$. Concretely, prove the existence of an explicit function $f_k(x)\to\infty$ (depending on $k$) such that
$$E_{k,2}(x,h)\;=\;\Omega\!\bigl(f_k(x)\bigr)$$
as $x\to\infty$, i.e. $\limsup_{x\to\infty}|E_{k,2}(x,h)|/f_k(x)>0$.

Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph. A list assignment for G is a function L that assigns to each vertex v ∈ V a finite set L(v) of allowed colors; L is called a k-list-assignment if |L(v)| = k for every v ∈ V. A proper L-coloring of G is a function f with f(v) ∈ L(v) for every v and f(u) ≠ f(v) whenever uv ∈ E.

An L-packing of size k is a collection (f_1, f_2, …, f_k) of proper L-colorings of G such that for every vertex v ∈ V the values f_1(v), f_2(v), …, f_k(v) are pairwise distinct (i.e., {f_1(v),…,f_k(v)} = L(v) when |L(v)| = k).

The list packing number χ_ℓ^*(G) is defined as the least integer k such that, for every k-list-assignment L of G, an L-packing of size k exists.

A graph G is planar if it admits an embedding in the plane with no edge crossings, and triangle-free if it contains no 3-cycle.

Question: Is it true that χ_ℓ^*(G) ≤ 4 for every triangle-free planar graph G?

$$d_k(n)=\#\{(a_1,\dots,a_k)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^k : a_1a_2\cdots a_k=n\},$$
so that $d(n)=d_2(n)$ is the usual divisor function and $d_3(n)$ is the ternary divisor function. For a real number $\kappa>0$, define the generalized divisor function $d_\kappa(n)$ as the $n$-th Dirichlet coefficient of $\zeta(s)^\kappa$, i.e. via the Dirichlet series
$$\zeta(s)^{\kappa}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{d_\kappa(n)}{n^s}\qquad(\Re s>1),$$
so that $d_\kappa$ is multiplicative with $d_\kappa(p^a)=\binom{\kappa+a-1}{a}$ for primes $p$ and $a\ge 0$.

Establish asymptotic formulas, as $x\to\infty$, for each of the following shifted convolution (additive divisor) sums:

(a) $\displaystyle\sum_{n\le x} d_3(n)\,d_3(n+1)$;

(b) $\displaystyle\sum_{n\le x} d(n)\,d(n+1)\,d(n+2)$;

(c) for every fixed $\kappa\in(0,1)$, $\displaystyle\sum_{n\le x} d_\kappa(n)\,d(n+1)\,d(n+2)$;

(d) for every fixed $\kappa\in(2,3)$, $\displaystyle\sum_{n\le x} d_\kappa(n)\,d_3(n+1)$.

In each case, identify the main term explicitly and obtain a power-saving error term.

Consider a soft amorphous material modeled as a disordered network or particle assembly subjected to quasi-static or finite-rate shear deformation. Assume the material is characterized by:

(i) a spatial distribution of structural heterogeneities, quantified by local order parameters such as local density, coordination number z(x), or local elastic modulus fluctuations;
(ii) a rigidity percolation transition controlled by mean coordination number z relative to the isostatic threshold z_c (e.g. z_c = 2d in d spatial dimensions for central-force networks), which governs the emergence of a system-spanning rigid cluster;
(iii) a stress propagation field σ(x) whose long-range correlations depend on the proximity to the rigidity transition and on the disorder distribution.

Under controlled structural disorder (parameterized, for instance, by the variance of local coordination or local stiffness), determine the relationship between these microscopic descriptors and the macroscopic mode of yielding. Specifically:

(a) Identify a quantitative criterion, in terms of the distance |z − z_c| from rigidity percolation and the amplitude/correlation length of structural heterogeneities, that predicts whether the material yields in a ductile fashion (smooth, spatially diffuse plastic flow) or in a brittle fashion (abrupt, system-spanning shear band formation with a macroscopic stress drop).

(b) Characterize how stress propagation — for example via the Eshelby-like quadrupolar kernel modified by structural disorder — mediates the transition between these two yielding modes.

(c) Determine whether the ductile-to-brittle transition coincides with, precedes, or follows the rigidity percolation transition as disorder is varied.

Consider an amorphous solid (e.g., a soft glassy material, foam, emulsion, colloidal glass, or metallic glass) subjected to an externally applied shear deformation. Two qualitatively different macroscopic responses are observed:

(i) Ductile yielding: as strain is increased, plastic deformation accumulates gradually and the stress-strain curve crosses smoothly from elastic to plastic flow, eventually reaching a steady plastic flow regime (the shear-induced solid-to-liquid transition).

(ii) Brittle yielding: as strain is increased, the material remains nearly elastic until a critical strain at which the stress drops abruptly via a system-spanning shear band, producing a discontinuous macroscopic signature.

The crossover from regime (i) to regime (ii) as a function of the initial preparation (degree of annealing/stability) of the amorphous solid is referred to as the ductile-to-brittle transition (DBT).

Question. Formulate a single non-equilibrium dynamical phase-transition framework that simultaneously describes:
 (a) the ductile-to-brittle transition (as a change in the order/character of the underlying non-equilibrium transition, e.g., from continuous/crossover to discontinuous, possibly terminating at a critical point), and
 (b) the shear-induced solid-to-liquid yielding transition in the ductile regime,
in such a way that both phenomena emerge as different macroscopic manifestations of one common dynamical critical/phase-transition mechanism, despite their qualitatively different macroscopic signatures. Prove (or disprove) that such a unified framework exists, and identify the universality class, order parameter(s), control parameters, and scaling laws that characterize it across the full range of amorphous materials and preparation protocols.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Significant progress has been made toward a unified picture: Ozawa et al. (PNAS 2018) proposed that a random critical point in the universality class of the quasistatically driven random-field Ising model separates brittle (discontinuous, first-order-like) and ductile (smooth crossover) yielding, controlled by the degree of annealing. Subsequent mean-field elastoplastic theories (e.g., Parisi–Procaccia–Lerner-type approaches and Hébraud–Lequeux–based descriptions, 2023–2024) extend this picture beyond RFIM by including elastic long-range interactions and dynamics. However, a fully validated unified non-equilibrium dynamical phase-transition framework simultaneously capturing the DBT and the shear-induced solid-to-liquid yielding transition across all amorphous materials, with established universality class and scaling, is not yet definitively established, and the question is still considered open in the soft-matter physics community.

Choose any subset $S\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,2k\}$ with $|S|=k$, and let $\bar S=\{1,2,\ldots,2k\}\setminus S$. The extended Petersen graph $XP(2n,S)$ has vertex set $V=\mathbb{Z}_n\times\{1,2\}$ and edge set
$$E=\{x_1y_1:d(x,y)\in S\}\cup\{x_2y_2:d(x,y)\in\bar S\}\cup\{x_1x_2:x\in\mathbb{Z}_n\},$$
where $x_i$ denotes $(x,i)$. Recall that the chromatic index $\chi'(G)$ is the minimum number of colors needed for a proper edge-coloring, and by Vizing's theorem $\chi'(G)\in\{\Delta(G),\Delta(G)+1\}$; $G$ is said to be of Class 1 if $\chi'(G)=\Delta(G)$ and Class 2 otherwise.

Prove or disprove: for every $k\geq 1$ and every admissible choice of $S$, the graph $XP(2n,S)$ is of Class 1, with the sole exception of the Petersen graph itself (the case $k=1$, $n=5$, $S=\{2\}$).

Let G be a finite, simple, connected graph. An edge-coloring of G (not necessarily proper) is called rainbow connected if for every pair of distinct vertices u, v of G there exists a u-v path all of whose edges receive pairwise distinct colors. The rainbow connection number rc(G) is the minimum number of colors in a rainbow connected edge-coloring of G. For a graph G of order n, let δ(G) denote the minimum degree.

(a) Does there exist an absolute constant c ≥ 0 such that every non-complete graph G of order n with δ(G) ≥ n/2 + c satisfies rc(G) = 2?

(b) In particular, does δ(G) ≥ n/2 already imply that rc(G) = 2 for every non-complete graph G of order n?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The best known result, due to Caro, Lev, Roditty, Tuza, and Yuster, is that δ(G) ≥ n/2 + log n implies rc(G) = 2 for non-complete graphs, with subsequent refinements involving lower-order logarithmic terms. Removing the logarithmic gap—i.e., obtaining a constant c (or c = 0) such that δ(G) ≥ n/2 + c forces rc(G) = 2—appears to remain unresolved in the literature.

Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph. The maximum degree of G is denoted Δ(G). A proper edge coloring of G with k colors is an assignment of one of k colors to each edge of G such that any two edges sharing a common vertex receive distinct colors. By Vizing's theorem, the chromatic index χ'(G) of G satisfies Δ(G) ≤ χ'(G) ≤ Δ(G) + 1. The graph G is called Class 1 if χ'(G) = Δ(G) and Class 2 if χ'(G) = Δ(G) + 1. A graph G is k-regular if every vertex has degree k, and G is k-edge-connected if |V| ≥ 2 and the removal of fewer than k edges leaves G connected.

Question: Does there exist a 5-edge-connected, 5-regular graph G that is Class 2, i.e., a 5-edge-connected 5-regular graph whose edges cannot be properly colored using only 5 colors?

Let an integrable system of partial differential equations be given, admitting an infinite hierarchy of generalized symmetries (in the sense of Olver), i.e., evolutionary vector fields whose characteristics depend on the dependent variables and finitely many of their derivatives. Such systems also typically admit a finite-dimensional Lie point symmetry algebra (whose invariant reductions are known to yield single-phase exact solutions such as solitary waves, single periodic cnoidal waves, and Painlevé-type self-similar reductions) as well as nonlocal symmetries (e.g., from potential or pseudopotential constructions).

Develop a systematic method that uses genuine generalized (higher-order, local) symmetries — rather than only Lie point symmetries or nonlocal symmetry constraints — to construct exact multi-wave solutions of the system. In particular:

1. Show whether invariance under suitable combinations of generalized local symmetries (or finite linear combinations of higher-order symmetry flows) can be used to characterize and explicitly construct N-soliton solutions for N ≥ 2.

2. Determine whether such generalized-symmetry reductions can produce multi-phase (quasi-periodic) wave solutions, including finite-gap / algebro-geometric solutions, going beyond single periodic cnoidal waves, solitary waves, and Painlevé-type reductions.

3. Provide either a general construction valid for a class of integrable PDEs (such as the KdV, modified KdV, sine-Gordon, or nonlinear Schrödinger hierarchies) or a proof of obstruction explaining why generalized local symmetries alone cannot yield multi-wave exact solutions.

Provide a structural characterization of all subcubic $K_3$-free graphs that are of Class 2. Equivalently, describe all triangle-free graphs $G$ with $\Delta(G) \le 3$ for which $\chi'(G) = 4$.

Consider a dilute dispersion or colloidal gel confined between two solid walls and subjected to a steady simple shear of rate $\dot\gamma$. The system consists of colloidal particles of characteristic size $a$ that aggregate into clusters of characteristic size $\xi(\dot\gamma)$ which may depend on the shear rate, and which together form a multiscale percolated network. At the bounding walls, the aggregates may simultaneously adhere, roll, and slide. Define the wall-slip velocity $v_s$ as the difference between the wall velocity and the extrapolated bulk fluid velocity at the wall, and the slip length $\ell_s = v_s/\dot\gamma$.

Question: Does there exist a generic coarse-grained constitutive framework that predicts $v_s$ (or $\ell_s$) for such dilute dispersions and gels purely in terms of a comparison of well-defined length scales — namely the particle size $a$, the static cluster size $\xi_0$, and the shear-dependent cluster scale $\xi(\dot\gamma)$ — relative to a wall-roughness or wall-interaction length, while consistently accounting for the coexistence of adhesion, rolling, and sliding of aggregates at the walls? If such a framework exists, identify which of these length scales controls the slip behavior in each regime.

A numerical semigroup is a cofinite submonoid $\Gamma \subseteq (\mathbb{N},+)$ containing $0$. Every numerical semigroup admits a unique minimal system of generators $\{n_1 < n_2 < \cdots < n_k\}$; the embedding dimension is $\operatorname{edim}(\Gamma) = k$ and the multiplicity is $\operatorname{mult}(\Gamma) = n_1$. Consider the surjective monoid homomorphism $\varphi : \mathbb{N}^k \to \Gamma$ sending the $i$-th standard basis vector to $n_i$, and let $\sigma = \ker \varphi \subseteq \mathbb{N}^k \times \mathbb{N}^k$ be its kernel congruence. A presentation of $\Gamma$ is a generating set of $\sigma$ as a congruence, and a minimal presentation is one of minimum cardinality; all minimal presentations have the same cardinality, denoted $\rho(\Gamma)$ (the number of relations of $\Gamma$).

For integers $e$ and $m$ with $3 \le e < m$, define
$$R(e,m) = \sup\{\,\rho(\Gamma) \;:\; \Gamma \text{ is a numerical semigroup with } \operatorname{edim}(\Gamma) = e+1 \text{ and } \operatorname{mult}(\Gamma) = m\,\}.$$

Determine $R(e,m)$ as an explicit function of $e$ and $m$.

Let $X$ be an arbitrary nonempty set. For a semigroup $S$, define the following equivalence relations on $S$ (called semigroup conjugacy relations):

(1) $a \sim_o b$ iff there exist $g,h \in S^1$ with $ag = gb$ and $bh = ha$.

(2) $a \sim_p b$ iff there exist $u,v \in S^1$ with $a = uv$ and $b = vu$.

(3) (Defined on epigroups, where each element $a$ has a power $a^n$ lying in a subgroup of $S$, with idempotent $a^\omega$ denoting the identity of that subgroup, and $a^{\omega+1} = a \cdot a^\omega$.) $a \sim_{tr} b$ iff there exist $g, h \in S$ such that $ghg = g$, $hgh = h$, $hg = a^\omega$, $gh = b^\omega$, and $g\, a^{\omega+1}\, h = b^{\omega+1}$.

A semigroup conjugacy relation $\sim$ is called partition-covering if for every partition $\mathcal{P}$ of $X$ there exists a semigroup structure on $X$ whose $\sim$-classes are exactly the blocks of $\mathcal{P}$.

Question: Are each of $\sim_o$, $\sim_p$, and $\sim_{tr}$ partition-covering?

For a numerical semigroup Γ ⊆ ℕ (a cofinite submonoid of (ℕ,+) containing 0), let mult(Γ) denote the multiplicity of Γ (the smallest positive element of Γ), let edim(Γ) denote the embedding dimension of Γ (the cardinality of its unique minimal system of generators), and let ρ(Γ) denote the reduction number of the maximal ideal of the associated local ring k[[Γ]] (equivalently, the least integer n such that (n+1)·mult(Γ) ∈ Γ + n·mult(Γ) in the standard sense used for one-dimensional local rings, i.e., the index from which the Hilbert function of the associated graded ring stabilizes).

For integers e and m with 3 ≤ e < m, define
   R(e,m) = sup { ρ(Γ) : Γ is a numerical semigroup with edim(Γ) = e+1 and mult(Γ) = m }.

Define the combinatorial quantity C(e,m) as follows. Let r be the unique positive integer such that
   C(e+r−1, r−1) ≤ m < C(e+r, r),
where C(a,b) denotes the binomial coefficient "a choose b". Set
   s = m − C(e+r−1, r−1).
Write s in its r-th Macaulay representation
   s = C(k_r, r) + C(k_{r−1}, r−1) + … + C(k_j, j),
with k_r > k_{r−1} > … > k_j ≥ j ≥ 1, and define
   s^{<r>} = C(k_r+1, r+1) + C(k_{r−1}+1, r) + … + C(k_j+1, j+1).
Finally let
   C(e,m) = C(e+r−1, r) + s^{<r>} − s.

It is known that R(e,m) ≤ C(e,m) for all such e,m. Determine exactly the set of pairs (e,m) with 3 ≤ e < m for which equality R(e,m) = C(e,m) holds.

A numerical semigroup is a cofinite subset $\Gamma \subseteq \mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that contains $0$ and is closed under addition. Every numerical semigroup admits a unique minimal system of generators $g_1 < g_2 < \cdots < g_e$ with $\gcd(g_1,\dots,g_e)=1$, and we write $\Gamma = \langle g_1,\dots,g_e\rangle$. The width of $\Gamma$ is defined by
$$\operatorname{width}(\Gamma) := g_e - g_1.$$
Consider the surjective monoid homomorphism $\varphi : \mathbb{N}^e \to \Gamma$ sending the $i$-th standard basis vector to $g_i$. The kernel congruence $\ker\varphi = \{(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}) \in \mathbb{N}^e \times \mathbb{N}^e : \varphi(\mathbf{a}) = \varphi(\mathbf{b})\}$ admits a minimal generating set (a minimal presentation) as a congruence, and all such minimal presentations have the same finite cardinality. Denote this cardinality by $\rho(\Gamma)$, the number of relations in a minimal presentation of $\Gamma$.

For each positive integer $w$, define
$$W(w) := \sup\{\rho(\Gamma) : \Gamma \text{ is a numerical semigroup with } \operatorname{width}(\Gamma) = w\}.$$

Determine $W(w)$ as a function of $w$ (in particular, decide whether it is finite, and if so give a closed-form expression or sharp bounds).

Let $\Gamma \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a numerical semigroup, that is, a cofinite submonoid of $(\mathbb{N},+)$ containing $0$. Write the (unique) minimal system of generators of $\Gamma$ as $n_1 < n_2 < \cdots < n_e$, and define the width of $\Gamma$ by
$$\mathrm{width}(\Gamma) = n_e - n_1.$$
Fix a field $k$, and let $k[\Gamma] = k[t^{n_1}, \ldots, t^{n_e}] \subseteq k[t]$ be the associated numerical semigroup ring, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m} = (t^{n_1}, \ldots, t^{n_e})$. Let
$$G_\Gamma = \mathrm{gr}_{\mathfrak{m}}(k[\Gamma]) = \bigoplus_{i \ge 0} \mathfrak{m}^i / \mathfrak{m}^{i+1}$$
be the associated graded ring (the coordinate ring of the tangent cone), regarded as a standard graded $k$-algebra. Let $b_1(G_\Gamma)$ denote the first Betti number of $G_\Gamma$ as a graded module over a polynomial ring surjecting onto $G_\Gamma$, i.e. the minimal number of generators of the defining ideal of $G_\Gamma$.

Prove or disprove: for every numerical semigroup $\Gamma$,
$$b_1(G_\Gamma) \;\le\; \binom{\mathrm{width}(\Gamma)+1}{2}.$$

Consider a soft glassy material (for example a colloidal gel) modeled as a disordered network of interacting mesoscopic constituents whose configuration is described by a microstructural tensor M(t) (such as the pair-correlation anisotropy or fabric tensor), and whose mechanical state is described by a stress tensor σ(t) obeying a constitutive relation that couples microstructure, local elasticity, and plastic relaxation events with a distribution of local relaxation times.

The sample is subjected to a steady simple shear of rate γ̇ for sufficiently long times that a non-equilibrium steady state is reached with anisotropic microstructure M_ss and stress σ_ss. At time t = 0 the shear is brought abruptly to zero (flow cessation) and the system is allowed to age while remaining mechanically isolated (zero strain boundary condition). After cessation one observes:
  (i) a frozen-in distorted microstructure M_∞ = lim_{t→∞} M(t) that differs from the isotropic quiescent state;
  (ii) a transient field of local stresses σ_loc(x,t) whose statistics relax over a broad spectrum of time scales;
  (iii) a non-vanishing macroscopic residual stress σ_res = lim_{t→∞} ⟨σ(t)⟩.

Problem. Establish a quantitative relationship, derived from a mesoscopic or continuum model of soft glassy/gel rheology, that links these three quantities. Specifically:
  (a) Express σ_res as a functional of the prior shear history {γ̇(t) : t < 0} and of the inherited anisotropy M_∞.
  (b) Derive the spectrum of local stress relaxation times after cessation from the structural anisotropy and characterize how heterogeneity in local relaxation produces the residual macroscopic stress.
  (c) Determine how, for gel-like networks with attractive interactions, the magnitude and sign of σ_res depend on the pre-cessation Weissenberg number and on the network connectivity, and identify the conditions under which σ_res vanishes despite M_∞ remaining anisotropic.

Background and definitions. A semigroup conjugacy is a function ∼ that assigns to each semigroup S an equivalence relation ∼_S on S, in such a way that ∼ generalizes the usual notion of conjugacy in groups (i.e., when S is a group, ∼_S coincides with the relation a ∼ b iff there exists g in S with b = g^{-1} a g). Many such semigroup-conjugacy relations have been studied in the literature; one example is the relation ∼_u defined on a monoid M by a ∼_u b iff there exists a unit g of M with b = g^{-1} a g.

Given a semigroup conjugacy ∼ and a semigroup S, the ∼-conjugacy classes of S form a partition of S. We say that ∼ is partition-covering if for every nonempty set X and every partition P of X, there exists a semigroup S with underlying set X such that the partition of S into ∼_S-classes is exactly P.

Problem. Does there exist a semigroup conjugacy ∼ that fails to be partition-covering, i.e., such that for some set X there is a partition P of X which cannot be realized as the partition of any semigroup structure on X into ∼-conjugacy classes?

Let $S$ be a semigroup. A binary relation $\sim$ on $S$ is called a semigroup conjugacy relation if it is an equivalence relation that, in the case $S$ is a group, reduces to ordinary group conjugacy, and that satisfies the standard structural axioms expected of a conjugacy notion on semigroups (in particular it agrees with group conjugacy on every subgroup of $S$).

Define the following two relations on $S$:

(1) Group-style conjugacy $\sim_g$: $a \sim_g b$ iff $a$ and $b$ lie in a common subgroup $H \le S$ and are conjugate in $H$ in the usual group-theoretic sense.

(2) Unit conjugacy $\sim_u$: $a \sim_u b$ iff there exists a unit $u \in S$ (i.e., an invertible element of the monoid generated by $S$, or more precisely an element of the group of units when $S$ is a monoid) such that $u^{-1} a u = b$ and $u b u^{-1} = a$.

One always has $\sim_g \subseteq \sim_u$.

Question: Is $\sim_u$ the smallest semigroup conjugacy relation strictly larger than $\sim_g$? Equivalently, must every semigroup conjugacy relation $\sim$ on $S$ with $\sim \ne \sim_g$ satisfy $\sim_u \subseteq \sim$?

2. Primary conjugacy: define $a\sim_p b$ iff there exist $u,v\in S^1$ with $a=uv$ and $b=vu$. Let $\sim_{p^*}$ denote the transitive closure of $\sim_p$ (it is already reflexive and symmetric).

3. Epigroup conjugacy $\sim_{\mathrm{tr}}$: an element $a\in S$ is called a group-bound (epigroup) element if some power $a^n$ lies in a subgroup of $S$; in that case the smallest such subgroup contains a unique idempotent $a^\omega$ and one defines $a^{\omega-1}$ to be the inverse of $a\cdot a^\omega$ in that subgroup, and writes $a^{\omega+k}=a^\omega a^k$ for $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ (when defined). For epigroup elements $a,b\in S$, declare $a\sim_{\mathrm{tr}} b$ iff there exist $g,h\in S^1$ such that $b=g\,a\,h$ and $a=h\,b\,g$, with the additional condition $g\,h\,a^\omega = a^\omega$ and $h\,g\,b^\omega=b^\omega$ (the standard "trace" / epigroup conjugacy relation extending Otto's conjugacy from monoids), and extend $\sim_{\mathrm{tr}}$ to all of $S$ in the usual way so that it becomes an equivalence relation.

Problem. Determine whether, for every semigroup $S$, the inclusion
$$\sim_{\mathrm{tr}}\;\cap\;\mathcal{H}\;\subseteq\;\sim_{p^*}$$
holds. Equivalently, must every pair of $\mathcal{H}$-related elements that are $\sim_{\mathrm{tr}}$-conjugate also be related by some finite chain of primary conjugations $a=c_0\sim_p c_1\sim_p\cdots\sim_p c_n=b$?

representations.normalized:
A numerical semigroup is a subset $\Gamma \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$. Let $G(\Gamma) = \{n_1 < n_2 < \cdots < n_e\}$ denote the unique minimal system of generators of $\Gamma$, and define the width of $\Gamma$ by
$$\mathrm{width}(\Gamma) = n_e - n_1.$$
Fix a field $k$ and consider the local numerical semigroup ring
$$R_\Gamma = k[\![t^{n_1}, t^{n_2}, \ldots, t^{n_e}]\!] \subseteq k[\![t]\!].$$
Viewing $R_\Gamma$ as a quotient of the local polynomial ring $S = k[\![x_1, \ldots, x_e]\!]$ via $x_j \mapsto t^{n_j}$, let $b_i(R_\Gamma) = \dim_k \mathrm{Tor}_i^S(R_\Gamma, k)$ denote the $i$-th Betti number of $R_\Gamma$.

Question: Is it true that for every numerical semigroup $\Gamma$ and every integer $i > 1$,
$$b_i(R_\Gamma) \;\leq\; \binom{\mathrm{width}(\Gamma) + 1}{i+1}\,?$$

Let $S$ be a semigroup. Define the following equivalence relations on $S$:

(1) Subgroup conjugacy $\sim_g$: elements $a,b\in S$ satisfy $a\sim_g b$ if there exist a subgroup $G$ of $S$ (i.e., a subsemigroup of $S$ that is a group) and an element $g\in G$ such that $a,b\in G$ and $b=g^{-1}ag$ (inverse taken in $G$).

(2) Unit conjugacy $\sim_u$: let $U(S)$ denote the group of units of $S$ (which exists when $S$ has an identity; otherwise adjoin one). Then $a\sim_u b$ if there exists $u\in U(S)$ with $b=u^{-1}au$.

(3) Green's relation $\mathcal H$: defined by $a\mathcal H b$ iff $a$ and $b$ generate the same principal left ideal and the same principal right ideal in $S^1$.

Question: Is it true that for every semigroup $S$ with $|S|<13$, the relations $\sim_u \cap\, \mathcal H$ and $\sim_g$ coincide on $S$?
