Let $n \ge 1$ and let $W$ be an $n \times n$ matrix drawn from the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (i.e., $W$ is symmetric with $W_{ii} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,2/n)$ and $W_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1/n)$ for $i < j$, all independent). Fix $\beta > 0$ and an external field vector $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and define the Gibbs measure on the hypercube $\{-1,+1\}^n$ by
$$\mu(\sigma) \;=\; \frac{1}{Z}\exp\!\Big(\tfrac{\beta}{2}\,\langle \sigma, W\sigma\rangle + \langle h,\sigma\rangle\Big),$$
where $Z$ is the normalizing partition function. The (single-site) Glauber dynamics is the discrete-time Markov chain on $\{-1,+1\}^n$ that at each step selects a coordinate $i \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$ uniformly at random and resamples $\sigma_i$ from its conditional law under $\mu$ given the remaining coordinates; this chain is reversible with respect to $\mu$.

The replica-symmetry-breaking threshold of the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model is $\beta^* = 1$.

Question: Is it true that for every $\beta < 1$ and for every external field $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the mixing time of Glauber dynamics for $\mu$ is bounded by a polynomial in $n$ (with high probability over $W$ as $n \to \infty$)?

The problem is open. The best known polynomial mixing-time bound for Glauber dynamics on the SK model holds only up to $\beta < 0.295$ (Anari–Koehler–Vuong, 2024). Setup. Let M be a smooth manifold and let L: TM → TM be a (1,1)-tensor field whose Nijenhuis torsion

  N_L(X,Y) := L^2[X,Y] − L[LX,Y] − L[X,LY] + [LX,LY]

vanishes identically; such an L is called a Nijenhuis operator. A function f ∈ C^∞(M) is called a conservation law of L if the 1-form L^* df is closed, i.e. d(L^* df) = 0. Given a Nijenhuis operator L, denote by K(L) the (real) vector space

  K(L) := { K: TM → TM (1,1)-tensor : N_{L+tK} ≡ 0 for all t ∈ ℝ, i.e. K is Nijenhuis-compatible with L },

equivalently the space of operators K such that L and K have vanishing mutual Nijenhuis torsion. For a fixed Nijenhuis operator V ∈ K(V) (so that V itself plays the role of the base element and K(V) is the space of operators compatible with V), one says that V is a conservation law for K ∈ K(V) in the sense that the trace coefficients of V provide closed 1-forms under K^*.

An element K ∈ K(V) is called Benenti-type if it is generated by V in a polynomial / standard fashion (so that conservation laws are inherited from V in a controlled way). Call K ∈ K(V) generically bad (non-Benenti) if at a generic point of M the algebraic type of K does not match the structure produced by Benenti-type elements of K(V), so that the standard mechanism for producing conservation laws from V fails.

Problem. Let V be a Nijenhuis operator on M and let K ∈ K(V) be a non-Benenti, generically bad element. It is known that V is a conservation law for K. Determine whether V is the only conservation law of K (up to the obvious functional dependencies), or whether K admits additional, functionally independent conservation laws. In the latter case, give a description of the space of all conservation laws of such a K — for instance, by characterising their construction, their functional dimension, or their dependence on V and on the algebraic invariants of K.

Let $\Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a compact embedded surface with non-empty boundary, having constant mean curvature $H \neq 0$ (a CMC surface), and assume that the boundary $\partial \Sigma = C$ is a closed Jordan curve lying in a plane $\Pi \subset \mathbb{R}^3$. The plane $\Pi$ divides $\mathbb{R}^3$ into two closed half-spaces $\Pi^+$ and $\Pi^-$. One says that $\Sigma$ lies on one side of $\Pi$ if $\Sigma \subset \Pi^+$ or $\Sigma \subset \Pi^-$.

(a) Determine geometric or topological hypotheses on the boundary curve $C$ (and possibly on $\Sigma$ near $C$, such as transversality conditions, contact-angle conditions with $\Pi$, or curvature/length conditions on $C$) that are sufficient to guarantee that every such compact embedded CMC surface $\Sigma$ spanning $C$ is contained entirely in one of the closed half-spaces determined by $\Pi$.

(b) Under the additional assumption that $C$ is a convex planar curve (i.e., $C$ bounds a convex region in $\Pi$), determine what further conclusions can be drawn about $\Sigma$: in particular, whether $\Sigma$ must be a topological disk, whether $\Sigma$ inherits the symmetries of $C$, and whether $\Sigma$ must be a graph over the planar domain bounded by $C$ or a spherical cap when $C$ is a circle.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general problem of identifying sharp boundary hypotheses ensuring one-sidedness of compact embedded CMC surfaces with planar boundary remains an active research topic. Partial results exist: when the boundary is a circle and the surface lies on one side, it is a spherical cap (Brito-Earp-Meeks-Rosenberg and others); locally convex CMC hypersurfaces with strictly convex planar boundary lie in a half-space; recent work (e.g. 2024 paper on Special Weingarten surfaces with planar convex boundary) extends some conclusions, but a complete characterization of sufficient boundary conditions is not established.

Consider the Euclidean Lie algebra $\mathfrak{e}(n+1) = \mathfrak{so}(n+1) \oplus \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, with elements written as pairs $(M,x)$ where $M \in \mathfrak{so}(n+1)$ is a skew-symmetric $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ matrix and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. Equip $\mathfrak{e}(n+1)^*$ with its standard linear (Lie–Poisson) bracket. Consider Hamiltonian systems of the form
$$H(M,x) \;=\; \operatorname{tr}(M^2) + V(x),$$
admitting a maximal collection of functionally independent first integrals (i.e. a superintegrable system) of the form
$$F_i(M,x) \;=\; \operatorname{tr}\bigl(C_i(M)\,M\bigr) + V_i(x), \qquad i = 1, 2, \ldots,$$
where each $C_i : \mathfrak{so}(n+1) \to \mathfrak{so}(n+1)$ is a symmetric linear operator (with respect to the trace form $\langle A,B\rangle = -\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}(AB)$) and the $V_i : \mathbb{R}^{n+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ are smooth potentials.

Problem: For each known superintegrable system on a constant-curvature space (sphere or Euclidean space) of dimension $n$ that can be transported to $\mathfrak{e}(n+1)$ in this manner, explicitly describe the family of symmetric operators $\{C_i\}$ on $\mathfrak{so}(n+1)$ together with the corresponding potentials $V$, $V_i$. Identify the algebraic structure (e.g. commutation relations, joint diagonalizability, dependence on auxiliary parameters) of the collection $\{C_i\}$ in these examples, and characterize which collections of symmetric operators $C_i : \mathfrak{so}(n+1) \to \mathfrak{so}(n+1)$ can arise from a superintegrable system of the above form.

Let $\Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a compact embedded surface of constant mean curvature with boundary $\partial \Sigma = C$, and assume that $\Sigma$ lies entirely on one side of $P$. Suppose further that there is a neighborhood $U$ of $C$ in $\Sigma$ such that $U$ is a vertical graph over a subset of $P \setminus D$ (i.e., $\Sigma$ is a graph on $P\setminus D$ near $C$).

Must $\Sigma$ be a bigraph in the following sense: does there exist a planar domain $\Omega \subset P$ with $D \subset \Omega$ such that $\Sigma = \Sigma_1 \cup \Sigma_2$, where $\Sigma_1$ is a vertical graph over $D$, and $\Sigma_2$ is an annulus that is a vertical graph over $\Omega \setminus D$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is listed as an open problem in a recent compilation of open problems on constant mean curvature surfaces with convex planar boundary. Web searches did not surface a published resolution; related results address existence of CMC graphs over convex planar domains but do not resolve the bigraph structure question near the boundary.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold equipped with a torsion-free affine connection $\nabla$. Two torsion-free connections $\nabla$ and $\widetilde{\nabla}$ on $M$ are said to be projectively equivalent if they share the same unparametrized geodesics; equivalently, there exists a 1-form $\omega$ on $M$ such that
$$\widetilde{\nabla}_X Y = \nabla_X Y + \omega(X)Y + \omega(Y)X$$
for all vector fields $X, Y$. A projective structure on $M$ is an equivalence class of such connections. A geometric tensor field of projective weight $w$ is a section of an appropriate density-twisted tensor bundle whose transformation rule under a change of projectively equivalent connections is governed by $\omega$ in the standard way.

For each integer $k \geq 1$, the "geometric Poisson structure of order $k$" on $M$ associated to a (pseudo-)Riemannian metric (or more generally to suitable geometric data) is a Poisson bracket on a function space on $M$ (in the formal/Hamiltonian formalism of hydrodynamic-type and higher-order systems) whose leading symbol in local coordinates is given by a contravariant tensor $g^{ij}$ accompanied by Christoffel-like coefficients, and which generalizes the Dubrovin–Novikov bracket (the case $k=1$).

Problem. Prove or disprove the following two assertions:

(a) For every integer $k > 1$, the geometric Poisson structure of order $k$ is projectively invariant, in the sense that it depends only on the projective class of the underlying connection.

(b) The leading coefficient $g^{ij}$ of every such geometric Poisson structure of order $k > 1$ admits an interpretation as a projectively invariant weighted tensor field of the appropriate projective weight.

Let $\Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a compact, smooth, immersed surface with boundary $\partial\Sigma$, and assume that $\Sigma$ has constant mean curvature $H$ (with respect to a chosen unit normal). Suppose that $\partial\Sigma$ is a round circle in some plane of $\mathbb{R}^3$.

Call $\Sigma$ stable if the second variation of the area functional is non-negative for every smooth normal variation of $\Sigma$ that fixes $\partial\Sigma$ pointwise and preserves the (signed) enclosed volume; equivalently, for every $f \in C^\infty(\Sigma)$ with $f|_{\partial\Sigma} = 0$ and $\int_\Sigma f\,dA = 0$,
$$ -\int_\Sigma f\,(\Delta_\Sigma f + |A|^2 f)\,dA \;\ge\; 0, $$
where $\Delta_\Sigma$ is the Laplace–Beltrami operator and $|A|^2$ is the squared norm of the second fundamental form of $\Sigma$.

Question: Must $\Sigma$ be either a flat planar disk bounded by the circle (when $H = 0$) or a spherical cap bounded by the circle (when $H \neq 0$)?

A constant-mean-curvature (CMC) surface in Euclidean 3-space $\mathbb{R}^3$ is an immersed surface $\Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ whose mean curvature $H$ is a nonzero constant. Kapouleas constructed, by a singular-perturbation / gluing technique, families of compact immersed (generally non-embedded, non-rotational) CMC surfaces of high genus whose boundary is a single round circle lying in a plane, obtained by desingularizing configurations of Delaunay unduloid pieces and spherical pieces joined along small catenoidal necks.

Task: Produce explicit numerical visualizations (i.e., computed triangulated or parametrically rendered pictures) of these Kapouleas CMC surfaces with circular boundary. Concretely, for representative members of the family (varying genus and the combinatorial data of the underlying graph of Delaunay/sphere pieces), numerically solve the CMC boundary value problem
$$ H(\Sigma) \equiv 1, \qquad \partial \Sigma = S^1 \subset \{z = 0\}, $$
and render the resulting surfaces, exhibiting their geometric features (necks, unduloidal segments, near-spherical bubbles, lack of rotational symmetry).

Let $C \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a simple closed curve of length $L$ contained in a plane $P$, and let $D \subset P$ denote the bounded planar domain whose boundary is $C$, with area $|D|$. An $H$-surface bounded by $C$ is a compact, connected, oriented immersed surface $\Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ with constant mean curvature equal to $H$ whose boundary $\partial \Sigma$ equals $C$. A standard flux/area argument shows that if such an $H$-surface exists, then $|H| \le L/(2|D|)$.

(a) Prove or disprove: for every $H \in [0,\, L/(2|D|)]$ there exists an $H$-surface bounded by $C$.

(b) Resolve the same question under the additional assumption that $C$ is a convex planar curve.

(c) Resolve the same question in the special case that $C$ is an ellipse.

Let $H\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$. An $H$-surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is a smooth compact orientable immersed surface $\Sigma\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ (possibly with boundary) whose mean curvature is identically equal to the constant $H$. A slab of width $w>0$ is a region $S_w=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3 : a\le z\le a+w\}$ between two parallel planes at distance $w$. A spherical cap is a compact piece of a round sphere of radius $1/|H|$ bounded by a circle; it is called a small spherical cap if it is contained in a closed hemisphere of that sphere (equivalently, if its boundary circle is a great circle or smaller and the cap lies on one side).

Let $\Sigma$ be a compact $H$-surface whose boundary $\partial\Sigma$ is a round circle $S^1(r)\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ of radius $r>0$ lying in some plane. Suppose $\Sigma$ is contained in a slab $S_w$ of width $w>0$.

(a) If $|H|<\tfrac{2}{w}$, must $\Sigma$ be a spherical cap?

(b) If the bound $|H|<\tfrac{2}{w}$ is replaced by $|H|< w\cdot\tfrac{1}{w}=1$ (equivalently, by the corresponding sharper threshold $w\!\cdot\!(1/w)$ in place of $2/w$), must $\Sigma$ be a small spherical cap?

Let H>0. An H-surface in Euclidean three-space ℝ³ is a smooth, immersed, oriented surface whose mean curvature is constantly equal to H. A slab of width w in ℝ³ is the closed region between two parallel planes at distance w apart. The round sphere of radius 1/H is a closed (compact, without boundary) H-surface that fits inside the closure of any slab of width 2/H whose bounding planes are tangent to it.

Prove or disprove: the round sphere of radius 1/H is the only closed H-surface contained in the closure of some slab of width 2/H in ℝ³.

representations.normalized:
Let $C \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a non-circular, closed, smooth, convex planar curve lying in a plane $P \subset \mathbb{R}^3$. A compact embedded constant-mean-curvature (cmc) disk $\Sigma$ spanning $C$ is a compact embedded surface of disk type with $\partial\Sigma = C$ and constant scalar mean curvature, and its (algebraic) volume $V > 0$ is the volume enclosed between $\Sigma$ and the planar disk in $P$ bounded by $C$.

Prove that there exists a constant $V_C > 0$, depending only on $C$, with the following threshold behavior. For every compact embedded cmc disk $\Sigma$ spanning $C$ with volume $V > 0$:

(1) If $V \le V_C$, then $\Sigma$ lies entirely in one of the two closed half-spaces determined by $P$.

(2) If $V = V_C$, then $\Sigma$ is tangent to $P$ at the points of $C$ where the curvature of $C$ attains its minimum.

(3) If $V > V_C$, then $\Sigma$ contains points strictly on both sides of $P$.

Let $C_1, C_2 \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be two simple, planar, convex closed curves lying in a common plane and bounding disjoint interior regions. A surface $\Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ is said to be a constant-mean-curvature (CMC) surface with boundary $C_1 \cup C_2$ if $\Sigma$ is a (sufficiently regular) compact surface with boundary equal to $C_1 \cup C_2$ and with mean curvature constant on $\Sigma$. Define the enclosed volume $V$ of such a $\Sigma$ in the standard way (e.g., as the algebraic volume bounded by $\Sigma$ together with the planar regions enclosed by $C_1$ and $C_2$).

Question: Does there exist a constant $V_0 > 0$ (depending on $C_1$ and $C_2$) such that every CMC surface $\Sigma$ with boundary $C_1 \cup C_2$ and volume $V < V_0$ is disconnected?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is posed as an open question concerning sharp geometric solvability criteria for the constant mean curvature Dirichlet equation over bounded convex planar domains. Known results provide existence under stronger conditions (e.g. $|\Omega|H^2 < \pi/2$ via cylinder barriers and Perron methods), and recent works (e.g. on sharp solvability criteria for mean curvature type Dirichlet problems) treat related but not identical thresholds. No source was found establishing existence under the precise hypotheses $|\Omega|H^2<\pi$, $LH^2<2\pi$, or $\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)<2/|H|$, so the problem appears still open.

representations.normalized:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded convex domain, and let $H>0$ be a constant. Consider the constant–mean–curvature Dirichlet problem
$$\operatorname{div}\!\left(\frac{Du}{\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}}\right) = 2H \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \quad \text{on } \partial\Omega,$$
whose solution $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline{\Omega})$ describes a graph of constant mean curvature $H$ spanning $\partial\Omega$. It is known that the level sets $\{u = c\}$ need not all be convex (an example due to X.-J. Wang exhibits non-convex level curves at heights related to $1/(4H)$).

(a) Give a quantitative description, in terms of the value $H$ (and geometric data of $\Omega$), of the distribution of those level curves $\{u = c\}$ that are convex: determine the range of heights $c \in [0, \max_{\overline{\Omega}} u]$ for which $\{u = c\}$ is a convex curve, and characterize the threshold(s) at which convexity is lost.

(b) Extend Wang's counterexample (which produces non-convex level curves of a CMC graph over a bounded convex domain) to the setting where $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is an unbounded convex domain, or show that no such extension is possible.

$$\operatorname{div}\!\left(\frac{Du}{\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}}\right) = 2H \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \quad \text{on } \partial\Omega,$$
whose solution $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline{\Omega})$ describes a graph of constant mean curvature $H$ spanning $\partial\Omega$. It is known that the level sets $\{u = c\}$ need not all be convex (an example due to X.-J. Wang exhibits non-convex level curves at heights related to $1/(4H)$).

(a) Give a quantitative description, in terms of the value $H$ (and geometric data of $\Omega$), of the distribution of those level curves $\{u = c\}$ that are convex: determine the range of heights $c \in [0, \max_{\overline{\Omega}} u]$ for which $\{u = c\}$ is a convex curve, and characterize the threshold(s) at which convexity is lost.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Wang's counterexample is known: solutions to the CMC Dirichlet problem on bounded convex planar domains can have non-convex level sets, with non-convexity appearing near height $1/(4|H|)$. Subsequent work (e.g., Jost–Ma–Ou and related papers on level curves of CMC graphs over convex domains) studies partial convexity results, but a complete quantitative control of the distribution of convex level curves in terms of $H$, as well as an extension of Wang's example to unbounded convex domains, does not appear to have been fully resolved in the literature.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded convex domain, and let $H$ be a nonzero real constant. Consider a function $u \in C^2(\overline{\Omega})$ that solves the constant mean curvature equation
$$\operatorname{div}\!\left(\frac{\nabla u}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla u|^2}}\right) = 2H \quad \text{in } \Omega,$$
with planar boundary, i.e. $u \equiv 0$ on $\partial\Omega$ (so the boundary curve of the graph lies in the plane $\{z=0\}$). Let $\Sigma = \{(x,y,u(x,y)) : (x,y) \in \overline{\Omega}\} \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ denote the graph of $u$, and let $K$ denote its Gauss curvature.

Determine geometric conditions on $\Omega$ (and possibly on $H$) that ensure $\Sigma$ is a convex surface, in the sense that $K > 0$ everywhere on $\Sigma$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general problem of identifying conditions on a bounded convex planar domain $\Omega$ that guarantee a CMC graph over $\Omega$ with planar boundary is convex appears to remain open in the Euclidean setting. Related convexity results are known in the Lorentz–Minkowski space (e.g., for spacelike CMC surfaces with pseudo-elliptic planar boundary), and counterexamples are known showing that strict convexity of the boundary alone is not sufficient. No comprehensive sufficient condition for the Euclidean CMC Dirichlet problem appears to be established.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The total positivity of the Eulerian triangle is a longstanding conjecture of Brenti (1996). Recent work (including a December 2024 paper developing planar network techniques for total positivity of combinatorial matrices) explicitly notes that this conjecture remains open, while proving total positivity for related matrices such as reversed Stirling triangles of the second kind, Lah numbers, and derangements.

$$2^*(s)=\frac{2(N-s)}{N-2}.$$
Fix parameters
$$0\leq s_1<s_2<2,\qquad 2<p\leq 2^*(s_1),\qquad 2<q\leq 2^*(s_2),\qquad \lambda>0,$$
and consider the Dirichlet problem
$$\begin{cases}-\Delta u=-\lambda\,|x|^{-s_1}\,|u|^{p-2}u+|x|^{-s_2}\,|u|^{q-2}u & \text{in }\Omega,\\ u=0 & \text{on }\partial\Omega.\end{cases}$$
Determine whether this problem admits a positive (classical or weak $H^1_0(\Omega)$) solution in the regime $s_1<s_2$ and $\lambda>0$. In particular, settle the case $p>q$, and most notably the critical case $p>q=2^*(s_2)$.

Let $F_m$ denote the free group of rank $m$ and let $T_{2m}$ denote its Cayley graph with respect to a free generating set, i.e. the regular $2m$-valent tree, equipped with the standard simplicial metric making it a CAT(0) (in fact, CAT($-\infty$)) space. Let $G = F_m \times \mathbb{Z}^n$ act on the CAT(0) space $X = T_{2m} \times \mathbb{R}^n$ by the product of the standard action of $F_m$ on $T_{2m}$ and the action of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ by translations. A subgroup $H \le G$ is called quasiconvex if there exists a constant $K \ge 0$ such that every geodesic in the Cayley graph of $G$ (with respect to some/any finite generating set) between two elements of $H$ stays in the $K$-neighbourhood of $H$. Given a basepoint $x_0 \in X$, let $\mathrm{Hull}(H x_0)$ denote the convex hull in $X$ of the orbit $H x_0$.

Question: Is it true that for every quasiconvex subgroup $H$ of $G = F_m \times \mathbb{Z}^n$ and every basepoint $x_0 \in X$, the action of $H$ on $\mathrm{Hull}(H x_0)$ is cocompact (so that, in particular, $H$ itself is a CAT(0) group)?

A finitely generated group $G$ is called a CAT(0) group if there exists a complete CAT(0) metric space $X$ on which $G$ acts properly discontinuously, cocompactly, and by isometries (a geometric action). Given a finitely generated group $G$ with a finite generating set $S$ and word metric $d_S$, a subgroup $H \le G$ is said to be quasiconvex (with respect to $S$) if there exists a constant $K \ge 0$ such that every geodesic in the Cayley graph $\mathrm{Cay}(G,S)$ between two points of $H$ stays within the $K$-neighborhood of $H$.

Question: Suppose $G$ is a CAT(0) group and $H \le G$ is a quasiconvex subgroup of $G$. Must $H$ itself be a CAT(0) group? Equivalently, must there exist a complete CAT(0) space on which $H$ acts geometrically?

Let $G$ be a virtually polycyclic group, i.e., a group that contains a polycyclic subgroup of finite index (recall that a group is polycyclic if it admits a finite subnormal series with cyclic factors). Equip $G$ with a proper left-invariant metric $d$ (any two such metrics on a finitely generated group are quasi-isometric, and properness means that balls are finite). For a subgroup $H \le G$ and two left cosets $aH, bH$, define their distance by $d(aH, bH) = \inf\{d(x,y) : x \in aH,\ y \in bH\}$.

A subgroup $H \le G$ is said to have bounded packing in $G$ if for every $r > 0$ there exists a positive integer $N = N(G,H,r)$ such that for any collection $g_1 H, g_2 H, \ldots, g_N H$ of $N$ distinct left cosets of $H$ in $G$, there exist indices $i \ne j$ with $d(g_i H, g_j H) \ge r$.

Prove or disprove: every subgroup $H$ of every virtually polycyclic group $G$ has bounded packing in $G$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The Hruska–Wise conjecture that every subgroup of a virtually polycyclic group has bounded packing has been established affirmatively in recent work. Partial results (e.g., for polycyclic groups of Hirsch length ≤ 3, and for nilpotent-by-polycyclic groups) appeared earlier, and the full conjecture is reported as settled. Related counterexamples are known for general solvable groups (derived length 3), showing the result does not extend beyond the polycyclic setting.

The question (in this full generality, for all subgroups of all solvable groups) has a negative answer. A finitely generated solvable group of derived length 3 has been constructed that contains a finitely generated subgroup failing bounded packing, refuting the broad version of the Hruska–Wise question. Consider the setting of coherent diffraction imaging (CDI) and ptychography. An unknown complex-valued object $O:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{C}$ is illuminated by one or more coherent probes, and the detector records only the squared magnitudes of the resulting far-field (Fraunhofer) diffraction patterns. In CDI a single magnitude measurement $I(\mathbf{q})=|\mathcal{F}\{P\cdot O\}(\mathbf{q})|^2$ is collected, where $\mathcal{F}$ denotes the Fourier transform and $P$ is the illumination function; in ptychography a set of such measurements $\{I_j(\mathbf{q})=|\mathcal{F}\{P(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_j)\cdot O(\mathbf{r})\}(\mathbf{q})|^2\}_j$ is collected over overlapping probe positions $\{\mathbf{r}_j\}$.

Define the "complexity" of the object $O$ as a quantitative measure of its structural intricacy (for example, its information content, sparsity in some basis, total variation, effective number of degrees of freedom, or any other statistic capturing how difficult $O$ is to represent or reconstruct).

Problem: Identify or design a statistic $\mathcal{C}$ that takes as input only the magnitude-only measurements $\{I_j\}$ (i.e., is computable directly from the diffraction data, before any phase-retrieval reconstruction of $O$) and provides a reliable estimate of the complexity of the underlying object $O$. Equivalently, determine which existing complexity statistics defined on objects can be approximated, or which new statistics can be defined, purely from the recorded intensities, and analyze their relationship to standard object-domain complexity measures.

Consider the discrete phase retrieval problem in the following setting. Let x ∈ C^N be an unknown signal (the "object"), and let A : C^N → R^M denote a measurement map of the form (A x)_k = |⟨a_k, x⟩|^2 for k = 1, …, M, where {a_k} is a fixed family of measurement vectors (e.g., Fourier samples possibly combined with masks or oversampling). Phase retrieval is the inverse problem of reconstructing x (up to a global phase) from y = A x. In practice, both the number of measurements required for unique/stable reconstruction and the convergence speed of iterative reconstruction algorithms (e.g., Gerchberg–Saxton, hybrid input–output, relaxed reflection methods, Wirtinger flow) depend strongly on structural properties of x such as its support geometry, edge regularity, and the homogeneity of its phase.

Define a notion of "object complexity" as any quantitative functional C(x) (or, ideally, a functional C(y) computable directly from the measurements y) intended to predict the intrinsic difficulty of reconstructing x from y, in terms of:
 (i) the minimal number M of measurements needed for injectivity or for stable inversion with prescribed noise tolerance, and
 (ii) the convergence rate and basin of attraction of standard iterative phase retrieval algorithms.

The problem is to develop a rigorous theory of object complexity for phase retrieval. Specifically:

1. Identify and prove which structural features of x (support size and shape, smoothness/sharpness of edges, sparsity, phase variation/inhomogeneity, dynamic range) provably control sample complexity and algorithmic convergence, and quantify these dependencies with matching upper and lower bounds.

2. Construct a complexity measure C that can be estimated from the measurements y alone (without knowledge of x), prove that C is a faithful predictor of reconstruction difficulty (in the senses (i) and (ii) above), and establish concentration or stability estimates for C under measurement noise.

3. Determine, in particular, how non-uniform phase fields and smooth (as opposed to sharp) object boundaries provably degrade the convergence of standard iterative algorithms, and characterize the precise dependence of convergence rates on such complexity parameters.

State which of the items 1–3 admit currently known rigorous theorems and which remain open.

Consider the phase retrieval problem: given measurements $y_k = |\langle a_k, x\rangle|^2$ for $k=1,\ldots,m$, where $\{a_k\}\subset\mathbb{C}^n$ is a known measurement ensemble and $x\in\mathbb{C}^n$ is an unknown signal, one seeks to recover $x$ (up to a global phase) by minimizing a nonconvex loss such as
$$ f(z) = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=1}^m \bigl(|\langle a_k, z\rangle|^2 - y_k\bigr)^2 $$
via iterative algorithms (e.g., gradient descent, Wirtinger flow, or related first-order schemes producing iterates $z_{t+1} = z_t - \eta\,\nabla f(z_t)$).

Introduce a quantitative notion of intrinsic complexity $\mathcal{C}(x)$ of the signal $x$ — for instance the effective sparsity, the support size, the Kolmogorov / description complexity, the entropy of its modulus distribution, or the number of distinct structural features in a real-space representation of $x$ (e.g., when $x$ encodes an image or a density).

Problem. Quantify how the complexity $\mathcal{C}(x)$ of the unknown object enters the reconstruction dynamics. Specifically:

(a) Establish a precise mechanism by which the complexity of $x$ manifests itself during the iterative reconstruction (for example through the local curvature of $f$ near $x$, the size of basins of attraction, the magnitude of spurious critical points, or the conditioning of the linearization of the phase-retrieval map at $x$).

(b) Derive explicit bounds of the form
$$ \|z_t - e^{i\theta_t} x\| \le \Phi\bigl(\mathcal{C}(x),\, m,\, n,\, t\bigr) $$

$$ f(z) = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=1}^m \bigl(|\langle a_k, z\rangle|^2 - y_k\bigr)^2 $$
via iterative algorithms (e.g., gradient descent, Wirtinger flow, or related first-order schemes producing iterates $z_{t+1} = z_t - \eta\,\nabla f(z_t)$).

Problem. Quantify how the complexity $\mathcal{C}(x)$ of the unknown object enters the reconstruction dynamics. Specifically:

(a) Establish a precise mechanism by which the complexity of $x$ manifests itself during the iterative reconstruction (for example through the local curvature of $f$ near $x$, the size of basins of attraction, the magnitude of spurious critical points, or the conditioning of the linearization of the phase-retrieval map at $x$).

(b) Derive explicit bounds of the form
$$ \|z_t - e^{i\theta_t} x\| \le \Phi\bigl(\mathcal{C}(x),\, m,\, n,\, t\bigr) $$
that exhibit the dependence of the convergence rate of the algorithm on $\mathcal{C}(x)$, and determine whether this dependence is necessary (matching lower bounds) or only sufficient.

Consider the phase retrieval problem: given measurements $y = |\mathcal{A} x^\star|^2 + \eta$, where $x^\star \in \mathbb{C}^n$ (or $\mathbb{R}^n$) is an unknown object (e.g. an image arranged on a pixel grid), $\mathcal{A}: \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}^m$ is a known linear measurement operator (such as an oversampled Fourier transform, coded-diffraction operator, or ptychographic operator), $|\cdot|^2$ is taken componentwise, and $\eta$ is a noise vector drawn from a known statistical model (e.g. additive Gaussian or Poisson). Suppose a reconstruction algorithm produces an estimator $\hat x = \hat x(y)$ of $x^\star$.

Develop a methodology that, for any prescribed confidence level $1-\alpha \in (0,1)$, attaches to the reconstruction $\hat x$ statistically meaningful confidence intervals — in particular, pixel-wise confidence intervals $[L_i(y), U_i(y)]$ for each coordinate (or pixel) $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ of $x^\star$ (or for the magnitude $|x^\star_i|$ and phase $\arg x^\star_i$ separately) — such that
$$\Pr\bigl(x^\star_i \in [L_i(y), U_i(y)] \text{ for all } i \in S \bigr) \ge 1-\alpha,$$
for an appropriate (joint, marginal, or false-coverage-controlled) coverage criterion, while accounting for the inherent global phase / sign / translation ambiguities of phase retrieval. Establish rigorous guarantees on the validity (coverage) and informativeness (width) of such intervals under realistic noise models, and thereby justify phase-retrieval reconstructions through quantitative uncertainty quantification.

Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph. A list assignment for G is a function L that assigns to every vertex v ∈ V a finite set L(v) of colors; if |L(v)| = k for every v ∈ V, then L is called a k-list-assignment. A proper L-coloring of G is a function c : V → ⋃_{v∈V} L(v) such that c(v) ∈ L(v) for every v ∈ V and c(u) ≠ c(v) whenever uv ∈ E. Two L-colorings c₁ and c₂ are said to be disjoint if c₁(v) ≠ c₂(v) for every v ∈ V. The list packing number χ⋆_ℓ(G) is defined as the least positive integer k such that for every k-list-assignment L of G there exist k pairwise disjoint proper L-colorings of G.

Prove or disprove: for every planar graph G, χ⋆_ℓ(G) ≤ 7.

  μ = Σ_{j=1}^N (δ_{x_j} ∗ f_j) + b,

From measurements of μ (for instance, magnitude-only Fourier measurements or other application-specific data), one would like to recover the locations x_j, the features f_j ∈ E, and the background b.

Consider a phase-retrieval model in which an unknown object is represented as a measure on $\mathbb{R}^d$ of the form
$$\rho \;=\; \rho_0 \;+\; \sum_{j=1}^{N} \sum_{k=1}^{K_j} c_{j,k}\, \mu_j(\,\cdot - x_{j,k}),$$
where:
- $\rho_0$ is a fixed (or separately estimated) background measure,
- $\{\mu_j\}_{j=1}^{N}$ is a finite collection of "feature template" measures (e.g., compactly supported probability measures or distributions modeling repeated structural motifs),
- $\{x_{j,k}\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ are translation parameters,
- $\{c_{j,k}\} \subset \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ are amplitude coefficients,
- $K_j \in \mathbb{N}$ counts the occurrences of template $\mu_j$.

The data consist of the squared modulus of the Fourier transform $|\widehat{\rho}(\xi)|^2$ measured on some sampling set $\Xi \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, possibly corrupted by noise.

Given a candidate library $\mathcal{L} = \{\nu_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ of admissible templates, devise and justify a principled procedure to:
(i) choose the number $N$ of distinct feature templates to include in the parametrized representation, and
(ii) select which specific templates $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_N \in \mathcal{L}$ should be used,
so that the resulting parametrized model recovers $\rho$ from the phaseless Fourier data in a manner that is identifiable, stable to noise, and parsimonious. Provide guarantees (such as consistency, identifiability, or error bounds) for the proposed selection rule.

$$\chi^{\star}_{\ell}(G) \le \chi^{\star}_{\ell}(G-v) + 2,$$
where $G-v$ is the graph obtained from $G$ by deleting the vertex $v$ (and all edges incident to it).

Let $\mathcal{E}$ be a fixed family of admissible "feature" templates, where each $\mu \in \mathcal{E}$ is a (complex-valued) tempered distribution or finite measure on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Consider the parametrized class of objects
$$f = \sum_{j=1}^{N} a_j \, \tau_{t_j} \mu_j,$$
where:
- $N \in \mathbb{N}$ is the number of features,
- $\mu_j \in \mathcal{E}$ are the feature types,
- $t_j \in \mathbb{R}^d$ are the feature locations, and $\tau_{t_j}$ denotes translation by $t_j$, i.e., $(\tau_{t_j}\mu_j)(x) = \mu_j(x - t_j)$,
- $a_j \in \mathbb{C}$ are the feature weights.

Suppose $f$ is observed only through phaseless (intensity) measurements, i.e., through the squared modulus of its Fourier transform
$$\mathcal{M}(f)(\xi) = |\hat f(\xi)|^2, \qquad \xi \in \mathbb{R}^d,$$
or, more generally, through $|\langle f, \varphi_\alpha\rangle|^2$ for a prescribed measurement family $\{\varphi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$.

Determine sufficient conditions on the feature dictionary $\mathcal{E}$, on the configuration $\{(a_j,\mu_j,t_j)\}_{j=1}^N$ (for example, separation of the locations $t_j$, linear independence properties of $\{\tau_{t_j}\mu_j\}$, genericity or non-degeneracy of the weights $a_j$, bounds on $N$), and on the measurement family under which the following hold:

(i) **Uniqueness:** the parameters $(N, \{a_j\}, \{\mu_j\}, \{t_j\})$ are uniquely determined by $\mathcal{M}(f)$, up to the unavoidable global symmetries of the phaseless problem (global phase, global translation, and reflection/conjugation).

(ii) **Stability:** there exists a constant $C > 0$ and a metric $d_{\text{par}}$ on the parameter space such that, for any two admissible parameter tuples $\theta, \theta'$ producing objects $f_\theta, f_{\theta'}$,
$$d_{\text{par}}(\theta,\theta') \;\le\; C \, \| \mathcal{M}(f_\theta) - \mathcal{M}(f_{\theta'}) \|,$$
modulo the same symmetries.

Formulate and prove such uniqueness and stability guarantees, identifying explicit sufficient conditions.

$$ A(f)(r,\xi) = \bigl|\mathcal{F}\bigl(f \cdot S_r w\bigr)(\xi)\bigr|^2, \qquad r \in R,\ \xi \in \Omega, $$

Consider a three-dimensional two-component (spin-↑ and spin-↓) Fermi gas with zero-range s-wave interactions characterized by the scattering length a, at temperature T. Let N_↑ and N_↓ denote the number of fermions in each spin component, N = N_↑ + N_↓ the total number, k_F the Fermi wavenumber associated with the total density (via n = k_F^3/(3π^2) for the equivalent unpolarized gas), and T_F = ℏ^2 k_F^2/(2 m k_B) the Fermi temperature. Suppose the gas is highly polarized, i.e. N_↑ − N_↓ scales extensively with N.

It is conjectured that in such a system pair condensation can occur not at zero center-of-mass momentum K_pair = 0, but rather in a coherent superposition of plane-wave pair states with nonzero center-of-mass momenta, producing a spatially modulated pair-condensed superfluid (a "supersolid"-like phase, of FFLO type).

Problem: Determine, as precisely as possible, the domain of existence of this spatially modulated pair-condensed superfluid phase in the three-dimensional parameter space
  (p, 1/(k_F a), T/T_F),  with p = (N_↑ − N_↓)/N ∈ (0,1],
including the boundary of the domain. The determination must account for the high sensitivity of the modulated phase to thermal fluctuations.

The FFLO/spatially-modulated superfluid phase has not been conclusively observed in 3D cold-atom experiments, and its precise domain of existence in (polarization, 1/k_F a, T/T_F) parameter space remains uncertain; theoretical predictions suggest only a narrow window in 3D, with strong sensitivity to thermal fluctuations. Let $G:\mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a (typically nonlinear) generative model whose image $\mathcal{R}(G) := \{G(z) : z \in \mathbb{R}^k\}$ is regarded as a low-dimensional prior set of "plausible" signals. Let $A:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ be a known (typically linear) forward measurement operator, let $f_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be an unknown true signal, and let $y = A f_0 + \eta \in \mathbb{R}^m$ be a measurement, where $\eta$ is noise. Consider the latent-space reconstruction
$$\tilde z \;\in\; \arg\min_{z \in \mathbb{R}^k}\; \|A\circ G(z) - y\|_2^2,$$
and define the reconstruction bias
$$\mathrm{Bias}(\tilde z;f_0) \;:=\; \|G(\tilde z) - f_0\|.$$
Crucially, the true signal $f_0$ is not assumed to lie in $\mathcal{R}(G)$ (e.g., $f_0$ may contain defects or anomalies not represented by the generative model).

Problem. Devise a procedure that, using only the generator $G$, the operator $A$, the measurement $y$, and the computed minimizer $\tilde z$ (and not the unknown $f_0$), either (a) detects whether the bias $\|G(\tilde z) - f_0\|$ is significantly nonzero (e.g., flags that $f_0 \notin \mathcal{R}(G)$ or that the reconstruction fails to capture $f_0$), or (b) provides a provable quantitative estimate or bound on $\|G(\tilde z) - f_0\|$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be Hilbert (or Banach) spaces. Consider an inverse problem in which one wishes to recover a ground-truth signal $f_0 \in X$ from noisy measurements
$$ y = A f_0 + \eta \in Y, \qquad \|\eta\|_Y \le \delta, $$
where $A : X \to Y$ is a (possibly nonlinear) measurement map. Let $G : Z \to X$ be a generative model defined on a latent space $Z$ (for instance a trained neural network, normalizing flow, or model-based prior), whose range $\mathcal{R}(G) \subset X$ serves as a learned signal class.

For parameters $\alpha,\beta > 0$, consider the unified variational reconstruction
$$ \hat f \in \arg\min_{f \in X} \Big\{ \tfrac12 \|A f - y\|_Y^2 + \alpha \, d\big(f,\mathcal{R}(G)\big)^2 + \beta\, \mathcal{R}(f) \Big\}, \qquad (\star) $$
which balances a measurement-fitting term against a penalty tying the reconstruction to the generative model (here $d(\cdot, \mathcal{R}(G))$ denotes distance to the range of $G$ and $\mathcal{R}$ is an optional regularizer).

Assume baseline reconstruction error guarantees of the form
$$ \|\hat f - f_0\|_X \;\le\; C_1\,\delta + C_2\, d(f_0, \mathcal{R}(G)) + C_3\,\varepsilon(G), $$
which can be derived under a global bi-Lipschitz assumption on $A$ (i.e. there exist $0 < c \le C < \infty$ with $c\|f-g\|_X \le \|Af - Ag\|_Y \le C\|f-g\|_X$ for all $f,g$ in a relevant set) together with Lipschitz/regularity assumptions on $G$.

Problem. Derive sharper theoretical error guarantees for the estimator $\hat f$ defined by $(\star)$ under realistic assumptions on $A$, $G$, and $f_0$. In particular:

(a) Establish quantitative reconstruction error bounds in the case where $A$ does not satisfy a global bi-Lipschitz property — for example, when $A$ is only locally bi-Lipschitz, satisfies a restricted isometry / range-restricted isometry condition on a neighborhood of $\mathcal{R}(G)$, or admits only a one-sided stability (modulus of injectivity / weak-type) estimate.

(b) Improve the constants and rates in such bounds for specific structured classes of generative models $G$, including (i) learned generative models such as ReLU neural network decoders, normalizing flows, score-based / diffusion generative models, and (ii) model-based generative models such as sparse synthesis dictionaries, low-rank models, or analytically prescribed manifolds, exploiting their geometric and approximation-theoretic properties.

State explicit hypotheses on $A$, $G$, and $f_0$ (including how well $f_0$ is approximated by $\mathcal{R}(G)$) under which the improved bounds hold, and identify regimes where the dependence on $\delta$, on the approximation error $d(f_0,\mathcal{R}(G))$, and on parameters of $G$ (depth, width, Lipschitz constant, latent dimension) is optimal.

Setup. Let $A:\mathbb{C}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m_{\ge 0}$ be a (possibly nonlinear) forward measurement operator, for instance the phase-retrieval operator $A(x)=(|\langle a_i,x\rangle|^2)_{i=1}^m$ for given sampling vectors $a_1,\dots,a_m\in\mathbb{C}^n$. Let $G:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{C}^n$ be a (typically nonlinear and non-convex) model map, e.g.\ a trained generative network, that produces approximate signals from a low-dimensional latent code $z\in\mathbb{R}^k$. Let $z_0\in\mathbb{R}^k$ be a target latent code, write the approximation bias $b:=G(z_0)-f_0$ where $f_0\in\mathbb{C}^n$ is the true signal, and assume the observed data are
$$y \;=\; A(f_0) + \varepsilon \;\in\;\mathbb{R}^m,$$
where $\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}^m$ is a noise vector (Gaussian, Poisson, or otherwise).

Reconstruction problem. Given a data-fidelity loss $\mathcal{L}$, a weighted regularizer $\mathcal{R}_W$ on the latent space depending on a positive weight matrix or schedule $W$, and a regularization parameter $\lambda>0$, consider the optimization problem
$$\min_{z\in\mathbb{R}^k}\; \mathcal{L}\bigl(A(G(z)),\,y\bigr) \;+\; \lambda\,\mathcal{R}_W(z). \qquad(\star)$$

Tasks.
(1) Design an iterative algorithm that solves $(\star)$ efficiently and prove convergence guarantees for it (e.g.\ convergence of iterates or of objective values, with explicit rates) under suitable assumptions on $A$, $G$, $\mathcal{L}$, and $\mathcal{R}_W$.

(2) Establish quantitative robustness bounds for the reconstructed $\hat z$ (and the corresponding signal estimate $G(\hat z)$) in terms of the noise level $\|\varepsilon\|$ and the generative bias $\|G(z_0)-f_0\|$, under different noise models.

(3) Because the signal-to-noise ratio $\|A(f_0)\|/\|\varepsilon\|$ is not known a priori, devise a rule that adapts the regularization parameter $\lambda=\lambda_t$ along the iterations $t=0,1,2,\dots$ so that the algorithm attains the same (or near-optimal) convergence and robustness guarantees as if the optimal $\lambda$ were known in advance.

Consider the complex phase retrieval problem in the high-dimensional proportional regime. Let n,m be positive integers with m/n → α > 0 as n → ∞ (α is called the oversampling ratio). Let f₀ be drawn uniformly at random from the complex unit sphere {f ∈ ℂⁿ : ‖f‖₂ = 1}. Let A ∈ ℂ^{m×n} be a random sensing matrix drawn from some prescribed ensemble (for instance, an i.i.d. Gaussian ensemble, a uniformly sampled partial unitary/Fourier ensemble, or, more generally, a right-unitarily-invariant ensemble characterized by a limiting singular value distribution). One observes the intensity measurements y = |A f₀|² ∈ ℝ^m (componentwise modulus squared, possibly with additional noise specified by a fixed channel). Let f̂(y, A) denote the Bayes-optimal estimator of f₀ (with respect to the global phase ambiguity, e.g. the estimator minimizing the expected projector distance to f₀), and let

   MMSE(α) = lim_{n→∞} 𝔼[ 1 − |⟨f̂, f₀⟩|² ].

Define:
 (a) the weak-recovery threshold α_WR as the infimum of α > 0 such that MMSE(α) is strictly smaller than the value attained by a uniformly random guess on the unit sphere;
 (b) the full-recovery threshold α_FR as the infimum of α > 0 such that MMSE(α) equals the smallest value achievable by any estimator for the given sensing model (i.e., the optimum over all measurable estimators in the chosen ensemble).

Determine, as explicit functionals of the statistical properties of the sensing ensemble (in particular its limiting singular value distribution), the values of α_WR and α_FR.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

For i.i.d. Gaussian sensing matrices the weak-recovery threshold is known to be α_WR = 1 and full/strong recovery occurs at α_FR = 2 (Mondelli–Montanari and follow-ups). For right-unitarily-invariant ensembles with general spectrum, recent works derive single-letter formulas for the Bayes-optimal MMSE and for the (algorithmic) weak-recovery threshold, giving partial answers depending on the spectrum (e.g. unitary/Fourier ensembles yield thresholds at 2, while structured ensembles can shift them). A complete characterization of both thresholds for arbitrary sensing-matrix statistics remains open.

Consider the phase retrieval problem in the high-dimensional asymptotic regime: a hidden signal $x^\star \in \mathbb{C}^n$ (drawn, say, uniformly from the complex sphere of radius $\sqrt{n}$) is observed through magnitude-only measurements
$$y = |A x^\star|^2 \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^m,$$
where $A \in \mathbb{C}^{m\times n}$ is a measurement matrix, $m = \alpha n$, and $\alpha>0$ is the oversampling ratio. The squared magnitude is taken entrywise.

For a sequence of estimators $\hat{x}=\hat{x}(y,A)$, define the (normalized) overlap
$$q(\hat{x},x^\star) = \frac{|\langle \hat{x}, x^\star\rangle|}{\|\hat{x}\|\,\|x^\star\|}.$$
The information-theoretic weak-recovery threshold is
$$\alpha_{\mathrm{WR}} = \inf\{\alpha>0 : \exists\,\hat{x}\text{ with }\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\,q(\hat{x},x^\star)^2 > 0\},$$
and the full-recovery threshold is
$$\alpha_{\mathrm{FR}} = \inf\{\alpha>0 : \exists\,\hat{x}\text{ with }\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\,q(\hat{x},x^\star)^2 = 1\}.$$
Algorithmic counterparts $\alpha_{\mathrm{WR}}^{\mathrm{alg}}$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{FR}}^{\mathrm{alg}}$ are defined analogously, restricting to polynomial-time estimators.

Now restrict the ensemble of measurement matrices to the physically structured "Fourier–diffuser" families:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] $A = F D F$, where $F$ is the (unitary) discrete Fourier transform on $\mathbb{C}^n$ and $D = \mathrm{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_n)$ with $d_i$ i.i.d.\ uniform on the unit circle in $\mathbb{C}$;
\item[(ii)] More generally, $A = F D_1 F D_2 \cdots F D_\ell$ for a fixed integer $\ell\geq 2$, where each $D_k$ is an independent diagonal matrix of i.i.d.\ uniform unit-modulus phases.
\end{itemize}
(For $m<n$, the construction is followed by sub-sampling $m$ rows; for $m>n$, by independent repetitions.)

Problem: Establish information-theoretic and algorithmic bounds (ideally, sharp values) for the weak-recovery threshold $\alpha_{\mathrm{WR}}$ and the full-recovery threshold $\alpha_{\mathrm{FR}}$ for the phase retrieval problem with measurement matrices drawn from the ensembles (i) and (ii).

Consider the probabilistic (Bayesian) phase retrieval problem in high dimensions. Let $f_0 \in \mathbb{R}^N$ (or $\mathbb{C}^N$) be an unknown object drawn from a prior distribution $P_0$, and let $A \in \mathbb{C}^{M \times N}$ be a sensing matrix with i.i.d. entries (e.g., complex Gaussian). One observes the intensity measurements
$$y_i = |(A f_0)_i|^2 + \text{noise}, \qquad i = 1,\dots,M,$$
and seeks to estimate $f_0$ from $(y, A)$. Let $\alpha = M/N$ denote the sampling ratio in the limit $N,M \to \infty$.

Define:
- the weak-recovery threshold $\alpha_{\mathrm{WR}}(P_0)$ as the infimum of $\alpha$ such that the Bayes-optimal MMSE estimator achieves strictly better mean-squared error than the trivial estimator using only the prior (i.e., nontrivial correlation with $f_0$ is achievable);
- the full-recovery threshold $\alpha_{\mathrm{FR}}(P_0)$ as the infimum of $\alpha$ such that the Bayes-optimal MMSE estimator achieves vanishing reconstruction error (perfect recovery up to global phase).

Determine how $\alpha_{\mathrm{WR}}$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{FR}}$ depend on the choice of object prior $P_0$. In particular, characterize the thresholds in each of the following cases:

1. Positivity prior: $f_0$ has nonnegative entries.
2. Support-constraint prior: $f_0$ is supported on a known subset $S \subset \{1,\dots,N\}$ of size $|S| = sN$ for some $s \in (0,1]$.
3. Generative prior: $f_0 = G(z_0)$, where $G:\mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^N$ is a known low-dimensional generative map (e.g., a deep neural network) with latent dimension $k \ll N$, and $z_0$ has a known distribution.

Give explicit formulas (or sharp upper and lower bounds) for $\alpha_{\mathrm{WR}}$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{FR}}$ as functions of the parameters of these priors, and compare them to the unstructured i.i.d. baseline $\alpha_{\mathrm{WR}} = \alpha_{\mathrm{FR}} = 1$ (Gaussian sensing) or $=2$ (random unitary sensing).

The dependence of weak- and full-recovery thresholds in probabilistic phase retrieval on structured object priors (positivity, support constraints, generative priors) is explicitly listed as an open problem in recent surveys of phase retrieval. While baseline thresholds for i.i.d. Gaussian and random-unitary sensing with separable priors are known (α_WR = α_FR = 1 and 2 respectively), no general theory characterizes these thresholds for non-separable priors such as low-dimensional generative priors; empirical and partial results indicate priors can lower both thresholds, but sharp formulas are not established.

Consider the following phase-retrieval measurement model motivated by event-driven four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D STEM) in the extremely low-dose regime. Let x ∈ ℂ^n be an unknown complex signal (representing, e.g., an exit wave or specimen transmission function) to be recovered, and let {a_i}_{i=1}^m ⊂ ℂ^n be a known collection of measurement vectors (modeling probe positions and detector pixels), with m ≫ n. For each i, the expected intensity is λ_i(x) = |⟨a_i, x⟩|^2, and the actual measurement y_i is a quantized (e.g., Poisson-counted) observation of λ_i with very small mean, so that Σ_i λ_i(x) (the total dose) is small and each y_i is typically 0 or 1.

Tasks:
(a) Design a computationally efficient reconstruction algorithm that, given (a_i, y_i)_{i=1}^m, produces an estimate x̂ of x up to a global phase.
(b) Prove theoretical guarantees of the form ‖x̂ − e^{iθ} x‖ ≤ ε(m, n, dose, noise) with high probability under a suitable random or structured model of the measurement vectors, and establish stability of the reconstruction with respect to perturbations and quantization errors in y.

Specify and justify the assumptions on {a_i}, the total dose, and the quantization noise model under which the guarantees hold.

Setup. Let $d\geq 2$ be an integer and identify $\mathbb{Z}_d$ with $\{0,1,\dots,d-1\}$. For a vector $u\in\mathbb{C}^d$, write $u[n]$ for its $n$-th coordinate (indices mod $d$). Define the cyclic shift operator $S_\xi:\mathbb{C}^d\to\mathbb{C}^d$ by $(S_\xi u)[n]=u[n-\xi]$, the entrywise conjugate-product $u\circ v$ by $(u\circ v)[n]=\overline{u[n]}\,v[n]$, and the discrete Fourier transform
$$\mathcal{F}[u][k]=\sum_{n=0}^{d-1} u[n]\,e^{-2\pi i nk/d}.$$
Fix a window $w\in\mathbb{C}^d$ and a signal $f\in\mathbb{C}^d$. The discrete ambiguity function of $f$ with window $w$ is the array
$$A_{w,f}[\xi,x] \;=\; \mathcal{F}\!\big[\,\overline{f}\cdot S_\xi f\,\big][x], \qquad (\xi,x)\in\mathbb{Z}_d\times\mathbb{Z}_d.$$
Ptychographic phase retrieval via Wigner distribution deconvolution recovers $f$ (up to a global unimodular constant) from $A_{w,f}$ by entrywise division by the window ambiguity factors
$$M_w[\xi,x] \;=\; \mathcal{F}\!\big[\,\overline{w}\cdot S_\xi w\,\big][x].$$
This procedure is well-posed at coordinates where $M_w[\xi,x]\neq 0$.

Question. Determine the maximum number $N(d)$ of pairs $(\xi,x)\in\mathbb{Z}_d\times\mathbb{Z}_d$ on which the window ambiguity factor $M_w[\xi,x]$ can vanish while still guaranteeing that the signal $f\in\mathbb{C}^d$ (generic, or in some specified class) is uniquely recoverable from the measurements $A_{w,f}$ up to a global phase. Equivalently, characterize the admissible zero patterns of $M_w$ that preserve uniqueness of recovery.

$$\mathcal{F}[u][k]=\sum_{n=0}^{d-1} u[n]\,e^{-2\pi i nk/d}.$$
Fix a window $w\in\mathbb{C}^d$ and a signal $f\in\mathbb{C}^d$. The discrete ambiguity function of $f$ with window $w$ is the array
$$A_{w,f}[\xi,x] \;=\; \mathcal{F}\!\big[\,\overline{f}\cdot S_\xi f\,\big][x], \qquad (\xi,x)\in\mathbb{Z}_d\times\mathbb{Z}_d.$$
Ptychographic phase retrieval via Wigner distribution deconvolution recovers $f$ (up to a global unimodular constant) from $A_{w,f}$ by entrywise division by the window ambiguity factors
$$M_w[\xi,x] \;=\; \mathcal{F}\!\big[\,\overline{w}\cdot S_\xi w\,\big][x].$$
This procedure is well-posed at coordinates where $M_w[\xi,x]\neq 0$.

Question. Determine the maximum number $N(d)$ of pairs $(\xi,x)\in\mathbb{Z}_d\times\mathbb{Z}_d$ on which the window ambiguity factor $M_w[\xi,x]$ can vanish while still guaranteeing that the signal $f\in\mathbb{C}^d$ (generic, or in some specified class) is uniquely recoverable from the measurements $A_{w,f}$ up to a global phase. Equivalently, characterize the admissible zero patterns of $M_w$ that preserve uniqueness of recovery.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is posed as an open problem about how many zero coefficients of the window ambiguity factor can be tolerated in Wigner distribution deconvolution for ptychographic phase retrieval. Web search reveals related work on WDD, uniqueness for phase objects, and noise/background suppression, but no source providing a definitive count or characterization addressing this specific tolerance question. Hence the problem appears to remain open.

Setup. Let $f \in \mathbb{C}^N$ be an unknown signal whose discrete Fourier transform $\hat f \in \mathbb{C}^N$ we wish to recover from intensity-only ptychographic measurements. In Wigner distribution deconvolution (WDD), one collects, for a known window/probe $w \in \mathbb{C}^N$ and a set of translates $\{T_\ell w\}_{\ell}$, the squared moduli $|\langle f, M_k T_\ell w\rangle|^2$, where $M_k$ and $T_\ell$ denote modulation and translation operators. These measurements give access, via a 2D Fourier transform, to entries of the Wigner-type matrix
$$X_{j,k} \;=\; \hat f(j)\,\overline{\hat f(j+k)}\,\cdot\, c_{j,k}(w),$$
where $c_{j,k}(w)$ are known coefficients depending on the window. After deconvolving by the known window factors, one obtains (a subset of) the rank-one matrix $\hat f \hat f^*$, from which $\hat f$ is recovered up to a global phase.

In practice some Fourier coefficients of the window vanish (or are too small to invert stably), so certain off-diagonals of $\hat f \hat f^*$ are missing. The subspace completion (SC) method exploits the rank-one structure of $\hat f \hat f^*$ to recover a small number of missing diagonals by solving a low-dimensional eigenvector problem on accessible blocks. Standard SC is designed for the case where only a few off-diagonals are inaccessible, and its operational cost grows rapidly with the number of missing off-diagonals.

Problem. Design and analyze a generalization of the subspace completion technique that provably recovers $\hat f$ (up to a global phase) from the available entries of $\hat f \hat f^*$ when an arbitrary number of off-diagonals (equivalently, an arbitrary subset of Fourier coefficients of the window) are missing, while keeping the total computational cost reasonable (e.g.\ polynomial in $N$, and ideally near-linear or matching the cost of a small number of FFTs). Provide both an algorithm and conditions on the missing-pattern under which exact or stable recovery is guaranteed.

Setup. Let $f \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ be an unknown signal and let $w \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ be a known window. For $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$, let $S_\xi$ denote the modulation/shift operator and define the windowed correlations $[w \cdot S_\xi w]_x = \overline{w(x)}\, w(x+\xi)$ (the window's ambiguity factor at shift $\xi$, evaluated at $x$). The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) of $f$ with window $w$ is
\[ V_w f(x,\omega) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f(t)\,\overline{w(t-x)}\, e^{-2\pi i \omega \cdot t}\, dt, \]
and its spectrogram is $|V_w f|^2$. Wigner Distribution Deconvolution (WDD) recovers $f$ (up to a global phase) from $|V_w f|^2$ by inverting, frequency-by-frequency, multiplication by the window ambiguity function $A_w(\xi,\eta) = \mathcal{F}_x[\,\overline{w(\cdot)}\, w(\cdot+\xi)\,](\eta)$. Recovery fails at frequencies where $A_w$ vanishes.

Problem.
(a) Determine a sufficient bandlimit hypothesis on $f$ (i.e., a condition of the form $\operatorname{supp}\widehat{f} \subseteq \Omega$ for some explicit set $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$) which, in the case of a symmetric window $w$ (so that $A_w$ may have non-trivial zero sets), guarantees that $f$ is uniquely determined (up to a global phase) by its spectrogram $|V_w f|^2$ via the WDD procedure.

(b) More generally, for an arbitrary window $w \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, establish a quantitative relationship between the size and location of the zero set $Z_w = \{(\xi,\eta) : A_w(\xi,\eta) = 0\}$ (where $A_w(\xi,\eta) = \big|\mathcal{F}[w \cdot S_\xi w]_x(\eta)\big|$ vanishes) and the band-limitedness of $f$ that suffices for unique recovery of $f$ from $|V_w f|^2$ through WDD.

Setting. Let $f \in \mathbb{C}^d$ denote an unknown object (signal) and $w \in \mathbb{C}^d$ denote a known window/probe. For a translation parameter $k \in \mathbb{Z}_d$ and frequency parameter $\ell \in \mathbb{Z}_d$, the ptychographic measurement is
$$ Y[k,\ell] \;=\; \Big| \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}_d} f[n]\, \overline{w[n-k]}\, e^{-2\pi i \ell n / d} \Big|^2 . $$
The classical Wigner distribution deconvolution (WDD) recovers $f$ (up to a global phase) from the full set of measurements $\{Y[k,\ell] : k,\ell \in \mathbb{Z}_d\}$ by taking a 2D Fourier transform in $(k,\ell)$, dividing pointwise by the corresponding Wigner transform of the probe, and then extracting $f$ from the lifted rank-one matrix $f f^*$. WDD has also been formulated when the translations $k$ are restricted to a subgroup (a regular sub-grid) of $\mathbb{Z}_d$.

Problem. Let $K \subset \mathbb{Z}_d$ be an arbitrary "physically reasonable" sampling pattern of translations (for instance, a non-uniform but covering set of probe positions), and consider only the measurements
$$ \{\, Y[k,\ell] \;:\; k \in K,\; \ell \in \mathbb{Z}_d \,\}. $$
Determine whether a Wigner distribution deconvolution-type inversion procedure can be derived that recovers $f$ (up to a global phase) from these measurements for general sampling patterns $K$ that are neither the full group $\mathbb{Z}_d$ nor a subgroup. Identify minimal/sufficient conditions on the pair $(K, w)$ and on the object $f$ (e.g., support, sparsity, smoothness, or non-vanishing assumptions) under which such a WDD-style reconstruction is well-posed and stable.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Recent work establishes a "discretization barrier": for general $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ functions, uniqueness in sampled STFT phase retrieval on any lattice is unachievable regardless of the single window chosen. Workarounds use multi-window Gabor systems, non-lattice sampling sets (e.g., square-root lattices), or restricted function classes. The general question of which single windows admit lattice-based recovery on structured subclasses remains open, with only partial results for Gaussians and special constructed windows.

forces $f$ and $g$ to agree up to a global phase.

Sampled STFT phase retrieval is a very active topic. It is known that uniform lattices never give uniqueness for a single window (Grohs–Liehr non-uniqueness theory), while alternatives such as square-root lattices, multi-window setups, and pairs of parallel lines have been shown to yield uniqueness. However, no general characterization of uniqueness sets in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is known, and uniqueness for spiral-like sampling sets does not appear to be established in the literature found. The problem appears to remain open.

Two functions $f, g \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ are said to be equal up to a global phase if there exists $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ with $g = e^{i\alpha} f$. Define
$$ \mathcal{R}_\Omega = \{\, f \in L^2(\mathbb{R}) : \text{if } g \in L^2(\mathbb{R}) \text{ satisfies } |Gg(x,\omega)| = |Gf(x,\omega)| \text{ for all } (x,\omega) \in \Omega, \text{ then } g = e^{i\alpha} f \text{ for some } \alpha \in \mathbb{R}\,\}, $$
the set of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ functions that can be recovered up to a global phase from the sampled Gabor magnitudes on $\Omega$. It is known that the Gaussian itself lies in $\mathcal{R}_\Omega$ while there is a dense subset of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ disjoint from $\mathcal{R}_\Omega$.

For $f \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and a window function $w \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) of $f$ with respect to $w$ is defined by
$$V_w f(x,\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f(t)\,\overline{w(t-x)}\, e^{-2\pi i t\cdot \xi}\,dt, \qquad (x,\xi) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d.$$
The associated spectrogram is $|V_w f|^2$. Phase retrieval seeks to reconstruct $f$ (up to a global unimodular phase factor $\alpha \in S^1 = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z|=1\}$) from magnitude measurements of $V_w f$.

Construct a window function $w \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, a sequence of finite sampling sets $\Omega_k = \{(x_j, \xi_j) : 1 \le j \le k\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d$, and a sequence of (practical, implementable) reconstruction maps
$$A_k : [0,\infty)^k \to L^2(\mathbb{R}^d),$$
such that there exists a dense subset $D \subset L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with the property that for every $f \in D$,
$$\inf_{\alpha \in S^1} \big\| \alpha f - A_k\big(|V_w f|^2 \big|_{\Omega_k}\big) \big\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)} \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } k \to \infty,$$
where $|V_w f|^2|_{\Omega_k} = (|V_w f(x_j,\xi_j)|^2)_{j=1}^k$.

Either exhibit such a triple $(A_k, w, \{\Omega_k\})$ or prove that no such practical scheme exists.

Several recent works provide partial answers: semidefinite programming based Gabor phase retrieval with accuracy guarantees from finitely many noisy samples, provably accurate spectrogram inversion algorithms for L^2([-π,π]), and provably convergent (accelerated) Griffin–Lim type iterations. These give practical algorithms with convergence/error guarantees in restricted settings (bandlimited or smooth functions on intervals, specific windows). A fully general construction yielding convergence on a dense subset of L^2(R^d) for all d with a unified practical scheme does not appear to be established, so the problem is best regarded as partially solved.

Let $n \geq 2$ and let $H^2(\mathbb{D}^n)$ denote the Hardy space on the unit polydisc $\mathbb{D}^n$. A closed subspace $\mathcal{S} \subseteq H^2(\mathbb{D}^n)$ is called a submodule if it is invariant under multiplication by each coordinate function $z_j$, $1\le j\le n$. For each $j$, define the bounded operators on $\mathcal{S}$:
- $R_{z_j} := M_{z_j}|_{\mathcal{S}}$, the restriction of multiplication by $z_j$ to $\mathcal{S}$;
- $E_{z_j} := P_{\mathcal{S}} \circ \mathrm{ev}_{z_j=0}|_{\mathcal{S}}$, the compression to $\mathcal{S}$ of the evaluation operator that sets the $j$-th variable to zero (equivalently, the projection onto the kernel of $R_{z_j}^*$ composed with the natural identification).

A single-variable inner function in the variable $z_i$ is a bounded holomorphic function $\phi_i:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{D}$ with unimodular radial boundary values almost everywhere, regarded as an element of $H^\infty(\mathbb{D}^n)$ depending only on $z_i$.

Given a nonempty subset $\Lambda \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, characterize precisely those submodules $\mathcal{S}$ admitting a representation
$$\mathcal{S} \;=\; \overline{\sum_{i\in\Lambda} \phi_i(z_i)\, H^2(\mathbb{D}^n)}$$
for some family $\{\phi_i\}_{i\in\Lambda}$ of one-variable inner functions. In particular, decide whether such a representation exists if and only if the following "defect" identities hold on $\mathcal{S}$:
$$(I_{\mathcal{S}} - E_{z_l}E_{z_l}^*)(I_{\mathcal{S}} - R_{z_l}R_{z_l}^*) = 0 \quad \text{for every } l \in \{1,\dots,n\}\setminus \Lambda,$$
$$(I_{\mathcal{S}} - E_{z_i}E_{z_i}^*)(I_{\mathcal{S}} - R_{z_i}R_{z_i}^*)(I_{\mathcal{S}} - E_{z_j}E_{z_j}^*)(I_{\mathcal{S}} - R_{z_j}R_{z_j}^*) = 0 \quad \text{for all distinct } i,j\in\Lambda.$$

Let $T$ be a rooted labelled tree on the vertex set $[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, regarded as a parking structure: each vertex is a parking space, and each non-root edge is oriented toward the root, giving each non-root vertex a unique outgoing edge. A sequence of $m\le n$ drivers arrives one by one; driver $j$ has a preferred space $s_j\in[n]$ and proceeds as follows: starting at vertex $s_j$, the driver parks there if it is unoccupied; otherwise the driver follows the directed edges toward the root, parking at the first unoccupied vertex encountered. If the driver reaches the root and it is occupied, the driver fails. The sequence $(s_1,\dots,s_m)\in[n]^m$ is called a parking sequence for $T$ with $m$ drivers if all $m$ drivers successfully park. Let
$$S(T,m)=\#\{(s_1,\dots,s_m)\in[n]^m:\text{all }m\text{ drivers park on }T\}.$$

Analogously, let $f:[n]\to[n]$ be a mapping (an $n$-mapping), with functional digraph having an edge from $i$ to $f(i)$ for each $i$. A driver with preference $s\in[n]$ starts at $s$ and follows the directed edges $i\mapsto f(i)$, parking at the first unoccupied vertex; if the driver returns to a previously visited (occupied) vertex without finding a free space, the driver fails. Define $S(f,m)$ as the number of sequences in $[n]^m$ for which all $m$ drivers successfully park.

Problem: Give a simple, general structural characterization of the counting functions $S(T,m)$ (for arbitrary rooted labelled trees $T$) and $S(f,m)$ (for arbitrary $n$-mappings $f$), beyond case-by-case formulas, bounds, or treatments of extremal cases.

Setup. Let $T$ be a rooted labelled tree on $n$ vertices, where the vertices serve as parking spaces and each edge is oriented toward the root (so each non-root vertex has a unique outgoing edge pointing to its parent). A parking function on $T$ is a sequence $(s_1,\dots,s_m)$ of vertices of $T$ (the preferred parking spots of $m$ drivers, $1\le m\le n$) defined by the following parking process: drivers arrive in order $1,2,\dots,m$; driver $i$ goes to vertex $s_i$ and, if it is empty, parks there; otherwise the driver moves along the directed edges toward the root, parking at the first empty vertex encountered. If the driver reaches the root and the root is occupied (or, more generally, leaves the tree without finding an empty vertex), the driver fails to park. The sequence $(s_1,\dots,s_m)$ is called a parking function (with $m$ successful drivers) if every driver succeeds in parking.

Two important families of size-$n$ rooted labelled trees are:
(a) labelled binary trees: rooted plane trees in which each vertex has at most two children, distinguished as left and right, with vertex labels forming a permutation of $\{1,\dots,n\}$;
(b) labelled ordered trees: rooted plane trees with an arbitrary number of linearly ordered children at each vertex, with vertex labels forming a permutation of $\{1,\dots,n\}$.

Let $F_n$ denote, for each family, the total number of pairs $(T,(s_1,\dots,s_n))$ where $T$ is a tree of size $n$ in the family and $(s_1,\dots,s_n)$ is a parking function on $T$ in which all $n$ drivers park successfully.

Problem. Determine, for each of the two families above, an exact formula and the asymptotic behaviour as $n\to\infty$ of $F_n$, by means of a generating-function or combinatorial-decomposition approach analogous to the one used for uniformly random labelled (Cayley) trees.

A closed subspace $\mathcal{S}\subseteq H^2(\mathbb{D}^n)$ is called a submodule if $M_{z_i}\mathcal{S}\subseteq \mathcal{S}$ for every $i=1,\ldots,n$. $$(I_{\mathcal{S}}-R_{z_i}R_{z_i}^{*})(I_{\mathcal{S}}-R_{z_j}R_{z_j}^{*})=0\qquad\text{for all }i\ne j.$$

Background. A simple tree family on the vertex set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$ is called an increasing tree family if every tree is rooted, the labels along any root-to-leaf path are strictly increasing, and the family is specified by a degree-weight generating function $\varphi(x)=\sum_{k\ge 0}\varphi_k x^k$ that assigns weight $\varphi_{d(v)}$ to a node of out-degree $d(v)$. Decreasing tree families are defined analogously with strictly decreasing labels. Recursive trees are the special case obtained by viewing increasing trees as unordered (i.e. children of a node form an unordered set), corresponding to $\varphi(x)=e^x$ in the exponential framework.

A parking function for a rooted labelled tree $T$ on $n$ vertices with $m\le n$ cars is a sequence $(s_1,\dots,s_m)\in V(T)^m$ of preferred parking spots such that the following process succeeds: car $i$ drives from $s_i$ toward the root, parking at the first unoccupied vertex it encounters; if all vertices on its path to the root are occupied, the process fails. The sequence is a parking function on $T$ when every car parks successfully. Let $P_{n,m}(T)$ denote the number of parking functions of length $m$ on $T$, and define the aggregate
$$ \mathcal{P}_{n,m}^{\mathcal{T}} \;=\; \sum_{T \in \mathcal{T}_n} w(T)\, P_{n,m}(T), $$
where $\mathcal{T}_n$ is the set of trees of size $n$ in a given increasing or decreasing tree family $\mathcal{T}$ and $w(T)$ is its combinatorial weight. One may also consider the sum-of-parking-function statistic $\sum_{(s_1,\dots,s_m)} (s_1+\cdots+s_m)$ summed over all parking functions of $T$, then averaged/summed over $\mathcal{T}_n$.

Problem. For increasing and decreasing tree families—and in particular for recursive trees (unordered increasing trees)—obtain a tractable determination of:
(a) the total number $\mathcal{P}_{n,m}^{\mathcal{T}}$ of parking functions, and
(b) related aggregate statistics such as the sums of parking-function values $\sum_T \sum_{(s_1,\dots,s_m)\in \mathrm{PF}(T)} (s_1+\cdots+s_m)$,
either by closed-form expressions, exact recursions, or asymptotic formulas (including possible phase-transition thresholds in $m/n$), despite the fact that the natural generating-function / differential-equation approach for recursive trees does not appear to yield directly solvable equations.

Let T be a rooted labeled tree on the vertex set [n] = {1, 2, ..., n} with root r, oriented so that every edge points toward the root; equivalently, let M : [n] → [n] be a mapping whose functional digraph has vertex set [n] with an edge from i to M(i). Each vertex is regarded as a parking space.

A sequence (a_1, a_2, ..., a_n) ∈ [n]^n of preferences for n drivers defines a parking process as follows. Drivers arrive in order 1, 2, ..., n. Driver k first attempts to park at vertex a_k. If that vertex is occupied, the driver moves along the directed edge to the next vertex (the parent in the tree case, or M applied repeatedly in the mapping case) and tries again, continuing until either an empty space is found (in which case the driver parks there) or no further moves are possible (in which case the process fails). The sequence is called a tree parking function for T (respectively a mapping parking function for M) if all n drivers successfully park.

Define the displacement d_k of driver k to be the number of directed edges traversed by driver k from a_k to the vertex where driver k actually parks. Define the total displacement to be D = d_1 + d_2 + ... + d_n.

For tree parking functions and for mapping parking functions, establish exact and/or asymptotic results for the distribution of:
(a) the total displacement D, and
(b) the individual displacement d_k of the k-th driver,
taken over uniformly random parking functions (and, where appropriate, over uniformly random underlying tree or mapping). In particular, determine generating functions, mean, variance, and limiting distributions of these statistics as n → ∞.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a cubic bipartite graph, i.e., a 3-regular graph whose vertex set admits a bipartition into two independent sets. A list assignment $L$ on $G$ assigns to each vertex $v\in V$ a set $L(v)$ of colors; it is a 3-list-assignment if $|L(v)|=3$ for every $v\in V$. A proper $L$-coloring of $G$ is a function $c:V\to\bigcup_{v}L(v)$ such that $c(v)\in L(v)$ for every $v\in V$ and $c(u)\neq c(v)$ whenever $uv\in E$. Three proper $L$-colorings $c_1,c_2,c_3$ are called pairwise disjoint if $c_i(v)\neq c_j(v)$ for every $v\in V$ and every $1\le i<j\le 3$.

Prove or disprove: For every cubic bipartite graph $G$ and every 3-list-assignment $L$ on $G$, there exist three pairwise disjoint proper $L$-colorings of $G$ (equivalently, the list packing number of every cubic bipartite graph is at most 3).

Setup. Let n and m be positive integers with m ≤ n. Consider one of the following two combinatorial structures on the vertex set [n] = {1,2,…,n}:

(A) Tree model. T is a rooted labelled tree on [n] with edges oriented toward the root. Each non-root vertex is regarded as a parking space, and the unique outgoing edge from a vertex points to the next space a driver tries upon finding the current space occupied.

(B) Mapping model. f : [n] → [n] is an arbitrary function, encoded by its functional digraph whose vertices are parking spaces and whose edges v → f(v) indicate where a driver moves when the current space is occupied.

Parking process. There are m drivers, and a "parking sequence" s = (s_1, …, s_m) ∈ [n]^m specifies, for each driver i, the preferred initial vertex s_i. Drivers arrive one by one. Driver i first attempts to park at s_i; if that vertex is already occupied, the driver moves along the directed edge to the next vertex, and continues until either finding an empty vertex (in which case the driver parks there) or returning to a vertex already visited / reaching a dead end without finding an empty space (in which case the driver is unsuccessful and leaves).

Defective parking functions. For a fixed nonnegative integer k, call a pair (T, s) (in model A) or (f, s) (in model B) a k-defective parking function if exactly k of the m drivers fail to park successfully.

Problem. Develop an enumerative theory of k-defective parking functions in these two settings. Specifically:

1. Determine the number T_{n,m,k} of pairs (T, s), where T ranges over rooted labelled trees on [n] and s ∈ [n]^m, such that exactly k drivers are unsuccessful.

2. Determine the analogous number M_{n,m,k} of pairs (f, s) with f : [n] → [n] and s ∈ [n]^m, in which exactly k drivers are unsuccessful.

3. Derive generating-function identities for these quantities, and obtain exact closed-form and asymptotic expressions, including a description of any phase transition occurring near m ≈ n/2.

Setup. Let T be a rooted tree on the vertex set {1,2,...,n} with a distinguished root. A parking function on T is a sequence (a_1, a_2, ..., a_n) of vertices of T (the preferences of n drivers) such that the following parking process succeeds: drivers arrive in order; driver i starts at vertex a_i and proceeds along the unique directed path from a_i toward the root, parking at the first unoccupied vertex encountered; the sequence is a parking function on T if every driver successfully parks. The same definition extends to parking functions on a mapping (functional digraph) f:[n]→[n], where each driver follows the iterated images of f until reaching an unoccupied vertex.

A "restricted" class of parking functions is a subfamily defined by combinatorial conditions on the preference sequence (a_1, ..., a_n) and/or on the underlying tree or mapping; examples of natural restrictions include: prime parking functions; parking functions with prescribed displacement statistics; parking functions whose preferences avoid given patterns; parking functions in which prescribed drivers must park at prescribed vertices; parking functions on trees of a fixed combinatorial family (ordered, unordered, binary, plane, etc.); and parking functions on mappings with constraints on cycle lengths or component sizes.

Problem. Develop exact and asymptotic enumeration formulas (for instance, closed-form counts, generating-function characterizations, or asymptotic equivalents as n→∞) for natural restricted classes of parking functions on rooted trees and on mappings, generalizing the known counting results that are available for the unrestricted case.
