Consider the Liar sentence L := "L is false." Rather than assigning L a single, time-independent truth value, model L as a discrete-time dynamical system whose state at step n is a truth value v_n ∈ {TRUE, FALSE}, updated by the involution v_{n+1} = ¬v_n, so that the trajectory unwinds the self-referential circle into a helix oscillating between TRUE and FALSE. Suppose an external cognitive observer evaluates L by repeatedly substituting the current truth value into the sentence at a discrete "frame rate" f_obs (evaluations per unit external time), producing one update of v_n per frame.

(a) Determine what intrinsic quantity, if any, sets the oscillator's own rate of time (its period or frequency in some natural time parameter), independent of any observer.

(b) Derive the precise relationship between the oscillation frequency f_L observed for L and the observer's frame rate f_obs, including the period in units of the observer's frames and any aliasing or relativistic-style dependence on f_obs.

(c) State conditions under which the oscillation rate is well-defined as an invariant of the sentence alone, versus conditions under which it is only definable relative to the observing cognitive system.

Call a formal modelling framework (a programming language, mathematical model, or metamodel) static if its syntax, semantics, and rule set are fixed once the framework is specified, so that any object expressed in it cannot alter its own description rules during execution. Call it dynamic if it provides intrinsic mechanisms by which the models, programs, or rules expressed in it can be modified at runtime as a function of the evolving state of the system being modelled. Call a system open-ended if, over time, it can produce qualitatively novel structures, behaviours, or organizational levels that are not enumerable in advance from its initial specification.

(a) Construct a dynamic programming language or dynamic metamodel L together with a generative procedure G such that, given a specification S of an open-ended system, G(S) produces a dynamic model (program) in L whose rules and state space evolve with the modelled system, and prove that the resulting model can faithfully track open-ended novelty in S in a precise sense to be made rigorous (e.g., that no fixed static model can simulate G(S) on arbitrary inputs without unbounded external reprogramming).

(b) Construct a dynamic metalanguage M, i.e., a formal system whose own syntactic and semantic rules can change at runtime, such that M itself generates dynamic languages of the type produced in (a), and these generated languages support open-ended self-modification (each generated language can, while in use, extend or revise its own syntax and semantics in response to the evolving system it models). Call a formal modelling framework (a programming language, mathematical model, or metamodel) static if its syntax, semantics, and rule set are fixed once the framework is specified, so that any object expressed in it cannot alter its own description rules during execution. Call it dynamic if it provides intrinsic mechanisms by which the models, programs, or rules expressed in it can be modified at runtime as a function of the evolving state of the system being modelled. Call a system open-ended if, over time, it can produce qualitatively novel structures, behaviours, or organizational levels that are not enumerable in advance from its initial specification.

Consider a dynamical system S that is self-modifying and open-ended in the following informal sense: at any time t, the behavior of S is described by some model M_t drawn from a (possibly unbounded) family of admissible models, together with an associated set of observables and measures μ_{M_t}. The system is called open-ended if, for every t and every choice of model M_t, there exists a future time t' > t at which the realized behavior of S lies outside the descriptive scope of M_t and cannot be quantified by any measure in μ_{M_t}.

Develop a formal framework of analysis tools (i.e., a class of model-independent observables, invariants, or detection procedures) capable of interrogating such self-modifying, evolving, open-ended systems even after their behavior has escaped any fixed model M_t and any measure based on M_t. Specifically:

(a) Give a rigorous definition of an "analysis tool" T that is well-defined on trajectories of S without requiring a fixed background model.

(b) Identify necessary and sufficient conditions under which such a tool T can detect, quantify, or classify novel behavior of S that lies outside the current model M_t.

(c) Construct at least one explicit example of such a tool, and prove that it remains informative across model transitions M_t → M_{t'}.

(d) Determine whether a universal analysis tool — one that remains informative for every open-ended system in a specified class — can exist, or prove an impossibility result analogous to model-based incompleteness.

Rosen's metabolism-repair systems (M,R-systems) model a living organism as a closed network of mappings in which metabolism, repair, and replication are mutually defining. Concretely, given sets A (inputs/metabolites) and B (outputs), one considers a metabolism map f : A → B, a repair map Φ : B → H(A,B) (where H(A,B) denotes the set of admissible maps A → B), and a replication map β : H(A,B) → H(B, H(A,B)), subject to the closure condition that the entire diagram be reproduced from within: there exist b ∈ B such that Φ(b) = f and β(f)(b) = Φ. Such systems can be assigned uniform solutions via the fixed-point combinator Y of the untyped λ-calculus, interpreted in Scott-style domain theory, and alternatively modelled coalgebraically using non-well-founded (anti-foundation) set theory.

Problem. (a) Construct an explicit mathematical bridge between the above formal sketches of self-referential organization (λ-calculus / domain-theoretic fixed points, and coalgebraic / non-well-founded set models of (M,R)-systems) and concrete classes of biological mechanisms (e.g. enzymatic reaction networks, autocatalytic chemical reaction systems, gene-regulatory feedback loops), in the form of a faithful interpretation functor or simulation theorem that preserves the closure-to-efficient-causation property of (M,R)-systems.

(b) Identify precise mathematical criteria under which a sequential, function-application based formalism (λ-calculus, ordinary recursion) is inadequate for modelling autopoietic organization, and must be replaced by a concurrent-process formalism (such as the π-calculus, CCS, Petri nets, or bigraphs); in particular, formulate and prove a separation theorem exhibiting an autopoietic phenomenon expressible in a concurrent-process model but not realisable as a fixed point of any sequential λ-term up to observational equivalence.

Develop a mathematical framework for game-theoretic systems in which the set of players is itself a dynamical variable that evolves in real time as a function of the players' actions. Concretely, formulate a model with the following ingredients:

(i) A time-indexed finite (or countable) set of agents N(t), each agent i ∈ N(t) endowed with a state x_i(t) in some measurable space X, an action a_i(t) chosen from an action set A_i(t), and a payoff/utility functional U_i depending on the trajectory of states, actions, and the population history.

(ii) Population-changing operations driven by the agents' actions: birth (creation of a new agent with inherited or initialized state and utility), death (removal of an agent), merging (two or more agents fuse into a single agent whose state, action set, and utility are determined by an aggregation rule), and splitting (one agent fissions into several agents whose states, action sets, and utilities are determined by a partition rule). The rates or triggers of these operations are functions of the current profile of actions and states.

(iii) A consistent notion of strategy and equilibrium that accounts for the fact that an agent's decision can change not only its own future payoff but also the cardinality and identity of the set of decision-makers that will exist and continue choosing actions, including possibly the agent itself ceasing to exist or being replaced by multiple successors.

The problem is to construct such a framework — specifying the appropriate state space, the dynamics of N(t), well-posed strategy spaces, an equilibrium concept (analogous to Nash, correlated, or evolutionarily stable equilibria) that is well-defined under variable player count, and existence/characterization theorems — and to demonstrate its applicability to systems such as biological tissues whose constituent decision-making units can merge, split, or generate new individuals as a result of their own actions.

Related but distinct theories (evolutionary games, mean-field games, population games, branching processes with control) handle exogenous or aggregate population dynamics rather than action-driven creation/destruction of individual decision-makers. The problem is posed as an open direction for which the requisite mathematics has not yet been developed.

A "rule-changing game" is an extensive form of strategic interaction in which the rules of the game (the set of admissible moves, payoff functions, and even the set of players) may themselves be modified by the moves of the players, so that the space of possible games is closed under such rule changes and admits self-reference (a game whose rules can refer to and alter the game itself).

One known approach to modeling such self-referential games is via domain theory: one seeks a domain D (a directed-complete partial order with a suitable bottom element) such that D is isomorphic to a space built from D using powerdomain constructions (e.g., the Plotkin, Smyth, or Hoare powerdomain) together with function-space and product constructors, so that elements of D represent games whose moves can lead to other elements of D. However, powerdomains do not in general yield set-theoretic powerset-like objects, and standard game-theoretic solution concepts (such as Nash equilibrium, subgame-perfect equilibrium, correlated equilibrium, or evolutionarily stable strategies) lifted to this domain-theoretic setting fail to fully capture their classical features.

Problem. Provide a mathematically rigorous framework for rule-changing games that:
(i) gives a precise definition of a rule-changing game as a mathematical object closed under rule modification and admitting self-reference;
(ii) defines analogues of standard solution concepts (at minimum a Nash-type equilibrium and a subgame-perfect-type refinement) within this framework;
(iii) proves existence theorems for these solution concepts under reasonable hypotheses; and
(iv) either resolves the obstructions arising from the non-set-theoretic character of powerdomain constructions when lifting these solution concepts, or replaces the powerdomain approach with an alternative construction that faithfully reproduces the desired classical game-theoretic features.

Treat "representation" as a candidate fundamental principle of living systems: a relation in which some physical structure or process within an organism stands for, refers to, or carries information about another state of affairs (internal or external). The task is twofold:

(1) Provide a precise formal definition of representation that is general enough to cover the diverse biological phenomena ordinarily called representational (e.g., genetic coding, signal transduction, neural firing patterns, immunological recognition, hormonal signaling), yet restrictive enough to distinguish a representation R of a target T from arbitrary physical correlations or causal couplings between R and T. The definition should specify the carrier, the represented content, the interpreting subsystem (if any), and the conditions under which the representation can misrepresent.

(2) Using this definition, give a mathematical account of how representation emerges from purely molecular-level dynamics in which individual molecules and their interactions exhibit no intrinsic distinction between "representation" and "thing represented." In particular, exhibit a coarse-graining or scale-transition procedure—mapping a microscopic dynamical description (e.g., a stochastic reaction network or molecular-mechanical system) to a macroscopic effective description—under which a well-defined representational relation appears at the macroscopic level but is absent microscopically, and characterize the conditions on the microscopic dynamics necessary and sufficient for such emergence.

Determine whether such a formalization and emergence theorem can be achieved, or prove obstructions showing that no single formal framework simultaneously satisfies (1) and (2) across the full range of biological representational phenomena.

Recall that a coalgebra for an endofunctor $F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}$ on a category $\mathcal{C}$ is a pair $(X,\gamma)$ consisting of an object $X\in\mathcal{C}$ together with a morphism $\gamma:X\to F(X)$, and that final $F$-coalgebras provide canonical models of self-referential and infinitely-unfolding behaviour (e.g.\ streams, transition systems, non-well-founded sets). A morphism of $F$-coalgebras $(X,\gamma)\to(Y,\delta)$ is a morphism $f:X\to Y$ with $F(f)\circ\gamma=\delta\circ f$.

Coalgebra in this fixed-functor sense describes the dynamics of a system whose "type of observations/transitions" $F$ is held constant. By a structurally evolving system we informally mean a system whose very state-space type changes over time, i.e.\ a family $\{F_t\}_{t\in T}$ of endofunctors indexed by a (possibly continuous or branching) parameter $t$, together with coalgebras $\gamma_t:X_t\to F_t(X_t)$ and coherent comparison data between different indices $t,t'\in T$.

Problem. Develop a mathematically precise framework — for instance based on indexed/fibred categories of coalgebras, lax or oplax natural transformations between the functors $F_t$, or bialgebraic/distributive-law techniques — that simultaneously
(i) retains the universal-property characterisation of self-reference enjoyed by final coalgebras for a single endofunctor, and
(ii) coherently models structural evolution, in which the endofunctor $F_t$ itself, and hence the carrier $X_t$, may change with $t$.
Then determine: to what extent can such a framework faithfully describe self-referential systems undergoing structural evolution? Specifically, identify necessary and sufficient conditions on the family $\{F_t\}$ and on the transition data under which a "final evolving coalgebra" exists and uniquely captures self-referential behaviour across structural change, or, conversely, prove obstructions showing that no such generalisation can preserve both clarity of self-reference and adequacy for structural evolution.

The question concerns developing practical hierarchical modeling frameworks for higher-order evolutionary change (rules changing, and rules-for-changing-rules changing). While related research exists (open-ended evolution, meta-dynamics, compositional/category-theoretic models of biology, e.g., Kauffman's adjacent possible, Andersen-Rasmussen-Sayama meta-dynamics), no widely accepted general practical framework has been established. The problem is broadly regarded as open in the theoretical biology and complex-systems communities.

representations.normalized:
Consider a parametric stochastic dynamical model M(θ) of an evolutionary process whose state space and dynamics admit multiple possible trajectories from a given initial condition (for instance, a model with bifurcating trajectories or branching stochastic dynamics). For a parameter θ in some admissible set Θ, let O(θ) denote the (possibly very large or infinite) set of qualitatively distinct outcomes that the model can produce with positive probability, and let p_θ be the induced probability distribution on O(θ). Suppose we are given an empirical dataset D = {d_1, …, d_N} consisting of observed outcomes from N independent realizations of the real system, where N ≪ |O(θ)| for all θ ∈ Θ; in particular, many outcomes that the model assigns positive probability are not represented in D.

The calibration problem is to choose θ (and to validate the structural form of M) using D. Two failure modes are to be distinguished:

(a) Structural correctness with under-sampling: M(θ*) is structurally correct for some θ* ∈ Θ, and the unobserved outcomes in O(θ*) \ D are genuinely possible-but-unrealized consequences of the true process. Then any calibration procedure that adjusts θ so as to concentrate p_θ on the observed outcomes D (e.g. by maximum likelihood on D treated as exhaustive, or by penalizing outcomes outside D) will mis-calibrate the model and destroy its ability to predict outcomes that could have happened but did not.

(b) Structural incorrectness: no θ ∈ Θ makes M structurally correct, and the would-be outcomes in O(θ) \ D are artifacts of a misspecified model that could not in fact occur in the real system. Then calibration that preserves probability mass on O(θ) \ D will produce a model that predicts impossible outcomes.

Develop a principled methodology — for example, an estimator θ̂(D), a model-validation criterion, or an identifiability theorem — that, given only the dataset D and the model class {M(θ) : θ ∈ Θ}, can either:

(i) consistently calibrate θ while correctly preserving probability mass on possible-but-unobserved outcomes when the model class contains a structurally correct member, and simultaneously
(ii) detect structural incorrectness, i.e. distinguish case (a) from case (b),

or else prove a no-go result showing that, under stated assumptions on (Θ, M, the sampling distribution of D), no procedure depending only on D can asymptotically distinguish (a) from (b) as N grows with N ≪ |O(θ)|.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of calibrating and validating stochastic/dynamical models with many more possible outcomes (e.g. bifurcating trajectories) than available datasets, and of distinguishing structural misspecification from under-sampling of a correct model, is a recognized open problem in the modeling of evolutionary and complex systems. No general-purpose method resolving this identifiability issue appears in the literature; related work on model validation under bifurcations and on simulation-based inference (ABC, neural posterior estimation) addresses parts of the issue but does not resolve the fundamental ambiguity between possible-but-unrealized and impossible outcomes.

[{"title": "Open Questions about Time and Self-reference in Living Systems", "url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11423", "snippet": "This is a problem that already arises in dynamical models with bifurcating trajectories and at present there is no known method for resolving it.", "claim": "The calibration/validation question for evolutionary models with many possible trajectories and few datasets is stated as currently unresolved."}]

Let $\mathcal{N}$ denote the family of univariate normal distributions
$$p(x;\mu,\sigma)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),\qquad \mu\in\mathbb{R},\ \sigma>0.$$
Identify $\mathcal{N}$ with the two-dimensional Lie group $G=\{(\mu,\sigma):\sigma>0\}$ whose group operation is
$$(\mu_1,\sigma_1)\cdot(\mu_2,\sigma_2)=(\mu_1+\sigma_1\mu_2,\ \sigma_1\sigma_2),$$
so that $G$ acts on itself by left translations $L_{(a,b)}(\mu,\sigma)=(a+b\mu,\,b\sigma)$. Equip $G$ with the Fisher information metric
$$g=\frac{d\mu\otimes d\mu+2\,d\sigma\otimes d\sigma}{\sigma^{2}},$$
which is left-invariant under the above action.

An affine connection $\nabla$ on $G$ is called left-invariant if $(L_{(a,b)})_{*}\nabla=\nabla$ for every $(a,b)\in G$. Such a connection $\nabla$ is said to be compatible with $g$ (in the statistical sense) if there exists a dual connection $\nabla^{*}$, also an affine connection on $G$, such that for all vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on $G$,
$$X\,g(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_{X}Y,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_{X}^{*}Z),$$
and such that both $\nabla$ and $\nabla^{*}$ are torsion-free.

Let $\mathcal{C}(G,g)$ denote the set of all left-invariant torsion-free affine connections on $G$ that are compatible with $g$ in this sense. The group of $g$-isometric Lie group automorphisms of $G$ acts on $\mathcal{C}(G,g)$ by pullback.

Determine, with explicit parametrization, the moduli space
$$\mathcal{M}(G,g)=\mathcal{C}(G,g)/\sim,$$
where $\sim$ denotes equivalence under this isometric automorphism action.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem was posed as an open problem at FDIG 2025. A 2025 paper by Furuhata–Inoguchi–Kobayashi establishes that the Amari–Chentsov α-connections are the only left-invariant affine connections on the univariate normal Lie group that are conjugate symmetric with respect to the Fisher metric, and a follow-up preprint (arXiv:2510.04442) studies moduli spaces of left-invariant statistical structures on related Lie groups, focusing on conjugate symmetric and dually flat structures. However, a complete description of the moduli space of all left-invariant Fisher-compatible affine connections on the univariate normal Lie group does not appear to have been carried out, so the problem appears partially solved.

Let $N$ denote the family of nondegenerate multivariate normal distributions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, parametrized by pairs $(\mu,\Sigma)$ with $\mu\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\Sigma$ a symmetric positive-definite $n\times n$ matrix. Endow $N$ with the Lie group structure obtained by identifying $(\mu,\Sigma)$ with the affine transformation $x\mapsto \Sigma^{1/2}x+\mu$, so that the group operation is $(\mu_1,\Sigma_1)\cdot(\mu_2,\Sigma_2)=(\mu_1+\Sigma_1^{1/2}\mu_2,\,\Sigma_1^{1/2}\Sigma_2\Sigma_1^{1/2})$, making $N$ a Lie group of dimension $n+n(n+1)/2$.

On the statistical manifold $N$, define the exponential connection $\nabla^{(e)}$ as the affine connection whose Christoffel symbols vanish in the natural (canonical) parameters $\theta$ of the exponential family representation of the multivariate normal; equivalently, $\nabla^{(e)}$ is the $\alpha=1$ member of Amari's family of $\alpha$-connections, characterized by the fact that the natural parameters of the exponential family form an affine coordinate system.

A semi-Riemannian metric $g$ on $N$ is called left-invariant if for every $h\in N$ the left translation $L_h:N\to N$ is an isometry of $g$. Each semi-Riemannian metric $g$ determines a unique torsion-free metric-compatible affine connection, its Levi-Civita connection $\nabla^g$.

Question: Does there exist a left-invariant semi-Riemannian metric $g$ on $N$ whose Levi-Civita connection $\nabla^g$ equals the exponential connection $\nabla^{(e)}$?

The general problem of characterizing which left-invariant connections on a Lie group are Levi-Civita connections of some left-invariant (semi-)Riemannian metric has been studied (e.g., by Pripoae and collaborators), but the specific case of the exponential connection on the multivariate normal Lie group does not appear to have a documented answer in the literature found.

A Hessian manifold is a triple $(M,\nabla,g)$ consisting of a smooth manifold $M$, a flat affine connection $\nabla$ on $M$, and a Riemannian metric $g$ on $M$ such that, locally around every point, there exist $\nabla$-affine coordinates $(x^1,\dots,x^n)$ and a smooth potential function $\varphi$ with
$$g_{ij} \;=\; \frac{\partial^2 \varphi}{\partial x^i\,\partial x^j}.$$
A standard source of Hessian manifolds is information geometry: given a parametric family of probability distributions $\{p(\,\cdot\,;\theta)\}_{\theta\in\Theta}$, the Fisher information metric on $\Theta$ together with the natural flat connection of an exponential family produces a Hessian structure; for instance, the family of binomial distributions $\mathrm{Bin}(N,\theta)$, $\theta\in(0,1)$, is the canonical example of a 1-dimensional Hessian manifold.

Problem. Classify, up to isomorphism of Hessian manifolds, all connected 1-dimensional Hessian manifolds $(M,\nabla,g)$. In particular, characterize which 1-dimensional Hessian manifolds arise (globally or locally) as statistical manifolds of parametric families of probability distributions, and identify the role of the binomial family within this classification.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Partial results exist: 1-dimensional exponential families on a finite set with constant Hessian sectional curvature have been classified, with binomial families playing the central role. However, a complete classification of all 1-dimensional Hessian manifolds, especially those arising from arbitrary probability distribution families, does not appear to be established in the literature.

Setup. Consider a continuous-time Markov jump process on a finite state space $\mathcal{X}$ with irreducible, reversible (or detailed-balance) transition rate kernel $Q(x,y)$ and invariant measure $\pi$. For probability densities $\rho:\mathcal{X}\to(0,\infty)$ and edge flows $j:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}$, the discrete optimal transport (Maas–Mielke–Chow) framework defines a Riemannian metric on the simplex of probabilities by
$$\|\dot\rho\|_\rho^2 \;=\; \inf_{j}\;\tfrac12\sum_{x,y} \frac{j(x,y)^2}{\theta\!\left(\rho(x)Q(x,y),\rho(y)Q(y,x)\right)} ,$$
where $\theta:(0,\infty)^2\to(0,\infty)$ is a symmetric mean (homogeneous of degree one), and the infimum is over $j$ satisfying the discrete continuity equation $\dot\rho(x)+\sum_y j(x,y)=0$. The choice $\theta(a,b)=\Lambda(a,b):=(a-b)/(\log a-\log b)$ (the logarithmic mean) is distinguished: it makes the heat flow of the Markov generator coincide with the gradient flow of the relative entropy $\mathrm{KL}(\rho\|\pi)$, and it yields a dual pair of dissipation potentials that are both quadratic. More generally, replacing $\Lambda$ by another mean $\theta$ produces a "generalized-mean" optimal-transport theory with its own dual variational structure.

Independently, in classical (parametric) information geometry on a smooth statistical manifold $\mathcal{M}$ of probability measures, Chentsov's theorem characterizes the Fisher–Rao metric and the $\alpha$-connections as the unique (up to scalar) Riemannian metric and family of affine connections that are invariant under sufficient statistics (Markov morphisms). The Kullback–Leibler divergence is the canonical divergence of the dually flat $(\pm 1)$-Amari–Chentsov structure.

Problem. Develop an information-geometric characterization of the discrete optimal-transport framework above that explains, intrinsically:

1. A "Chentsov-type" uniqueness/invariance theorem singling out the logarithmic mean $\Lambda$ among all admissible symmetric means $\theta$ used to define the metric tensor on the simplex, analogous to the way Chentsov's theorem singles out the Fisher metric.

2. An interpretation of the special role of the relative entropy $\mathrm{KL}(\rho\|\pi)$ in the $\Lambda$-based theory as the canonical divergence of a dually flat structure, paralleling its role in classical information geometry.

3. For a generalized mean $\theta\neq\Lambda$, an associated pair of dual affine connections (an "Amari–Chentsov-type" $\pm$ structure) on the space of probability densities and edge flows, together with a canonical divergence whose Bregman/Hessian geometry recovers the dual variational structure of the $\theta$-optimal transport.

Prove or disprove the existence of such an information-geometric framework that uniformly accounts for the variants of optimal transport for Markov jump processes, and identify the resulting invariance principle that selects the logarithmic mean.

Let $\mathcal{S}$ denote the manifold of faithful density operators on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$. A monotone (quantum Fisher) Riemannian metric on $\mathcal{S}$ is, by Petz's classification, in one-to-one correspondence with an operator monotone function $f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ satisfying $f(1)=1$ and $f(t)=tf(1/t)$, via the formula
$$\langle A,B\rangle_\rho^f = \mathrm{Tr}\bigl(A^*\, c_f(L_\rho,R_\rho)^{-1}\, B\bigr),\qquad c_f(x,y)=y\,f(x/y),$$
where $L_\rho$ and $R_\rho$ denote left and right multiplication by $\rho$, and $A,B$ are tangent vectors at $\rho$ (traceless self-adjoint operators). Each such $f$ corresponds to an operator mean $m_f(x,y)=c_f(x,y)$ in the sense of Kubo–Ando, and one obtains a wide variety of monotone metrics by choosing $f$ to be a "generalized mean" (e.g. arithmetic, geometric, harmonic, logarithmic, power means).

Problem: Construct an information-geometric framework — comprising a manifold structure, a family of (possibly non-symmetric) divergences, and a pair of dually coupled affine connections $(\nabla, \nabla^*)$ with respect to a Riemannian metric $g$ — that simultaneously realizes the entire family $\{\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle^f_\rho\}_f$ of generalized-mean quantum Fisher metrics on $\mathcal{S}$ as instances of a single unified construction, in such a way that the classical dualistic structure of Amari–Chentsov is recovered in commutative limits and the standard (SLD, BKM, right-logarithmic-derivative, geometric-mean) cases appear as distinguished members of the family.

Setup. Let $\mathcal{H}_A$ and $\mathcal{H}_B$ be finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces of dimensions $m$ and $n$, and let $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{H})$ denote the set of (full-rank) density matrices on $\mathcal{H}$, i.e. positive-definite Hermitian operators of unit trace. A completely positive trace-preserving map (or, more generally, a completely positive map specified by Kraus operators) $\Phi:\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_A)\to \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_B)$ is said to be doubly stochastic if it preserves the maximally mixed state and its adjoint does as well. The operator Sinkhorn algorithm (Gurvits' operator scaling) takes as input a completely positive map $\Phi$ and iteratively rescales it by alternately conjugating with positive-definite operators $L\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_A)$ and $R\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_B)$ so that $\Phi(I)$ and $\Phi^{*}(I)$ are alternately driven to the identity; i.e. it produces a sequence of scalings converging (when scalable) to a doubly stochastic map.

For ordinary (commutative) matrix scaling, the Sinkhorn iteration is well known to coincide with alternating minimization of the Kullback–Leibler divergence
$$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=\sum_{i,j} P_{ij}\log\frac{P_{ij}}{Q_{ij}}-P_{ij}+Q_{ij}$$
over the affine sets of nonnegative matrices with prescribed row sums and prescribed column sums, respectively.

Question. Does there exist a divergence $D(\rho\|\sigma)$ defined on pairs of (full-rank) density matrices — for instance a quantum analogue of the Kullback–Leibler divergence such as the Umegaki relative entropy, the Belavkin–Staszewski relative entropy, or any other smooth contrast function on $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{H}_A)\times\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{H}_B)$ (or on the space of completely positive maps) — such that the operator Sinkhorn algorithm coincides with alternating minimization of $D$ over two suitable affine (or e-flat) families associated with the marginal constraints $\Phi(I)=I$ and $\Phi^{*}(I)=I$?

Equivalently, given that the space of density matrices, equipped with the natural dually flat structures coming from quantum information geometry, has non-vanishing torsion, determine whether the operator Sinkhorn iteration admits a representation as alternating $D$-projections for some divergence $D$, or prove that no such divergence exists.

Background. In classical information geometry, a statistical manifold is endowed with a Riemannian metric $g$ together with a pair of torsion-free affine connections $
abla$ and $
abla^{*}$ that are mutually dual with respect to $g$, meaning that for all vector fields $X,Y,Z$,
$$Xg(Y,Z)=g(
abla_{X}Y,Z)+g(Y,
abla^{*}_{X}Z).$$
For such a dualistic structure, when the manifold is dually flat one can introduce a canonical (Bregman-type) divergence $D$ and prove the generalized Pythagorean theorem: if $p,q,r$ are points such that the $
abla$-geodesic from $q$ to $p$ is $g$-orthogonal at $q$ to the $
abla^{*}$-geodesic from $q$ to $r$, then
$$D(p\,\Vert\,r)=D(p\,\Vert\,q)+D(q\,\Vert\,r).$$

Problem. Formulate and prove an analogue of the generalized Pythagorean theorem in a setting where one is given a smooth manifold equipped with a divergence (or, more generally, a contrast/yoke function) but where one does not assume the existence of a pair of mutually dual affine connections. Specifically, identify intrinsic geometric data (replacing the dual pair $(
abla,
abla^{*})$) — for instance derived directly from the divergence, from a single connection together with auxiliary structure, or from a generalized notion of orthogonality — under which a decomposition identity of Pythagorean type
$$D(p\,\Vert\,r)=D(p\,\Vert\,q)+D(q\,\Vert\,r)$$
(or a suitable generalization thereof) holds for triples $(p,q,r)$ satisfying an appropriate orthogonality condition at $q$.

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold equipped with a family of torsion-free affine connections $\{
abla^{(\alpha)}\}_{\alpha\in\mathbb{R}}$ such that, writing $
abla^{(0)}$ for the Levi-Civita connection of $g$ and $T$ for a totally symmetric $(0,3)$-tensor (the Amari–Chentsov tensor), one has
$$g(
abla^{(\alpha)}_X Y, Z) \;=\; g(
abla^{(0)}_X Y, Z) \;-\; 	frac{\alpha}{2}\, T(X,Y,Z)$$
for all vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on $M$. The connections $
abla^{(\alpha)}$ and $
abla^{(-\alpha)}$ are mutually dual with respect to $g$. The triple $(M,g,
abla^{(\alpha)})$ is called a statistical manifold; it is dually flat (for the parameter $\alpha$) if both $
abla^{(\alpha)}$ and $
abla^{(-\alpha)}$ are flat (zero curvature and torsion). When $M$ is a parametric family of probability distributions, $g$ the Fisher information metric, and $T$ the Amari–Chentsov skewness tensor, the structure is moreover required to be invariant under sufficient statistics (i.e., invariant in the sense of Chentsov).

Question: Exhibit a non-trivial example of an invariant statistical manifold $(M,g,
abla^{(\alpha)})$ that is dually flat for some value $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ with $\alpha
eq \pm 1$, or prove that no such example exists beyond the classical exponential/mixture ($\alpha=\pm 1$) cases.

Let $X$ be a Polish space (a separable, completely metrizable topological space) equipped with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and let $\mathcal{P}(X)$ denote the space of Borel probability measures on $X$, endowed with the topology of weak convergence. Fix a reference probability measure $\mu \in \mathcal{P}(X)$ and let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be i.i.d. random variables with law $\mu$. Two classical large-deviation principles concerning the empirical data are:

(i) Sanov's theorem: the empirical measures $L_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \delta_{X_i} \in \mathcal{P}(X)$ satisfy a large-deviation principle on $\mathcal{P}(X)$ with rate function the relative entropy $H(\nu \,\|\, \mu) = \int \log\!\frac{d\nu}{d\mu}\, d\nu$ (with $H(\nu\|\mu) = +\infty$ when $\nu \not\ll \mu$).

(ii) Cramér's theorem: when $X$ is a separable Banach space and $\mathbb{E}\,e^{\langle \xi, X_1\rangle} < \infty$ for all $\xi$ in the dual, the empirical means $S_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ satisfy a large-deviation principle with rate function the Cramér transform $\Lambda^*(x) = \sup_{\xi}\bigl\{\langle \xi, x\rangle - \log \mathbb{E}\,e^{\langle \xi, X_1\rangle}\bigr\}$.

Both rate functions are convex, lower semicontinuous functionals on infinite-dimensional spaces and are linked by a Legendre-type duality.

Question. Construct, or prove the impossibility of, an intrinsic infinite-dimensional differential-geometric structure on $\mathcal{P}(X)$ (respectively on the Banach space $X$) — for example, a Banach/Fréchet manifold structure together with a (possibly degenerate) Riemannian or dually-flat affine connection pair $(\nabla, \nabla^*)$ in the sense of information geometry — such that:

(a) the relative entropy $H(\,\cdot\,\|\,\mu)$ arises as the canonical divergence (or contrast function) associated with this structure, recovering Sanov's rate function as a geometric object on $\mathcal{P}(X)$;

(b) the Cramér rate function $\Lambda^*$ arises as the Legendre dual potential under the dually-flat (or analogous) structure, recovering Cramér's rate function on $X$;

(c) the duality between Sanov's and Cramér's theorems is realized as the duality between the two flat connections (or analogous geometric duality) in this infinite-dimensional setting, extending the finite-dimensional dually-flat exponential/mixture geometry of Amari–Chentsov to arbitrary Polish sample spaces.

Determine whether such a unifying infinite-dimensional differential-geometric framework underlies the functional-analytic extensions of Sanov's and Cramér's theorems on Polish spaces.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$ be a measurable sample space (typically infinite, e.g. $\Omega=\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Borel $\sigma$-algebra) and let $\mathcal{P}(\Omega)$ denote a suitable space of probability measures on $\Omega$ that admits the structure of an infinite-dimensional Banach (or Fréchet) manifold in the sense of information geometry — for instance the Pistone–Sempi exponential statistical manifold, where $\mathcal{P}_\mu = \{p\,\mu : p>0,\ \int p\,d\mu=1\}$ is modeled on Orlicz spaces with the Young function $\Phi(x)=\cosh(x)-1$, equipped with the Fisher–Rao metric and the dual exponential/mixture connections $\nabla^{(e)}, \nabla^{(m)}$.

A finite-dimensional statistical model is a smooth injective immersion $\iota: \Theta \hookrightarrow \mathcal{P}(\Omega)$ from an open set $\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, so that $\iota(\Theta)$ is a $d$-dimensional submanifold of $\mathcal{P}(\Omega)$.

Problem. Develop a framework in which finite-dimensional statistical models on infinite sample spaces are systematically studied as submanifolds of such an infinite-dimensional manifold $\mathcal{P}(\Omega)$, and determine whether this viewpoint yields genuine simplifications or new insights for probabilistic and statistical questions about those models. Concretely:

(a) Identify natural geometric invariants of the embedding $\iota(\Theta)\subset\mathcal{P}(\Omega)$ — such as the second fundamental form with respect to $\nabla^{(e)}$ and $\nabla^{(m)}$, the normal bundle, and curvature of the ambient manifold restricted to $\iota(\Theta)$ — and relate them to classical statistical quantities (efficiency, information loss, robustness, asymptotic expansions of estimators).

(b) Show whether projection operators (e.g. $m$- or $e$-projections from $\mathcal{P}(\Omega)$ onto $\iota(\Theta)$) provide a unified treatment of maximum likelihood estimation, model misspecification, and the EM algorithm that is strictly more transparent than purely finite-dimensional parametric arguments.

(c) Exhibit at least one concrete probabilistic or statistical statement about a finite-dimensional model on an infinite sample space whose proof is materially simplified, or whose conclusion is strengthened, by viewing the model as a submanifold of $\mathcal{P}(\Omega)$ rather than as an abstract finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold.

Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space and let $\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H})$ denote the manifold of strictly positive (invertible) density operators on $\mathcal{H}$, i.e., self-adjoint positive-definite operators of unit trace. The tangent space $T_\rho \mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H})$ at $\rho \in \mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H})$ is naturally identified with the space of traceless self-adjoint operators on $\mathcal{H}$.

Equip $\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H})$ with:
(i) a monotone Riemannian metric $g$, i.e., a Riemannian metric whose induced distance is contractive under every completely positive trace-preserving map (such metrics are classified, up to normalization, by Petz's theorem via operator-monotone functions);
(ii) the m-connection $\nabla^{(m)}$, defined as the flat affine connection inherited from the natural embedding $\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H}) \hookrightarrow \{A = A^* : \operatorname{tr} A = 1\}$ as an affine subspace of self-adjoint operators;
(iii) the e-connection $\nabla^{(e)}$, defined as the dual connection of $\nabla^{(m)}$ with respect to $g$, in the sense that for all vector fields $X, Y, Z$,
$$X\, g(Y,Z) = g(\nabla^{(m)}_X Y, Z) + g(Y, \nabla^{(e)}_X Z).$$

A submanifold $M \subseteq \mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H})$ is called $\nabla^{(e)}$-autoparallel if for every pair of vector fields $X, Y$ tangent to $M$, the covariant derivative $\nabla^{(e)}_X Y$ is also tangent to $M$.

Determine all $\nabla^{(e)}$-autoparallel submanifolds of $\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H})$. Equivalently, characterize the pairs $(\rho, V)$, where $\rho \in \mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H})$ and $V$ is a linear subspace of $T_\rho \mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H})$, for which there exists a $\nabla^{(e)}$-autoparallel submanifold of $\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H})$ passing through $\rho$ with tangent space $V$ at $\rho$.

The problem is posed as an open problem in quantum information geometry. Existing literature (notably work on autoparallelity of quantum statistical manifolds) emphasizes that, unlike the classical case, the quantum e-connection generally has non-vanishing torsion, creating obstructions to the existence of e-autoparallel submanifolds; partial results exist for specific monotone metrics (e.g., SLD, BKM), but a general characterization of admissible pairs $(\rho, V)$ remains unresolved.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a measurable space with a $\sigma$-finite reference measure $\nu$, and let $T:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^d$ be a measurable statistic. The associated exponential family is the set of probability densities
$$p_\theta(x)=\exp\bigl(\langle \theta, T(x)\rangle - \psi(\theta)\bigr),\qquad \theta\in\Theta,$$
where $\Theta=\{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^d : \psi(\theta):=\log\int_\mathcal{X}\exp\langle\theta,T(x)\rangle\,d\nu(x)<\infty\}$ is the natural parameter space (which is always convex), and the expectation parameter space is
$$M=\{\mathbb{E}_\theta[T(X)] : \theta\in\Theta\}\subset\mathbb{R}^d.$$
While in standard regular cases $M$ is open and convex, there exist exponential families for which $M$ fails to be convex.

Develop a systematic theory describing the class of exponential families whose expectation parameter space $M$ is non-convex. In particular: characterize, in terms of the sufficient statistic $T$, the dominating measure $\nu$, and the geometry of $\Theta$, necessary and sufficient conditions under which $M$ is non-convex; describe the possible topological and geometric shapes that $M$ can take in such cases; and analyze the consequences of non-convexity for maximum likelihood estimation, the existence and uniqueness of the MLE, and the information-geometric structure (dual flatness, Bregman divergence, Legendre transform $\theta\leftrightarrow\mu$) of the family.

Let $\mathcal{E} = \{p_\theta(x) = \exp(\langle \theta, t(x)\rangle - F(\theta))\,h(x) : \theta \in \Theta\}$ be an exponential family on a measurable space $(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{B}, \mu)$, where $t : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}^d$ is the sufficient statistic, $h \geq 0$ is a base measure density, and
$$\Theta = \{\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d : F(\theta) := \log \int_\mathcal{X} \exp(\langle \theta, t(x)\rangle)\, h(x)\, d\mu(x) < \infty\}$$
is the natural parameter space (which is convex). The expectation parameter space is
$$M = \{\eta(\theta) := \nabla F(\theta) : \theta \in \mathrm{int}(\Theta)\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d.$$
The family $\mathcal{E}$ is called steep when $\|\nabla F(\theta_n)\| \to \infty$ for every sequence $\theta_n \in \mathrm{int}(\Theta)$ converging to a boundary point of $\Theta$; equivalently, $M$ equals the interior of the convex hull of the support of the pushforward of $\mu$ under $t$. When $\mathcal{E}$ is steep, $M$ is automatically convex; when $\mathcal{E}$ is non-steep, $M$ may fail to be convex.

Provide a complete geometric and topological characterization of the possible shapes of the expectation parameter space $M$ that can arise from non-steep exponential families, both in the bounded case and in the unbounded case. Specifically, determine which subsets of $\mathbb{R}^d$ are realizable as $M = \nabla F(\mathrm{int}(\Theta))$ for some non-steep exponential family.

General references on exponential families establish that the natural parameter space is always convex and that the expectation parameter space coincides with the interior of the convex hull of the support exactly when the family is steep. For non-steep exponential families, the expectation parameter space can be non-convex, but no general characterization of the possible shapes (bounded or unbounded) appears in the standard literature, and the question is posed as an open problem.

$$p_\kappa(x;\theta)=\exp_\kappa\!\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n\theta^i F_i(x)-\psi_\kappa(\theta)\Big),\qquad \theta\in\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^n,$$
together with its induced information geometry (Fisher–Rao metric, dual affine connections, divergence, etc.).

Question: Provide a systematic framework in which the deformation parameter $\kappa$ itself is treated as an additional coordinate of the statistical manifold, so that one studies the enlarged $(n+1)$-parameter family $\{p_\kappa(x;\theta):(\theta,\kappa)\in\Theta\times K\}$. $$p(x;\theta) = \exp_\lambda\!\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n \theta^i F_i(x) - \psi(\theta)\Big),$$

Form the disjoint union
$$M = \bigsqcup_\lambda M_\lambda,$$
viewed as a foliated manifold whose leaves are the individual $\lambda$-exponential families.

(i) restricts on each leaf $M_\lambda$ to the deformed information geometry of the $\lambda$-exponential family, and
(ii) is genuinely useful for problems of statistical inference across leaves (such as estimation, model selection, or hypothesis testing involving the deformation parameter $\lambda$)?

Background. Recall that the 2-Wasserstein distance between two Borel probability measures μ, ν on R^n with finite second moments is

  W_2(μ, ν)^2 = inf_{π ∈ Π(μ,ν)} ∫_{R^n × R^n} |x − y|^2 dπ(x, y),

where Π(μ, ν) denotes the set of couplings of μ and ν. The set P_2(R^n) of such measures, equipped with W_2, is a metric space (the Wasserstein space) on which a rich infinite-dimensional Riemannian-type geometry has been developed (formal Riemannian metric on tangent spaces of absolutely continuous measures, Otto calculus, geodesics given by displacement interpolation, etc.).

The subspace G(n) of nondegenerate Gaussian measures N(m, Σ) on R^n (with m ∈ R^n and Σ ∈ Sym_+^n positive definite) is a totally geodesic, finite-dimensional submanifold of P_2(R^n). On G(n), the 2-Wasserstein distance has the closed form

  W_2(N(m_1, Σ_1), N(m_2, Σ_2))^2 = |m_1 − m_2|^2 + tr(Σ_1 + Σ_2 − 2(Σ_1^{1/2} Σ_2 Σ_1^{1/2})^{1/2}),

and G(n) carries an explicit Riemannian metric (the Bures–Wasserstein metric on Sym_+^n combined with the Euclidean metric on R^n), with explicit geodesics, curvature, exponential and logarithm maps, and barycenter theory.

A probability measure μ on R^n is called elliptical with location m ∈ R^n, scatter Σ ∈ Sym_+^n, and radial generator (a probability law ρ on [0, ∞)) if μ is the law of m + Σ^{1/2} R U, where U is uniform on the unit sphere S^{n−1} and R ∼ ρ is independent of U. Fix a radial law ρ with finite second moment, and let E_ρ(n) ⊂ P_2(R^n) be the family of all elliptical distributions on R^n with this generator ρ, parametrized by (m, Σ) ∈ R^n × Sym_+^n.

Problem. Develop a Wasserstein geometry of E_ρ(n) parallel to that of the Gaussian submanifold G(n). In particular, address the following:

(i) Show that E_ρ(n) is a totally geodesic submanifold of (P_2(R^n), W_2), and identify the W_2-geodesics within E_ρ(n) explicitly in terms of (m, Σ).

(ii) Derive a closed-form expression for W_2(μ_1, μ_2) when μ_1, μ_2 ∈ E_ρ(n), as a function of (m_1, Σ_1), (m_2, Σ_2), and the moments of ρ.

(iii) Equip E_ρ(n) with the induced Riemannian metric and compute its sectional curvature, exponential and logarithm maps, and Wasserstein barycenters of finite families of elliptical measures.

(iv) Determine to what extent the Otto-type formal Riemannian structure, the displacement convexity of standard functionals (entropy, potential, interaction energies), and gradient-flow formulations on the Gaussian submanifold extend to E_ρ(n), and identify any genuinely non-Gaussian phenomena.

Several aspects of the proposed program are already known: the 2-Wasserstein distance between two elliptical distributions sharing the same radial generator admits a closed form involving the Bures metric on covariance matrices (analogous to the Gaussian case), and this has been used in applied work on elliptical embeddings and elliptical processes. Let $N\ge 3$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be a smoothly bounded domain, and let $2^*=	frac{2N}{N-2}$ denote the critical Sobolev exponent. Consider the Brezis–Nirenberg problem
$$-\Delta u=\lambda u+|u|^{2^*-2}u\ 	ext{in }\Omega,\qquad u=0\ 	ext{on }\partial\Omega,$$
with parameter $\lambda>0$. In the special case $N=3$ and $\Omega=B(0,1)\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ (the open unit ball), it is known that for every $\lambda>0$ there exist infinitely many non-radial sign-changing solutions; the existing proof of this fact is constructive and uses a Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction with sign-changing nodal bubbles built from solutions of the Yamabe problem.

Provide a direct variational proof of the following statement: for $N=3$, $\Omega=B(0,1)$, and every $\lambda>0$, the above problem admits infinitely many non-radial sign-changing weak solutions $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. Specifically, construct (e.g., via a min–max/critical point scheme on a suitable subspace of $H^1_0(B(0,1))$ invariant under a nontrivial subgroup of $O(3)$ that excludes radial symmetry) an unbounded sequence of critical values of the energy functional
$$J_\lambda(u)=	frac12\int_{B(0,1)}|
abla u|^2\,dx-	frac{\lambda}{2}\int_{B(0,1)}u^2\,dx-	frac{1}{2^*}\int_{B(0,1)}|u|^{2^*}\,dx,$$
whose corresponding critical points are non-radial and sign-changing, without relying on a perturbative reduction argument.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a bounded domain (which may be assumed convex if necessary), and let $2^* = 6$ denote the critical Sobolev exponent in dimension three. Consider the Brezis–Nirenberg problem
$$
\begin{cases}
-\Delta u = \lambda u + |u|^{2^*-2} u & \text{in } \Omega, \\
u = 0 & \text{on } \partial\Omega.
\end{cases}
$$
A weak solution $u \in H_0^1(\Omega)$ is called sign-changing if both $u^+ = \max(u,0)$ and $u^- = \max(-u,0)$ are nontrivial. The energy of a solution is
$$
E(u) = \frac{1}{2}\int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2 \, dx - \frac{\lambda}{2}\int_\Omega u^2\, dx - \frac{1}{2^*}\int_\Omega |u|^{2^*}\, dx.
$$
Prove or disprove: for every $\lambda > 0$, the problem above admits infinitely many sign-changing solutions whose energies are unbounded above.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^4$ be a bounded smooth domain, and consider the Brezis–Nirenberg problem at the critical Sobolev exponent $2^* = \frac{2N}{N-2} = 4$ in dimension $N=4$:
$$
\begin{cases}
-\Delta u = \lambda u + |u|^{2}u & \text{in } \Omega,\\
u = 0 & \text{on } \partial\Omega,
\end{cases}
$$
where $\lambda > 0$ is a real parameter. Let $\sigma(-\Delta)$ denote the Dirichlet spectrum of $-\Delta$ on $\Omega$, i.e. the set of eigenvalues of $-\Delta$ acting on $H^1_0(\Omega)$. A weak solution $u \in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is called sign-changing if both $u^+ = \max(u,0)$ and $u^- = \max(-u,0)$ are nontrivial.

It is known that for every $\lambda > 0$ with $\lambda \notin \sigma(-\Delta)$ the above problem admits a sign-changing solution.

Question: For every $\lambda \in \sigma(-\Delta)$ with $\lambda > 0$, does the problem above admit a sign-changing solution?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

For N ≥ 7, Schechter–Zou established infinitely many sign-changing solutions for all λ > 0. For low dimensions N ∈ {4,5,6}, only finitely many solutions (at least N+1 pairs, by Devillanova–Solimini and Clapp–Weth) are known, with no information on their nodal nature. Recent works (e.g., on dimension six) explicitly list this as an open question, and the problem of whether infinitely many sign-changing solutions exist on a general bounded domain when N ≤ 6 remains open.

$$-\Delta u = \lambda u + |u|^{2^*-2}u \ \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad u=0 \ \text{ on } \partial\Omega,$$
where $2^* = 6$ is the critical Sobolev exponent in dimension three. The associated energy functional is
$$E_\lambda(u) = \frac{1}{2}\int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2\,dx - \frac{\lambda}{2}\int_\Omega u^2\,dx - \frac{1}{6}\int_\Omega |u|^6\,dx.$$
A family $\{u_\lambda\}$ of solutions is said to blow up with finite energy at a fixed parameter $\bar\lambda \in (0,\lambda_1(\Omega))$ if
$$\|u_\lambda\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)} \to +\infty \quad \text{and} \quad E_\lambda(u_\lambda) \text{ remains bounded as } \lambda \to \bar\lambda.$$
Druet has identified a specific threshold value $\lambda^*=\lambda^*(\Omega) \in (0,\lambda_1(\Omega))$ at which finite-energy single blow-up can occur in dimension three.

Question: Does there exist a bounded smooth domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ (possibly required to be convex) and a value $\bar\lambda \neq \lambda^*(\Omega)$ for which one can construct a family of solutions $u_\lambda$ to the Brezis–Nirenberg problem above that blows up with finite energy at $\bar\lambda$?

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be a bounded smooth domain with $N\ge 7$, and let $2^*=\frac{2N}{N-2}$ denote the critical Sobolev exponent. Consider the Brezis–Nirenberg problem
$$-\Delta u = \lambda u + |u|^{2^*-2}u \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u=0 \quad \text{on } \partial\Omega,$$
where $\lambda>0$ is a real parameter. The associated energy functional is
$$E_\lambda(u) = \frac{1}{2}\int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2\,dx - \frac{\lambda}{2}\int_\Omega u^2\,dx - \frac{1}{2^*}\int_\Omega |u|^{2^*}\,dx, \qquad u\in H^1_0(\Omega).$$

The question of whether finite-energy blow-up solutions to the Brezis–Nirenberg problem exist at a fixed positive parameter in dimensions $N\ge 7$ on a general (possibly convex) bounded domain is explicitly listed as open. Let $N \geq 3$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ be a bounded smooth domain (which may be assumed convex, or even strictly star-shaped, if needed), and let $2^* = \frac{2N}{N-2}$ denote the critical Sobolev exponent. Consider the Brezis–Nirenberg problem
$$
\begin{cases}
-\Delta u = \lambda u + |u|^{2^*-2} u & \text{in } \Omega,\\
u = 0 & \text{on } \partial \Omega,
\end{cases}
$$
with parameter $\lambda > 0$ fixed. Suppose $(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a family of (possibly sign-changing) weak solutions of this problem at a fixed $\lambda > 0$ that blows up, i.e. $\|u_n\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)} \to \infty$, while having uniformly bounded energy
$$
E(u_n) = \frac{1}{2}\int_\Omega |\nabla u_n|^2 \, dx - \frac{\lambda}{2}\int_\Omega u_n^2 \, dx - \frac{1}{2^*}\int_\Omega |u_n|^{2^*}\, dx \leq C < \infty.
$$
Determine the complete asymptotic behavior of such finite-energy blow-up sequences: classify the possible numbers, locations, signs, and profiles of the bubbles, the rates at which their concentration parameters degenerate, and the relationships these quantities satisfy with $\lambda$ and the geometry of $\Omega$ (in particular, the Robin function of $\Omega$).

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ be a bounded smooth domain (possibly with nontrivial topology) and consider the Brezis–Nirenberg problem
$$ -\Delta u = \lambda u + |u|^{2^*-2} u \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \quad \text{on } \partial\Omega, $$
where $2^* = 2N/(N-2)$ is the critical Sobolev exponent. For $\mu > 0$ and $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^N$, let
$$ W_{\mu,\xi}(x) = \alpha_N \left( \frac{\mu}{\mu^2 + |x-\xi|^2} \right)^{(N-2)/2} $$
denote the standard Aubin–Talenti bubbles (with the normalizing constant $\alpha_N = (N(N-2))^{(N-2)/4}$ that makes $W_{\mu,\xi}$ a positive solution of $-\Delta W = W^{2^*-1}$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$).

Fix $N \ge 6$ and a parameter $\lambda \ge 0$ (in the admissible range so that $-\Delta - \lambda$ is coercive on $H_0^1(\Omega)$). Question: Does there exist a sign-changing solution $u_\lambda \in H_0^1(\Omega)$ of the above problem of the form
$$ u_\lambda \;\approx\; u_0 \;-\; \sum_{j=1}^{k} W_{\mu_j(\lambda),\,\xi_j(\lambda)}, $$
where $u_0$ is a fixed (positive or sign-changing) solution of the same equation, $k \ge 1$, $\mu_j(\lambda) \to 0$, and the concentration points $\xi_j(\lambda)$ approach the boundary $\partial\Omega$ (i.e. $\mathrm{dist}(\xi_j(\lambda), \partial\Omega) \to 0$)?

Equivalently: construct sign-changing solutions of the Brezis–Nirenberg problem exhibiting boundary concentration at a fixed value of $\lambda \ge 0$ in dimensions $N \ge 6$.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ be a bounded smooth domain with $N \geq 4$, and consider the Brezis–Nirenberg problem
$$-\Delta u = \lambda u + |u|^{2^*-2} u \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \text{ on } \partial \Omega,$$
where $2^* = \frac{2N}{N-2}$ is the critical Sobolev exponent and $\lambda > 0$. A "bubble-tower sign-changing solution blowing up at a point $x_0 \in \Omega$" is a family $\{u_\lambda\}$ of sign-changing solutions which, as $\lambda \to 0^+$, decomposes as
$$u_\lambda(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{k} (-1)^{j+1}\, \alpha_N\, \mu_{j,\lambda}^{(N-2)/2}\bigl(\mu_{j,\lambda}^2 |x-x_0|^2 + 1\bigr)^{-(N-2)/2} + o(1)$$
in $H_0^1(\Omega)$, with $k \geq 2$ concentration parameters satisfying $\mu_{1,\lambda},\dots,\mu_{k,\lambda} \to \infty$ and $\mu_{j+1,\lambda}/\mu_{j,\lambda} \to \infty$ (so at least two bubbles concentrate at the same point $x_0$ on different scales), where $\alpha_N$ is the standard normalization constant for the Aubin–Talenti bubbles.

Prove or disprove: for every bounded smooth domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$, bubble-tower sign-changing solutions of the above form (with at least two bubbles concentrating at a common point) can exist as $\lambda \to 0^+$ only if $N \geq 7$.

The conjecture is partially established. Iacopetti and Pacella proved nonexistence of bubble-tower sign-changing solutions (with two bubbles at the same point) in low dimensions N=4,5,6 as λ→0. Existence constructions of such tower-of-two-bubbles sign-changing solutions are known for N≥7 (e.g., in symmetric/general domains). However, ruling out bubble-towers with more than two bubbles at the same point in arbitrary bounded domains in low dimensions, and the full statement of the conjecture in general domains, does not appear to have been completely settled in the literature available through 2025.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^4$ be a bounded domain with smooth boundary (which may be assumed convex, or even strictly star-shaped, if necessary). Consider the Brezis–Nirenberg problem in dimension $N=4$:
$$-\Delta u = \lambda u + |u|^{2^*-2}u \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \quad \text{on } \partial\Omega,$$
where $2^* = \tfrac{2N}{N-2} = 4$ is the critical Sobolev exponent. Let $\sigma(-\Delta)$ denote the Dirichlet spectrum of $-\Delta$ on $\Omega$, i.e., the sequence of eigenvalues $0<\lambda_1<\lambda_2\le\lambda_3\le\cdots$ of $-\Delta$ with zero boundary conditions on $\Omega$.

The associated energy functional on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is
$$I_\lambda(u) = \tfrac{1}{2}\int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2\,dx - \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\int_\Omega u^2\,dx - \tfrac{1}{4}\int_\Omega u^4\,dx.$$
Define the sign-changing Nehari manifold
$$\mathcal{M}_\lambda = \bigl\{u\in H^1_0(\Omega):\, u^\pm\not\equiv 0,\; \langle I'_\lambda(u),u^+\rangle = \langle I'_\lambda(u),u^-\rangle = 0\bigr\},$$
where $u^+=\max\{u,0\}$ and $u^-=\min\{u,0\}$. A function $\hat u\in\mathcal{M}_\lambda$ is called a least-energy sign-changing solution if $\hat u$ is a critical point of $I_\lambda$ with $\hat u^\pm\not\equiv 0$ and
$$I_\lambda(\hat u) = \inf\{I_\lambda(u):\, u\in\mathcal{M}_\lambda\}.$$

Question: For every $\lambda\in\sigma(-\Delta)$, does there exist a least-energy sign-changing solution of the above problem?

A locally finite graded poset $P$ with minimum element $\hat{0}$ is called an $r$-differential poset (for a positive integer $r$) if it satisfies the following conditions:
1. $P$ has a unique minimum element $\hat{0}$, every maximal chain from $\hat{0}$ to a given element has the same length, and every rank $P_n = \{x \in P : \mathrm{rank}(x) = n\}$ is finite.
2. For every pair of distinct elements $x, y \in P$, the number of elements that cover both $x$ and $y$ equals the number of elements covered by both $x$ and $y$.
3. For every $x \in P$, if $x$ covers exactly $k$ elements of $P$, then $x$ is covered by exactly $k + r$ elements of $P$.

Equivalently, letting $U, D : \mathbb{Z}P \to \mathbb{Z}P$ be the linear up- and down-operators on the free abelian group on $P$, $P$ is $r$-differential if and only if $DU - UD = r \cdot I$.

Standard examples include Young's lattice (which is $1$-differential), the Young–Fibonacci lattice (which is $1$-differential), and finite Cartesian products of $r_i$-differential posets (which are $(\sum r_i)$-differential).

Problem: Classify all $r$-differential posets, for every positive integer $r$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is widely regarded as open. There are uncountably many 1-differential posets (Lewis, 2007), making a clean classification of general differential posets unlikely. Even the restricted question of classifying $r$-differential lattices for $r \ge 1$ remains open: it is unknown whether any $r$-differential lattice exists other than products of Young's lattice and the Young–Fibonacci lattice.

A shifted standard Young tableau of size n is a filling of the shifted Young diagram of a strict partition λ = (λ₁ > λ₂ > ⋯ > λₖ > 0) with λ₁ + ⋯ + λₖ = n (the diagram has row i indented i−1 places to the right and contains λᵢ boxes) by the integers 1, 2, …, n, each used exactly once, such that entries strictly increase along every row and every column.

Build a rooted tree T whose vertices are all shifted standard Young tableaux of all sizes n ≥ 0, where the root is the unique empty tableau (n = 0), and the parent of a shifted standard Young tableau S of size n ≥ 1 is the shifted standard Young tableau of size n−1 obtained by deleting the box containing the entry n from S. (Equivalently, vertices are ordered by containment of the underlying labeled fillings, and the tree structure is generated by this containment.) The rank of a vertex is its size n; for a vertex v, let cₖ(v) denote the number of descendants of v at rank rank(v) + k for each k ≥ 0, and call the sequence (cₖ(v))_{k≥0} the census of the subtree rooted at v.

Resolve the following two assertions:

(a) The only automorphism of T, viewed as an unlabeled rooted tree, is the identity.

(b) Every vertex v of T is uniquely determined among all vertices of T by the census (cₖ(v))_{k≥0} of the subtree rooted at v.

representations.normalized:
Background. A graded poset $P = \bigsqcup_{n\ge 0} P_n$ with $|P_0|=1$ is called $r$-differential (in the sense of Fomin/Stanley) if its up- and down-operators $U,D\colon \mathbb{C}P \to \mathbb{C}P$, defined by $Ux = \sum_{y \gtrdot x} y$ and $Dx = \sum_{y \lessdot x} y$, satisfy $DU - UD = r\,\mathrm{Id}$. The Young lattice $\mathbb{Y}^{(r)}$ consisting of all integer partitions with at most $r$ rows, ordered by inclusion of Young diagrams, is known to be $r$-differential. From the general theory of $r$-differential posets one obtains an RSK-type bijection between $r$-colored permutations of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ (i.e., pairs $(\sigma, c)$ where $\sigma \in S_n$ and $c\colon\{1,\dots,n\}\to\{1,\dots,r\}$, equivalently elements of the wreath product $\mathbb{Z}/r\mathbb{Z} \wr S_n$) and pairs $(P,Q)$ of suitably weighted standard tableaux of the same shape $\lambda \in \mathbb{Y}^{(r)}$ with $|\lambda| = n$.

Problems.
(1) Define a notion of jeu de taquin for standard (and skew) Young tableaux whose shapes are restricted to lie in $\mathbb{Y}^{(r)}$, in such a way that it interacts compatibly with the above RSK-type correspondence on $r$-colored permutations, in analogy with classical jeu de taquin for Young diagrams and Sagan–Worfley's jeu de taquin for shifted Young diagrams.

(2) Formulate and prove a Greene-type invariant for $r$-colored permutations: i.e., describe an explicit combinatorial statistic on $r$-colored permutations (analogous to the maximum total length of a union of $k$ increasing subsequences in the classical Greene theorem) whose value depends only on the insertion tableau $P$ produced by the above RSK algorithm, and which characterizes the shape of $P$. Equivalently, give a combinatorial description of the equivalence relation on $r$-colored permutations consisting of those producing the same $P$-tableau.

Let $\mathcal{D}_n$ denote the set of strict partitions of $n$, i.e., partitions $\lambda = (\lambda_1 > \lambda_2 > \cdots > \lambda_{\ell(\lambda)} > 0)$ of $n$ into distinct positive parts; identify each such partition with its shifted Young diagram (the diagram with $\lambda_i$ cells in row $i$, where row $i$ is shifted $i-1$ units to the right). For $\lambda \in \mathcal{D}_n$, let:
- $g^\lambda$ be the number of standard shifted Young tableaux of shape $\lambda$ (uncolored),
- $c_\lambda = 2^{|\lambda|-\ell(\lambda)}$, where $|\lambda|=n$ and $\ell(\lambda)$ is the number of parts of $\lambda$.

For each weight function $w \in \{1,\ g^\lambda,\ (g^\lambda)^2,\ c_\lambda,\ g^\lambda c_\lambda,\ (g^\lambda)^2 c_\lambda\}$, define the probability measure on $\mathcal{D}_n$ by $\mathbb{P}^{(w)}_n(\lambda) = w(\lambda) / Z^{(w)}_n$, where $Z^{(w)}_n = \sum_{\mu \in \mathcal{D}_n} w(\mu)$.

Embed each shifted diagram $\lambda$ into $\mathbb{R}^2$ as the union of unit cells, and rescale by the factor $1/\sqrt{n}$ in both coordinate directions, obtaining a region $\widetilde{\lambda}_n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$.

For each of the six measures, determine whether there exists a deterministic limit shape $\Omega^{(w)} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ such that, as $n \to \infty$, the rescaled random shifted diagram $\widetilde{\lambda}_n$ (with $\lambda$ drawn from $\mathbb{P}^{(w)}_n$) converges in probability to $\Omega^{(w)}$ in the sense that for every point in the interior of $\Omega^{(w)}$ the probability of belonging to $\widetilde{\lambda}_n$ tends to $1$ and for every point outside $\Omega^{(w)}$ this probability tends to $0$. Identify each limit shape $\Omega^{(w)}$ explicitly, and determine which of the six measures yield the same limit shape (in particular, whether — analogously to the unshifted case where the weights $1$, $f^\lambda$, and $(f^\lambda)^2$ all give the same limit shape — some or all of the six shifted measures coincide).

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Limit shapes are individually known for several of the six measures: for the uniform measure on strict partitions (weight 1), the limit shape was established by Vershik (building on Erdős–Lehner and Szalay–Turán); for the shifted Plancherel measure (weight $(g^\lambda)^2 c_\lambda /n!$), a limit shape was obtained by Borodin and others, and is studied e.g. by Matsumoto and in Petrov's work on random strict partitions and random shifted tableaux. However, a unified comparative analysis showing whether all six listed weightings yield the same (or different) limit shape does not appear to have been carried out in the literature, so the question as posed is partially solved.

Fix an integer r ≥ 1. An r-colored permutation of length n is a pair (σ, c) where σ ∈ S_n is a permutation and c : {1,...,n} → {1,2,...,r} is an arbitrary coloring. To each r-colored permutation one associates a Young diagram with at most r rows via a colored analogue of the Robinson–Schensted correspondence (the colors determine which of r interleaved insertion procedures the corresponding letter participates in, so that the resulting recording shape has at most r rows).

Equip the set of r-colored permutations of length n with the uniform probability measure, and let λ^{(n)} denote the random Young diagram (with at most r rows) obtained from a uniform random r-colored permutation of length n.

Problem. Develop a theory of limit shapes for Young diagrams with at most r rows analogous to the Vershik–Kerov–Logan–Shepp theorem for unrestricted Young diagrams under Plancherel measure. Concretely:

(a) Determine the asymptotic behavior, as n → ∞, of the row lengths λ_1^{(n)} ≥ λ_2^{(n)} ≥ ... ≥ λ_r^{(n)} of λ^{(n)}, including their typical growth rates.

(b) Identify a deterministic scaling (a_n, b_n) such that the rescaled boundary of λ^{(n)} (viewed as a Young diagram in the plane, with rows scaled by 1/a_n and columns by 1/b_n) converges, in an appropriate sense (e.g. in probability with respect to uniform or Hausdorff distance on the boundary curve), to a deterministic limit shape Φ_r supported on a region of the plane.

(c) Describe the limit shape Φ_r explicitly.

The case r = ∞ (no row restriction, with appropriate normalization corresponding to Plancherel measure on partitions of n) reduces to the classical Vershik–Kerov–Logan–Shepp limit shape; the goal is to produce the analogous theory for each finite r ≥ 1.

Background. The Young–Fibonacci lattice YF is the graded poset whose elements at rank k are the words on the alphabet {1,2} whose digits sum to k (Fibonacci words of size k). The covering relations are: a word w covers w' if w' is obtained from w either by deleting the leftmost 1 of w, or by replacing the leftmost 2 (occurring before any 1) of w by 1 (equivalently, reading covers from below: from a word v one builds a covering w by either prepending a 1 to v, or by changing the first 1 of v into a 2). The Hasse diagram of YF endows the set of Fibonacci words with a graph distance d. For an integer r ≥ 1, let YF_r denote the r-differential analogue of the Young–Fibonacci lattice (the dual graded graph obtained from the unique weighting equal to 1 on YF, augmented with r colors when applicable; in the case of YF_r as dual graded graphs there is a unique weighting and no nontrivial coloring of tableaux). For each k let YF^{(k)}_r be the set of words of size k.

Problem.
(a) Define a notion of scaling (a "doubling map") for YF_r: construct, for every k, an embedding D : YF^{(k)}_r → YF^{(2k)}_r such that
  (i) D is nearly isometric: there exist constants C, C' (independent of k) such that for all words u, v ∈ YF^{(k)}_r,
        |d(D(u), D(v)) − 2·d(u, v)| ≤ C,
   and conversely any pair of words near each other in the image corresponds to a pair of words near each other in YF^{(k)}_r;
  (ii) D is nearly surjective: every word w ∈ YF^{(2k)}_r lies within distance ≤ C' of D(YF^{(k)}_r).

(b) Using such a doubling map, form the corresponding inverse/direct limit metric space (the "limit space"). Considering each of the three natural probability distributions on Young–Fibonacci diagrams of size n (the Plancherel-type measure coming from r-colored permutations and the other two distributions naturally associated to YF_r as dual graded graphs), determine whether a uniformly random r-colored permutation of size n yields, after appropriate rescaling via D, a limit shape inside this limit space. If a limit shape exists, identify it explicitly.

Let $k\geq 1$ be a fixed integer. A standard Young tableau (SYT) of size $n$ with at most $k$ rows is a filling of the cells of a Young diagram $\lambda \vdash n$, with $\lambda$ having at most $k$ rows, by the integers $1,2,\dots,n$ such that entries strictly increase along rows (left to right) and down columns. Define the rooted tree $T_k$-SYT as follows:

- The vertex set is the set of all standard Young tableaux with at most $k$ rows (including the empty tableau of size $0$).
- The empty tableau is the root.
- For each SYT $T$ of size $n\geq 1$, its parent in the tree is the SYT of size $n-1$ obtained by deleting the cell containing the entry $n$ from $T$ (this cell is necessarily a corner cell, and the resulting tableau still has at most $k$ rows).

Regard $T_k$-SYT as an unlabeled rooted tree (i.e., forget the SYT labels of the vertices and remember only the abstract rooted tree structure given by the parent–child relation).

Determine the automorphism group $\operatorname{Aut}(T_k\text{-SYT})$ of this unlabeled rooted tree, for every integer $k\geq 1$.

representations.normalized:
The Young–Fibonacci lattice YF is the graded lattice whose elements at rank n are the words (compositions) of 1's and 2's summing to n (with the empty word at rank 0), and whose covering relation w ⋖ w' (with rank(w') = rank(w) + 1) holds when w' is obtained from w either by prepending a 1, or by changing the leftmost run-prefix of 2's followed by changing a 1 just after that prefix into a 2 (equivalently: w' covers w iff w is obtained from w' by either deleting the leftmost 1 of w', or by changing a 2 of w' that lies in the leftmost block of consecutive 2's into a 1 and removing one such 2 — i.e., the standard Fomin/Stanley covering rule for the Young–Fibonacci lattice). A standard Young–Fibonacci tableau of shape w (rank n) is a saturated chain ∅ = w_0 ⋖ w_1 ⋖ ⋯ ⋖ w_n = w in YF.

Define SYFT to be the rooted tree whose vertices are all standard Young–Fibonacci tableaux (of all shapes, including the empty tableau as the root), with an edge between a tableau T of length n and a tableau T' of length n+1 whenever T' extends T by one additional cover. Equivalently, SYFT is the tree of upward paths from ∅ in the Young–Fibonacci lattice.

Forget all vertex labels, retaining only the abstract rooted (or unrooted) tree structure of SYFT. Determine the automorphism group of SYFT as an unlabeled tree.

For a permutation $w \in S_n$, let $\mathfrak{S}_w(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ denote its Schubert polynomial, and define
$$\nu_w := \mathfrak{S}_w(1, 1, \dots, 1),$$
the sum of its coefficients. It is known that $\nu_w = 1$ if and only if $w$ is $132$-avoiding (i.e. dominant): there is no triple of indices $i < j < k$ with $a_i < a_k < a_j$, where $w = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ in one-line notation.

Prove or disprove: $\nu_w = 2$ if and only if the one-line notation $w = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ contains exactly one occurrence of the pattern $132$, i.e., exactly one triple of indices $i < j < k$ such that $a_i < a_k < a_j$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The conjecture was proved by Anna Weigandt (2018), who showed that $\nu_w$ equals the number of reduced pipe dreams (or equivalently is bounded below by/related to the number of $132$-patterns), establishing in particular that $\nu_w = 2$ iff $w$ has exactly one $132$-pattern.

with the lower bound improved to approximately $0.2932362762$ and the upper bound improved to approximately $0.37$.

Determine the exact asymptotic growth rate of $u(n)$. Specifically, determine whether the limit
$$\alpha := \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{\log_2 u(n)}{n^2}$$
exists, and if so, find its value $\alpha \in [1/4, 1/2]$ such that $u(n) \sim 2^{\alpha n^2}$, and improve the known upper and lower bounds on $\alpha$.

For a permutation $w \in S_n$, let $\mathfrak{S}_w(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{n-1}) \in \mathbb{Z}[x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}]$ denote the Schubert polynomial of $w$, defined recursively by $\mathfrak{S}_{w_0} = x_1^{n-1} x_2^{n-2} \cdots x_{n-1}$ for the longest permutation $w_0 \in S_n$, and $\mathfrak{S}_{w s_i} = \partial_i \mathfrak{S}_w$ whenever $\ell(w s_i) < \ell(w)$, where $s_i = (i, i+1)$ and $\partial_i f = (f - s_i f)/(x_i - x_{i+1})$ is the divided difference operator. Define the principal specialization at $1$:
$$\nu_w := \mathfrak{S}_w(1, 1, \ldots, 1),$$
which equals the sum of all coefficients of $\mathfrak{S}_w$. For each positive integer $n$, set
$$u(n) := \max_{w \in S_n} \nu_w.$$

(a) For each $n$, determine all permutations $w \in S_n$ that achieve $\nu_w = u(n)$.

(b) Determine whether, as $n \to \infty$, the maximizing permutations $w \in S_n$ (suitably rescaled, viewed as permutation matrices in $[0,1]^2$) admit a limit shape, and if so describe it explicitly.

Let $r$ be a positive integer. A locally finite graded poset $P$ with a unique minimum element $\hat 0$ is called an $r$-differential poset if it satisfies the following two conditions:

(D1) For every pair of distinct elements $x, y \in P$, the number of elements covered by both $x$ and $y$ equals the number of elements that cover both $x$ and $y$.

(D2) For every $x \in P$, if $x$ covers exactly $k$ elements, then $x$ is covered by exactly $k + r$ elements.

A crown in $P$ is a configuration consisting of three elements $u_1, u_2, u_3$ at some rank $n$ together with three elements $v_1, v_2, v_3$ at rank $n+1$ such that each $v_i$ covers exactly two of the $u_j$'s (so the bipartite covering relation between $\{u_1,u_2,u_3\}$ and $\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}$ forms a 6-cycle). We say that $P$ contains a crown covering a crown if there exist a crown $(u_1,u_2,u_3; v_1,v_2,v_3)$ at ranks $n, n+1$ and a crown $(v_1,v_2,v_3; w_1,w_2,w_3)$ at ranks $n+1, n+2$ sharing the middle triple.

Prove or disprove: an $r$-differential poset $P$ is a lattice if and only if $P$ does not contain a crown covering a crown.

Two basic examples are Young's lattice $Y$ (the lattice of integer partitions ordered by inclusion of Young diagrams), which is $1$-differential, and its $r$-fold Cartesian product $Y^{\times r}$, which is $r$-differential.

Fix $r \in \mathbb{P}$ and $n \ge 0$. Determine the minimum value of $|P_n|$ as $P$ ranges over all $r$-differential posets. In particular, decide whether this minimum is attained by $P = Y^{\times r}$.

Stanley's 1988 conjecture posits that the rank sizes of any r-differential poset lie between those of Y^{×r} (lower bound) and the Young–Fibonacci lattice YF_r (upper bound). For an integer $n\geq 0$, let $\Lambda_n$ denote the set of all integer partitions of $n$ (so $|\Lambda_n|=p(n)$). Partially order $\Lambda_n$ by refinement: for $\lambda,\rho\in\Lambda_n$, declare $\lambda\leq\rho$ if and only if $\lambda$ can be obtained from $\rho$ by partitioning each part of $\rho$ into a sum of positive integers (equivalently, the parts of $\lambda$ can be grouped so that the sums of the groups give the parts of $\rho$). With this order, $\Lambda_n$ is a finite poset with minimum element $\langle 1^n\rangle$ (the partition into $n$ ones) and maximum element $\langle n\rangle$. Let $\mu$ denote the Möbius function of $\Lambda_n$, defined recursively by $\mu(\lambda,\lambda)=1$ and $\mu(\lambda,\rho)=-\sum_{\lambda\leq\sigma<\rho}\mu(\lambda,\sigma)$ for $\lambda<\rho$, and $\mu(\lambda,\rho)=0$ otherwise.

Problem: Determine, in closed combinatorial form, the Möbius function $\mu(\lambda,\rho)$ of the refinement poset $\Lambda_n$ for arbitrary $\lambda,\rho\in\Lambda_n$.

A lattice $L$ is a partially ordered set in which every pair of elements $x, y$ has a least upper bound (join) $x \vee y$ and a greatest lower bound (meet) $x \wedge y$. The lattice $L$ is called modular if for all $x, y, z \in L$ with $x \le z$ one has
$$ x \vee (y \wedge z) = (x \vee y) \wedge z. $$
For $a \le b$ in $L$, the interval $[a,b]$ is the sublattice $\{x \in L : a \le x \le b\}$. The dual of a lattice $(L, \le)$ is the lattice $(L, \ge)$ with the order reversed; $L$ is self-dual if it is isomorphic to its dual. A lattice is finitary if every interval $[a,b]$ is finite, and it has finite covers if every element covers and is covered by only finitely many elements.

(a) Classify all finite modular lattices $L$ with the property that every interval $[a,b] \subseteq L$ is self-dual.

(b) Classify all finitary modular lattices with finite covers having the same property: every interval is self-dual.
