Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ (with $n \geq 2$) be a bounded domain with smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$. Fix a point $P$ in the interior of $\Omega$, chosen generically. Consider the billiard flow inside $\Omega$: a "photon" emitted from $P$ in some unit direction $v \in S^{n-1}$ travels along a straight line at unit speed, and upon hitting $\partial\Omega$ undergoes specular (optical) reflection (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection); thereafter it continues, reflecting again at every subsequent boundary encounter. For each $t > 0$, define the time-$t$ wave front $F_t(P) \subset \overline{\Omega}$ as the set of all positions reached at time exactly $t$ by such trajectories, taken over all initial unit directions $v \in S^{n-1}$.

Question: Does $F_t(P)$ become dense in $\overline{\Omega}$ as $t \to \infty$? That is, is it true that for every nonempty open set $U \subset \Omega$ there exists $T > 0$ such that $F_t(P) \cap U \neq \emptyset$ for all $t \geq T$ (equivalently, $\bigcup_{t \geq T} F_t(P)$ is dense, or the appropriate density formulation)?

Let $\gamma$ be a smooth strictly convex closed curve in the plane (an oval), bounding a convex region $K$. For each integer $n \geq 3$, define
$$f(n) = \min_{P} \operatorname{area}(K \triangle P),$$
where the minimum is taken over all convex $n$-gons $P$ (one may consider separately the inscribed case $P \subset K$, the circumscribed case $K \subset P$, or the unrestricted case), and $K \triangle P = (K \setminus P) \cup (P \setminus K)$ denotes the symmetric difference.

It is known that the analogous minimal-approximation functions in which the deviation between $K$ and $P$ is measured by the difference of perimeters or by the difference of areas (in the inscribed or circumscribed setting) are realized as the minimal actions (with respect to a generating function) of four billiard-like dynamical systems on the boundary $\gamma$: the classical Birkhoff billiard, the outer billiard, the symplectic billiard, and the outer length billiard. Each of these is a twist map of an annulus whose generating function corresponds, respectively, to inscribed perimeter, circumscribed perimeter, inscribed area, and circumscribed area, and whose minimal $n$-periodic action recovers the corresponding approximation function.

Problem: Determine whether the function $f(n)$, measuring the optimal area of the symmetric difference between $K$ and an $n$-gon, can likewise be realized as the minimal $n$-periodic action of some billiard-like dynamical system on $\gamma$ (i.e., a twist map generated by an appropriate geometric generating function on pairs or tuples of points of $\gamma$). If so, describe such a system explicitly; if not, prove that no such system exists.

representations.normalized:
Consider the symmetric Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou-β (FPUT-β) chain: a one-dimensional lattice of N classical particles with positions q_i and momenta p_i (i = 1, …, N), governed by the Hamiltonian
  H = Σ_i [ p_i^2 / 2 + (1/2)(q_{i+1} − q_i)^2 + (β/4)(q_{i+1} − q_i)^4 ],
with β > 0 and (for definiteness) periodic boundary conditions. Because the on-site potential is even in the relative displacement, the only nonlinearity is quartic (no cubic asymmetry).

It is well documented numerically that the equilibrium energy current correlations exhibit anomalous (super-diffusive) decay, so that the finite-size thermal conductivity κ(N) diverges as κ(N) ∼ N^{α} with an exponent α consistent with the kinetic-theory / mode-coupling prediction (often quoted as α = 2/5 for the symmetric case). One may also study the associated stochastic interface obtained by integrating the local energy fluctuations in space, and ask which kinetic roughening universality class (characterized by growth, roughness, and dynamical exponents) this interface belongs to.

Empirically, the large-scale fluctuations of this interface match neither the Kardar–Parisi–Zhang (KPZ) class (with dynamical exponent z = 3/2 and the standard Tracy–Widom / Baik–Rains height statistics) nor the linear Edwards–Wilkinson (EW) class (with z = 2 and Gaussian height fluctuations) predicted by nonlinear fluctuating hydrodynamics for momentum-conserving anharmonic chains, even though the heat-transport exponent agrees with mode-coupling / kinetic-theory predictions.

Problem. Identify and rigorously characterize the universality class governing the large-scale scaling behavior of heat transport and the associated interface dynamics in the symmetric FPUT-β chain. In particular:
(a) Determine the correct dynamical, growth, and roughness exponents of the energy-fluctuation interface.
(b) Provide the limiting scaling functions (analogous to the KPZ or EW scaling functions) describing space–time correlations of the energy current and the height statistics of the interface.
(c) Reconcile this universality class with the observed transport exponent α (compatible with kinetic theory) while explaining why both KPZ and EW predictions fail.

representations.normalized:
Consider a one-dimensional anharmonic oscillator chain of N sites with Hamiltonian
  H = Σ_i [ p_i^2/(2m) + V(q_{i+1} - q_i) ],
where V is a nonlinear nearest-neighbor interaction potential (for instance the Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou potential V(r) = (1/2)r^2 + (α/3)r^3 + (β/4)r^4, with α ≥ 0 and β > 0). The chain is coupled at its two ends to Langevin heat baths at temperatures T_L and T_R, and after a long time it reaches a nonequilibrium stationary state with a heat current J(N) and an effective finite-size thermal conductivity
  κ(N) = J(N) N / (T_L − T_R).
For nonintegrable potentials, κ(N) is expected to diverge as κ(N) ∼ N^δ for large N, with the exponent δ determined by a hydrodynamic universality class (δ = 1/3 for asymmetric potentials in the KPZ class, δ = 1/2 for symmetric potentials).

Now superimpose on the deterministic Hamiltonian dynamics a "conservative" stochastic noise that, at independent random times, exchanges the momenta of randomly chosen neighboring particles (or, more generally, applies random rotations to neighboring momentum pairs). This noise preserves total momentum and total kinetic energy at every event, and in the limit where it dominates one obtains a stochastic system whose hydrodynamic universality class for energy transport is rigorously known and is argued to coincide with that of the purely deterministic chain.

Problem. Provide a quantitative explanation of the following empirical observation. When the conservative momentum-exchange noise is added to the FPUT chain, the apparent finite-size exponent δ_eff(N) extracted from κ(N) ∼ N^{δ_eff(N)} on accessible system sizes can shift toward values different from (and in particular larger than) the deterministic one, even though the asymptotic universality class is unchanged. Specifically:

(a) Identify the mechanism by which adding a conservative noise — which on physical grounds should reduce the conductivity by introducing additional momentum scrambling — instead accelerates the apparent convergence of κ(N) and modifies its effective growth exponent at finite N.

(b) Derive (or characterize) how the crossover length N* separating the preasymptotic regime from the true asymptotic anomalous regime depends on the noise rate γ, and explain why N* can decrease with γ even when the long-wavelength hydrodynamic exponent δ does not depend on γ.

(c) Reconcile (a) and (b) with the statement that the conservative noise leaves the long-distance hydrodynamic universality class invariant.

Consider a one-dimensional chain of N classical particles with displacements q_i and momenta p_i (i = 1, ..., N) governed by the Hamiltonian

  H = Σ_i p_i^2/(2 m_i) + (1/2) Σ_{i ≠ j} K_{ij} V(q_i - q_j) + Σ_i U(q_i),

where V is a nonlinear pair potential of Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou type, e.g. V(x) = x^2/2 + α x^3/3 + β x^4/4. Consider two extensions of the standard nearest-neighbor, homogeneous case:

(a) Long-range couplings: K_{ij} = |i - j|^{-s} for some exponent s > 0 (with appropriate Kac-type rescaling for s ≤ 1), and otherwise homogeneous masses m_i = m, no on-site potential (U = 0).

(b) Disorder plus nonlinearity: nearest-neighbor couplings only, but with random masses m_i (or random on-site potentials U(q_i) = ε_i q_i^2/2) drawn i.i.d. from a non-degenerate distribution, together with α ≠ 0 or β ≠ 0.

Let $M\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be a nonempty compact set and $r>0$. A connected closed set $\Sigma\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ is called a maximal distance minimizer for $M$ with radius $r$ if it minimizes the one-dimensional Hausdorff length $\mathcal{H}^1(\Sigma)$ among all connected closed sets $\Sigma'\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ satisfying $\max_{x\in M}\mathrm{dist}(x,\Sigma')\le r$.

For $R>0$, the $R$-stadium is the set $M=\partial(N_R([AB]))$, the boundary of the closed $R$-neighborhood of a line segment $[AB]\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ of positive length. A horseshoe is a planar set consisting of an arc of a circle of radius $R-r$ together with two segments of tangent lines to that arc.

Tasks:
(a) For every $r$ with $r<R<5r$, describe all maximal distance minimizers for the $R$-stadium with radius $r$.
(b) Determine the sharp threshold $R_1(r)$ such that for all $R\le R_1(r)$ there exists a maximal distance minimizer (for the $R$-stadium with radius $r$) that is not a horseshoe, and the sharp threshold $R_2(r)$ such that for all $R\ge R_2(r)$ every maximal distance minimizer is a horseshoe. More generally, for closed convex curves $M\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ with prescribed minimal radius of curvature, determine the sharp thresholds guaranteeing existence of non-horseshoe minimizers and, respectively, guaranteed horseshoe-only minimizers.

Let $M \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a non-empty compact set and let $r > 0$. For a closed set $\Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, define
$$F_M(\Sigma) = \sup_{y \in M} \mathrm{dist}(y, \Sigma), \qquad \mathrm{dist}(y,\Sigma) = \inf_{x \in \Sigma} |y-x|.$$
A maximal distance minimizer (MDM) for the pair $(M, r)$ is a connected compact set $\Sigma^* \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ that minimizes the one-dimensional Hausdorff measure $\mathcal{H}^1(\Sigma)$ among all connected compact sets $\Sigma$ satisfying the covering constraint $F_M(\Sigma) \le r$, i.e.
$$\Sigma^* \in \arg\min\{\mathcal{H}^1(\Sigma) : \Sigma \text{ connected, compact, } F_M(\Sigma) \le r\}.$$

Determine, explicitly, the set of all MDMs in each of the following cases:
(a) $M = B_R \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ is a closed ball of radius $R$, for $d \ge 2$ and all $r \in (0,R)$;
(b) $M$ is the boundary of a rectangle in $\mathbb{R}^2$, in the regime of small $r > 0$;
(c) $M$ is a regular $n$-gon in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (i.e., its boundary or its closed convex hull), for each $n \ge 3$ and all $r > 0$ (it is conjectured that each MDM is a finite polyline whose junctions form angles at least $2\pi/3$; prove or disprove this and identify the minimizers explicitly, including the case $n = 3$).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ be separable Hilbert spaces, and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a class of (e.g., Lipschitz or higher-regularity) operators $F:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$. Suppose we observe i.i.d. noisy input–output pairs
$$ (X_i, Y_i)_{i=1}^n, \qquad Y_i = F^\star(X_i) + \xi_i, $$
where $F^\star\in\mathcal{F}$ is the unknown target operator, $X_i$ is drawn from some probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{X}$, and $\xi_i$ is centered noise on $\mathcal{Y}$ (e.g., Gaussian with bounded covariance) independent of $X_i$. For an estimator $\widehat{F}_n$ depending only on the data, define the squared $L^2(\mu)$-risk
$$ \mathcal{R}(\widehat{F}_n, F^\star) = \mathbb{E}\,\|\widehat{F}_n - F^\star\|_{L^2(\mu;\mathcal{Y})}^2. $$
Standard statistical-learning analyses of empirical risk minimization over $\mathcal{F}$ produce upper bounds on $\sup_{F^\star\in\mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(\widehat{F}_n, F^\star)$ that decay no faster than $n^{-1/2}$, even when the complexity of $\mathcal{F}$ would otherwise allow a faster nonparametric rate in the noiseless setting.

Question: Determine whether the rate $n^{-1/2}$ is a genuine minimax barrier for noisy operator learning, i.e., whether
$$ \inf_{\widehat{F}_n}\;\sup_{F^\star\in\mathcal{F}}\;\mathcal{R}(\widehat{F}_n, F^\star) \;\gtrsim\; n^{-1/2} $$
holds for natural infinite-dimensional regularity classes $\mathcal{F}$, or whether this $n^{-1/2}$ ceiling is merely an artifact of the proof technique used in the statistical-learning upper-bound analysis and can be improved by a different estimator or analysis.

Recent work (arXiv:2512.17805, "Towards Sharp Minimax Risk Bounds for Operator Learning") makes substantial progress: it establishes a curse of sample complexity for Lipschitz/Hölder operator classes, showing that for generic finite-regularity operator classes the minimax risk cannot decay at algebraic rates, while for more restrictive holomorphic classes ERM achieves rates faster than $n^{-1/2}$ such as $n^{-(1/p - 1/2)}$. Let $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ be separable Hilbert spaces (for instance, $L^2$ spaces over compact domains in $\mathbb{R}^d$), and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a class of (possibly nonlinear) operators $F:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$. Given $n$ i.i.d. input–output pairs $(X_i, Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ where $X_i$ is drawn from a probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{X}$ and $Y_i = F^\star(X_i) + \varepsilon_i$ for some unknown $F^\star\in\mathcal{F}$ and centered noise $\varepsilon_i$, define the minimax risk
$$ R_n(\mathcal{F}) \;=\; \inf_{\widehat{F}_n}\;\sup_{F^\star\in\mathcal{F}}\; \mathbb{E}\,\bigl\|\widehat{F}_n - F^\star\bigr\|_{L^2(\mu;\mathcal{Y})}^2, $$
where the infimum is over all measurable estimators $\widehat{F}_n$ based on the sample.

A class $\mathcal{F}$ is said to admit an algebraic minimax sample-complexity rate if there exist constants $c,C>0$ and an exponent $\alpha>0$ such that
$$ c\, n^{-\alpha} \;\le\; R_n(\mathcal{F}) \;\le\; C\, n^{-\alpha} \qquad \text{for all sufficiently large } n. $$
Many natural function-space classes (e.g.\ general Lipschitz operators between infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces) suffer from infinite-dimensional curse-of-dimensionality phenomena and only admit logarithmic rates in $n$.

Problem. Identify classes $\mathcal{F}$ of operators arising in scientific applications—such as solution operators of parametric partial differential equations, Hamiltonian flow maps, homogenization operators, or parameter-to-observable maps in inverse problems—that are
(i) practically relevant to scientific computing, and
(ii) sufficiently structured (through smoothness, low effective dimension, holomorphic parameter dependence, multiscale structure, etc.) that the minimax risk $R_n(\mathcal{F})$ obeys an algebraic decay $n^{-\alpha}$ with explicit exponent $\alpha>0$ independent of any ambient infinite dimension.

Provide such a class, together with matching upper and lower bounds establishing the algebraic rate.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be (real or complex) separable Banach spaces and let $K \subset X$ be a compact subset (for example, the unit ball of a compactly embedded subspace). Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a class of continuous operators $F : K \to Y$. Given $n \in \mathbb{N}$ "sampling points" $x_1,\dots,x_n \in K$ chosen by the learner (adaptively or non-adaptively), the learner observes the noiseless data $\{(x_i, F(x_i))\}_{i=1}^n$ and produces an estimator $\widehat{F}_n : K \to Y$. Define the sampling (worst-case) width
$$ s_n(\mathcal{F}) \;=\; \inf_{\widehat{F}_n}\; \sup_{F\in\mathcal{F}}\; \sup_{x\in K}\, \|F(x)-\widehat{F}_n(x)\|_Y, $$
where the infimum runs over all measurable reconstruction maps based on $n$ point evaluations. An algorithm is called minimax-optimal in this noiseless sampling-width formulation if the rate of its worst-case error over $\mathcal{F}$ matches $s_n(\mathcal{F})$ as $n\to\infty$ up to constants (or up to logarithmic factors).

Empirical risk minimization (ERM) refers to estimators of the form
$$ \widehat{F}_n \;\in\; \arg\min_{G\in\mathcal{H}_n}\; \sum_{i=1}^n \|G(x_i)-F(x_i)\|_Y^2, $$
where $\{\mathcal{H}_n\}$ is a suitable sequence of hypothesis classes (e.g., neural-network or polynomial surrogate model classes) chosen to approximate $\mathcal{F}$.

It is known that for certain classes of holomorphic operators on infinite-dimensional Banach spaces, ERM-based reconstructions achieve the minimax sampling-width rate. The question is:

Determine whether ERM is minimax-optimal, in the sense of the sampling width $s_n(\mathcal{F})$ above, for operator classes $\mathcal{F}$ beyond holomorphic ones. In particular, settle this for:

(i) classes of infinitely Fréchet-differentiable ($C^\infty$) operators $F : K \to Y$ with prescribed bounds on all Fréchet derivatives;

(ii) classes of solution operators arising from specific parametric PDE problems, namely operators $F$ mapping a coefficient/parameter $a \in K$ to the solution $u(a) \in Y$ of a parametric elliptic, parabolic, or hyperbolic PDE under standard well-posedness assumptions.

In each case, identify the minimax sampling-width rate and prove matching upper bounds achieved (or not achieved) by ERM with an appropriate hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}_n$.

Let $A \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a finite set of points (called terminals). A Steiner tree for $A$ is a connected set $S \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ containing $A$, and a minimizing Steiner tree is one that achieves the infimum of the one-dimensional Hausdorff measure (total length) among all such connected sets. Equivalently, in the network setting, given a connected weighted graph $G = (V,E,w)$ and a subset $A \subseteq V$ of terminals, a minimizing Steiner tree is a subtree of $G$ that contains $A$ and minimizes the total edge weight.

Question: For a "general" (generic) input $A$, is the minimizing Steiner tree unique? More precisely, does there exist a notion of genericity (e.g., a residual or full-measure subset of the configuration space of finite terminal sets) such that for every input in this generic class, the minimizing Steiner tree is unique?

Setup. Let $\varrho$ be a Borel probability measure on a separable Hilbert space $\mathcal{X}$ and let $\mathcal{Y}$ be a separable Hilbert space. Consider learning an unknown operator $G:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ from $n$ i.i.d. noisy input–output samples $(x_i,y_i)$, $x_i\sim\varrho$, $y_i=G(x_i)+\eta_i$, with the loss measured in $L^2_\varrho(\mathcal{X};\mathcal{Y})$.

For a parameter $\alpha>0$, define the Fourier-neural-operator approximation class $\mathcal{K}^\alpha_{\mathrm{FNO}}$ as the set of operators $G$ such that there exists a sequence $\{G_M\}_{M\in\mathbb{N}}$ of Fourier neural operators of complexity (number of parameters / Fourier modes) at most $M$ with
$$\|G-G_M\|_{L^2_\varrho}\;\le\; C\, M^{-\alpha}.$$

For an estimator $\widehat G_n$ based on $n$ samples, define the minimax risk
$$R_n(\alpha)\;=\;\inf_{\widehat G_n}\sup_{G\in\mathcal{K}^\alpha_{\mathrm{FNO}}}\mathbb{E}\,\|\widehat G_n-G\|^2_{L^2_\varrho},$$
and let the optimal algebraic minimax-rate exponent be
$$\beta^\star(\alpha)\;=\;\sup\{\beta\ge 0:\, R_n(\alpha)=O(n^{-\beta})\}.$$

It is known that $\beta^\star(\alpha)\le 1/2$ for all $\alpha$, and that $\beta^\star(\alpha)\to 1/2$ as $\alpha\to\infty$, while existing lower bounds (proved via empirical risk minimization arguments) leave a gap at finite $\alpha$.

Question. Determine whether the upper bound $\beta^\star(\alpha)=1/2$ is sharp for finite $\alpha>0$. Equivalently, does there exist a finite $\alpha$ and an estimator achieving an algebraic rate exponent strictly larger than the currently established lower-bound exponent, possibly attaining $1/2$, or can one prove a strict separation $\beta^\star(\alpha)<1/2$ for finite $\alpha$?

Setup. Let $A:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}^M$ be a linear measurement operator and consider the inverse problem
$$y = A\hat x + e, \qquad \hat x \in \Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^N,$$
where $\Sigma$ is a (low-dimensional) proximinal model set and $e\in\mathbb{R}^M$ is noise.

Generalized projection. A (possibly set-valued) map $P_\Sigma:\mathbb{R}^N\rightrightarrows \Sigma$ is called a generalized projection onto $\Sigma$. It is said to have the restricted $\beta$-Lipschitz property with respect to $\Sigma$ if
$$\forall z\in\mathbb{R}^N,\ \forall x\in\Sigma,\ \forall u\in P_\Sigma(z): \quad \|u-x\|_2 \le \beta \,\|z-x\|_2.$$
Let $P_\Sigma^{\perp}$ denote an orthogonal projection onto $\Sigma$ (a selection minimizing $\|z-\cdot\|_2$ over $\Sigma$).

Modified RED iteration. For step sizes $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\mu>0$, and an initial point $x_0\in\mathbb{R}^N$, define
$$z_n = (1-\lambda)x_n + \lambda P_\Sigma(x_n), \qquad x_{n+1} = z_n - \mu A^\top(Az_n - y).$$

Known result. Let $\beta = \beta_\Sigma(P_\Sigma)$ be the restricted Lipschitz constant and let $\delta=\delta_\Sigma(\mu A^\top A)$ be a restricted contraction constant of $I-\mu A^\top A$ on $\Sigma$. Assume $\|P_\Sigma - P_\Sigma^{\perp}\|_2 \le \eta$ in the sense that any selection of $P_\Sigma$ stays within distance $\eta$ of $P_\Sigma^{\perp}$. If
$$r := \delta\beta + |1-\lambda|\,\|I-\mu A^\top A\|_{op} < 1,$$
then
$$\|x_n-\hat x\|_2 \le r^n \|x_0-\hat x\|_2 + \frac{1}{1-r}\bigl(|1-\lambda|\,\|I-\mu A^\top A\|_{op}\,\eta + \mu\,\|A^\top e\|_2\bigr).$$

Question. Drop the closeness-to-orthogonality assumption $\|P_\Sigma - P_\Sigma^\perp\|_2 \le \eta$. Does the modified RED iteration above still converge to a stable solution of the inverse problem under only the assumption that $P_\Sigma$ is a generic restricted-$\beta$-Lipschitz generalized projection onto the proximinal set $\Sigma$ (i.e., in the same generality as the generalized projected-gradient-descent setting), and if so, under what conditions on $\lambda,\mu,\beta,A,\Sigma$ can one obtain a quantitative error bound analogous to the one above but without the $\eta$ term?

Let $M \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a finite set of points called terminals. A Steiner tree for $M$ is a connected set $S \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ of minimal total length (one-dimensional Hausdorff measure) containing $M$. It is classical that any Steiner tree $S$ is a finite union of straight line segments meeting only at terminals or at so-called Steiner (branching) points; every branching point has degree exactly $3$ and the three incident segments meet pairwise at $120^\circ$ angles, while terminals have degree $1$, $2$, or $3$.

Fix a point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and a radius $r > 0$, and consider the closed ball $B_r(x)$. Assume that the Steiner tree $S$ has no terminal inside $B_r(x)$ (the "terminal-free ball" setting). For a parameter $t \in (0,1)$, consider the smaller concentric ball $B_{tr}(x)$.

Question: Over all finite terminal sets $M \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, all Steiner trees $S$ for $M$, and all balls $B_r(x)$ containing no terminal of $M$, what is the supremum (in particular for $t = 1/2$, and more generally for $t \in (0,1)$) of the number of branching (Steiner) points of $S$ contained in $B_{tr}(x)$?

Setup. Let A : R^N → R^m be a linear measurement operator and consider the inverse problem y = A x̂ + e, where x̂ belongs to a (possibly nonconvex) low-dimensional model set Σ ⊂ R^N and e ∈ R^m is a noise vector. Let P_Σ : R^N → Σ denote a (not necessarily orthogonal) projection onto Σ, i.e., P_Σ(x) ∈ argmin_{z∈Σ} ‖x − z‖.

Generalized projected gradient descent (GPGD) for this problem is defined by the iteration
  x_{n+1} = P_Σ(x_n) − μ A^T(A P_Σ(x_n) − y),
where μ > 0 is a step size. Assume A satisfies a restricted isometry property on Σ − Σ and that P_Σ satisfies a restricted Lipschitz property, so that under these hypotheses the GPGD iterates converge linearly to a neighborhood of x̂ whose radius is controlled by ‖e‖ (stable recovery with linear rate).

Define a denoiser f : R^N → R^N by f(x) = P_Σ(x). The classical Regularization by Denoising (RED) iteration with parameter λ ≥ 0 is
  x_{n+1} = x_n − μ [ A^T(A x_n − y) + λ (x_n − f(x_n)) ],
and a modified RED iteration (in which the data-fidelity gradient is evaluated at the denoised point) is
  x_{n+1} = x_n − μ [ A^T(A f(x_n) − y) + λ (x_n − f(x_n)) ].
When λ = 1, modified RED coincides with GPGD; admissible values λ ≠ 1 yield strictly slower linear convergence rates and weaker identifiability guarantees in this analysis, and analogous convergence results for classical RED require still more restrictive hypotheses.

Problem. Identify a theoretical regime — i.e., a class of measurement operators A, model sets Σ, denoisers f, and parameters λ — in which using either the classical RED iteration or the modified RED iteration with some λ ≠ 1 is provably preferable to running GPGD (λ = 1). More precisely, exhibit hypotheses under which a (classical or modified) RED scheme attains a strictly better convergence rate, a strictly better stability/identifiability constant, or recovery guarantees that GPGD provably cannot achieve; or alternatively prove that no such regime exists, so that GPGD always dominates RED under the present hypotheses.

Design a conversational question answering (ConvQA) system that, given a multi-turn dialogue history and a current user query, produces accurate answers across heterogeneous target domains (for example, customer service, healthcare, and education) under the following requirements:

1. Cross-domain generalization without extensive retraining: The system must achieve competitive answer-quality performance on previously unseen domains using only lightweight adaptation (e.g., a small number of in-domain examples, prompts, or adapter modules) rather than full model retraining.

2. Domain-sensitivity: The system must condition its responses on domain-specific context, terminology, conventions, and constraints (e.g., medical safety considerations in healthcare, pedagogical scaffolding in education, policy compliance in customer service).

3. Modular scalability: The architecture must support adding new domains through modular components (such as domain adapters, retrievers, or knowledge modules) whose number of trainable parameters and computational cost scale sublinearly with the number of domains supported.

4. Continual improvement from interaction: The system must improve over time by learning from realistic multi-domain interaction logs and user feedback signals (explicit ratings, corrections, or implicit signals) while avoiding catastrophic forgetting of previously learned domains.

Provide (a) a formal specification of the system (input/output spaces, training objective, adaptation procedure, and feedback-incorporation mechanism), (b) an evaluation protocol that simultaneously measures cross-domain generalization, domain-specific accuracy, modular scalability, and continual-learning stability, and (c) theoretical or empirical guarantees that the proposed design satisfies requirements (1)–(4) jointly.

Design a conversational question answering framework that supports multi-turn reasoning over heterogeneous multimodal inputs. Formally, let a dialogue be a finite sequence of turns $(u_1, r_1, u_2, r_2, \ldots, u_T)$, where each user turn $u_t$ is associated with a context $C_t = (X_t^{\text{txt}}, X_t^{\text{img}}, X_t^{\text{vid}}, X_t^{\text{aud}})$ consisting of (possibly empty) textual, image, video, and audio components. The task is to construct a model $f$ that, given the dialogue history $H_t = (u_1, r_1, \ldots, u_{t-1}, r_{t-1})$ together with the multimodal context $C_t$ and the current question $u_t$, produces a response $r_t = f(H_t, C_t, u_t)$ such that:

1. (Cross-modal grounding) $r_t$ is consistent with the joint semantic content of $X_t^{\text{txt}}, X_t^{\text{img}}, X_t^{\text{vid}}, X_t^{\text{aud}}$, meaning no claim in $r_t$ contradicts evidence available in any single modality or across modalities.
2. (Coherence) $r_t$ is logically and topically consistent with all previous turns in $H_t$, including resolution of coreference and ellipsis whose antecedents may occur in any modality.
3. (Evaluation performance) On standardized multimodal multi-turn QA benchmarks, $f$ achieves answer accuracy, grounding fidelity, and dialogue-coherence scores that meet or exceed predefined performance thresholds reflective of realistic deployment requirements.

Provide explicit architectural, training, and evaluation principles for $f$, and prove (empirically or theoretically) that the resulting system simultaneously satisfies the cross-modal consistency, coherence, and performance conditions above in realistic application settings.

Setup. Consider an N-party quantum key agreement (MQKA) protocol involving parties P_1,...,P_N (N ≥ 3). Each party P_i contributes a private input bit-string x_i and the protocol uses a quantum communication network whose underlying interaction graph is one of the following sparse topologies, each having O(N) quantum channels: a ring (cycle), a chain, a tree, or a star. After execution of the protocol, every honest party outputs the same final key K ∈ {0,1}^ℓ.

Security definitions.
(i) Correctness: when all parties are honest, all outputs equal a common key K which is uniformly distributed and statistically close to uniform from the viewpoint of any external eavesdropper.
(ii) Information-theoretic fairness against (N−1)-collusions: for every proper subset S ⊊ {P_1,...,P_N} with |S| = N−1, and for every (computationally unbounded) joint strategy of the parties in S, including any adaptive choice of inputs and any allowed quantum operations on the channels they touch, the probability that the coalition can either (a) force the honest party's output to equal a value K* chosen in advance by the coalition, or (b) predict the honest party's output K with advantage greater than a negligible function of the security parameter, is itself negligible. The fairness must not depend on any hidden trust assumption (e.g., a third party assumed honest beyond the protocol's stated model).
(iii) Efficiency / key rate: the asymptotic key length per quantum-channel-use should remain bounded below by a positive constant independent of N (no superpolynomial degradation in N).

Problem. Determine whether there exists an MQKA protocol whose communication graph is one of the topologies above (ring, chain, tree, or star), or any other topology with O(N) quantum channels, that simultaneously achieves correctness (i), information-theoretic fairness against arbitrary (N−1)-coalitions (ii), and the constant-rate efficiency property (iii).

If no such protocol exists, prove an information-theoretic impossibility result that quantifies the tradeoff: identify a lower bound demonstrating that for graphs with O(N) edges, any protocol satisfying (i) and (ii) must incur a key-rate loss that grows unboundedly with N, or equivalently must rely on an unverifiable trust assumption. If a relaxed notion of approximate fairness (allowing the coalition's predictive/forcing advantage to be bounded by some explicit function ε(N)) is the best one can attain, characterize the optimal achievable ε(N) as a function of N for each of the listed topologies.

Design a conversational question-answering system, modeled as a function that maps a user identifier u, a dialogue history H_u = (q_1, a_1, ..., q_{t-1}, a_{t-1}), and a current query q_t to an answer a_t, together with an evolving user profile P_u. The profile P_u is required to encode user-specific attributes including (i) preferred response formats (e.g., concise vs. detailed, textual vs. structured), (ii) inferred domain expertise levels, (iii) emotional tone preferences, (iv) recurring topics of interest, and (v) long-term goals expressed or implied across sessions. Specify and analyze algorithms for updating P_u online from interaction signals (explicit feedback, implicit behavior, linguistic cues), and for conditioning answer generation on P_u so that answers improve, under suitable evaluation metrics, in personalization and context-awareness relative to a non-personalized baseline.

The system must simultaneously satisfy formal guarantees in the following four directions:
1. Privacy: profile updates and storage admit a quantifiable privacy guarantee (for example, (ε, δ)-differential privacy with respect to any single user utterance, or an equivalent formal notion), and no user-specific attribute can be reconstructed from released model outputs beyond a stated bound.
2. Transparency: there exists an inspection mechanism providing, on request, a human-readable account of which elements of P_u influenced a given answer a_t.
3. Fairness: for a specified collection of protected attribute groups G_1, ..., G_k, the answer quality metric Q satisfies a stated group-fairness criterion (e.g., |E[Q | G_i] − E[Q | G_j]| ≤ η for all i, j).
4. Bias resistance: there is a quantitative bound on the probability that the system, conditioned on any profile P_u, produces outputs flagged as harmful by a fixed harmfulness classifier, uniformly over admissible profiles.

Construct such a system, prove that the four guarantees can be achieved jointly with provable personalization gain, or alternatively establish impossibility/trade-off theorems characterizing the achievable region among these objectives.

Consider a conversational question answering (ConvQA) system that maintains an internal knowledge representation K_t and a response policy π_t at interaction step t. The system receives a stream of user turns (q_1, q_2, ...) and must produce answers (a_1, a_2, ...) while continuously updating (K_t, π_t) in real time. Design and analyze an online adaptation framework that integrates one or more of the following learning paradigms — reinforcement learning (with reward signals derived from user feedback), active learning (with selective query/clarification strategies), continual/lifelong learning (with mechanisms against catastrophic forgetting such as elastic weight consolidation, replay buffers, or parameter isolation), self-supervised learning (with auxiliary objectives from conversational context), retrieval-augmented generation (with a dynamically updatable external memory or index), and federated learning (with decentralized updates that never expose raw user data) — such that the resulting system simultaneously satisfies the following criteria:

(i) Accuracy: expected answer quality on a held-out evaluation distribution does not degrade across t.
(ii) Robustness: performance remains stable under distribution shift and adversarial or noisy user inputs.
(iii) Privacy preservation: updates from any individual user satisfy a quantifiable privacy guarantee (e.g., differential privacy with budget ε).
(iv) Resistance to catastrophic forgetting: performance on previously encountered topics or skills does not deteriorate by more than a prescribed tolerance after adaptation to new ones.

Provide an explicit algorithmic procedure together with theoretical or empirical guarantees that jointly establish properties (i)–(iv), and characterize the trade-offs (e.g., privacy–utility, plasticity–stability, exploration–exploitation) inherent in such a real-time adaptive ConvQA system.

Let n ≥ 2 and 1 ≤ k ≤ n−1 be integers. The Dicke state |D^n_k⟩ is the symmetric n-qubit pure state defined by

  |D^n_k⟩ = C(n,k)^{−1/2} · Σ_{x ∈ {0,1}^n, |x|=k} |x⟩,

where the sum is over all binary strings of length n with Hamming weight exactly k. A multiparty quantum key agreement (MQKA) protocol among n parties is a protocol producing a common shared classical key K such that:
 (i) Correctness: all honest parties output the same K;
 (ii) Security: any external eavesdropper learns negligible information about K;
 (iii) Strong fairness under collusion: for every proper subset S ⊊ {1,…,n} of dishonest participants (possibly all but one honest party), the colluding set S cannot bias, predetermine, or determine K alone, and every honest party contributes equally to K;
 (iv) The protocol may be analyzed in three security models: device-dependent (DD), measurement-device-independent (MDI), and semi-device-independent (SDI);
 (v) The protocol may be deployed on different network architectures: star (one central node connected to n−1 leaves), tree (general rooted tree topology), and hybrid (combinations thereof, possibly client–server).

Open problem: Construct an MQKA protocol in which the fundamental entangled resource consumed in each round is a Dicke state |D^n_k⟩ (rather than GHZ or Bell states), and rigorously prove that it satisfies correctness, security, and strong fairness against any collusion of up to n−1 participants, with security and fairness guarantees comparable to existing GHZ-based and Bell-based MQKA protocols. Furthermore, characterize quantitatively, as functions of (n,k), the protocol's:
 (a) qubit efficiency (key bits per transmitted qubit),
 (b) asymptotic and finite-size key rates under realistic channel noise and loss,
 (c) noise and loss tolerance thresholds,
 (d) resilience to collusion of size up to n−1,
 (e) performance trade-offs across the star, tree, and hybrid architectures, and
 (f) achievable security guarantees in each of the DD, MDI, and SDI models.

representations.normalized: Consider a conversational question answering system that processes a sequence of user-system interaction turns t_1, t_2, ..., t_n, where each turn t_i consists of a user utterance u_i and a system response r_i. At each new query u_{n+1}, the system must produce an answer r_{n+1} that depends on relevant prior context drawn from the interaction history H_n = (t_1, ..., t_n). Because |H_n| grows unboundedly with n while computational and memory budgets for context are finite, the system needs a dynamic history-management policy π that, given H_n and u_{n+1}, outputs a transformed compact context C_n with |C_n| ≤ B (for a fixed budget B) by applying operations from the set {retain turn t_i verbatim, summarize a subset of turns into a shorter abstract, compress a turn or group of turns into a lossy representation, discard a turn}. The policy must satisfy the following desiderata simultaneously: (i) C_n preserves the information in H_n most relevant for correctly answering u_{n+1}; (ii) π tracks evolving user goals and topic shifts, i.e., adapts its retain/summarize/compress/discard decisions when the conversational focus changes; (iii) π remains computationally tractable and answer-quality-preserving as n → ∞ in prolonged real-world dialogues. Design such a policy π (or prove fundamental limits on it), and provide a framework with provable or empirically validated guarantees that jointly achieve (i)–(iii).

Consider a conversational question answering (ConvQA) system modeled as a function that, given a dialogue history $h$ and a user query $q$, produces a response $r$ together with auxiliary metadata. Assume the system has access to an information source (e.g., a knowledge base, document corpus, or learned language model) from which candidate answers $\{a_1, \ldots, a_k\}$ can be retrieved or generated, each associated with an estimated confidence $c_i \in [0,1]$. Suppose that some queries are ambiguous (admit multiple distinct correct interpretations) and that some retrievable information is uncertain (low confidence, conflicting, or incomplete).

Design and rigorously analyze a response policy $\pi$ for such a ConvQA system that simultaneously addresses the following requirements:

1. (Multiple plausible answers) When the posterior over interpretations or answers is multimodal, $\pi$ outputs a calibrated set of plausible answers rather than a single one.
2. (Confidence and explanation) Each answer is annotated with a confidence score $c_i$ that is calibrated in the sense that, conditionally on $c_i = c$, the empirical accuracy equals $c$, together with an explanation tracing the answer to supporting evidence.
3. (Clarification) When the ambiguity of $q$ given $h$ (measured, e.g., by the entropy of the posterior over interpretations) exceeds a threshold $\tau_{\mathrm{amb}}$, $\pi$ issues a clarifying follow-up question that maximally reduces expected ambiguity.
4. (Contradiction detection) If retrieved evidence $E$ contains mutually inconsistent statements, $\pi$ flags the contradiction and abstains from asserting either branch as fact.
5. (Selective prediction in high-stakes domains) In domains designated as high-stakes (e.g., medical or legal advice), $\pi$ declines to answer whenever the top confidence $\max_i c_i$ falls below a domain-specific threshold $\tau_{\mathrm{hs}}$, with provable bounds on the residual risk.

The problem is to specify such a policy $\pi$, prove calibration and risk guarantees (e.g., a PAC-style bound on the probability of confidently asserting an incorrect answer in high-stakes settings), and characterize the trade-off between answer coverage, clarification frequency, and risk.

Setting. Consider $n \geq 3$ mutually distrustful parties $P_1, \ldots, P_n$ who wish to agree on a common secret bit string $K \in \{0,1\}^\ell$ via a quantum protocol. Each party holds an untrusted measurement device (a black box accepting classical inputs and returning classical outputs) and access to quantum states distributed by an untrusted source over an authenticated classical broadcast channel. Let $P(a_1,\ldots,a_n \mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ denote the joint conditional distribution of outputs $a_i$ given inputs $x_i$ realized by the devices in a given run.

A multiparty quantum key agreement (MQKA) protocol is fully device-independent (DI) if its security and correctness guarantees are derived solely from statistical features of $P$ (e.g., violations of multipartite Bell-type inequalities), without any assumption on the Hilbert-space dimension, the internal state preparation, or the form of measurements implemented by the devices. The protocol must satisfy:

(i) Correctness: with probability at least $1-\varepsilon_c$, all honest parties output the same key $K$.

(ii) Secrecy (against an eavesdropper Eve and against any coalition $C \subsetneq \{P_1,\ldots,P_n\}$ of dishonest insiders, possibly controlling the source and devices of $C$): the trace distance between the joint state of $K$ and the side information held by Eve $\cup\, C$, conditioned on the protocol not aborting, is at most $\varepsilon_s$.

(iii) Fairness: no proper subset of parties (honest or dishonest) can bias the final key toward a value of their choice; formally, for every proper coalition $C$, the conditional distribution of $K$ given $C$'s view is $\varepsilon_f$-close to uniform on $\{0,1\}^\ell$, and every honest party contributes equally to $K$ in a sense made precise by a chosen fairness functional.

Question. Does there exist an $n$-party protocol $(n \geq 3)$ in this fully device-independent model that, given only the observed $n$-partite nonlocal correlations $P$, simultaneously achieves correctness, secrecy, and fairness with $\varepsilon_c, \varepsilon_s, \varepsilon_f \to 0$ in the asymptotic limit, while remaining robust to (a) loophole-free multipartite Bell-test constraints (finite detection efficiency, finite statistics, no signaling), (b) arbitrary insider coalitions $C$ of size up to $n-1$, and (c) bounded quantum and classical resources? In particular, exhibit such a protocol together with a positive secret-key rate as a function of the observed Bell-inequality violation, or prove an impossibility result.

Subproblem. Identify semi-device-independent variants—e.g., where sources are trusted but measurements are untrusted (measurement-device-independent MQKA), or where the Hilbert-space dimension is bounded—under which the above three guarantees can be provably achieved with experimentally realistic parameters, and quantify the trade-off between the strength of the relaxed device assumptions and the achievable key rate.

Recent literature treats fully device-independent multiparty quantum key agreement (DI-MQKA) as an active, unresolved research frontier. Device-independent conference key agreement protocols using GHZ states and generalized CHSH-type inequalities have been proposed, and measurement-device-independent and semi-DI MQKA schemes exist, but no protocol simultaneously establishes secrecy, fairness against arbitrary insider coalitions, and loophole-free experimental feasibility. Surveys identify DI-MQKA among the principal open challenges for future quantum-internet key agreement.

Setup. Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph with |V| = n vertices, each vertex assigned to one of n parties. The associated graph (cluster) state is the n-qubit pure state

  |G⟩ = (∏_{(u,v)∈E} CZ_{u,v}) |+⟩^{⊗n},

where |+⟩ = (|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and CZ_{u,v} is the controlled-Z gate acting on qubits u and v. A multiparty quantum key agreement (MQKA) protocol based on |G⟩ is a procedure in which the n parties each hold one qubit of (possibly many copies of) |G⟩, perform local measurements (single-qubit Pauli or adaptive measurements as in measurement-based quantum computation), and through classical post-processing (sifting, parameter estimation, error correction, privacy amplification) produce an identical bit-string of length ℓ that is secret from any eavesdropper, including dishonest insiders.

Noise model. Fix a hardware noise model N consisting of: (i) an independent photon-loss / qubit-erasure rate η ∈ [0,1] per qubit; (ii) a depolarizing or Pauli error channel with rate p ∈ [0,1/2] applied per qubit before measurement; and (iii) measurement error rate q ∈ [0,1/2]. Let R(G, N) denote the asymptotic secret-key rate per copy of |G⟩ achievable by the optimal cluster-state MQKA protocol against general coherent attacks (composable security), let η*(G) denote the maximum loss rate η for which R(G, N) > 0 holds (with p = q = 0), and let p*(G) denote the maximum Pauli error rate p for which R(G, N) > 0 (with η = q = 0).

Problem. Provide closed-form or efficiently computable expressions, or matching upper and lower bounds, for the three functionals

  R(G, N),  η*(G),  p*(G),

as functions of the graph topology of G (e.g. degree sequence, girth, vertex connectivity, expansion, or local-Clifford equivalence class) and of the parameters (η, p, q) of the noise model N. In particular, determine whether for natural graph families (paths, stars, complete graphs, 2D and 3D lattices) one can rigorously establish:

(a) an explicit secret-key-rate formula R(G, N) achievable by an explicit protocol;
(b) loss-tolerance thresholds η*(G) and error thresholds p*(G) that scale favorably with n for at least one infinite family of graphs;
(c) a topological criterion on G that is necessary and sufficient for the resulting MQKA protocol to support measurement-based routing (i.e. distillation of an n-party GHZ-type secret-sharing primitive between any chosen subset of parties) under the noise model N.

representations.normalized:
A multiparty quantum key agreement (MQKA) protocol is a protocol in which n mutually distrustful parties P_1,...,P_n jointly establish a common secret key K such that (i) every party contributes equally to K (fairness), (ii) no proper subset of parties can predetermine or bias K (collusion resistance), and (iii) security against external eavesdroppers is guaranteed by the laws of quantum mechanics.

Investigate whether the design principles and security guarantees of MQKA can be lifted to the following three multiparty cryptographic primitives, and in each case either construct a protocol meeting the stated security goals or prove an impossibility result:

1. (t,n)-threshold key schemes. Design an MQKA-based protocol that produces shares s_1,...,s_n of a key K such that any t shares reconstruct K while any t-1 shares reveal no information about K, with security (against both outside adversaries and coalitions of up to t-1 dishonest parties) reducible to quantum-mechanical assumptions rather than computational ones, and quantify the advantage over classical (t,n)-threshold secret sharing.

2. Quantum private comparison (QPC). Using MQKA-style fairness and collusion resistance, construct a protocol allowing n parties holding private inputs x_1,...,x_n to compute a comparison predicate (e.g. equality of all x_i) while revealing nothing else about the inputs, even under arbitrary collusions of up to n-1 participants and an untrusted assistant, and characterize the optimal trade-offs among round complexity, qubit cost, and tolerated collusion size.

3. Hybrid classical–quantum distributed ledgers. Define a distributed ledger consensus protocol in which transaction validity and authentication are derived from a fairness-aware MQKA subroutine, and prove security properties analogous to safety, liveness, and resistance to coalitions controlling a bounded fraction of parties, identifying the precise quantum-cryptographic assumption (e.g. authenticated quantum channels, no-cloning, monogamy of entanglement) that gives a provable advantage over purely classical Byzantine consensus.

The overarching question is: do quantum mechanics together with the MQKA notions of fairness and collusion resistance yield concrete, provable security advantages over the best classical schemes for key recovery, private comparison, authentication, consensus, and transaction validity in the multiparty setting?

Fix integers $r \ge 1$ and $p \ge 2$, and let $d, n \ge 1$. A tensor $T \in (\mathbb{R}^d)^{\otimes r}$ is called symmetric if its entries $T_{i_1 \dots i_r}$ are invariant under all permutations of the indices. For a symmetric tensor $T$ define its symmetric injective $\ell_p$ norm by
$$\|T\|_{I_p} \;=\; \max_{\substack{x \in \mathbb{R}^d \\ \|x\|_p \le 1}} \bigl|\langle T, x^{\otimes r}\rangle\bigr|, \qquad \langle T, x^{\otimes r}\rangle \;=\; \sum_{i_1,\dots,i_r=1}^{d} T_{i_1\dots i_r}\, x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_r}.$$
Let $T_1, \dots, T_n \in (\mathbb{R}^d)^{\otimes r}$ be deterministic symmetric tensors, and let $g_1, \dots, g_n$ be independent standard Gaussian random variables. Determine whether there exists a constant depending only on $r$ and $p$, together with polylogarithmic factors in $d$ and $n$ (denoted $\widetilde{O}_{r,p}$), such that
$$\mathbb{E}\, \Bigl\| \sum_{i=1}^n g_i\, T_i \Bigr\|_{I_p} \;\le\; \widetilde{O}_{r,p}\!\left( d^{\,1/2 - 1/p}\, \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^n \|T_i\|_{I_p}^{\,2}\Bigr)^{\!1/2}\right)$$
holds for every choice of $d$, $n$, and symmetric tensors $T_1, \dots, T_n$.

For a positive integer $n$, a circulant graph on the vertex set $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ is determined by a symmetric "connection set" $S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \setminus \{0\}$ (with $S = -S$): vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent iff $i - j \in S$. Sample a random dense circulant graph $G$ on $n$ vertices by choosing $S$ uniformly at random among all symmetric subsets of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ (equivalently, by independently including each unordered pair $\{k,-k\}$ with $k \neq 0$ in $S$ with probability $1/2$).

For a graph $G$, the Lovász theta number $\vartheta(G)$ is defined by
$$\vartheta(G) = \max \sum_{i,j \in V(G)} X_{ij},$$
where the maximum is taken over all positive semidefinite matrices $X = (X_{ij})$ indexed by $V(G)$ such that $\operatorname{tr}(X) = 1$ and $X_{ij} = 0$ whenever $i \neq j$ and $\{i,j\}$ is an edge of $G$.

Question: Does
$$\mathbb{E}[\vartheta(G)] = (1 + o(1))\sqrt{n}$$
hold as $n \to \infty$, where the expectation is over the random circulant graph $G$ defined above?

For a real matrix A ∈ R^{N×M} with rows A_1, …, A_N ∈ R^M, and for any subset S ⊆ [N] := {1, …, N}, let A_S denote the submatrix of A formed by the rows indexed by S, and let σ_M(A_S) denote the smallest singular value of A_S (with σ_M(A_S) := 0 if A_S has fewer than M rows). Let S^c = [N] \ S. Define
   ω(A) = min { σ_M(A_S) : S ⊆ [N] and rank(A_{S^c}) < M }.
Assume A has the property that every subset of M of its rows spans R^M (equivalently, A satisfies the "complement property" ensuring injectivity of the squared-magnitude measurement map).

Question: Do there exist universal constants C > 0 and 0 < β < 1 (independent of M and of A) such that, for every M > 1 and every such matrix A ∈ R^{(2M−1)×M},

A finite collection of unit vectors $\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}\subset\mathbb{C}^d$ is called an equiangular tight frame (ETF) if there exist constants $\alpha\geq 0$ and $\beta>0$ such that $|\langle v_i,v_j\rangle|=\alpha$ for all $i\neq j$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n v_iv_i^*=\beta\,I_d$. Equivalently, when $n=d^2$, such a configuration corresponds to a symmetric informationally complete positive operator-valued measure (SIC-POVM): a set of $d^2$ rank-one operators $\Pi_i=\frac{1}{d}v_iv_i^*$ summing to $I_d$ with $|\langle v_i,v_j\rangle|^2=\frac{1}{d+1}$ for $i\neq j$.

Prove or disprove: for every positive integer $d$, there exists an equiangular tight frame in $\mathbb{C}^d$ consisting of exactly $d^2$ unit vectors (equivalently, a SIC-POVM exists in every finite complex dimension $d$).

Let $G_{p,1}$ denote the "1-localization" of $G_p$: the induced subgraph of $G_p$ on the set $N(0) = \{x \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times : x \text{ is a nonzero quadratic residue mod } p\}$ of vertices adjacent to $0$.

Recall that the Lovász theta number $\vartheta(H)$ of a graph $H$ on vertex set $V$ is defined by
$$\vartheta(H) = \max \sum_{i,j \in V} B_{ij},$$
where the maximum is over symmetric positive semidefinite matrices $B \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times V}$ with $\mathrm{tr}(B) = 1$ and $B_{ij} = 0$ whenever $i \neq j$ and $\{i,j\}$ is an edge of $H$.

Determine whether
$$\vartheta(G_{p,1}) \sim \sqrt{p/2} \qquad \text{as } p \to \infty \text{ through primes } p \equiv 1 \pmod 4.$$

Let p be an odd prime with p ≡ 1 (mod 4). The Paley graph G_p has vertex set F_p (the finite field of order p), with two distinct vertices u, v adjacent if and only if u − v is a nonzero quadratic residue in F_p. Let ω(G_p) denote the clique number of G_p.

For a graph G on vertex set V = {1,…,n}, the degree-4 Sum-of-Squares (SoS) relaxation of the clique number is the optimal value of the following pseudo-expectation problem: maximize Ẽ[∑_{i∈V} x_i] over linear functionals Ẽ on the space of polynomials in x_1,…,x_n of degree ≤ 4 satisfying
 (i) Ẽ[1] = 1;
 (ii) Ẽ[x_i^2 − x_i] = 0 for every i ∈ V (Boolean constraints);
 (iii) Ẽ[x_i x_j · q(x)] = 0 for every edge {i,j} ∉ E(G) (i.e., every non-edge) and every polynomial q with deg(x_i x_j q) ≤ 4 (independent-set constraint);
 (iv) Ẽ[p(x)^2] ≥ 0 for every polynomial p with deg(p) ≤ 2.
Denote this optimum by SoS_4(G).

It is classical (via the Hoffman/Lovász-type spectral bound) that SoS_4(G_p) = O(√p), and a lower bound SoS_4(G_p) = Ω(p^{1/3}) is known.

Question: Does there exist a constant ε > 0 such that
 SoS_4(G_p) = O(p^{1/2 − ε})
as p ranges over primes with p ≡ 1 (mod 4)?

Let $\mu$ be a log-concave probability measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$, i.e. a Borel probability measure whose density $f$ with respect to Lebesgue measure (when restricted to its support) satisfies $f(\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y) \ge f(x)^\lambda f(y)^{1-\lambda}$ for all $x,y$ in the support and $\lambda \in [0,1]$. Assume $\mu$ has finite second moments and let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ denote its covariance matrix, with operator norm $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. The isoperimetric (Cheeger) constant of $\mu$ is defined by
$$\psi_\mu \;=\; \inf_{S \subset \mathbb{R}^n} \frac{\mu^+(\partial S)}{\min(\mu(S), 1-\mu(S))},$$
where the infimum runs over all Borel sets $S$ and $\mu^+(\partial S) = \liminf_{\varepsilon \to 0^+}\frac{\mu(S_\varepsilon)-\mu(S)}{\varepsilon}$ is the Minkowski boundary measure (with $S_\varepsilon$ the open $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of $S$).

Prove or disprove: there exists a universal constant $C>0$, independent of $n$ and of $\mu$, such that for every log-concave probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$,
$$\psi_\mu \;\ge\; \frac{C}{\sqrt{\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}}}.$$

For a group (or more generally a semigroup) $G$, the power semigroup $\mathcal{P}(G)$ is the semigroup whose underlying set is the collection of all nonempty subsets of $G$, equipped with the multiplication
$$A\cdot B=\{ab:a\in A,\ b\in B\}$$
for $A,B\subseteq G$ nonempty. A group is called periodic if every element has finite order. A semigroup $S$ is said to embed into a semigroup $T$ if there is an injective homomorphism $S\hookrightarrow T$.

It is known that not every finite semigroup embeds into a power semigroup over some finite group, although every semigroup is a divisor (a homomorphic image of a subsemigroup) of the power semigroup over some periodic group, and the property of being a divisor of the power semigroup of some finite group is algorithmically decidable for finite semigroups.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm which, given as input a finite semigroup $S$ (e.g., by its multiplication table), decides whether $S$ embeds into the power semigroup $\mathcal{P}(G)$ for some finite group $G$? More generally, does there exist such an algorithm deciding whether $S$ embeds into $\mathcal{P}(G)$ for some periodic group $G$?

Let a predicate $P$ on semigroups be a property of pairs (or tuples) of elements, such as the equality predicate $x = y$, the divisibility predicates $x \mid y$ (right, left, or two-sided), membership in a given (principal) ideal, membership in a maximal subgroup, conjugacy, or other commonly studied semigroup-theoretic relations.

A semigroup $S$ is said to be residually finite with respect to a predicate $P$ if, whenever $P$ fails on a tuple of elements of $S$, there exists a homomorphism $\varphi: S \to F$ onto a finite semigroup $F$ such that $P$ also fails on the image tuple in $F$. (For the equality predicate this recovers the classical notion of residual finiteness.)

A variety $\mathcal{V}$ of semigroups is called locally residually finite with respect to $P$ if every finitely generated semigroup in $\mathcal{V}$ is residually finite with respect to $P$.

The problem: For each of the standard semigroup predicates (equality, the various divisibility predicates, membership in principal ideals, membership in maximal subgroups, and other classically considered predicates), give an explicit description—preferably in terms of identities or other effectively verifiable conditions—of all semigroup varieties that are locally residually finite with respect to that predicate.

A semigroup is called regular if for every element $a$ there exists an element $x$ such that $axa = a$. A semigroup variety is a class of semigroups closed under taking subsemigroups, homomorphic images, and direct products; equivalently, it is the class of all semigroups satisfying a given set of identities. A semigroup variety $\mathcal{V}$ is called periodic if every member of $\mathcal{V}$ is a periodic semigroup, i.e. for every element $a$ there exist positive integers $m, r$ with $a^{m+r} = a^m$. For a class $\mathcal{K}$ of semigroups, let $\mathrm{var}(\mathcal{K})$ denote the smallest variety containing $\mathcal{K}$.

Problem: Give an explicit description (for instance, by identities, by structural invariants, or by a combinatorial characterization) of all periodic semigroup varieties $\mathcal{V}$ of the form $\mathcal{V} = \mathrm{var}(\mathcal{R})$, where $\mathcal{R}$ is a class (equivalently, a single member) of regular semigroups.

(For comparison, an analogous description is known when $\mathcal{R}$ is restricted to consist of completely $0$-simple semigroups; the task is to extend such a description to arbitrary regular semigroups.)

By the Rees theorem, every finite completely $0$-simple semigroup is isomorphic to a Rees matrix semigroup $\mathcal{M}^0(G; I, \Lambda; P)$ over a finite group $G$ with a regular sandwich matrix $P$ over $G \cup \{0\}$.

A semigroup is said to be finitely based if the variety it generates can be defined by finitely many identities (i.e., its identities admit a finite basis).

Identifying finite completely $0$-simple semigroups over Abelian groups with their finite descriptions as Rees matrix semigroups $\mathcal{M}^0(A; I, \Lambda; P)$ where $A$ is a finite Abelian group, decide whether the set of (codes of) finite finitely based completely $0$-simple semigroups over finite Abelian groups is a recursive (decidable) subset. An ordered semigroup is a triple $(S,\cdot,\le)$ where $(S,\cdot)$ is a semigroup and $\le$ is a partial order on $S$ that is compatible with the multiplication, i.e., $a\le b$ implies $ca\le cb$ and $ac\le bc$ for all $a,b,c\in S$. A variety of ordered semigroups is a class of ordered semigroups defined by a set of inequalities $u\le v$ between semigroup terms, equivalently a class closed under taking ordered subsemigroups, order-preserving homomorphic images, and direct products (with componentwise order). The collection of all varieties of ordered semigroups, ordered by inclusion, forms a complete lattice $\mathcal{L}$. For two varieties $\mathcal{U}\subsetneq \mathcal{V}$ in $\mathcal{L}$, $\mathcal{V}$ is called a cover of $\mathcal{U}$ if there is no variety $\mathcal{W}$ with $\mathcal{U}\subsetneq \mathcal{W}\subsetneq \mathcal{V}$. A variety $\mathcal{U}\in\mathcal{L}$ is said to "have a cover" if there exists at least one variety $\mathcal{V}\in\mathcal{L}$ that is a cover of $\mathcal{U}$.

Problem. Give a complete description (characterization) of all varieties of ordered semigroups that have a cover in the lattice $\mathcal{L}$ of varieties of ordered semigroups.

Call $S$ a Lesokhin semigroup if every endomorphism of $S$ is a power function. An element $e \in S$ is idempotent if $e^2 = e$.

Give a complete description (classification) of all finitely generated Lesokhin semigroups that contain no idempotent elements.

(It is known that within the separative case, every such semigroup is isomorphic to a subsemigroup of an infinite monogenic semigroup; the problem asks for a description in the general finitely generated case without idempotents.)

Let $S$ be a commutative semigroup, and let $\operatorname{End}(S)$ denote the set of all semigroup endomorphisms $S \to S$, equipped with the pointwise multiplication operation $(\varphi \cdot \psi)(x) = \varphi(x)\psi(x)$, which makes $\operatorname{End}(S)$ into a commutative semigroup. Let $S$ be a semigroup. Define a relation $<$ on $S$ by $a < b$ if and only if $a \neq b$ and $a = ab = ba$. This relation is a strict partial order on any semigroup without idempotents. The chain rank of $S$ is defined as the supremum of the lengths $n$ for which there exist elements $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n \in S$ with $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_n$; the chain rank is infinite if such chains can be made arbitrarily long.

It is known that every finitely generated commutative semigroup without idempotents has finite chain rank.

Question: Does every finitely generated semigroup without idempotents have finite chain rank? More restrictively, does every finitely presented semigroup without idempotents have finite chain rank?

For a mathematical structure $A$ (for example, a partially ordered set, a relatively free algebra, or another algebraic or relational structure), let $\mathrm{End}(A)$ denote the semigroup of all endomorphisms of $A$ under composition, and let $\mathrm{Aut}(A)$ denote the group of all automorphisms of $A$. A class $\mathcal{K}$ of structures is said to be determined up to isomorphism by endomorphism semigroups if, for any $A,B\in\mathcal{K}$, an isomorphism $\mathrm{End}(A)\cong\mathrm{End}(B)$ of semigroups implies $A\cong B$. More generally, given an assignment that to each structure $A$ associates a subsemigroup $S(A)\subseteq\mathrm{End}(A)$, the structures in $\mathcal{K}$ are said to be determined up to isomorphism by $S$ if $S(A)\cong S(B)$ as semigroups implies $A\cong B$ for all $A,B\in\mathcal{K}$.

For natural classes of mathematical structures — in particular, classes of ordered sets and classes of relatively free algebras — solve the following two problems:

(1) Identify those subclasses $\mathcal{K}$ that are determined up to isomorphism by their endomorphism semigroups $\mathrm{End}(A)$, $A\in\mathcal{K}$.

(2) Identify those distinguished subsemigroups $S(A)\subseteq\mathrm{End}(A)$ (defined uniformly across the class) such that the assignment $A\mapsto S(A)$ determines the structures of $\mathcal{K}$ up to isomorphism.

Let $X$ be a nonempty set and let $T(X)$ denote the full transformation monoid on $X$, i.e. the set of all maps $X \to X$ under composition. Endow $T(X)$ with the pointwise convergence topology: a net $(f_\alpha)$ converges to $f$ if and only if $f_\alpha(x) = f(x)$ eventually for every $x \in X$. Equivalently, $T(X)$ carries the product topology inherited from $X^X$ where $X$ is given the discrete topology. A subsemigroup $S \subseteq T(X)$ is said to be closed in the pointwise topology if it is closed as a subset of $T(X)$ in this topology. It is known that the closed subsemigroups of $T(X)$ in the pointwise topology are exactly the endomorphism monoids of relational (or first-order) structures with universe $X$.

Now let $\mathcal{A}$ be an algebraic structure (e.g. a group, semigroup, ring, or universal algebra), and let $\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{A})$ be its monoid of endomorphisms. The Zariski-type topology on $\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{A})$ is the topology whose subbasis of closed sets consists of the "equation solution sets"
$$V(u,v) = \{\, \varphi \in \mathrm{End}(\mathcal{A}) : u(\varphi(a_1),\ldots,\varphi(a_n)) = v(\varphi(a_1),\ldots,\varphi(a_n))\,\},$$
where $u, v$ are terms in the signature of $\mathcal{A}$ and $a_1,\ldots,a_n \in \mathcal{A}$. The Zariski-type topology is in general weaker than the pointwise convergence topology on $\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{A})$.

Solve the following two problems.

(1) Give an intrinsic description (e.g. in terms of algebraic, combinatorial or model-theoretic invariants) of those subsemigroups of $T(X)$ that are closed in the pointwise convergence topology.

(2) Give an intrinsic description of those submonoids of $\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{A})$ (for $\mathcal{A}$ ranging over a natural class of algebraic structures) that are closed in the Zariski-type topology defined above.

Background and definitions.

(a) A finite semigroup S is called 0-simple if it has a zero element 0 and its only ideals are {0} and S, and S^2 ≠ {0}. By the Rees theorem, every finite 0-simple semigroup is isomorphic to a Rees matrix semigroup M^0(G; I, Λ; P) over a finite group G (the structure group) with a Λ × I sandwich matrix P having entries in G ∪ {0}. A finite Brandt semigroup is a finite 0-simple inverse semigroup; equivalently, it has the form B(G, n) where the sandwich matrix is the n × n identity matrix over G ∪ {0}.

(b) A pseudovariety of finite groups is a class of finite groups closed under taking finite direct products, subgroups, and homomorphic images. A pseudovariety H is said to have decidable universal theory if there is an algorithm that, given a universal first-order sentence φ in the language of groups, decides whether φ holds in every group of H.

(c) Let C be a class of finite semigroups closed under isomorphism. A Birkhoff operator is one of the standard class operators sending a class X of (finite) algebras to one of: H(X) (homomorphic images), S(X) (subalgebras), P_fin(X) (finite direct products), or any finite composition of such operators. Given a finite semigroup presentation Φ = ⟨A | R⟩, let K(Φ) denote the set of those finite semigroups in K that satisfy the relations R for some assignment of generators (equivalently, the membership/word problem associated with the operator class K applied to Φ). The class C is said to be completely solvable if for every Birkhoff operator K and every finite presentation Φ, the set K(Φ) is recursive (i.e., membership in K(C) is uniformly decidable from the presentation Φ).

Problem. Decide each of the following:

(1) Let H be a pseudovariety of finite groups with decidable universal theory, and let C_H be the class of finite 0-simple semigroups whose structure group lies in H. Is C_H completely solvable?

(2) Let H be a pseudovariety of finite groups with decidable universal theory, and let B_H be the class of finite Brandt semigroups whose maximal subgroups lie in H. Is B_H completely solvable?

A class K of finite semigroups is said to be completely solvable if there exists an algorithm that, given a finite semigroup S (presented, say, by its multiplication table), decides whether S belongs to K, and moreover decides membership in K for every finitely generated subsemigroup-defining problem associated with K (i.e., the membership problem for K is decidable in a uniform algorithmic sense).

Recall the following definitions:
- A semigroup S is regular if for every a ∈ S there exists x ∈ S with a x a = a.
- An element e ∈ S is idempotent if e² = e; the set of idempotents of S is denoted E(S).
- A regular semigroup S is orthodox if E(S) is a subsemigroup of S (equivalently, the product of any two idempotents of S is again idempotent).
- A variety of idempotent semigroups (band variety) is a class of semigroups satisfying e² = e together with some additional set of identities, closed under taking subsemigroups, homomorphic images, and direct products.

Determine whether each of the following classes of finite semigroups is completely solvable:

(1) The class of all finite regular orthodox semigroups.

(2) For a fixed variety V of idempotent semigroups, the class of all finite regular semigroups S such that the band E(S) (with the multiplication inherited from S) belongs to V.

For a group (or semigroup) $G$, let $\mathcal{P}(G)$ denote the power semigroup of $G$: the set of all nonempty subsets of $G$ equipped with the multiplication
$$A \cdot B = \{ab : a \in A,\ b \in B\}.$$
A semigroup $S$ is called periodic if for every $s \in S$ there exist positive integers $m \neq n$ with $s^m = s^n$ (equivalently, every monogenic subsemigroup of $S$ is finite). A group $G$ is periodic if every element has finite order.

Question: Does every periodic commutative semigroup $S$ embed (as a semigroup) into $\mathcal{P}(G)$ for some periodic Abelian group $G$?

representations.normalized:
Background. A class of semigroups is called an inclusive variety if it can be axiomatised by a set of identical inclusions, i.e. by formulas of the form w₁ ⊆ w₂ where w₁, w₂ are semigroup words and w₁ ⊆ w₂ in a semigroup S means that for every assignment of the variables to elements of S, the value of the word w₁ is contained (as an element) in the subsemigroup generated by the value of w₂ — equivalently, every value of w₁ can be written as a value of w₂. The collection of all inclusive subvarieties of a fixed inclusive variety V, ordered by inclusion, forms a complete lattice L_in(V).

Problem. Describe (classify) all inclusive varieties V of semigroups for which the lattice L_in(V) of inclusive subvarieties is at most countable; in particular, give a characterisation of those V for which L_in(V) is finite, and of those for which L_in(V) is countably infinite.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

A partial characterisation is known: for inclusive varieties of abelian groups, a complete description of when the lattice of inclusive subvarieties is finite has been obtained (Mashevitzky, "Nonelementary inclusive varieties of groups and semigroups", Algebra Universalis 86 (2025), no. 14). A full classification for arbitrary inclusive varieties of semigroups does not appear to be available in the literature, so the problem remains only partially solved.

representations.normalized:
Background and definitions. Let $S$ be a semigroup. An identical inclusion on $S$ is a formal expression of the form
$$ w(x_1,\dots,x_n) \in \{w_1(x_1,\dots,x_n),\, w_2(x_1,\dots,x_n),\,\dots\}, $$
where $w$ and the $w_i$ are words in the free semigroup on the variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$. The semigroup $S$ is said to satisfy this identical inclusion if for every assignment of the variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ to elements of $S$, the value of $w$ in $S$ coincides with the value of $w_i$ for at least one index $i$. (Thus an ordinary identity $w = w_1$ is the special case in which the right-hand set is a singleton.)

Two semigroups $S$ and $T$ are called inclusively equivalent if they satisfy exactly the same identical inclusions. Equivalently, they generate the same inclusive variety, where the inclusive variety generated by a class of semigroups is the class of all semigroups satisfying every identical inclusion satisfied by every member of the generating class.

Problem. For each of the following basic classes of semigroups, give a complete classification of its members up to inclusive equivalence:

(a) nilsemigroups,
(b) nilpotent semigroups,
(c) periodic Clifford semigroups (semilattices of groups whose maximal subgroups are periodic),
(d) finite groups,
(e) cyclic $p$-groups (for each prime $p$).

That is, in each class describe explicitly the equivalence classes of the inclusive-equivalence relation, equivalently parametrize the inclusive varieties generated by single members of the class.

representations.normalized:
Background and definitions. Let $X = \{x_1, x_2, \ldots\}$ be a countably infinite alphabet and let $X^+$ denote the free semigroup on $X$. An identity is a formal expression $u = v$ with $u, v \in X^+$; an identical inclusion (in the sense of Lyapin) is a formal expression of the form
$$u \in \{w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_k\},$$
where $u, w_1, \ldots, w_k \in X^+$. A semigroup $S$ satisfies the identical inclusion $u \in \{w_1, \ldots, w_k\}$ if for every homomorphism $\varphi : X^+ \to S$ one has $\varphi(u) \in \{\varphi(w_1), \ldots, \varphi(w_k)\}$.

A (semigroup) variety $\mathcal{V}$ is, as usual, a class of semigroups defined by some set of identities; for each $n \geq 1$, the $n$-generated free semigroup of $\mathcal{V}$ is denoted $F_n(\mathcal{V})$. Say that the finitely generated free semigroups of $\mathcal{V}$ are separated from each other by identical inclusions if for every pair of positive integers $m \neq n$ there exists an identical inclusion that is satisfied in exactly one of $F_m(\mathcal{V})$ and $F_n(\mathcal{V})$.

Problem. Describe all (ordinary) semigroup varieties $\mathcal{V}$ with the property that the finitely generated free semigroups $F_1(\mathcal{V}), F_2(\mathcal{V}), F_3(\mathcal{V}), \ldots$ are pairwise separated from each other by identical inclusions. (As a known instance, the variety of semilattices has this property.)

Work in the signature of semigroups (a single binary associative operation). A class K of semigroups is called an inclusive variety if it is closed under taking subsemigroups, homomorphic images, and arbitrary direct products. An inclusive variety is called elementary if it can be axiomatized by a set of first-order sentences in the language of semigroups. A variety of semigroups is, as usual, a class defined by a set of identities (which is automatically an inclusive variety).

For a semigroup variety V, let V_fin denote the class of all finite members of V, and let V_fg denote the class of all finitely generated members of V.

Question: Does there exist a variety V of semigroups such that V_fin is an elementary inclusive variety? Equivalently (as a parallel question), does there exist a variety V of semigroups such that V_fg is an elementary inclusive variety?

representations.normalized:
Background and definitions.

Let S be a semigroup. An identical inclusion over S (in the sense of Lyapin) is a universally closed expression of the form
   w(x_1,…,x_n) ∈ {w_1(x_1,…,x_n), w_2(x_1,…,x_n), …, w_k(x_1,…,x_n)},
where w, w_1, …, w_k are semigroup words in the variables x_1,…,x_n. A semigroup S satisfies this identical inclusion if, for every assignment of the variables x_1,…,x_n to elements of S, the value of w equals the value of at least one of the words w_i. An identical inclusion is called elementary if k is finite (only finitely many words appear on the right-hand side).

A class K of semigroups is called an inclusive variety if it is the class of all semigroups satisfying some (possibly infinite) system Σ of identical inclusions. The inclusive variety generated by a set X of semigroups is the smallest inclusive variety containing X, equivalently the class of all semigroups satisfying every identical inclusion that holds in every member of X.

An inclusive variety V is said to be finitely based by elementary identical inclusions if there is a finite system Σ of elementary identical inclusions such that V is exactly the class of all semigroups satisfying Σ.

Problem.

Decide the following question algorithmically: given as input a finite list S_1, S_2, …, S_m of finite semigroups (each presented by its multiplication table), determine whether the inclusive variety generated by {S_1,…,S_m} is finitely based by elementary identical inclusions. Either exhibit such an algorithm, or prove that no such algorithm exists.

representations.normalized:
A partial groupoid (pargoid) is a set P equipped with a partial binary operation, i.e. a partial map · : P × P ⇀ P. A semigroup S is called an outer extension of a pargoid P if P ⊆ S and, for all a, b ∈ P with a · b defined in P, the product ab in S equals a · b; equivalently, the partial operation on P is the restriction of the multiplication of S.

Given a semigroup S, its set E(S) of idempotents (elements e ∈ S with e² = e) inherits from S the partial operation defined by: e * f is defined and equals ef whenever e, f ∈ E(S) and ef ∈ E(S). The resulting pargoid is called the pargoid of idempotents of S.

Solve the following characterization problems.

(1) Pargoids of projections. Let X be a set and let T(X) be the full transformation semigroup on X (all maps X → X under composition). The idempotents of T(X) are called projections of X. Give an abstract characterization, in purely pargoid-theoretic terms, of those pargoids that are isomorphic to the pargoid of idempotents of T(X) for some set X.

(2) Pargoids of matrix units. For a set I, the matrix-unit semigroup on I is the set M(I) = (I × I) ∪ {0} with multiplication (i, j)(k, l) = (i, l) if j = k and 0 otherwise (and 0 absorbing). Characterize, in pargoid-theoretic terms, those pargoids that arise as the pargoid of idempotents (equivalently, of matrix units together with 0) of M(I) for some set I.

(3) Pargoids of idempotents of basic classes of semigroups. For each of the standard classes of semigroups (e.g. groups, completely simple semigroups, completely 0-simple semigroups, inverse semigroups, regular semigroups, commutative semigroups, bands), give an intrinsic abstract characterization of those pargoids which occur, up to isomorphism, as the pargoid of idempotents of some semigroup in the given class.

A pargoid is a set equipped with a partial binary operation, i.e., a partial groupoid: a set $P$ together with a partial map $\cdot : D \to P$ defined on some subset $D \subseteq P \times P$. A pargoid of transformations on a set $X$ is a pargoid whose elements are (total or partial) transformations of $X$, where the operation is the usual composition of transformations restricted to those pairs $(f,g)$ for which the composition is required to lie in the pargoid (so the composition $f\cdot g$ is defined in the pargoid precisely when this composed transformation belongs to the pargoid).

A semigroup extension of a pargoid $(P,\cdot)$ is a semigroup $(S,*)$ such that $P \subseteq S$ and, for all $a,b \in P$ with $a\cdot b$ defined in $P$, one has $a*b = a\cdot b$. Such an extension is called internal if $S$ is itself a semigroup of transformations of $X$ extending $P$, with $*$ given by composition of transformations.

Problem. Give a characterization (by necessary and sufficient conditions, intrinsic to the pargoid) of those pargoids of transformations that admit an internal semigroup extension.
