A semigroup extension of a pargoid $(P,\cdot)$ is a semigroup $(S,*)$ such that $P \subseteq S$ and, for all $a,b \in P$ with $a\cdot b$ defined in $P$, one has $a*b = a\cdot b$. Such an extension is called internal if $S$ is itself a semigroup of transformations of $X$ extending $P$, with $*$ given by composition of transformations.

Problem. Give a characterization (by necessary and sufficient conditions, intrinsic to the pargoid) of those pargoids of transformations that admit an internal semigroup extension.

The shaping of asymmetric (bipolar, multipolar, point-symmetric) planetary nebulae remains an active and unresolved question in stellar astrophysics. The leading paradigm increasingly favors binary/companion interactions (common envelope, jets, wind Roche-lobe overflow) imprinting asymmetries during the late-AGB or proto-PN phase, supported by ALMA and HST imaging showing structure already in pre-PN sources, but no single mechanism is established as universally responsible, and the precise onset epoch is still debated. Around certain planetary nebulae and proto-planetary nebulae one observes systems of concentric arcs and quasi-circular rings, as well as bipolar lobes that sometimes appear along two distinct symmetry axes (a "primary" and a "secondary" bipolar axis). Assuming that these concentric arcs/rings are imprints of repeated, quasi-periodic mass-loss episodes from the central evolved star (asymptotic giant branch or post-AGB phase), address the following:

(a) Identify the physical mechanism that sets the recurrence timescale between successive mass-loss episodes responsible for the concentric arcs and rings. In particular, determine which stellar process — e.g. thermal pulses of the helium-burning shell, large-amplitude radial pulsations, magnetic activity cycles, hydrodynamical wind instabilities, or binary-companion interactions — produces inter-ring spacings consistent with the observed range of a few hundred to ~2000 years, and derive (or otherwise characterize) the predicted period as a function of stellar parameters.

(b) Identify the physical mechanism that causes successive episodic outflows (jets or bipolar lobes) to change orientation between a primary bipolar axis and a secondary bipolar axis. In particular, determine whether such reorientation is driven by precession of an accretion disk in a binary or triple system, by misalignment between stellar rotation and magnetic axes, by tidal/orbital evolution of a companion, or by another mechanism, and predict the angular relation and timescale between successive lobe directions.

A complete solution should give a self-consistent physical model linking the recurrence period of the rings/arcs to the reorientation of bipolar lobes, with quantitative predictions that can be compared to observed nebular morphologies.

Around the central stars of certain planetary nebulae, and in the equatorial regions of various bipolar and multipolar planetary nebulae, observations reveal compact gaseous/dusty disks or torus-like structures, often accompanied by directional (jet-like) outflows that appear to shape the host nebula into narrow-waist bipolar or multipolar morphologies.

(a) Identify the physical mechanism(s) responsible for the formation of these compact circumstellar disks and torus-like structures. Specifically, determine which of the following processes (or which combination thereof) accounts for their existence: (i) Roche-lobe overflow and accretion in a binary system containing the post-AGB primary; (ii) common-envelope evolution and its ejecta; (iii) tidal disruption or engulfment of a sub-stellar or planetary companion; (iv) wind-Roche-lobe overflow; (v) magnetically channelled mass loss from a single rotating AGB/post-AGB star; or (vi) some other process.

(b) Determine whether and how such disks (or related accretion structures) generate and collimate the observed directional outflows. In particular, specify the launching mechanism (e.g., magneto-centrifugal disk winds, magnetic-tower jets, radiation- or line-driven jets, accretion-powered outflows, or hydrodynamic focusing by an equatorial density enhancement of a wide spherical fast wind as in generalized interacting-stellar-winds models), and quantitatively relate the disk properties (mass, size, lifetime, magnetic field, accretion rate) to the resulting outflow's velocity, mass-loss rate, opening angle, and degree of collimation needed to produce the observed narrow-waist bipolar or multipolar nebular morphologies.

Consider a star transitioning from the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) phase to the planetary nebula phase. During and after this post-AGB evolution, the surrounding circumstellar envelope expands and reaches very low gas densities (typically below about 10^6 particles per cm^3), with the synthesis phase lasting on the order of only 10^3 years. Spectroscopic observations of planetary nebulae reveal a family of unidentified infrared emission (UIE) bands (notably near 3.3, 6.2, 7.7, 8.6, and 11.3 μm) whose carriers are believed to be complex organic compounds with mixed aromatic and aliphatic structures (e.g., polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon–like nanoparticles or mixed aromatic/aliphatic organic nanoparticles). These UIE bands are absent or weak in AGB progenitors but appear strongly in planetary nebulae, indicating that substantial chemical synthesis takes place during the short post-AGB transition.

Problem: Formulate and justify a physical/chemical mechanism explaining how complex organic compounds containing both aromatic ring systems and aliphatic side chains can be synthesized in such low-density circumstellar environments on timescales of order 10^3 years during or after the post-AGB phase. The mechanism should account for (i) the rapid growth of aromatic ring networks starting from simple precursors such as acetylene, (ii) the attachment and preservation of aliphatic groups, (iii) the role (if any) of UV photochemistry, shocks, grain-surface reactions, or non-equilibrium processes given the prevailing temperature, density, and radiation field, and (iv) the observed contrast between AGB and post-AGB/planetary-nebula spectra.

A proto-planetary nebula (proto-PN) is the short-lived transitional object produced when a star evolves off the asymptotic giant branch toward the planetary-nebula phase. Many proto-PNe display strikingly axisymmetric or point-symmetric morphologies (bipolar lobes, jets, multipolar structures) that are widely modeled as being shaped by interaction with a binary (or substellar) companion to the central evolved star. However, no direct detection of a close stellar companion has yet been made for any proto-PN central source.

Formulate and answer the following question. Within the population of proto-planetary nebulae whose morphologies indicate companion-driven shaping:

(a) Identify, observationally, the binary companions of the central stars of proto-planetary nebulae.

(b) If such companions remain undetected by current methods, determine whether they are predominantly:
   (i) very low-mass companions, namely stellar objects with mass M < 0.2 M_sun, brown dwarfs, or planets; or
   (ii) stellar companions on long orbital periods, P > 30 yr,
or some combination of (i) and (ii), and quantify the relative frequencies of these populations.

Provide observational or theoretical evidence sufficient to discriminate among these possibilities for the proto-PN sample.

Consider a hierarchical triple stellar system, i.e., a gravitationally bound system consisting of an inner binary (two stars in a relatively tight orbit) together with a third (outer) star orbiting the center of mass of the inner binary on a much wider orbit, with the orbits arranged so that the system is dynamically stable on secular timescales. Each star evolves through standard stellar evolutionary phases, eventually possibly reaching the asymptotic giant branch (AGB), during which the star develops an extended convective envelope and undergoes heavy mass loss via stellar winds, and the subsequent planetary nebula (PN) phase, in which the ejected envelope is ionized by the hot stellar core and observed as an expanding nebular outflow.

Within this setting, develop a quantitative theory describing the joint orbital and stellar evolution of hierarchical triples from the main-sequence stage up to and through the AGB and PN phases of one of their members, accounting for the following coupled physical mechanisms:

1. Secular gravitational dynamics of the triple, including von Zeipel–Lidov–Kozai eccentricity/inclination oscillations of the inner binary driven by the outer companion, and their interaction with tidal dissipation and stellar structure changes.
2. Hardening of the inner binary through tides, mass transfer, and common-envelope evolution, possibly leading to a stellar merger of the two inner components.
3. The fate of the outer (tertiary) component, including the conditions under which it remains bound, is dynamically ejected, or is engulfed/captured during AGB mass loss and envelope expansion.
4. The morphological and kinematic imprint left on the resulting planetary nebula outflow as a function of the triple's orbital parameters and evolutionary outcome (e.g., axisymmetric versus point-symmetric structures, jets, rings, or departures from bipolar symmetry).

Specifically, determine:
(a) The distribution over physically reasonable initial triple configurations (component masses, inner and outer semi-major axes, eccentricities, mutual inclination) of the dynamical state in which the system enters the AGB phase.
(b) The branching ratios among the qualitatively distinct evolutionary endpoints (stable triple with AGB primary, inner-binary merger before AGB, common-envelope-induced hardening, ejection or capture of the tertiary).
(c) The resulting predicted morphological classes of planetary nebulae produced by each endpoint, and observable diagnostics that distinguish triple-shaped PNe from those shaped by single stars or isolated binaries.

The planetary-nebula luminosity function (PNLF) is the distribution N(M) of planetary nebulae as a function of absolute magnitude M in the [O III] λ5007 emission line. Empirically, the PNLF in a wide variety of galaxies is well described, near its bright end, by a function that truncates sharply at an absolute magnitude M*, and the value of M* is observed to be remarkably similar (within a few tenths of a magnitude) across host stellar populations whose mean ages differ by an order of magnitude — from young, star-forming spiral disks to old elliptical galaxies in which star formation effectively ceased more than ~5 Gyr ago.

Standard stellar-evolution theory predicts that planetary nebulae descend from asymptotic-giant-branch progenitors whose central-star mass, post-AGB luminosity, and post-AGB transition timescale all decrease with the age of the parent population. As a consequence, the predicted [O III] luminosity of the brightest planetary nebulae in a coeval population should decrease substantially with population age, producing a fainter PNLF cutoff M* in old systems and (under some assumptions) an excess of nebulae brighter than the observed cutoff in young systems. Even when one incorporates the faster post-AGB evolution given by modern post-AGB tracks (which shortens transition times for low-mass cores and partially raises their peak luminosities), a fully self-consistent stellar-evolutionary mechanism that reproduces the observed near-invariance of M* across all population ages — and in particular accounts for the existence of [O III]-bright planetary nebulae in stellar populations older than ~5 Gyr — has not been established.

The planetary-nebula luminosity function (PNLF) is the distribution N(M) of planetary nebulae as a function of absolute magnitude M in the [O III] λ5007 emission line. Empirically, the PNLF in a wide variety of galaxies is well described, near its bright end, by a function that truncates sharply at an absolute magnitude M*, and the value of M* is observed to be remarkably similar (within a few tenths of a magnitude) across host stellar populations whose mean ages differ by an order of magnitude — from young, star-forming spiral disks to old elliptical galaxies in which star formation effectively ceased more than ~5 Gyr ago.

The age-invariance of the PNLF bright-end cutoff has been a long-standing puzzle. Faster post-AGB evolutionary tracks (Miller Bertolami 2016) showed that lower-mass, longer-lived central stars can reach higher luminosities, partially closing the gap, and recent work (2025) argues that circumnebular dust extinction in younger populations, together with revised post-AGB tracks, plays a critical role in maintaining a near-invariant cutoff. However, a fully consistent explanation accounting for [O III]-bright planetary nebulae in old (>5 Gyr) populations is not yet established, and recent VLT-MUSE PNLF studies (2025) of early-type galaxies continue to investigate residual stellar-population dependence. The problem is therefore best characterized as partially solved.

Let $\mathbb{T}^2 = [-\pi,\pi]^2$ be the two-dimensional torus, with all functions assumed $2\pi$-periodic in each variable. For a function $\theta\in L^2(\mathbb{T}^2)$ define the Fourier coefficients
$$\hat\theta(n) = \int_{\mathbb{T}^2} \theta(x,y)\, e^{-i n\cdot (x,y)}\, dx\, dy, \qquad n\in\mathbb{Z}^2,$$
and the homogeneous $\dot H^{-1}$ norm by
$$\|\theta\|_{\dot H^{-1}(\mathbb{T}^2)}^2 = \sum_{\substack{n\in\mathbb{Z}^2\\ |n|>0}} \frac{|\hat\theta(n)|^2}{|n|^2}.$$
Determine whether there exist:
(i) a nonzero function $\theta_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb{T}^2)$ with $\int_{\mathbb{T}^2}\theta_0(x,y)\,dx\,dy = 0$,
(ii) a shear velocity field $u(y,t)\in L^\infty_t W^{1,1}_y(\mathbb{T})$, that is, a measurable function $u:\mathbb{T}\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfying $\int_{\mathbb{T}} |\partial_y u(y,t)|\,dy \le C$ for some constant $C$ uniformly in $t$,
such that the unique solution $\theta(x,y,t)$ of the transport equation
$$\partial_t \theta + u(y,t)\,\partial_x\theta = 0, \qquad \theta(x,y,0) = \theta_0(x,y)$$
satisfies
$$\|\theta(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{\dot H^{-1}(\mathbb{T}^2)} \le C_1\, e^{-C_2 t}\qquad \text{for all } t\ge 0,$$
for some constants $C_1, C_2 > 0$. Prove either that such a configuration exists, or that no such $(\theta_0, u)$ can exist.

It is classical that a pure shear velocity field $u(y,t)\partial_x$ cannot mix exponentially: the solution is $\theta(x,y,t)=\theta_0(x-\int_0^t u(y,s)\,ds, y)$, and the $y$-profile of each Fourier mode in $x$ is preserved, so the decay of $\|\theta(t)\|_{\dot H^{-1}}$ is at most algebraic (typically $t^{-1/2}$) under bounded variation/$W^{1,1}$ control on $u$. Recent work on "Exponential Mixing by Shear Flows" achieves exponential mixing only by alternating horizontal and vertical shears, not a single shear in $y$. Thus exponential mixing is impossible under the stated single-direction shear and $W^{1,1}_y$ assumption.

Let $E$ be a closed bounded subset of the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$ whose complement $\mathbb{C}_\infty\setminus E$ (in the Riemann sphere) is simply connected, and let $G(z)$ denote the Green function of $\mathbb{C}_\infty\setminus E$ with pole at infinity. For each $R>1$, let
$$E_R=\{z\in\mathbb{C}: G(z)<\log R\}\cup E$$
be the finite region bounded by the level curve $G(z)=\log R$. For nonnegative integers $m,n$, let $R_{mn}(f;z)$ denote a rational function of type $(m,n)$ (numerator degree at most $m$, denominator degree at most $n$) of best uniform approximation to $f$ on $E$, and consider the table $\{R_{mn}\}$ as $m,n\to\infty$.

The classical theory establishes the following: if $f$ is analytic on $E$ and meromorphic in $E_R$ with exactly $\nu$ poles in $E_R\setminus E$ (counted with multiplicity), then convergence and degree-of-approximation theorems for the rows and diagonals of the table $\{R_{mn}\}$ hold, paralleling the polynomial approximation theory of Walsh-type for analytic functions and giving rates governed by $R$ and the pole locations.

Problem: Does an analogous theory of best rational approximation $R_{mn}$ on $E$ hold when $f$ is analytic on $E$ and meromorphic in $E_R$ with infinitely many poles in $E_R\setminus E$? Specifically, formulate and prove (or disprove) convergence and degree-of-approximation theorems for $R_{mn}(f;\cdot)\to f$ in the case where the set of poles of $f$ in $E_R$ is infinite.

Let $f$ be a continuous real-valued function on the interval $[-1,1]$. For nonnegative integers $m$ and $n$, let $\mathcal{R}_{m,n}$ denote the set of rational functions $r=p/q$ with real coefficients, where $p$ is a polynomial of degree at most $m$ and $q$ is a polynomial of degree at most $n$, with $q$ not identically zero. By a classical theorem, there exists a unique rational function $r_{m,n}^*\in\mathcal{R}_{m,n}$ that minimizes the uniform error
$$\|f-r\|_{[-1,1]}=\sup_{x\in[-1,1]}|f(x)-r(x)|$$
over all $r\in\mathcal{R}_{m,n}$. Call $r_{m,n}^*$ the best rational approximant of type $(m,n)$ to $f$, and arrange these into the table $R=(r_{m,n}^*)_{m,n\ge 0}$.

Problem: Describe, for a general continuous (or sufficiently smooth) function $f$ on $[-1,1]$, the location in the complex plane of the poles of $r_{m,n}^*$ as $(m,n)$ varies. In particular, determine the asymptotic distribution of the poles of $r_{m,n}^*$ along rays of the table (e.g.\ as $m,n\to\infty$ with $m/n$ tending to a fixed ratio), identifying where the poles cluster, whether they remain bounded away from $[-1,1]$, and how their distribution relates to the analytic properties of $f$.

For specific classes of functions—most notably $f(x)=|x|^\alpha$ on $[-1,1]$ and functions with fast rational approximability—the asymptotic distribution of poles of best rational approximants has been determined (Stahl and others). For nonholomorphic $f\in C[-1,1]$ with bounded denominator degree, the zero/pole distribution is governed by the equilibrium measure of $[-1,1]$. However, for general continuous functions and for general ray sequences in the table, the question of where the poles lie remains without a complete answer; the problem is partially solved.

Question: Is it true that for every space-constructible function $S(n)$ with $S(n) \geq \log n$, one has
$$\mathrm{DSPACE}(S(n)) \;=\; \mathrm{NSPACE}(S(n))?$$
In particular, in the special case $S(n) = n$ (the linear-bounded automaton, or LBA, problem), does $\mathrm{DSPACE}(n) = \mathrm{NSPACE}(n)$ hold?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The LBA problem (whether DSPACE(n) = NSPACE(n)) and the more general question of whether DSPACE(S(n)) = NSPACE(S(n)) for all S(n) ≥ log n remain longstanding open problems in complexity theory. Savitch's theorem gives NSPACE(S) ⊆ DSPACE(S^2), and the Immerman–Szelepcsényi theorem (1987–88) shows NSPACE(S) is closed under complement, but equality with DSPACE(S) is still unresolved.

A two-way counter machine is a finite-state device equipped with a read-only two-way input tape (with end markers) and a single counter that holds a nonnegative integer. In one step the machine reads the current input symbol and the sign-status of the counter (zero or positive), then chooses a next state, a head movement (left, stay, or right), and a counter operation (increment, decrement, or no change). The machine is deterministic if its transition function assigns at most one move to each configuration (a 2DC machine) and nondeterministic otherwise (a 2NC machine). A language is accepted by such a machine if, on input w, the machine has at least one computation that enters an accepting state.

Let 2DC denote the class of languages accepted by two-way deterministic counter machines, and 2NC the class of languages accepted by two-way nondeterministic counter machines. Decide whether
2DC = 2NC,
that is, whether every language accepted by some two-way nondeterministic counter machine is also accepted by some two-way deterministic counter machine.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Chrobak (MFCS 1984, "Nondeterminism is essential for two-way counter machines", LNCS 176, pp. 240–244) proved that two-way nondeterministic counter automata are strictly more powerful than two-way deterministic ones, i.e., 2DC ⊊ 2NC. Thus the equality question is settled in the negative.

Define the following classes of formal languages over a finite input alphabet, where each machine has read-only access to its input bracketed by left and right end markers and may move its input head in either direction.

- 2NPDA: the class of languages recognized by two-way nondeterministic pushdown automata.
- 2DC: the class of languages recognized by two-way deterministic counter machines, i.e. machines as above whose auxiliary storage is a single counter that can be incremented, decremented, and tested for zero, with deterministic transitions and a two-way input head.

Consider the following families of languages, defined for each integer n ≥ 1:

(a) L_n^{det} = { w ∈ {a, b, c, #}^* : w = x_1 # x_2 # … # x_k for some k ≥ 1 with each x_i ∈ {a,b}^*, and there exist indices 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k with j − i = n and x_i = x_j }, with deterministic recognizability witnessed by a 2DPDA.

(b) L_n^{nond} = an analogous family of 2NPDA-recognizable languages parameterized by n, obtained by allowing nondeterministic guessing of the matching index pair.

(More generally, let {F_n}_{n≥1} be any family of 2DPDA-languages, and let {G_n}_{n≥1} be any family of 2NPDA-languages.)

Question: Does there exist an integer n ≥ 1 such that L_n^{det} ∈ 2DC? Equivalently, is at least one member of the family {F_n} (respectively {G_n}) recognizable by a two-way deterministic counter machine?

Decide, for the families above, whether some member belongs to 2DC, or prove that no member of the family belongs to 2DC.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem was settled negatively. Jiang and Li (1996), "k One-Way Heads Cannot Do String-Matching" (J. Comput. representations.normalized:
Consider the exact string matching problem: given a pattern of length m and a text of length n over some alphabet (with N = n + m the total input length), report all occurrences of the pattern in the text. We work in the standard parallel models of computation:

- A PRAM (Parallel Random Access Machine) consists of p synchronous processors sharing a common memory; concurrent reads of the same location are allowed but concurrent writes are not.
- A WRAM (also called CRCW PRAM) is the same model except that concurrent writes to the same memory location are also allowed (under some standard convention, e.g. the common-write rule).

A parallel algorithm using p processors and running in worst-case time t is called optimal if pt = O(n).

It is known that there exist optimal parallel algorithms for string matching in the ranges
  p ≤ n / log n on a WRAM, and
  p ≤ n / log² n on a PRAM.

Question: Do there exist optimal parallel string-matching algorithms (i.e. with pt = O(n)) for larger ranges of processors, in particular
  (a) for all p ≤ n on a WRAM, and
  (b) for all p ≤ n / log n on a PRAM?

The recognition question for bipartite degree sets is settled: it is known that for every finite nonempty set S of positive integers there exists a bipartite graph G with D(G) = S. This is established in the literature on bipartite graphs and their degree sets (e.g., Manoussakis and Patil, "Bipartite graphs and their degree sets," and subsequent works on minimum orders of such bipartite graphs). Hence the recognition problem has a trivial affirmative answer, and refinements (minimum order, connectedness, unicyclic, etc.) have also been characterized.

Let G be a finite simple graph on p ≥ 3 vertices. For an integer k with 0 ≤ k ≤ p − 3, the graph G is called k-Hamiltonian if for every set S of vertices with |S| ≤ k the graph G − S is Hamiltonian (so 0-Hamiltonian means Hamiltonian). The graph G is called Hamiltonian-connected if for every pair of distinct vertices u, v of G there exists a Hamiltonian path in G from u to v.

Determine the smallest nonnegative integer k with the property that every k-Hamiltonian graph (on a sufficiently large number of vertices, p ≥ k + 3) is Hamiltonian-connected.

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk, and let $S$ be the class of analytic univalent functions $g$ on $\mathbb{D}$ normalized by $g(z)=z+a_2z^2+a_3z^3+\cdots$. For $\psi\in[-\pi,\pi]$, a function $g\in S$ is said to be convex in the direction $\psi$ if its image $g(\mathbb{D})$ has the property that, for every $w_0\in\mathbb{C}$, the intersection of $g(\mathbb{D})$ with the line $\{w_0+te^{i\psi}:t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ is connected (possibly empty). Let $C_\psi\subset S$ denote the subclass of functions convex in the direction $\psi$. The Hadamard convolution of two analytic functions $f(z)=\sum_{k\ge 0}a_kz^k$ and $g(z)=\sum_{k\ge 0}b_kz^k$ on $\mathbb{D}$ is defined by $(f*g)(z)=\sum_{k\ge 0}a_kb_kz^k$. Define the class
$$\mathrm{DCP}=\{f\text{ analytic on }\mathbb{D}:\,f*g\in C_\psi\text{ for every }\psi\in[-\pi,\pi]\text{ and every }g\in C_\psi\}.$$
For every positive integer $n$, determine whether the truncated exponential polynomial
$$P_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(1+z)^k}{k!}$$
belongs to $\mathrm{DCP}$.

Let $f_\lambda : \widehat{\mathbb{C}} \to \widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ be a holomorphic family of rational maps (or, more generally, of transcendental meromorphic maps $f_\lambda : \mathbb{C} \to \widehat{\mathbb{C}}$) depending holomorphically on a parameter $\lambda$ in some complex manifold $\Lambda$. Recall that a Herman ring of $f_\lambda$ is a periodic Fatou component $U$ of period $p \geq 1$ that is conformally isomorphic to a round annulus $A_r = \{z : 1 < |z| < r\}$ via a conformal map $\varphi : U \to A_r$ that conjugates $f_\lambda^p|_U$ to an irrational rotation $z \mapsto e^{2\pi i \alpha} z$ of $A_r$ for some $\alpha \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$.

Address the following:

(a) Describe the bifurcation mechanisms by which Herman rings are created and destroyed under perturbation of $\lambda$. In particular, identify the local dynamical phenomena (e.g., collisions of boundary components with the postsingular set, parabolic implosions, quasiconformal surgeries, breakdowns of invariant curves) responsible for the appearance or disappearance of a Herman ring as $\lambda$ varies, and give a classification of such bifurcations.

(b) For a given natural holomorphic family $\{f_\lambda\}_{\lambda \in \Lambda}$ (for example, the family of degree-$d$ Blaschke-product-like rational maps with a fixed rotation number, the complex standard family $f_\lambda(z) = \lambda z \exp\!\left(\tfrac{a}{2}(z - 1/z)\right)$, or natural families of transcendental meromorphic maps), determine the topological structure, measure-theoretic size (Lebesgue measure, Hausdorff dimension), and analytic properties (e.g., quasi-conformal rigidity, density, accessibility) of the set
$$\mathcal{H}(\{f_\lambda\}) = \{\lambda \in \Lambda : f_\lambda \text{ has a Herman ring}\}.$$
In particular, determine whether $\mathcal{H}$ has positive Lebesgue measure, whether it has nonempty interior, and how its slices by rotation number compare with the corresponding Arnold tongue structure of the associated circle dynamics.

Background and setup. In the semantic-subtyping approach to designing type systems, types are interpreted as subsets of a model D, and subtyping S ≤ T is defined to hold exactly when the interpretation of S is contained in the interpretation of T. The type language is closed under the boolean connectives (union, intersection, and negation), so the set of denotable types forms a boolean algebra (modulo semantic equivalence) and the subtyping relation is the induced lattice order. A denotable type T is called atomic if T is not equivalent to the empty type and the only denotable subtypes of T are T itself and the empty type; equivalently, T is a minimal nonzero element of the subtype lattice. Concrete instances include the lambda-calculus system "CDuce" and pi-calculus systems based on semantic subtyping, in which deciding S ≤ T is reduced to emptiness checks that, in known decidability proofs, ultimately rely on enumerating the (finitely many) atomic types contained in a denotable type.

Problem. Provide a mathematical explanation of the following three intertwined questions about semantic-subtyping systems whose type interpretation lies in a model D as above.

(1) Identify the structural phenomenon that forces the recurrent appearance of atomic types in semantic-subtyping decision procedures: characterize, in terms of properties of the model D and of the boolean algebra of denotable types (e.g. atomicity, atomicness, completeness, descending chain conditions, definability of singletons, or finite-model properties), why every currently known decidability proof for semantic subtyping reduces to enumerating atoms of denotable types.

(2) Determine how tightly the semantic-subtyping technique is tied to the decidability of atomicity: exhibit either a general theorem showing that decidability of S ≤ T in a semantic-subtyping system implies decidability of "is T atomic?" (and effectiveness of an enumeration of the atoms below T), or a counterexample consisting of a semantic-subtyping system with decidable subtyping in which atomicity of denotable types is undecidable or in which atoms cannot be effectively enumerated.

(3) Construct, if possible, a non-trivial semantic-subtyping system in which no denotable type is atomic — equivalently, in which the subtype lattice (restricted to nonempty denotable types) is dense, meaning that whenever S < T are denotable and S is not equivalent to the empty type, there exists a denotable U with S < U < T — while still admitting a sound and decidable subtyping algorithm for a useful programming-language type discipline (covering, e.g., product, function, and recursive types). Alternatively, prove that no such system can exist under reasonable expressiveness assumptions.

Background. In the design of typed programming languages, a subtyping relation between types is traditionally defined syntactically by a deductive system: one fixes a grammar of types (typically with constructors such as products, arrows, recursive types, and possibly Boolean combinators ∨, ∧, ¬) and gives a set of inference rules deriving judgements t ≤ s. The "semantic subtyping" approach instead proceeds as follows. One fixes a class of models in which every type t is mapped to a subset ⟦t⟧ of some domain D (an "extensional interpretation"), required to commute with the Boolean type connectives in the set-theoretic way (⟦t∨s⟧ = ⟦t⟧∪⟦s⟧, ⟦¬t⟧ = D∖⟦t⟧, etc.) and to interpret each non-Boolean type constructor in a way faithful to its operational meaning. Subtyping is then defined extensionally by

  t ≤ s  ⇔  ⟦t⟧ ⊆ ⟦s⟧  in every such model.

Problem. Address the following two interrelated questions about the expressive power and structure of this approach.

(a) Determine whether the semantic-subtyping methodology is essentially a different presentation of subtyping relations that could equivalently be obtained by a syntactic deductive system, or whether it produces type systems whose subtyping relations cannot be captured by any reasonable finite syntactic axiomatization. More precisely, give either:
  (i) a general theorem showing that for every type system arising from a semantic-subtyping construction (in a suitably formalized class) there exists an equivalent finitely axiomatized syntactic subtyping system; or
  (ii) an explicit example of a type system definable by semantic subtyping whose induced subtyping relation provably admits no such syntactic axiomatization, together with a characterization of the obstruction.

(b) Provide a systematic theory of the extensional interpretation. That is, formalize a general framework that takes as input a signature of type constructors together with their intended operational behavior and outputs a canonical extensional interpretation ⟦·⟧ together with sufficient conditions ensuring (1) soundness with respect to the operational semantics, (2) decidability of the induced subtyping relation, and (3) uniqueness or canonicity of the resulting interpretation. Identify the precise degrees of freedom (parameters, choices) available in the construction of such interpretations and characterize the boundary cases where the method fails or yields non-canonical alternatives.

representations.normalized:
Background. The semantic subtyping approach defines a subtyping relation on types by interpreting each type as a set of values and declaring s ≤ t whenever the interpretation of s is contained in that of t. This yields a set-theoretic account of unions, intersections, and negations of types, and is typically developed for languages featuring:
  (i) a type-case construct of the form "(x ∈ t) ? e1 : e2" that, at runtime, branches according to whether the value bound to x belongs to the type t, and
  (ii) explicit type annotations on values whose semantic type is not syntactically apparent — for instance, λ-abstractions annotated with their full intersection-of-arrows interface (λ^{⋂_i s_i → t_i} x. e) and communication channels annotated with the type of messages they carry.

These features are normally used in essential ways: the type-case is what gives observational meaning to fine-grained set-theoretic distinctions among types, and the annotations enable the model-based interpretation of values to be recovered from syntax (so that, e.g., a function annotated with Odd→Odd ∧ Even→Even is observably distinct from the same code annotated only with Int→Int).

Problem. Determine the extent to which the semantic-subtyping methodology is intrinsically tied to the presence of a type-case construct and to explicit type annotations on values such as λ-abstractions and channels. Concretely:

(a) Exhibit a useful programming language (e.g. a λ-calculus or process calculus with set-theoretic types including union, intersection, and negation) equipped with a semantic subtyping relation, in which there is no type-case construct, yet the semantic distinctions induced by the set-theoretic interpretation of types remain observable and the model-theoretic account of types is preserved; or prove that no such language exists, in the sense that without type-case the semantic-subtyping interpretation collapses to (or is indistinguishable from) a coarser, syntactic notion of subtyping.

(b) Determine whether the semantic-subtyping approach is compatible with any nontrivial form of (partial) type reconstruction — that is, a system in which type annotations on λ-abstractions and channels may be omitted (in whole or in part) and recovered by inference, while still admitting a sound and complete semantic interpretation of types as sets of values and preserving principal-type or minimum-typing-style properties.

Provide either constructions establishing the positive answers, or impossibility/lower-bound results delineating the precise dependence of semantic subtyping on type-case and on explicit annotations.

Let $b:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be a Sobolev vector field (with bounded divergence) and let $X(t,x)$ denote its associated regular Lagrangian flow, i.e., the unique (up to Lebesgue-negligible sets) Borel map satisfying $\partial_t X(t,x)=b(t,X(t,x))$ with $X(0,x)=x$ and the bounded compressibility condition $X(t,\cdot)_\#\mathcal{L}^n\le C\,\mathcal{L}^n$.

Recall that a Borel map $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ is said to be differentiable in measure at $x$ with derivative the matrix $A(x)$ if, for every $y\in\mathbb{R}^n$,
$$\frac{|f(x+ry)-f(x)-rA(x)y|}{r}\xrightarrow[r\downarrow 0]{}0\quad\text{locally in measure.}$$

Suppose that for each $t\in[0,T]$ the map $x\mapsto X(t,x)$ is differentiable in measure, so that there exists a matrix-valued Borel map $A(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ with
$$X(t,x+ry)=X(t,x)+r\,A(t,x)\,y+o(r)\qquad\text{locally in measure as }r\downarrow 0,\;\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n.$$

Determine the nature of the matrix-valued map $A(t,x)$: identify a canonical equation it must satisfy (for instance, an ODE along trajectories of the form $\frac{d}{dt}A(t,x)=M(t,X(t,x))\,A(t,x)$ for an appropriate matrix field $M$ derived from the distributional derivative $Db$, together with $A(0,x)=I$), and characterize its regularity.

Setting. Let $b:[0,T]\times \mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ be a Borel vector field belonging to $L^1_t(W^{1,p}_{x,\mathrm{loc}})$ with $p>1$, satisfying suitable global growth and bounded-divergence conditions ensuring existence and uniqueness of a regular Lagrangian flow. Recall that a regular Lagrangian flow associated to $b$ is a Borel map $X:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ such that:
(i) for $\mathcal{L}^d$-a.e.\ $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$, the curve $t\mapsto X(t,x)$ is an absolutely continuous integral solution of $\dot X(t,x)=b(t,X(t,x))$ with $X(0,x)=x$;
(ii) there exists a constant $L\ge 0$ such that $X(t,\cdot)_\#\mathcal{L}^d\le L\,\mathcal{L}^d$ for every $t\in[0,T]$.

Known fact (differentiability in measure). For such flows there exists a Borel map $W:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ such that, for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\frac{X(t,x+h)-X(t,x)-W(t,x)h}{|h|}\xrightarrow[h\to 0]{}0\quad\text{in measure on bounded sets}, \tag{$\ast$}$$
i.e.\ the flow is differentiable in measure in the sense of Ambrosio–Malý.

Question. Can the differentiability-in-measure property $(\ast)$ be strengthened to a measure-theoretic local Lipschitz regularity statement for $X(t,\cdot)$? Precisely: does there exist, for every $\varepsilon>0$ and every bounded set $B\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, a Borel set $E_\varepsilon\subset B$ and a constant $L_\varepsilon$ such that $\mathcal{L}^d(B\setminus E_\varepsilon)<\varepsilon$ and, for $\mathcal{L}^d$-a.e.\ $x\in E_\varepsilon$, there is a measurable neighborhood (in the density / measure-theoretic sense) of $x$ on which $X(t,\cdot)$ admits a Lipschitz representative with Lipschitz constant $\le L_\varepsilon$? More generally, formulate and prove a version of "local Lipschitz" regularity—understood in a measure-theoretic rather than topological sense—that follows from $(\ast)$ in the $W^{1,p}$ Sobolev setting with $p>1$.

For Sobolev vector fields in $W^{1,p}$ with $p>1$, Crippa–De Lellis established a quantitative Lusin–Lipschitz estimate: outside a set of arbitrarily small measure $\varepsilon$, the regular Lagrangian flow coincides with a Lipschitz map (with constant $\sim e^{C/\varepsilon}$). This provides a measure-theoretic local Lipschitz regularity in the $W^{1,p}$, $p>1$ case, addressing the question affirmatively in that regime. The deeper question of strengthening differentiability-in-measure to local Lipschitz regularity in more general weakly differentiable settings (e.g. $W^{1,1}$ or BV) remains open; differentiability in measure has more recently been established for nearly incompressible BV fields, but a corresponding measure-theoretic Lipschitz regularity is not known.

Let $M$ be a closed orientable hyperbolic 3-manifold whose isometry group $\mathrm{Isom}(M)$ is non-solvable. Recall that for a prime $p$, $M$ is said to be a $p$-fold cyclic branched covering of a knot $K \subset S^3$ if there is a $\mathbb{Z}/p$-action on $M$ whose quotient is $S^3$ and whose branch locus projects to $K$. A knot $K \subset S^3$ is called strongly invertible if it admits an orientation-preserving involution of $S^3$ that reverses the orientation of $K$ and has fixed-point set an unknotted circle meeting $K$ in two points. A knot $K$ is said to have symmetric period $p$ if there exists a periodic orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $h$ of $(S^3,K)$ of order $p$ whose fixed-point set $F$ is a nonempty connected 1-submanifold of $S^3$ disjoint from $K$, and such that the image of the 2-component link $K \cup F$ in the quotient $S^3/\langle h\rangle \cong S^3$ is a 2-component link $\overline{K}\cup\overline{F}$ admitting an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of $S^3$ that exchanges its two components.

Assume that for every prime $p$ and every knot $K$ such that $M$ is a $p$-fold cyclic branched covering of $K$, the knot $K$ is not strongly invertible but does have symmetric period $p$.

(a) Determine an explicit upper bound, depending only on the above hypotheses, for the cardinality of the set of pairs $(K,p)$ that can arise in this way for a single such manifold $M$.

(b) Determine all groups that can occur as $\mathrm{Isom}(M)$ for such an $M$.

Let $\mu$ be a finite positive Borel measure on the real line (or on the unit circle) whose support is compact, and assume that $\mu$ is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure (so that its absolutely continuous part vanishes). Let $\{p_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ denote the sequence of monic orthogonal polynomials associated with $\mu$, defined by $\int p_n p_m \, d\mu = 0$ for $n\ne m$. Denote by $Z_n = \{x_{n,1},\dots,x_{n,n}\}$ the zero set of $p_n$.

It is classical (Mhaskar–Saff and others) that the global (bulk) asymptotic distribution of $Z_n$ is governed by potential-theoretic equilibrium measures. The problem is to describe the fine structure of $Z_n$ as $n\to\infty$ when $\mu$ is singular: namely, determine the local spacing and clustering behavior of consecutive zeros of $p_n$, the existence (or failure) of "clock behavior" (i.e. asymptotically equally-spaced zeros at the natural microscopic scale) at points in the support of $\mu$, and how the singular nature of $\mu$ (e.g. pure point components, singular continuous components, or singular parts supported on Cantor-type sets) is reflected in the local arrangement of the zeros.

Concretely: give a detailed description of the local distribution and organization of the zeros $\{x_{n,k}\}$ at scale $1/n$ (or the appropriate microscopic scale) for orthogonal polynomials with respect to a general singular measure $\mu$.

The question of the fine (microscopic) structure of zeros of orthogonal polynomials for singular measures is an active research area. Partial results exist: clock behavior has been established for random Verblunsky coefficients and under BLS-type conditions, and local zero behavior near algebraic singularities of the measure has been analyzed. representations.normalized:
Consider the classical three-dimensional Skyrme model. A static field is a map φ : ℝ³ → S³ ⊂ ℝ⁴ with φ(x) → φ_∞ as |x| → ∞ for some fixed point φ_∞ ∈ S³, so that φ extends continuously to a map from the one-point compactification S³ ≅ ℝ³ ∪ {∞} into S³. The Skyrme energy is

  E(φ) = ∫_{ℝ³} ( (1/2) Σ_{i=1}^{3} |∂_i φ|² + (1/4) Σ_{1 ≤ i < j ≤ 3} |∂_i φ ∧ ∂_j φ|² ) dx,

where ∂_i φ ∧ ∂_j φ denotes the wedge product of the two ℝ⁴-valued vectors ∂_i φ and ∂_j φ in ⋀² ℝ⁴, with norm taken in ⋀² ℝ⁴. Each finite-energy configuration φ has an integer topological degree

  Q(φ) = deg(φ : S³ → S³) ∈ π₃(S³) ≅ ℤ.

For each integer N ∈ ℤ, set

  E_N = inf { E(φ) : φ : ℝ³ → S³ with E(φ) < ∞ and Q(φ) = N }.

Question: For every integer N, does there exist a finite-energy static map φ_N with Q(φ_N) = N and E(φ_N) = E_N? That is, is the infimum E_N attained for every topological degree N ∈ ℤ?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The existence of Skyrme energy minimizers in every degree N is a long-standing question. Partial results exist: minimizers are known to be attainable for degree ±1 and, more generally, whenever the energy levels satisfy a strict "substantial inequality" preventing energy splitting (Lin–Yang and related work). However, attainability of E_N for every integer degree N in the classical 3D Skyrme model has not been established in full generality and remains open, since concentration-compactness arguments can fail to rule out splitting into well-separated lower-degree pieces.

Consider the time-dependent Skyrme model on Minkowski space $\mathbb{R}^{1+3}$ with metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$. The field is a map $U:\mathbb{R}^{1+3}\to SU(2)$, and the Lagrangian density is
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Sk}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{tr}(R_\mu R^\mu)+\tfrac{1}{16}\,\mathrm{tr}\big([R_\mu,R_\nu][R^\mu,R^\nu]\big),$$
where $R_\mu=U^{-1}\partial_\mu U$ takes values in $\mathfrak{su}(2)$. The corresponding Euler–Lagrange equations form a quasilinear hyperbolic system for $U$.

Consider also the Faddeev submodel, in which the field is a map $\mathbf{n}:\mathbb{R}^{1+3}\to S^2\subset\mathbb{R}^3$, $|\mathbf{n}|=1$, with Lagrangian density
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Fa}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\partial_\mu\mathbf{n}\cdot\partial^\mu\mathbf{n}-\tfrac{1}{4}\,F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu},\qquad F_{\mu\nu}=\mathbf{n}\cdot(\partial_\mu\mathbf{n}\times\partial_\nu\mathbf{n}),$$
whose Euler–Lagrange equation is a quasilinear hyperbolic equation for $\mathbf{n}$.

The associated conserved energies are
$$E_{\mathrm{Sk}}[U]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Big(-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}(R_iR_i)-\tfrac{1}{16}\mathrm{tr}([R_i,R_j][R_i,R_j])\Big)\,dx,$$
$$E_{\mathrm{Fa}}[\mathbf{n}]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}\partial_i\mathbf{n}\cdot\partial_i\mathbf{n}+\tfrac{1}{4}F_{ij}F_{ij}\Big)\,dx,$$
which are finite for the relevant Cauchy data.

Establish a mathematical well-posedness theory for the Cauchy problems associated to these two hyperbolic systems with finite-energy initial data $(U,\partial_t U)|_{t=0}$ and $(\mathbf{n},\partial_t\mathbf{n})|_{t=0}$, including:
(a) local and global existence of solutions;
(b) uniqueness in a suitable class;
(c) regularity (propagation of Sobolev regularity, persistence of smoothness);
(d) qualitative dynamical behavior such as long-time asymptotics, scattering, stability of solitons, or singularity formation.

A general well-posedness theory for the full (3+1)-dimensional Skyrme and Faddeev hyperbolic Euler–Lagrange systems with arbitrary finite-energy data appears to remain open. Partial progress is available: Geba–Nakanishi–Rajeev and others established global existence and scattering for Skyrme wave maps with small critical data, and Li (Duke Math. Consider the static Skyrme energy on $\mathbb{R}^3$ for maps $U:\mathbb{R}^3 \to SU(2) \cong S^3$ satisfying $U(x) \to I$ as $|x|\to\infty$, given by
$$E(U) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{tr}(\partial_i U^{-1}\partial_i U) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{16}\,\mathrm{tr}\big([\partial_i U^{-1}\,\partial_j U,\,\partial_j U^{-1}\,\partial_i U]\big)\Big)\,dx,$$
(written here up to a positive constant normalization of the Skyrme term). Each finite-energy configuration $U$ has a well-defined integer topological degree $N \in \pi_3(S^3) \cong \mathbb{Z}$. For each integer $N$, the hedgehog ansatz takes the form
$$U_N(x) = \cos f(r)\, I + i\, \sin f(r)\, \big(\hat{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\big)^{(N)},$$
where $r=|x|$, $\hat{x}=x/r$, $\boldsymbol{\sigma}=(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3)$ are the Pauli matrices, the superscript $(N)$ denotes the standard degree-$N$ extension consistent with topological charge $N$, and $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ is a profile function with $f(0)=N\pi$ and $f(\infty)=0$. It is known that for every integer $N$ there exists a profile $f$ minimizing the Skyrme energy within the radially symmetric (hedgehog) class of degree $N$, yielding a static critical point $U_N$ of $E$.

Question: For some (or any) integer $N$, is the hedgehog critical point $U_N$ an absolute minimizer of $E$ among all finite-energy configurations $U:\mathbb{R}^3 \to SU(2)$ of topological degree $N$ (not merely among radially symmetric ones)?

For topological degrees $|N|\geq 2$, numerical and analytical studies (e.g., toroidal, Platonic-symmetric Skyrmions) indicate that the energy minimizers are not radially symmetric, so the hedgehog is not the absolute minimizer in those sectors. For $N=\pm 1$, the hedgehog is widely believed to be the absolute minimizer, but a rigorous mathematical proof in the full unconstrained class does not appear to be established. For a measurable map $n:\mathbb{R}^3\to S^2$ (where $S^2$ denotes the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$), define the Faddeev energy
$$E(n)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\bigl(|\nabla n|^2+|n^{*}\omega|^2\bigr)\,dx,$$
where $n^{*}\omega$ is the pullback by $n$ of the standard area form $\omega$ on $S^2$, i.e., $(n^{*}\omega)_{ij}=n\cdot(\partial_i n\wedge\partial_j n)$, and $|n^{*}\omega|^2=\sum_{i<j}|(n^{*}\omega)_{ij}|^2$. Let
$$X=\{\,n:\mathbb{R}^3\to S^2 \ \text{measurable} : E(n)<\infty\,\}.$$
Question: Does every $n\in X$ admit a sequence of smooth maps $n_j\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3,S^2)$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\sup_{j} E(n_j)<\infty$, and
\item $n_j\to n$ in $H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^3,S^2)$ as $j\to\infty$?
\end{enumerate}
Equivalently, are smooth $S^2$-valued maps with uniformly bounded Faddeev energy $H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$-dense in the finite-energy class $X$?

Consider the following two geometric variational problems.

(1) Skyrme model. Let $u : \mathbb{R}^3 \to S^3 \subset \mathbb{R}^4$ be a finite-energy map with $u(x) \to (1,0,0,0)$ as $|x|\to\infty$, so that $u$ extends to a map $S^3 \to S^3$ and has a well-defined topological degree $\deg(u) \in \mathbb{Z}$. The Skyrme energy is
$$E_S(u) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} \Bigl( \tfrac{1}{2} |\nabla u|^2 + \tfrac{1}{4} \sum_{i<j} |\partial_i u \wedge \partial_j u|^2 \Bigr)\, dx,$$
where $\partial_i u \wedge \partial_j u$ denotes the antisymmetric wedge product of the vector-valued partial derivatives. For a fixed integer $N \neq 0$, let $u_*$ be a minimizer of $E_S$ in the class $\{u : \deg(u) = N\}$ (assumed to exist).

(2) Faddeev model. Let $n : \mathbb{R}^3 \to S^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a finite-energy map with $n(x) \to (0,0,1)$ as $|x|\to\infty$, so that $n$ extends to a map $S^3 \to S^2$ with Hopf invariant $Q(n) \in \mathbb{Z}$. The Faddeev energy is
$$E_F(n) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} \bigl( |\nabla n|^2 + |F_n|^2 \bigr)\, dx, \qquad (F_n)_{ij} = n \cdot (\partial_i n \times \partial_j n).$$
For a fixed integer $N \neq 0$, let $n_*$ be a minimizer of $E_F$ in the class $\{n : Q(n) = N\}$ (assumed to exist).

The natural variational framework only guarantees that $u_*$ and $n_*$ lie in the finite-energy Sobolev-type space associated with the respective functional.

Question. Must any such absolute energy minimizer $u_*$ (respectively $n_*$) be smooth, or at least enjoy strong regularity (e.g., $C^\infty$, real analytic, or Hölder continuous classical solution of the Euler–Lagrange equations) on all of $\mathbb{R}^3$, beyond the weak regularity inherited from finite energy?

The regularity of absolute energy minimizers for the Skyrme and Faddeev models is widely cited as a fundamental open problem. Existence of minimizers is known in various topological classes (e.g., Lin–Yang results for the Faddeev model), and partial regularity results exist for related relaxed energies, but full smoothness of unconstrained absolute minimizers in arbitrary topological classes does not appear to have been established. Recent work (e.g., 2025 results on global minimality of the Hopf map in the strong-coupling regime) addresses special cases but not the general regularity question.

Consider the unconstrained optimization problem
   minimize f(x),  x ∈ ℝⁿ,
where f : ℝⁿ → ℝ is continuously differentiable and bounded below. Let g(x) = ∇f(x). A nonlinear conjugate gradient (CG) method generates iterates
   x_{k+1} = x_k + α_k d_k,   k = 0, 1, 2, …,
where α_k > 0 is a step length determined by a line search, and the search directions are defined by
   d_{k+1} = −g_{k+1} + β_k s_k,
with g_k = g(x_k), s_k = x_{k+1} − x_k, and β_k ∈ ℝ a CG update parameter (e.g., Hestenes–Stiefel, Fletcher–Reeves, Polak–Ribière, Dai–Yuan, etc.). The standard convention takes the initial search direction to be the steepest-descent direction:
   d_0 = −g_0.

Provide a rigorous theoretical or algorithmic justification, valid for general (non-quadratic, non-convex) continuously differentiable objectives bounded below, that explains:

(a) Why the choice d_0 = −g_0 is critical to the global convergence and the practical efficiency of nonlinear CG methods, beyond the classical finite-termination/conjugacy arguments that apply only to strictly convex quadratic f.

(b) Precise conditions on an alternative initial direction d_0 ≠ −g_0 (for instance, conditions such as a sufficient-descent inequality g_0ᵀ d_0 ≤ −c‖g_0‖² for some c > 0, or angle/normalization conditions) under which the resulting nonlinear CG iteration retains its global convergence properties and competitive numerical performance, and conditions under which these properties are lost.

State and prove the corresponding convergence results, or exhibit explicit counterexamples showing degradation when d_0 is chosen arbitrarily.

Surveys and recent works on nonlinear conjugate gradient methods (e.g., Andrei's monograph and survey, and Kimiaei's 2025 work on restarting nonlinear CG) continue to assume d_0 = −g_0 and treat the role of the initial direction for general nonlinear objectives as an unresolved issue. Consider a nonlinear conjugate gradient (CG) method for minimizing a continuously differentiable function f: R^n -> R. Starting from x_0 in R^n, the method generates iterates x_{k+1} = x_k + alpha_k d_k, where d_0 = -grad f(x_0), the search directions are updated by d_{k+1} = -grad f(x_{k+1}) + beta_k d_k for some scalar beta_k characterizing the CG variant (e.g., Fletcher–Reeves, Polak–Ribière–Polyak, Hestenes–Stiefel, Dai–Yuan, etc.), and alpha_k > 0 is a step length determined by a line search satisfying standard (e.g., Wolfe or strong Wolfe) conditions.

Empirically, across a wide range of test problems and CG variants, the sequence {alpha_k} is observed to vary in a highly irregular (apparently unpredictable) manner from iteration to iteration, and individual values of alpha_k can differ from 1 by up to two orders of magnitude (i.e., alpha_k as small as ~10^{-2} or as large as ~10^{2}), with the direction and magnitude of this departure depending sensitively on the scaling of the problem and on the specific instance.

Provide a rigorous theoretical explanation for the following:
(a) Why, in a nonlinear CG method, the step length sequence {alpha_k} typically fails to concentrate near 1 and can differ from 1 by as much as two orders of magnitude, with the deviation depending on problem scaling.
(b) Why the variation of {alpha_k} from one iteration to the next tends to be erratic rather than monotonic or asymptotically stable.
(c) Why this behavior contrasts sharply with Newton, quasi-Newton (e.g., BFGS), and limited-memory quasi-Newton (e.g., L-BFGS) methods, in which the unit step length alpha_k = 1 is asymptotically accepted by the line search under standard assumptions.

The goal is a structural/analytical explanation tying the behavior of {alpha_k} to the geometry of the search directions d_k generated by CG (which, unlike Newton-type methods, are not approximations to a Newton direction and do not carry curvature information of consistent scale), to the dependence of beta_k on gradient information, and to the scaling properties of the underlying objective.

Consider the unconstrained minimization problem
    min { f(x) : x ∈ R^n },
where f : R^n → R is continuously differentiable with gradient g(x) = ∇f(x). A nonlinear conjugate gradient method generates iterates
    x_{k+1} = x_k + α_k d_k,
with d_0 = -g_0 and, for k ≥ 1,
    d_{k+1} = -g_{k+1} + β_k d_k,
where α_k > 0 is a step length (typically chosen via a line search satisfying the standard Wolfe or strong Wolfe conditions) and β_k ∈ R is the conjugate gradient parameter. Classical choices of β_k (Hestenes–Stiefel, Fletcher–Reeves, Polak–Ribière–Polyak, Dai–Yuan, Liu–Storey, conjugate descent, etc.) are functions only of the gradients g_k = g(x_k) and g_{k+1}, the difference y_k = g_{k+1} - g_k, the displacement s_k = x_{k+1} - x_k, and inner products and norms built from these vectors; they do not involve the objective function values f(x_k) and f(x_{k+1}).

Problem. Design a nonlinear conjugate gradient algorithm in which the parameter β_k explicitly depends on the function-value information f(x_k) and f(x_{k+1}) (for instance through the difference f(x_k) - f(x_{k+1}) or quantities derived from it), prove that the resulting method generates descent directions and is globally convergent on a suitable class of objective functions under a standard line-search condition, and demonstrate that it offers competitive numerical performance compared with established conjugate gradient schemes.

Several conjugate gradient algorithms incorporate function-value information indirectly via modified secant conditions, e.g. using z_k = y_k + (η_k/||s_k||^2) s_k with η_k = 2(f_k - f_{k+1}) + (g_k + g_{k+1})^T s_k (as in accelerated hybrid CG schemes). (P3) For all a, b ∈ K, (b' + (a + b)) ∈ T.
(P4) For all a, b ∈ K, ((a + b)' + (b + a)) ∈ T.
(P5) For all a, b, c ∈ K, ((b' + c)' + ((a + b)' + (a + c))) ∈ T.
(P6) For all a, b ∈ K, if (a' + b) ∈ T and (b' + a) ∈ T, then a = b.

Let Postulate 1.1 be the statement: for all a, b ∈ K, if a ∈ T and (a' + b) ∈ T, then b ∈ T.

Question: Is Postulate 1.1 independent of the postulates (P2)–(P6)? Equivalently, does there exist a system (K, T, +, ') that satisfies (P2)–(P6) but does not satisfy Postulate 1.1?

Consider the unconstrained optimization problem
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x),
\]
where $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuously differentiable and bounded below, with gradient $g(x)=\nabla f(x)$. A nonlinear conjugate gradient (CG) method generates iterates
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_k d_k,
\]
where $\alpha_k>0$ is a step size satisfying a standard line search (e.g. Wolfe or strong Wolfe conditions), and the search directions are
\[
d_0=-g_0,\qquad d_{k+1}=-g_{k+1}+\beta_k d_k,\quad k\ge 0.
\]
Classical choices for the scalar $\beta_k$ include
\[
\beta_k^{FR}=\frac{\|g_{k+1}\|^2}{\|g_k\|^2},\quad
\beta_k^{PRP}=\frac{g_{k+1}^\top y_k}{\|g_k\|^2},\quad
\beta_k^{HS}=\frac{g_{k+1}^\top y_k}{d_k^\top y_k},\quad
\beta_k^{DY}=\frac{\|g_{k+1}\|^2}{d_k^\top y_k},
\]
where $y_k=g_{k+1}-g_k$. A hybrid conjugate gradient method defines $\beta_k$ either by a projection rule (e.g. $\beta_k=\max\{0,\min\{\beta_k^{A},\beta_k^{B}\}\}$ for some classical $\beta^A,\beta^B$) or by a convex combination
\[
\beta_k=(1-\theta_k)\beta_k^{A}+\theta_k\beta_k^{B},\qquad \theta_k\in[0,1],
\]
where $\theta_k$ may depend on $g_k,g_{k+1},d_k,s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k,y_k$.

Problem. Determine which hybrid nonlinear conjugate gradient algorithm—across all projection-type and convex-combination-type schemes built from the Fletcher–Reeves, Polak–Ribière–Polyak, Hestenes–Stiefel, Dai–Yuan and related formulas—achieves the best overall balance of global convergence guarantees (under standard line search assumptions) and computational performance on general smooth unconstrained problems. In particular, identify an optimal rule for choosing the combination parameter $\theta_k$ (or the projection scheme) that simultaneously preserves global convergence and yields the strongest practical efficiency.

   x_{k+1} = x_k + α_k d_k,  d_{k+1} = -g_{k+1} + β_k d_k,

where g_k = ∇f(x_k), α_k > 0 is determined by a (possibly inexact) line search, and β_k is a CG update parameter (e.g. Fletcher–Reeves, Polak–Ribière, Hestenes–Stiefel, Dai–Yuan, etc.).

Determine the most suitable termination rule for such an algorithm. Specifically, compare and decide among the following candidate stopping criteria, given a tolerance ε > 0:

   (a)  ‖g_k‖_∞ ≤ ε,
   (b)  ‖g_k‖_2 ≤ ε,
   (c)  ‖g_k‖ ≤ ε · max{1, ‖g_0‖} (a relative criterion tied to the initial gradient, in either the ∞- or 2-norm),

Identify which of these criteria, or which combination of them, best balances:
   (i) correctness (reliably certifying approximate first-order optimality),
   (ii) computational efficiency, and
   (iii) appropriateness across both large-scale and small-scale instances of the problem,
and justify the choice for finite-precision implementations of nonlinear CG methods.

Consider the unconstrained optimization problem of minimizing a smooth function f : R^n → R for large n, with gradient g(x) = ∇f(x). Two classical iterative families are used:

(1) Nonlinear conjugate gradient (CG) methods, which generate iterates x_{k+1} = x_k + α_k d_k with search directions of the form d_0 = -g_0 and d_{k+1} = -g_{k+1} + β_k d_k, where the scalar β_k is chosen by formulas such as Fletcher–Reeves, Polak–Ribière–Polyak, Hestenes–Stiefel, Dai–Yuan, etc., and α_k is determined by a line search.

(2) Quasi-Newton (QN) methods, which generate iterates x_{k+1} = x_k - α_k H_k g_k, where H_k is an approximation to the inverse Hessian updated by a secant formula such as BFGS, DFP, or SR1; in the limited-memory variant (e.g. L-BFGS), H_k is represented implicitly via a small number m of stored vector pairs {(s_i, y_i)} with s_i = x_{i+1} - x_i and y_i = g_{i+1} - g_i.

Establish a precise theoretical relationship between nonlinear CG methods and (limited-memory) quasi-Newton methods. In particular:
(a) Characterize, in terms of the choice of β_k and the line search, exact conditions under which a nonlinear CG iteration coincides with, or can be reformulated as, a (limited-memory) quasi-Newton iteration with a specific implicit Hessian approximation H_k, and conversely identify which limited-memory QN updates reduce to a CG-type recursion.
(b) Using this correspondence, design a hybrid algorithm that combines features of both families and prove for it global convergence, a rate-of-convergence estimate (e.g. n-step quadratic or superlinear convergence under standard assumptions), and per-iteration cost and storage requirements comparable to those of CG and L-BFGS, so that the resulting method inherits the low memory footprint of CG together with the curvature-tracking robustness of quasi-Newton methods on large-scale problems.

Consider the three-dimensional autonomous quadratic system of ordinary differential equations
  x' = y^2 - z^2,
  y' = x,
  z' = y,
which is equivalent to the third-order ("jerk") scalar equation
  z''' = (z')^2 - z^2.
A smooth dynamical system is called chaotic if it possesses a bounded invariant set on which the flow exhibits sensitive dependence on initial conditions together with topological transitivity (or, more concretely, has a positive topological entropy / a horseshoe). Numerical experiments suggest that the system above admits a single unstable periodic orbit and that all other trajectories are unbounded.

Prove rigorously that this system is non-chaotic, or else exhibit a chaotic invariant set for it.

which is equivalent to the third-order ("jerk") scalar equation

Prove rigorously that this system is non-chaotic, or else exhibit a chaotic invariant set for it.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

A 2008 result by Malasoma ("Non-chaotic behaviour for a class of quadratic jerk equations", Chaos, Solitons & Fractals) proves that every jerk equation z''' = j(z, z', z'') in which j is a quadratic polynomial with at most two monomials cannot be chaotic. Since j(z, z') = (z')^2 - z^2 is exactly such a two-term quadratic polynomial, this result settles the conjecture in the affirmative: the system is non-chaotic. Earlier work of Yang–Chen (2002) handled the homogeneous two-term case, and Heidel–Zhang's program had reduced the problem to this single remaining exception.

Consider continuous autonomous dynamical systems
    x'(t) = f(x(t)),    x ∈ ℝ^N,  t ∈ [0, ∞),
where f : ℝ^N → ℝ^N is continuous (so that solutions exist for t ∈ [0, ∞)). Informally, a solution x(t) is called "chaotic" if it exhibits sensitive dependence on initial conditions and complicated long-term behavior, while a "non-chaotic" solution is any solution that does not display such behavior.

A known partial criterion for non-chaoticity reads as follows. Suppose the system has no cluster points in its set of isolated fixed points. Then the system has no bounded chaos provided that, for every solution, at least N − 2 of its components x_{i_1}(t), …, x_{i_{N−2}}(t) eventually satisfy at least one of the following:
 (i) tend to a finite limit as t → ∞;
 (ii) are periodic or asymptotic to a periodic function;
 (iii) are unbounded; or
 (iv) exhibit one of certain prescribed finite-time behaviors (e.g., blow-up in finite time, finite-time termination, or oscillations of unbounded frequency on a finite interval).
This criterion is widely accepted for N = 3 but remains unverified for N > 3, and even when valid it fails to capture many forms of non-chaotic behavior.

Problem. Formulate a universal definition of "non-chaotic solution" for the system x' = f(x) on ℝ^N, valid for every dimension N (in particular for N > 3), that:
 (a) reduces to or is consistent with the accepted notion of non-chaoticity in dimension N = 3;
 (b) encompasses every solution covered by the criterion above as a special case;
 (c) also includes the broad classes of non-chaotic solutions that the above criterion fails to detect; and
 (d) is intrinsic, i.e., expressible purely in terms of the qualitative dynamics of x(t) (such as its ω-limit set, recurrence structure, entropy, or sensitivity properties) without reference to the particular form of f.

representations.original:
Consider continuous autonomous dynamical systems
    x'(t) = f(x(t)),    x ∈ ℝ^N,  t ∈ [0, ∞),
where f : ℝ^N → ℝ^N is continuous (so that solutions exist for t ∈ [0, ∞)). Informally, a solution x(t) is called "chaotic" if it exhibits sensitive dependence on initial conditions and complicated long-term behavior, while a "non-chaotic" solution is any solution that does not display such behavior.

A known partial criterion for non-chaoticity reads as follows. Suppose the system has no cluster points in its set of isolated fixed points. Then the system has no bounded chaos provided that, for every solution, at least N − 2 of its components x_{i_1}(t), …, x_{i_{N−2}}(t) eventually satisfy at least one of the following:
 (i) tend to a finite limit as t → ∞;
 (ii) are periodic or asymptotic to a periodic function;
 (iii) are unbounded; or
 (iv) exhibit one of certain prescribed finite-time behaviors (e.g., blow-up in finite time, finite-time termination, or oscillations of unbounded frequency on a finite interval).
This criterion is widely accepted for N = 3 but remains unverified for N > 3, and even when valid it fails to capture many forms of non-chaotic behavior.

Problem. Formulate a universal definition of "non-chaotic solution" for the system x' = f(x) on ℝ^N, valid for every dimension N (in particular for N > 3), that:
 (a) reduces to or is consistent with the accepted notion of non-chaoticity in dimension N = 3;
 (b) encompasses every solution covered by the criterion above as a special case;
 (c) also includes the broad classes of non-chaotic solutions that the above criterion fails to detect; and
 (d) is intrinsic, i.e., expressible purely in terms of the qualitative dynamics of x(t) (such as its ω-limit set, recurrence structure, entropy, or sensitivity properties) without reference to the particular form of f.

Equivalently, provide a precise mathematical definition of non-chaoticity that, taken as the negation of "chaotic," yields a workable universal notion of chaotic solution for continuous autonomous ODE systems on ℝ^N.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of giving a universal definition of non-chaotic (equivalently, chaotic) solutions for continuous autonomous ODE systems on ℝ^N is widely recognized as an open conceptual problem in dynamical systems. The Heidel–Zhang criterion is established for N = 3 but not verified for N > 3, and even there it misses many non-chaotic behaviors. No accepted universal definition has been published; the question remains open.

Consider autonomous polynomial ordinary differential systems on R^N of the form

   x_i'(t) = P_i(x_1, ..., x_N),    i = 1, ..., N,

where each P_i is a polynomial of total degree at most k. Call such a system "chaotic" if it admits a bounded invariant set on which the flow exhibits sensitive dependence on initial conditions and a dense orbit (i.e., a chaotic attractor or chaotic invariant set in the standard dynamical-systems sense). Call the system "conservative" if its flow preserves volume (equivalently, div(P) ≡ 0) and "dissipative" if the time-average of div(P) on the attractor is strictly negative.

Two systems are considered equivalent under the following natural group actions:

(a) For N = 3: the diagonal scaling group acting by x_1 = a X_1, x_2 = b X_2, x_3 = c X_3, t = δ τ (with a,b,c,δ nonzero reals), together with the cyclic/symmetric permutation group S_3 acting on coordinates.

(b) For N > 3: the diagonal scaling group acting by x_i = a_i X_i, t = δ τ together with the full symmetric group S_N permuting coordinates.

(c) In general (N ≥ 3): the affine group acting by x = A y + b with A ∈ GL_N(R), b ∈ R^N, combined with time rescaling t = δ τ.

Solve the following:

1. For N = 3 and each fixed k, classify all equivalence classes (under (a)) of polynomial systems of degree at most k that admit chaotic solutions; in particular, determine the exact (finite or otherwise) number of such chaotic equivalence classes, and within them count how many are conservative and how many are dissipative.

2. For each N > 3 and each fixed k, give the analogous classification and counts under the equivalence (b).

3. For each N ≥ 3 and each fixed k, give the analogous classification and counts under the affine equivalence (c).

4. Determine which topological/dynamical types of chaotic attractors (for example Lorenz-type or Rössler-type) can arise among the systems above for each N and k.

The classification and counting of chaotic polynomial ODE systems up to scaling, permutation, or affine equivalence is a long-standing open program. The problem remains open.

Consider a vector field on R^3 of the form x' = f(x), where either f is a polynomial map or f ∈ C^n(R^3, R^3) for some nonnegative integer n. Suppose a trajectory of this system is asymptotic (as t → +∞) to a two-dimensional C^r invariant manifold M ⊂ R^3, where r ≥ 1 is an integer. Address the following:

(a) Can such a trajectory be chaotic (in the sense of sensitive dependence on initial conditions together with topological transitivity, or any standard equivalent notion)?

(b) If chaotic asymptotic trajectories of this type exist, what is the minimal topological complexity required of the 2D invariant manifold M that contains or attracts them? Here topological complexity is measured in the sense that, for example, a torus is considered more complicated than a plane (e.g., via genus or other topological invariants).

(c) In particular, can a quadratic polynomial vector field on R^3 leaving a 2-torus invariant exhibit chaotic dynamics on that torus?

(d) More generally, on a 2-torus invariant under a smooth vector field, can a single trajectory be topologically more complicated than a space-filling curve (i.e., have a closure or orbit-structure exceeding that of a dense, area-filling orbit)?

Determine which of these phenomena are possible, and if possible, exhibit explicit examples; if impossible, prove the corresponding obstructions.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Classical results (Denjoy, Schwartz, Peixoto) imply that a C^2 flow on the 2-torus cannot be chaotic, so smooth trajectories confined to a 2-torus are not chaotic and orbit closures are at most the whole torus. However, the question as posed concerns trajectories in R^3 only asymptotic to a 2D invariant manifold, where the manifold need not be smoothly embedded as a flow-invariant 2-torus in the classical sense, and the question of minimal topological complexity of such 2D manifolds containing/attracting chaos remains an open problem listed in the survey of open problems on quadratic and higher-degree polynomial ODE systems. No published resolution was located.

Consider the two autonomous three-dimensional quadratic ODE systems

(I)  x' = y² − z + A,   y' = z,   z' = x,

where A ∈ ℝ is a real parameter, and

(II) x' = y,   y' = −x + y z,   z' = 1 − y².

Numerical experiments suggest that system (I) admits at least one bounded trajectory whose successive intersections with the Poincaré section {x = 0} accumulate on a set of nonzero "thickness" (i.e. not contained in a smooth one-dimensional curve), and likewise that system (II) admits at least one bounded trajectory whose successive intersections with the Poincaré section {z = 0} accumulate on a set of nonzero "thickness".

(a) Prove rigorously that for some choice of parameter A and some initial condition, the corresponding Poincaré return set of system (I) on {x = 0} has non-integer Hausdorff (or box-counting) dimension strictly between 1 and 2.

(b) Prove the analogous statement for system (II): there exists an initial condition whose Poincaré return set on {z = 0} has fractal (non-integer) dimension strictly between 1 and 2.

(c) Determine, with proof, whether either of these systems is genuinely chaotic in the sense of possessing a positive topological entropy or a positive Lyapunov exponent on an invariant set, and in particular whether the observed "thickness" of the Poincaré sections implies genuine chaotic dynamics.

representations.normalized:
For a complex parameter $\lambda \in \mathbb{C} \setminus \{-1, -2, -3, \ldots\}$, define the infinite matrix $H_\lambda = (a_{mn})_{m,n=0}^\infty$ with entries
$$a_{mn} = \frac{1}{m + n + 1 - \lambda}, \qquad m, n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots.$$
Assume that, for the values of $\lambda$ and $p$ considered, $H_\lambda$ defines a bounded linear operator on the sequence space $\ell^p$ (for $1 \le p < \infty$, $\ell^p$ is the Banach space of complex sequences $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ with $\sum_n |x_n|^p < \infty$).

Fix $p$ with $2 < p < \infty$. Determine, for each admissible $\lambda$:
(a) the spectrum $\sigma(H_\lambda)$ of $H_\lambda$ acting on $\ell^p$;
(b) the point spectrum $\sigma_p(H_\lambda)$ (the set of eigenvalues);
(c) the essential spectrum $\sigma_e(H_\lambda)$.

In particular, decide whether the following conjecture holds: for every real $\lambda < 1$,
$$\sigma(H_\lambda) = \left\{\, \pi \sec(\pi u) : u \in \mathbb{C},\ |\operatorname{Re} u| \le \tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{p}\,\right\},$$
the point spectrum $\sigma_p(H_\lambda)$ equals the interior of this set, and the essential spectrum $\sigma_e(H_\lambda)$ equals its boundary.

Let $B_r(0)\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ ($N\ge 2$) denote the open ball of radius $r>0$ centered at the origin. Fix parameters $\alpha>0$ (mainly the case $0<\alpha<1$ is of interest), $0<p<1$, and $\lambda>0$, and consider the singular semilinear elliptic Dirichlet problem
$$
-\Delta u + \frac{1}{u^{\alpha}} = \lambda\, u^{p} \quad \text{in } B_r(0), \qquad u>0 \text{ in } B_r(0), \qquad u=0 \text{ on } \partial B_r(0).
$$
Because the absorption term $1/u^{\alpha}$ is singular where $u$ vanishes, the classical moving-plane / Gidas–Ni–Nirenberg symmetry argument is not directly applicable, so a priori non-radial positive solutions are not excluded.

Question: Does this problem admit a positive (weak/classical, in an appropriate sense) solution $u:B_r(0)\to(0,\infty)$ that is not radially symmetric about the origin? Equivalently, determine whether every positive solution must be radially symmetric, or exhibit values of $N$, $r$, $\alpha\in(0,1)$, $p\in(0,1)$, and $\lambda>0$ for which a non-radial positive solution exists.

Let Ω = B_r(0) ⊂ ℝ^N be the open ball of radius r > 0 centered at the origin, and fix a constant β ∈ (0,1). Consider the singular semilinear elliptic problem with absorption

(II)    −Δu + u^{−β} χ_{{u>0}} = λ g(u) in Ω,    u ≥ 0 in Ω,    u = 0 on ∂Ω,

where λ > 0 is a real parameter and g : [0,∞) → [0,∞) is a fixed continuous nonlinearity (for instance g(s) = s^q with q ∈ (0,1) or another sublinear/superlinear model giving the bifurcation diagram described below). A solution u to (II) is called a free-boundary solution if the set {u = 0} ∩ Ω has nonempty interior and on its boundary one has u = 0 and ∇u = 0 simultaneously; otherwise u is called strictly positive (lying in the positive cone, with u > 0 in Ω).

Assume that the radial bifurcation diagram of (II) has the following structure: there exist 0 < λ_* < λ_{**} < ∞ such that
(a) for every λ ∈ (λ_*, λ_{**}) there exist exactly two radial solutions u_1(·;λ) < u_2(·;λ) of (II), both strictly positive in Ω;
(b) for every λ > λ_{**} only the upper radial solution u_2(·;λ) exists;
(c) as λ ↑ λ_{**}, the lower radial branch u_1(·;λ) remains strictly positive inside Ω and converges to a limit profile u_1(·;λ_{**}) which still satisfies u_1 > 0 in Ω, vanishes on ∂Ω, and has zero normal derivative on ∂Ω, i.e. ∂u_1/∂ν = 0 on ∂Ω.

Let Ω = B_r(0) ⊂ ℝ^N be the open ball of radius r > 0 centered at the origin, and fix a constant β ∈ (0,1). Consider the singular semilinear elliptic problem with absorption

(II)    −Δu + u^{−β} χ_{{u>0}} = λ g(u) in Ω,    u ≥ 0 in Ω,    u = 0 on ∂Ω,

where λ > 0 is a real parameter and g : [0,∞) → [0,∞) is a fixed continuous nonlinearity (for instance g(s) = s^q with q ∈ (0,1) or another sublinear/superlinear model giving the bifurcation diagram described below). A solution u to (II) is called a free-boundary solution if the set {u = 0} ∩ Ω has nonempty interior and on its boundary one has u = 0 and ∇u = 0 simultaneously; otherwise u is called strictly positive (lying in the positive cone, with u > 0 in Ω).

Assume that the radial bifurcation diagram of (II) has the following structure: there exist 0 < λ_* < λ_{**} < ∞ such that
(a) for every λ ∈ (λ_*, λ_{**}) there exist exactly two radial solutions u_1(·;λ) < u_2(·;λ) of (II), both strictly positive in Ω;
(b) for every λ > λ_{**} only the upper radial solution u_2(·;λ) exists;
(c) as λ ↑ λ_{**}, the lower radial branch u_1(·;λ) remains strictly positive inside Ω and converges to a limit profile u_1(·;λ_{**}) which still satisfies u_1 > 0 in Ω, vanishes on ∂Ω, and has zero normal derivative on ∂Ω, i.e. ∂u_1/∂ν = 0 on ∂Ω.

Question. Determine and rigorously justify the analytic/geometric mechanism that forces the lower radial branch λ ↦ u_1(·;λ) to terminate exactly at λ = λ_{**}: that is, explain why this branch cannot be continued to values λ > λ_{**} even though, at λ = λ_{**}, u_1 still belongs to the positive cone and only meets the boundary tangentially (with simultaneous vanishing of u and of ∂u/∂ν on ∂Ω).

Let $N \ge 3$ and let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ be a bounded star-shaped domain with smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$, and let $n$ denote the outward unit normal to $\partial\Omega$. Fix exponents $\alpha,\beta$ with $0 < \alpha < \beta < 1$, and assume the dimensional condition
$$N \;>\; \frac{2(1+\alpha)(1+\beta)}{(1-\alpha)(1-\beta)}.$$
Consider the singular semilinear Dirichlet problem
$$-\Delta u + u^{\alpha} \;=\; \lambda\, u^{\beta} \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega,$$
with $\lambda > 0$, where solutions are sought among nonnegative functions $u \ge 0$ in $\Omega$ (with the convention $u^\alpha, u^\beta$ defined by $0$ where $u=0$).

It is known that for some value of $\lambda$ there exists a positive solution $w_\lambda$ which is not identically zero and which satisfies $\partial w_\lambda/\partial n \not\equiv 0$ on $\partial\Omega$ (so $w_\lambda$ is not a "flat" free-boundary solution).

Question: Must every such solution $w_\lambda$ actually satisfy the stronger pointwise boundary inequality
$$\frac{\partial w_\lambda}{\partial n}(x) \;\le\; 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in \partial\Omega\,?$$
