Let $a > 0$ be a real parameter, and consider the second-order rational delay difference equation
$$x_{n+1} \;=\; \frac{a}{x_n^{2}} \;+\; \frac{1}{x_{n-1}}, \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots,$$
with arbitrary positive initial conditions $x_{-1}, x_{0} \in (0, \infty)$. This recurrence has a unique positive equilibrium $\bar{x} > 0$, namely the unique positive solution of $\bar{x} = a/\bar{x}^{2} + 1/\bar{x}$, equivalently $\bar{x}^{3} - \bar{x} - a = 0$.

Recall that the equilibrium $\bar{x}$ is said to be globally asymptotically stable if it is locally stable (every neighborhood of $\bar{x}$ contains a forward-invariant neighborhood) and globally attracting (for every choice of positive initial conditions $x_{-1}, x_{0}$, the solution $\{x_n\}_{n \geq -1}$ satisfies $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = \bar{x}$).

Determine the set of all values of the parameter $a > 0$ for which the unique positive equilibrium $\bar{x}$ of the above equation is globally asymptotically stable.

Consider the following construction of a "cyclic pentagonal tiling" of the plane. Start with the standard square lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ and choose a point $p$ in the interior of the unit square $[0,1]^2$ that is not its center. For each unit square cell of the lattice, place a translated copy of $p$ inside it; together with the four corners of that cell, these five points form a (generically) cyclic pentagon (i.e., a pentagon whose vertices lie on a common circle). Replacing each square by the corresponding congruent cyclic pentagon yields an arrangement of congruent cyclic pentagons that covers the plane (with possible overlaps), called a cyclic pentagonal tiling.

A generalized tiling billiard trajectory in such an arrangement is defined as follows: a particle moves in straight line segments inside a pentagonal cell; whenever it crosses an edge $e$ of a pentagon, it is refracted by reflecting its direction across $e$ (equivalently, the trajectory is continued into the centrally symmetric copy of the pentagon glued along $e$), and motion continues in straight lines, refracting at each subsequent edge crossing.

Determine the generic dynamical behavior of trajectories of this generalized tiling billiard system in cyclic pentagonal tilings: for a generic choice of the shifted lattice point $p$ and a generic initial condition (starting point and direction), describe the long-term behavior of the trajectory (e.g., whether it is bounded, escapes to infinity, follows an asymptotic direction, has linear or sublinear deviations, is periodic, etc.).

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Recent work (Jay, "Deviations for generalized tiling billiards in cyclic polygons", arXiv:2402.15765, IMRN 2025) studies generalized tiling billiards in cyclic N-gons with N ≥ 5, including pentagonal cases. It exhibits an open set of trajectories that deviate sublinearly from their asymptotic direction (a behavior strikingly different from triangular and quadrilateral tilings, where almost every trajectory stays bounded distance from a line) and establishes deviation rates in generic and certain non-generic cases. This provides substantial progress but does not yet give a complete description of the generic behavior of trajectories in the cyclic pentagonal tilings, so the problem appears partially resolved.

Fix a finite "shape" α, defined as a graph on a vertex set partitioned into two ordered tuples (left and right boundary vertices) U_α and V_α together with additional internal vertices W_α, with edge set E(α). For each integer n ≥ 1 let {ε_{i,j} : 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n} be independent ±1 (or independent standard Gaussian) random variables, with ε_{j,i}=ε_{i,j}. The graph matrix M_α associated to α is the matrix whose rows are indexed by injective tuples I ∈ [n]^{|U_α|} and columns by injective tuples J ∈ [n]^{|V_α|}, with entry
   (M_α)_{I,J} = Σ_{φ} ∏_{{u,v} ∈ E(α)} ε_{φ(u),φ(v)},
where the sum runs over all injective maps φ from the vertex set of α into [n] that extend the given assignments on U_α and V_α, and the entry is 0 unless I and J are disjoint as required.

Question: For every fixed shape α, do there exist constants f(α) ∈ ℝ and g(α) ∈ ℝ, depending only on α, such that the expected operator (spectral) norm satisfies
   E‖M_α‖ = Θ(n^{f(α)} (log n)^{g(α)})
as n → ∞? Equivalently, determine the exact polynomial exponent f(α) and the exact polylogarithmic exponent g(α) for every fixed shape α.

Let $A>0$, $p>0$, and $k\in\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$ be parameters. Consider the delay difference equation
$$x_{n+1}=\frac{A}{x_n^{2}}+\frac{1}{x_{n-k}^{\,p}},\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots,$$
with positive initial conditions $x_{-k},x_{-k+1},\ldots,x_0\in(0,\infty)$. The equation has a unique positive equilibrium $\bar x$, namely the unique positive solution of $\bar x=A/\bar x^{2}+1/\bar x^{p}$.

Determine explicit conditions on the parameters $A$, $p$, and $k$ under which the positive equilibrium $\bar x$ is globally asymptotically stable; that is, conditions ensuring that $\bar x$ is locally asymptotically stable and that for every choice of positive initial conditions the corresponding solution $\{x_n\}_{n\ge -k}$ satisfies $\lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=\bar x$.

A finite semigroup S with zero is called 0-simple if S^2 ≠ {0} and S has no two-sided ideals other than {0} and S. By the Rees theorem every finite 0-simple semigroup is isomorphic to a Rees matrix semigroup M^0(G; I, Λ; P) over a finite group G, with index sets I and Λ and a regular Λ×I sandwich matrix P with entries in G ∪ {0}. A finite Brandt semigroup is a finite 0-simple inverse semigroup; equivalently, it is a Rees matrix semigroup M^0(G; I, I; P) with P the I×I identity matrix over G.

Recall that a semigroup T is called a divisor of a semigroup S if T is a homomorphic image of a subsemigroup of S. For a class K of semigroups let D(K) denote the class of all divisors of members of K, i.e. all semigroups isomorphic to a homomorphic image of a subsemigroup of some S ∈ K.

Problem. Give an explicit structural description (for instance by a system of universal first-order formulas, or by a list of forbidden divisors / structural invariants) of the class D(K) in each of the following two cases:

(1) K is the class of all finite Brandt semigroups.

(2) K is the class of all finite 0-simple semigroups whose sandwich matrix in some Rees matrix representation has all entries equal to 0 or 1 (i.e. M^0({1}; I, Λ; P) with P a 0–1 matrix, viewed as a Rees matrix semigroup over the trivial group).

Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $X$ be an $n$-element set. The full transformation semigroup $T(n)$ is the semigroup of all functions $f : X \to X$ under composition. A semigroup identity is a formal equation $u = v$, where $u$ and $v$ are words in a countable alphabet of variables; a semigroup $S$ satisfies the identity $u = v$ if every substitution of elements of $S$ for the variables makes the two sides equal in $S$. The set of all identities satisfied by $T(n)$ generates the equational theory (variety) of $T(n)$.

Problem: Give an explicit description of all identities satisfied by the full transformation semigroup $T(n)$ on an $n$-element set, for each $n \geq 2$ (equivalently, describe a basis of identities for the variety generated by $T(n)$).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of describing the identities of the full transformation semigroup T(n) is a long-standing open question in semigroup theory. Only partial results are known: certain classes of identities have been described, and short identities (shorter than the natural unary ones) have been constructed for infinitely many n, but no full description / identity basis is known for general n. The problem connects to the words separation problem in automata theory.

A semigroup variety is a class of semigroups closed under taking subsemigroups, homomorphic images, and direct products; equivalently, it is the class of all semigroups satisfying a given set of identities. A semigroup S with zero 0 is called 0-simple if S^2 ≠ {0} and the only ideals of S are {0} and S. Fix a positive integer n, and let RS_n denote the semigroup variety generated by the class of all 0-simple semigroups that satisfy the identity x^2 = x^{n+2}. The lattice of all semigroup varieties is ordered by inclusion; given a variety V, a cover of V (in a fixed lattice of varieties) is a variety W properly containing V such that no variety lies strictly between V and W.

Problem: Describe explicitly all covers of the variety RS_n
(a) in the lattice of all semigroup varieties, and
(b) in the lattice of all semigroup varieties satisfying the identity x^2 = x^{n+2}.

(It is known that in the lattice (b) the set of covers of RS_n is finite, and that every subvariety of RS_1 has only finitely many covers.)

A Boolean circuit over the full binary basis B_2 (the set of all Boolean functions {0,1}^2 → {0,1}) is a directed acyclic graph whose sources are labeled by input variables x_1, …, x_n or constants, whose internal nodes (gates) have fan-in 2 and are labeled by functions in B_2, and which has a designated output node; the size of the circuit is the number of gates. The "gate elimination" method is the standard inductive technique for proving circuit-size lower bounds: one identifies a small set of input variables whose restriction (substituting constants 0/1) is guaranteed to eliminate at least k gates from any optimal circuit for the function, yielding by induction a lower bound of the form k·n − O(1) on the circuit size of an explicit family of Boolean functions f_n : {0,1}^n → {0,1}.

Question: Does there exist an explicit family of Boolean functions f_n : {0,1}^n → {0,1} for which a pure gate-elimination argument can prove that every B_2-circuit computing f_n has size at least 4n − O(1)?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Lower bounds of 4n−O(1), 4.5n−o(n) (Lachish–Raz), and 5n−o(n) (Iwama–Morizumi) have been proved using gate-elimination style arguments, but these are over the U_2 basis (B_2 minus parity/its negation), not the full binary basis B_2 considered here. Over B_2 the best known bound is 3.1n−o(n) (Li–Yang, STOC 2022), and works such as "On the Limits of Gate Elimination" (Golovnev et al., MFCS 2016) explicitly establish barriers for the gate-elimination technique over B_2. Whether a 4n lower bound over B_2 is achievable via pure gate elimination appears to remain open.

Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $A^+$ denote the set of finite non-empty words over $A$. A substitution is a map $\sigma : A 	o B^+$ (for some alphabet $B$) extended to a monoid homomorphism $A^+ 	o B^+$ by concatenation. A word $w \in B^\omega$ (finite or infinite) is said to contain a substitution image of $u \in A^+$ if there exist a substitution $\sigma : A 	o B^+$ and a factor $v$ of $w$ such that $v = \sigma(u)$; otherwise $w$ avoids all substitution images of $u$.

A word $u \in A^+$ is called blocking if every sufficiently long word over any finite alphabet contains a substitution image of $u$ (equivalently, no infinite word over any finite alphabet avoids all substitution images of $u$); otherwise $u$ is called non-blocking.

For a word $u$, let $c(u)$ denote the number of distinct letters occurring in $u$, and define
$$ m(u) = \min\{|B| : 	ext{there exists an infinite word over } B 	ext{ that contains no substitution image of } u\},$$
where the minimum is taken over all finite alphabets $B$ (with $m(u) = \infty$ if $u$ is blocking).

Problem. Determine $m(u)$ for every non-blocking word $u$, expressed as a function of $u$ (and in particular of $c(u)$).

For a Boolean function $f:\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^m$, let $C(f)$ denote the minimum number of gates in such a circuit computing $f$. The strongest known explicit lower bound for single-output functions ($m=1$) is of the form $(3+\tfrac{1}{86})n - o(n)$.

Exhibit an explicit family of multi-output Boolean functions $\{f_n:\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^{m(n)}\}$ (with $m(n) \ge 2$, e.g., $m(n) = O(n)$) together with a proof that $C(f_n) \ge c \cdot n$ for some constant $c$ strictly larger than the best known constant for single-output functions, or more generally prove a superlinear lower bound on $C(f_n)$ for some explicit multi-output family. Equivalently: can one leverage multiple outputs to obtain circuit-size lower bounds in the unrestricted model that exceed those currently known for single-output Boolean functions?

Let $(S,\cdot,\le)$ be an ordered semigroup, i.e. a semigroup equipped with a partial order $\le$ that is compatible with multiplication: $a\le b$ implies $ca\le cb$ and $ac\le bc$ for all $a,b,c\in S$.

For variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$, an identical inequality (also called an identical relation of precedence) on a class $\mathcal{K}$ of ordered semigroups is an expression $u(x_1,\dots,x_n)\le v(x_1,\dots,x_n)$, where $u,v$ are semigroup words, that holds in every $S\in\mathcal{K}$ for every substitution of $x_i$ by elements of $S$. An identity is an expression $u=v$ that holds for every such substitution. A system $\Sigma$ of identical inequalities is said to be equivalent to a system $\mathcal{I}$ of identities (over the class of all ordered semigroups) if a given ordered semigroup satisfies all members of $\Sigma$ if and only if it satisfies all members of $\mathcal{I}$.

Problem: Find necessary and sufficient conditions on a system $\Sigma=\{u_i\le v_i : i\in I\}$ of identical inequalities under which there exists a system of identities equivalent to $\Sigma$ in the class of ordered semigroups. (The case $|I|=1$, i.e. systems consisting of a single identical inequality, is known to be settled.)

representations.normalized:
A Boolean circuit on n inputs is a directed acyclic graph whose sources are labeled with input variables x_1,...,x_n (or constants), whose internal nodes (gates) are labeled with binary Boolean operations chosen from the full binary basis B_2 (all functions {0,1}^2 -> {0,1}), and which has one designated output node. The size of the circuit is the number of gates. The circuit satisfiability problem (Circuit-SAT) takes as input such a circuit C and asks whether there exists an assignment a in {0,1}^n with C(a) = 1.

Brute-force search solves Circuit-SAT in time 2^n · poly(|C|) by trying every input assignment.

Question: Does there exist a (possibly randomized) algorithm that, given as input a Boolean circuit C over the basis B_2 of size at most 4n on n input variables, decides whether C is satisfiable in time 2^{(1-ε)n} · poly(n) for some absolute constant ε > 0, thereby improving on brute-force search?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Known improved Circuit-SAT algorithms (e.g., Calabro–Impagliazzo–Paturi and follow-ups) beat brute force for circuits of constant depth with cn gates, but these techniques degrade and become no better than 2^n once the circuit size grows to roughly 4n or beyond for general (unrestricted-depth) circuits over B_2. No known algorithm improves on brute-force search for Circuit-SAT on general size-4n circuits; the question is widely cited as open in the circuit complexity literature.

A Boolean circuit (over the standard De Morgan basis with AND, OR, NOT gates of fan-in at most 2) on n input bits is said to have size s if it consists of at most s gates. Fix a constant c > 0. A "non-trivial satisfiability algorithm" for the class of Boolean circuits of size cn on n inputs is a deterministic algorithm that, given as input a description of such a circuit C, decides whether there exists x ∈ {0,1}^n with C(x) = 1, in worst-case time 2^n / s(n) for some superpolynomial (or otherwise non-trivial) function s(n) → ∞ — that is, an algorithm that beats exhaustive search by a non-trivial factor on this circuit class.

Question: Does the existence, for every constant c > 0, of a non-trivial satisfiability algorithm for Boolean circuits of size cn on n inputs imply that there is a language in some "natural" complexity class (e.g., E^{NP}, NEXP, or similar) that, for every constant c > 0, requires Boolean circuits of size at least cn (i.e., linear lower bounds with arbitrarily large constant)?

Equivalently: prove or refute the implication

   "for every c, a non-trivial SAT algorithm exists for size-cn circuits"  ⟹  "for every c, there is an explicit function requiring circuits of size cn".

For a positive integer n, let B_n denote the set of Boolean functions f : {0,1}^n → {0,1}, and let gates(f) denote the minimum number of gates in an unrestricted Boolean circuit (over the full binary basis) computing f. For positive integers r and n and a function f ∈ B_n, define r × f : {0,1}^{rn} → {0,1}^r to be the function that applies f independently to r disjoint input blocks of length n, producing r output bits. One says that the "mass production effect" occurs for f when gates(r × f) is much smaller than r · gates(f); equivalently, computing r independent copies of f is significantly cheaper than computing r separate copies.

Characterize, or exhibit explicit examples of, Boolean functions f that avoid the mass production effect: that is, families of functions f for which gates(r × f) = (1 - o(1)) · r · gates(f) (or, more strongly, gates(r × f) ≥ r · gates(f) - o(r · gates(f))) as r grows. In particular, identify structural properties of f that force the circuit complexity of r × f to grow essentially linearly in r times the circuit complexity of f, with no asymptotic savings from computing multiple independent copies in parallel.

Consider Boolean circuits over the standard basis (AND, OR, NOT) with bounded fan-in (say fan-in 2), computing Boolean functions $f:\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$. The size of a circuit is the number of gates, and its depth is the length of the longest path from an input to the output gate.

Exhibit an explicit family of Boolean functions $\{f_n\}_{n\ge 1}$, with $f_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ computable by some uniform algorithm (e.g., in NP, or even just in some explicit complexity class), together with a function $s(n) = \omega(n)$, such that any Boolean circuit of depth $O(\log n)$ computing $f_n$ must have size at least $s(n)$.

Equivalently: prove that there exists an explicit Boolean function family that cannot be computed by Boolean circuits of simultaneously linear size $O(n)$ and logarithmic depth $O(\log n)$, with a superlinear size lower bound holding for all $O(\log n)$-depth circuits computing it.

A linear Boolean circuit (over $\mathbb{F}_2$) is a directed acyclic graph in which every non-input gate has fan-in 2 and computes the XOR (parity) of its two inputs; the input nodes are labeled by variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$, and a designated set of $n$ output gates produces the output. The size of such a circuit is its number of gates. For a matrix $A \in \{0,1\}^{n\times n}$, the linear map $f_A: \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^n$ defined by $f_A(x) = Ax$ (with arithmetic over $\mathbb{F}_2$) can be computed by some linear Boolean circuit; let $L(A)$ denote the minimum size of any such circuit computing $f_A$.

It is known that for a uniformly random $A \in \{0,1\}^{n\times n}$ one has $L(A) = \Theta(n^2/\log n)$ with high probability, while for every explicit family of matrices $\{A_n\}$ the best known unconditional lower bound on $L(A_n)$ is only $3n - o(n)$.

Problem: Exhibit an explicit family of matrices $\{A_n\}_{n\ge1}$ with $A_n \in \{0,1\}^{n\times n}$ together with a proof that
$$L(A_n) \;=\; \omega(n),$$
i.e., prove a superlinear lower bound on the size of any linear Boolean circuit (using only parity gates of fan-in 2) computing the multi-output linear map $x \mapsto A_n x$.

    mc(f_n) ≥ n,
and, more ambitiously, to prove a lower bound of the form
    mc(f_n) ≥ (1 + ε) n
for some absolute constant ε > 0 and all sufficiently large n.

$$\frac{|\partial_{\mathbf{b}}^m F(z)|}{m!\,L(z)^m}\le \max_{0\le k\le m_0}\frac{|\partial_{\mathbf{b}}^k F(z)|}{k!\,L(z)^k}\qquad\text{for all }m\in\mathbb{Z}_+\text{ and all }z\in\mathbb{C}^n.$$

Let S be a commutative semigroup. The set End(S) of all endomorphisms of S (semigroup homomorphisms S → S) becomes a semigroup under pointwise multiplication, defined by (φ·ψ)(s) = φ(s)ψ(s) for all s ∈ S. A semigroup F is called free if there is a subset X ⊆ F such that every element of F can be written uniquely as a finite product of elements of X (i.e., F is freely generated by X in the variety of semigroups).

Problem: Characterize (describe) all commutative semigroups S for which the endomorphism semigroup End(S), equipped with pointwise multiplication, is a free semigroup.

Fix a direction $b \in \mathbb{C}^n \setminus \{0\}$. For a positive continuous function $L: \mathbb{C}^n \to (0,\infty)$ and $\eta > 0$, define the regularity quantity
$$\lambda_b(\eta) = \sup\!\left\{ \frac{L(z + t_2 b)}{L(z + t_1 b)} : z \in \mathbb{C}^n,\ t_1, t_2 \in \mathbb{C},\ |t_1 - t_2| \le \frac{\eta}{L(z + t_1 b)} \right\},$$
and let $Q_b^n$ denote the class of all such $L$ for which $\lambda_b(\eta) < \infty$ for every $\eta > 0$.

An entire function $F: \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ is said to be of bounded $L$-index in the direction $b$ if there exists an integer $m_0 \ge 0$ such that for every $z \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and every nonnegative integer $m$,
$$\frac{|\partial_b^m F(z)|}{m!\, L(z)^m} \le \max_{0 \le k \le m_0} \frac{|\partial_b^k F(z)|}{k!\, L(z)^k},$$
where $\partial_b F(z) = \sum_{j=1}^n b_j \partial F/\partial z_j$.

Let $L \in Q_b^n$ and let $F$ be an entire function on $\mathbb{C}^n$. Prove or disprove: $F$ is of bounded $L$-index in the direction $b$ if and only if there exist constants $R > 0$, $P_2(R) \ge 1$, and $\eta(R) \in (0, R)$ such that for every $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}^n$ there is some $r = r(z_0) \in [\eta(R), R]$ with
$$\max\{|F(z_0 + t b)| : |t| = r/L(z_0)\} \le P_2(R)\, \min\{|F(z_0 + t b)| : |t| = r/L(z_0)\}.$$

Let $(M,\omega)$ be a closed (compact, without boundary) symplectic manifold, and let $\varphi : M \to M$ be a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism, i.e. the time-one map of a smooth time-dependent Hamiltonian flow on $M$. A fixed point $x$ of $\varphi$ is called homologically necessary (or Arnold–Floer forced) if its existence is guaranteed by the Arnold conjecture lower bounds derived from Floer/Morse homology of $M$ (for instance, by the rank of $H_*(M;\mathbb{Q})$ or the sum of Betti numbers). Suppose that $\varphi$ has at least one fixed point in addition to those forced by Arnold–Floer theory — for example, a hyperbolic fixed point, or a non-contractible fixed point (a fixed point whose associated orbit loop is not contractible in $M$) — and assume that the presence of this extra fixed point forces $\varphi$ to possess infinitely many periodic points (i.e. integer $k \geq 1$ and fixed points of $\varphi^k$ giving distinct periodic orbits).

A primitive periodic orbit of $\varphi$ of period $k$ is an orbit $\{x, \varphi(x), \dots, \varphi^{k-1}(x)\}$ where $k$ is the minimal positive integer with $\varphi^k(x) = x$. Let $N(T)$ denote the number of primitive periodic orbits of $\varphi$ of minimal period at most $T$.

Question: Under the hypotheses above, must one have a quadratic lower bound
$$N(T) \geq c\, T^2$$
for some constant $c > 0$ and all sufficiently large $T$?

Let $b \in \mathbb{C}^n \setminus \{0\}$ be a fixed direction, let $F: \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be an entire function (not identically zero), and let $L: \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{R}_+$ be a positive continuous function. For $z \in \mathbb{C}^n$ consider the slice function $g_z(t) = F(z + tb)$, $t \in \mathbb{C}$, and let $n_z(\rho)$ denote the number of zeros of $g_z$ in the disc $\{t \in \mathbb{C} : |t| < \rho\}$ (counted with multiplicities), assuming $g_z \not\equiv 0$. Define
$$n(r) \;=\; \sup_{z \in \mathbb{C}^n} n_z\!\left(\frac{r}{L(z)}\right), \qquad r > 0,$$
and the "exceptional set"
$$G^b_r(F) \;=\; \bigcup_{w \in \mathbb{C}^n : F(w)=0} \Big\{ w + tb : |t| < \tfrac{r}{L(w)} \Big\}.$$
Let $\partial F(z)/\partial b$ denote the directional derivative of $F$ along $b$, and let $\lambda_b(r)$ be the directional regularity quantity
$$\lambda_b(r) \;=\; \sup\!\left\{ \frac{L(z_1)}{L(z_2)} \,:\, z_1 = z_2 + tb,\ |t| \le \frac{r}{\min\{L(z_1),L(z_2)\}} \right\}.$$
Set
$$r_0 \;=\; \sup_{r>0} \frac{r}{2\, n(r)\, \lambda_b(r)}.$$

Question: Do there exist an entire function $F$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$ and a positive continuous function $L: \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{R}_+$ such that both of the following hold?
\begin{enumerate}
\item There exist $r_1 > r_0$ and $P > 0$ such that
$$\frac{1}{|F(z)|}\left|\frac{\partial F(z)}{\partial b}\right| \;\le\; P\, L(z) \qquad \text{for every } z \in \mathbb{C}^n \setminus G^b_{r_1}(F).$$
\item For every $r_2 < r_0$,
$$\sup_{z \in \mathbb{C}^n \setminus G^b_{r_2}(F)} \frac{1}{|F(z)|\, L(z)} \left|\frac{\partial F(z)}{\partial b}\right| \;=\; +\infty,$$
and $n(r_2) \in (0, +\infty)$.
\end{enumerate}
In other words, is the threshold $r_0$ sharp in the sense that an entire function exhibiting this exact transition between bounded and unbounded normalized directional logarithmic derivative on the complement of the tube $G^b_r(F)$ actually exists?

A finite semigroup is called aperiodic if every subgroup contained in it is trivial (equivalently, for every element $s$ there exists $n\ge 1$ with $s^n = s^{n+1}$). A semigroup is called regular if for every element $a$ there exists an element $x$ such that $a x a = a$.

A class $\mathcal{C}$ of finite semigroups is said to be completely solvable if there exists an algorithm which, given a finite semigroup $S \in \mathcal{C}$ presented by its multiplication table, decides every basic algorithmic predicate for $S$ — in particular, given any finite subset $A \subseteq S$ and an element $b \in S$, decides whether $b$ belongs to the subsemigroup of $S$ generated by $A$ (the membership/divisibility problem), whether $b$ lies in the ideal generated by $A$, and whether $b$ lies in the maximal subgroup determined by $A$.

Question: Is the class of all finite regular aperiodic semigroups completely solvable?

Consider a periodic polygonal tiling of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, in which the plane is partitioned into polygonal cells whose collection is invariant under a lattice $\Lambda \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ of translations. A generalized tiling billiard trajectory is a piecewise-linear oriented curve in $\mathbb{R}^2$ that moves along straight segments inside each cell and, upon crossing an edge $e$ shared by two adjacent cells, refracts according to Snell's law with refraction coefficient $-1$: if $\theta$ is the angle that the incoming segment makes with $e$, the outgoing segment makes angle $-\theta$ with $e$ (equivalently, the refracted ray is the reflection of the incoming ray with respect to the edge $e$, but continuing into the neighboring cell rather than bouncing back).

A trajectory is called:
- periodic if it is a closed curve;
- linearly escaping (drift-periodic) if it is invariant under a non-trivial translation of $\Lambda$ and escapes to infinity;
- dense in an open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ if its closure contains $U$.

Call a "generic dynamical archetype" for a given periodic polygonal tiling a qualitative description of the asymptotic behavior of trajectories that holds for a full-measure (or otherwise generic) set of initial conditions; examples include "every generic trajectory is periodic", "every generic trajectory is linearly escaping", or "the closure of a generic trajectory contains an open set".

Question: As the periodic polygonal tiling of the plane varies over all such tilings, does the collection of generic dynamical archetypes that occur for generalized tiling billiards with Snell refraction coefficient $-1$ form a finite list?

For a class $\Phi$ of semigroups, let $H$, $S$, $P$, $P_S$ denote the standard Birkhoff-style class operators: $H(\Phi)$ is the class of all homomorphic images of members of $\Phi$, $S(\Phi)$ the class of all subsemigroups of members of $\Phi$, $P(\Phi)$ the class of all direct products of members of $\Phi$, and $P_S(\Phi)$ the class of all subdirect products of members of $\Phi$. Composing these one forms the operators

$$HP,\quad HP_S,\quad SHP,\quad SHP_S,$$

applied in the indicated order to $\Phi$. The variety generated by a semigroup $M$ is $HSP(M)$.

Given a class $\mathcal{C}$ of semigroups, define its kernel by
$$\operatorname{Cor}(\mathcal{C}) \;=\; \{\,M \in \mathcal{C} \;:\; HSP(M) \subseteq \mathcal{C}\,\}.$$

A class $\mathcal{D}$ of finite semigroups is called decidable if there exists an algorithm that, on input a finite semigroup $M$ (given by its multiplication table), decides whether $M \in \mathcal{D}$.

Problem. Let $K \in \{HP,\, HP_S,\, SHP,\, SHP_S\}$ and let $\Phi$ be an arbitrary finite class of finite semigroups. Is the class $\operatorname{Cor}(K(\Phi))$ always decidable?

Consider the tiling of the plane by unit squares arranged so that the squares in every other horizontal row are translated horizontally by a fixed parameter θ ∈ [0,1) (a "brick tiling" with offset θ). A tiling billiard trajectory is the piecewise-linear path of a point particle that travels in straight lines inside each tile and, upon crossing an edge between two adjacent tiles, refracts according to the law of negative refraction (the reflected direction is the reflection of the incoming direction across the edge being crossed, so the trajectory crosses the edge with the angle of incidence equal to the angle of refraction but on the opposite side of the normal).

It is known that when θ ∈ ℚ, every (nonsingular) trajectory of this billiard system is periodic (in fact, with a uniform bound on the period depending on the denominator of θ).

Problem: Determine the dynamical behavior of tiling billiard trajectories on the brick tiling with shift parameter θ when θ is irrational. In particular, describe whether trajectories are periodic, drift-periodic, bounded, escaping, recurrent, equidistributed, etc., and identify the underlying dynamical structure (e.g. interval exchange, rotation, or otherwise) governing their long-term behavior.

For a group $G$, the power semigroup $\mathcal{P}(G)$ is the semigroup whose elements are the nonempty subsets of $G$ with multiplication
$$A\cdot B = \{ab : a\in A,\ b\in B\}.$$
A group $G$ is called periodic if every element of $G$ has finite order. A semigroup $S$ is said to be regular if for every $s\in S$ there exists $t\in S$ with $sts=s$, and completely regular if every element lies in a subgroup of $S$. A semigroup is periodic if every element generates a finite subsemigroup, and an inverse-having (or "inversive") completely regular semigroup is one in which each element $x$ has a (group) inverse $x^{-1}$ within its $\mathcal{H}$-class.

It is known that a completely regular semigroup embeds into $\mathcal{P}(G)$ for some periodic group $G$ if and only if it is inversive and periodic.

Problem. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on a regular semigroup $S$ for there to exist a periodic group $G$ such that $S$ embeds (as a semigroup) into the power semigroup $\mathcal{P}(G)$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $T^*M$ denote its cotangent bundle, equipped with the canonical symplectic form $\omega_0 = d\lambda$, where $\lambda$ is the tautological one-form. Let $\pi : T^*M \to M$ be the projection, and let $\eta$ be a closed one-form on $M$, whose pullback to $T^*M$ we also denote by $\eta$. The pair $(T^*M, \omega_0)$ together with $\eta$ defines a locally conformal symplectic (LCS) structure via the Lichnerowicz differential $d_\eta \alpha := d\alpha + \eta \wedge \alpha$. For a smooth function $H : T^*M \to \mathbb{R}$, the LCS Hamiltonian vector field $X_H$ is defined by $\iota_{X_H} \omega_0 = -d_\eta H$.

Assume that $H$ is a Tonelli Hamiltonian, i.e. $H$ is $C^2$, fiberwise strictly convex, and superlinear in the fibers of $T^*M$. Let $L : TM \to \mathbb{R}$ be the Legendre-dual Tonelli Lagrangian of $H$. Writing the LCS Hamilton equations in local canonical coordinates $(q,p)$ on $T^*M$ with $\eta = \eta_i(q)\,dq^i$, one obtains a system of the form
$$\dot q = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p}, \qquad \dot p = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial q} - L(q,\dot q)\,\eta(q),$$
so that, relative to the standard Hamilton equations on $T^*M$, an additional force term equal to $-L(q,\dot q)\,\eta(q)$ appears.

Problem: Give a physical interpretation of the additional force term $-L(q,\dot q)\,\eta$ appearing in these simplified locally conformal symplectic cotangent-bundle equations for a Tonelli Hamiltonian with $\eta$ pulled back from the base. In particular, identify a mechanical or thermodynamic mechanism (e.g. a friction/dissipation law, a non-conservative external forcing, or a gauge/conformal rescaling effect) that naturally produces a force proportional to minus the instantaneous Lagrangian times the one-form $\eta$, and justify the identification.

Background. A semigroup is a set equipped with an associative binary operation. An identical inclusion (over a countable alphabet X) is a formal expression of the form w ⊆ {w₁, …, wₙ}, where w, w₁, …, wₙ are words in X⁺. A semigroup S satisfies this inclusion if, for every homomorphism φ : X⁺ → S, one has φ(w) ∈ {φ(w₁), …, φ(wₙ)}. A class K of semigroups is called an inclusive variety if there exists a (possibly infinite) set Σ of identical inclusions such that K consists exactly of those semigroups that satisfy every inclusion in Σ. It is known that every inclusive variety is closed under taking subsemigroups and under homomorphic images.

Birkhoff's classical HSP theorem characterizes equational varieties of algebras as exactly those classes that are closed under homomorphic images (H), subalgebras (S), and direct products (P).

Problem. Establish an analogue of Birkhoff's theorem for inclusive varieties of semigroups. That is, exhibit a (minimal) collection 𝒪 of class operators such that, for every class K of semigroups, K is an inclusive variety if and only if K is closed under each operator in 𝒪.

Background and definitions.

Let $S$ be a semigroup, and let $X = \{x_1, x_2, \dots\}$ be a countably infinite set of variables. Denote by $X^+$ the free semigroup on $X$. An identical inclusion (also called an inclusive identity) over $S$ is a formal expression of the form
$$ w \subseteq \{u_1, u_2, \dots, u_k\}, $$
where $w, u_1, \dots, u_k \in X^+$. The semigroup $S$ is said to satisfy this identical inclusion if for every homomorphism (substitution) $\varphi : X^+ \to S$ one has
$$ \varphi(w) \in \{\varphi(u_1), \varphi(u_2), \dots, \varphi(u_k)\}. $$
The set of all identical inclusions satisfied by $S$ is called the inclusive theory of $S$.

Two semigroups $S$ and $T$ are said to satisfy the same identical inclusions if their inclusive theories coincide. A semigroup $S$ is determined by its identical inclusions up to isomorphism if every semigroup $T$ satisfying exactly the same identical inclusions as $S$ is isomorphic to $S$.

Known examples of semigroups that are determined by their identical inclusions up to isomorphism include:
- the two-element semilattice;
- every quasicyclic group (Prüfer $p$-group) $\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)$;
- every finite group.

Problem. Within the basic classes of semigroups (such as semilattices, bands, completely simple semigroups, inverse semigroups, periodic semigroups, commutative semigroups, etc.), characterize, or exhibit further families of, the semigroups that are determined up to isomorphism by their identical inclusions.

A semigroup is called idempotent (or a band) if every element x satisfies x² = x. An identical inclusion over a countable alphabet X is a formal expression of the form w ⊆ W, where w is a word in X⁺ and W ⊆ X⁺ is a (possibly infinite) set of words; a semigroup S satisfies the inclusion w ⊆ W if, for every homomorphism φ : X⁺ → S, one has φ(w) ∈ φ(W). A class K of semigroups is called an inclusive variety if it can be defined by a (possibly infinite) system of identical inclusions, i.e. K is the class of all semigroups satisfying every inclusion in some prescribed set Σ of identical inclusions. An inclusive variety K is called elementary if it is also axiomatizable by a set of first-order formulas in the language of semigroups; otherwise it is called nonelementary.

Question: Does there exist a nonelementary inclusive variety K of idempotent semigroups, that is, an inclusive variety K consisting entirely of bands such that K cannot be axiomatized by any set of first-order sentences?

Let X be a nonempty set and let T(X) denote the monoid of all self-maps X → X under composition. By a pargoid of transformations on X we mean any subset P ⊆ T(X) (typically closed under composition, so a subsemigroup of T(X), and possibly satisfying additional natural closure conditions such as containing the identity, being closed under inverses when applicable, etc.). Given a mathematical structure A on the underlying set X (for example, a partially ordered set, lattice, topological space, graph, group, ring, vector space, module, metric space, etc.), several "natural" pargoids are associated to A, such as:
 • End(A), the semigroup of all endomorphisms of A,
 • Aut(A), the group of all automorphisms of A,
 • the semigroup of all closure operators on A (when A is a poset),
 • the semigroup of all continuous self-maps (when A is a topological space),
 • the semigroup of all order-preserving self-maps (when A is a poset),
and similar canonical constructions.

Two structures A and B (of the same type) on possibly different underlying sets are said to be determined up to isomorphism by an associated pargoid construction P(·) if whenever P(A) and P(B) are isomorphic (as semigroups, or as groups in the case of automorphism groups), there exists an isomorphism A ≅ B of the structures.

Solve the following two problems for the main natural classes C of mathematical structures (posets, lattices, topological spaces, graphs, groups, rings, modules, metric spaces, etc.) and the main natural pargoid constructions P:

(1) Characterise, for each pair (C, P), the subclass of structures A ∈ C that are determined up to isomorphism by their pargoid P(A).

(2) Characterise the pargoids of transformations on a set X that are themselves determined up to isomorphism (as a pargoid) by their endomorphism semigroup End(P) or by their automorphism group Aut(P).

(A known partial result, due to E. S. Lyapin, is that every partially ordered set is determined up to isomorphism by the pargoid of its closure operators.)

An involuted semigroup is a semigroup $(S,\cdot)$ equipped with a unary operation ${}^*:S\to S$ satisfying $(xy)^*=y^*x^*$ and $(x^*)^*=x$ for all $x,y\in S$. Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a variety of involuted semigroups (i.e. a class defined by identities in the signature $\{\cdot,{}^*\}$). For an algebra $A$ in some signature, say that a model of $A$ is representable in $\mathcal{V}$ if $A$ embeds into a member of $\mathcal{V}$ via the natural interpretation of its operations. The class of all such representable models forms a quasivariety (a class defined by quasi-identities, i.e. universal Horn formulas with equality).

Problem: Characterize all varieties $\mathcal{V}$ of involuted semigroups with the property that the quasivariety of models representable in $\mathcal{V}$ is finitely axiomatizable, i.e. can be defined by finitely many quasi-identities.

A planetary nebula is an expanding shell of ionized gas, dust, and molecules ejected by a low- to intermediate-mass star at the end of its asymptotic-giant-branch evolution. Observationally, such a nebula is accessible only through (i) two-dimensional images obtained by projecting its three-dimensional emissivity distribution along the line of sight, and (ii) line-of-sight kinematic data (e.g., position–velocity diagrams obtained from Doppler-shifted emission lines), which provide the radial velocity component of the gas at each projected position. Different intrinsic three-dimensional shapes (for example, bipolar, elliptical, or multipolar geometries) can produce nearly identical two-dimensional projected images depending on the orientation relative to the observer, and additional lobes or structures may remain undetected in shallow optical imaging while becoming visible only in deeper or infrared observations.

Formulate and solve the following inverse problem: given a planetary nebula modeled as a three-dimensional emissivity field ε(x, y, z) together with a velocity field v(x, y, z) supported on a bounded region of ℝ³, and given as data the projected surface brightness I(X, Y) = ∫ ε ds along lines of sight together with position–velocity information specifying, for each projected pixel, the distribution of line-of-sight velocity components weighted by ε, determine

(a) under what conditions on (ε, v) the pair (ε, v) can be uniquely reconstructed (up to natural symmetries such as reflection along the line of sight) from this combined imaging plus kinematic data, and

(b) provide a constructive, observationally practical reconstruction procedure that recovers the intrinsic three-dimensional morphology of the nebula, including the detection of faint multipolar lobes, from such two-dimensional images and kinematic measurements.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The recovery of true three-dimensional structures of planetary nebulae from 2D imaging and kinematic data is a long-standing open observational and modeling problem. Tools such as SHAPE (Steffen et al.) provide morpho-kinematic reconstructions but require assumptions (e.g., homologous expansion) and do not give unique recoveries; recent reviews continue to list 3D morphology and projection ambiguities as unresolved.

Consider a planetary nebula formed at the end of the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) phase of a low- or intermediate-mass star, surrounded by a circumstellar envelope produced by prior AGB mass loss. Observations of certain planetary nebulae reveal highly collimated fast outflows, including narrow rotating jets and multiple pairs of bipolar lobes oriented along distinct axes (point-symmetric or multipolar morphologies), and in some cases recurrent ejection events separated in time. The fast wind from the hot central star, however, is observed to be approximately spherically symmetric, and a single binary stellar merger does not naturally account for ejection episodes that recur in time or that are oriented along different axes.

Identify and characterize the physical mechanism (or combination of mechanisms—e.g., accretion disks around a companion, magnetic launching and collimation, common-envelope nozzle confinement, precessing jets, triple-star interactions, etc.) that:
(a) launches highly collimated fast outflows from a system whose stellar fast wind is essentially spherical;
(b) explains rotating (precessing) jets;
(c) accounts for multiple bipolar lobe pairs at different orientations within a single nebula; and
(d) permits recurrent, temporally separated collimated ejection events.

Provide a model that simultaneously satisfies (a)–(d), including the energy and angular-momentum source, the launching geometry, the collimation agent, and the mechanism producing axis reorientation between successive ejections.

representations.normalized:
In the late stages of stellar evolution, a low- or intermediate-mass star ascends the asymptotic giant branch (AGB), where it loses mass through a slow, dense, dusty wind. After the AGB phase, the central star's effective temperature rises rapidly, ionizing the surrounding circumstellar envelope and producing a planetary nebula (PN). Many observed planetary nebulae contain small-scale, high-density structures embedded in or surrounding the ionized gas, in the form of cometary globules (dense neutral or molecular knots with ionized tails pointing away from the central star) and dense clumps.

Two competing scenarios for the origin of these globules and knots are:

(A) In situ formation during the PN phase. The clumps form after the onset of ionization, e.g., through hydrodynamic or radiative instabilities at the ionization front separating the ionized wind/nebular gas from the neutral AGB envelope (such as thin-shell, Rayleigh–Taylor, or ionization-front instabilities), so that the observed knots are a product of PN-phase physics.

(B) Inheritance from the AGB wind. Dense clumps already form in the AGB wind itself (e.g., via dust-driven wind instabilities, convective cells, or chromospheric activity) and persist through the post-AGB transition into the PN phase, becoming the observed cometary globules and knots. A complication for this scenario is that such AGB clumps are generally not in pressure equilibrium with the surrounding tenuous wind and may dissipate before the PN phase begins.

Problem. Determine which of scenarios (A) and (B) is responsible for the cometary globules and dense clumps observed in planetary nebulae. Concretely:

1. Establish whether instabilities at an ionization front propagating into a smooth (or mildly inhomogeneous) AGB envelope can, under realistic PN conditions (ionizing photon luminosities, density profiles, expansion velocities, and timescales), produce a population of clumps with the observed sizes, densities, masses, spatial distributions, and cometary morphologies.

2. Establish whether clumps formed in the AGB wind can survive the post-AGB transition — including the rapid increase in central-star temperature, the onset of a fast tenuous wind, and ionization — given that they are not initially in pressure equilibrium with their surroundings, and whether the surviving clumps reproduce the observed properties of PN knots.

3. On the basis of (1) and (2), decide between scenario (A), scenario (B), or a quantified combination of the two.

For a finite string (word) $w$ over a finite alphabet, a run (also called a maximal repetition) is a maximal occurrence of a periodic factor of exponent at least $2$, i.e., a substring $w[i..j]$ with smallest period $p \le (j-i+1)/2$ that cannot be extended to the left or to the right while preserving the period $p$. Let $\rho(n)$ denote the maximum, taken over all strings of length $n$ over any alphabet, of the number of runs occurring in the string. It is known that the limit superior
$$ \alpha := \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{\rho(n)}{n} $$
exists and is finite (in fact $\rho(n)<n$ for all $n\ge 1$). Prove or disprove the following: for every positive integer $n$,
$$ \frac{\rho(n)}{n} < \alpha. $$
That is, the asymptotic upper bound of $\rho(n)/n$ is never attained for any finite $n$.

A planetary nebula consists of an ionized gaseous component (typically observed in optical emission lines such as Hα and [O III]) surrounding a hot post-asymptotic-giant-branch central star, together with a neutral component composed of molecular gas (e.g., H2, CO), atomic gas, and dust. While the ionized component can be readily imaged in the optical, the spatial distribution of the neutral component is much less well constrained.

Determine, for representative planetary nebulae spanning the observed morphological classes (round, elliptical, bipolar, multipolar), the full three-dimensional spatial distribution of the molecular gas, dust, and other neutral material relative to the three-dimensional distribution of the ionized optical nebula. Using these distributions, address the following:

(a) What is the true total mass distribution (ionized plus neutral) of each nebula, and how does the inclusion of the neutral component modify mass estimates derived from the ionized component alone?

(b) To what extent does the neutral component physically confine the optical lobes, in the sense of providing a denser surrounding medium that bounds the ionized cavities?

(c) What role does the neutral component play in collimating and shaping bipolar (and more generally axisymmetric or multipolar) outflows from the central star–nebula system?

Provide a quantitative model linking the observed three-dimensional neutral-gas and dust distributions to the morphology, kinematics, and mass budget of the ionized nebula.

A planetary nebula is the ionized circumstellar envelope ejected by a low- or intermediate-mass star (initial mass roughly 1–8 solar masses) during its transition from the asymptotic giant branch to the white dwarf stage. Around a subset of planetary nebulae, observations reveal extended outer features whose linear sizes reach parsec scales (and whose angular extent on the sky can reach degree scales), often shaped as giant bipolar lobes, jets, or filamentary haloes, and which are observed to be expanding at hypersonic velocities (kinematic expansion speeds far exceeding the local sound speed of the surrounding medium, in some cases of order hundreds of km/s).

Formulate and answer the following two-part problem:

(a) Identify the physical mechanisms — for example, eruptive mass-loss episodes from the central star, jets driven during or after a common-envelope binary interaction, magnetohydrodynamic launching from an accretion disk around a binary companion, or other proposed processes — that can quantitatively reproduce both the very large spatial scales (≳1 pc) and the hypersonic expansion velocities of these outer structures and giant bipolar lobes around planetary nebulae. Provide a hydrodynamic or magnetohydrodynamic model whose predicted morphologies, sizes, and velocity fields are consistent with the observed parsec/degree-scale outflows.

(b) Estimate the rate of occurrence (per planetary-nebula progenitor, or per unit time per unit stellar mass) of the eruptive and/or post-common-envelope events capable of launching such large-scale structures, and compare this rate with the observed fraction of planetary nebulae that exhibit such giant outer features.

Background. A planetary nebula (PN) is the ionized circumstellar shell ejected by a low- to intermediate-mass star (initial mass roughly 0.8–8 solar masses) at the end of its asymptotic giant branch (AGB) evolution, illuminated by the hot, exposed stellar core that becomes a white dwarf. A proto-planetary nebula (pPN) is the brief transitional object between the AGB and PN phases, in which the central star has not yet become hot enough (T_eff ≳ 30000 K) to ionize its expelled envelope. A close binary central star of a planetary nebula (CSPN) is a central star whose companion has an orbital period short enough (typically less than a few days) to imply that the system has previously undergone common-envelope (CE) evolution: a short-lived phase in which the AGB primary engulfs its companion, leading to rapid orbital shrinkage and ejection of the shared envelope.

Two candidate channels for forming a PN from an AGB progenitor are:
(i) Gradual post-AGB evolution: a single star (or a very wide binary) loses its envelope by a slow superwind, then crosses the HR diagram on a timescale of order 10^3–10^4 years through an identifiable pPN stage before ionization.
(ii) Common-envelope evolution: a close companion spirals inward inside the AGB envelope, ejecting it on a timescale ≲ 10^3 years, producing a PN with a close binary central star.

Problem. Provide a quantitative astrophysical model that simultaneously answers the following:

(a) Identify the stellar progenitor population of planetary nebulae that host close binary central stars, given that the currently observed sample of proto-planetary nebulae does not appear to evolve into this population (e.g. due to mismatched luminosities, kinematics, chemical abundances, envelope masses, or expansion timescales). Specify the AGB initial mass range, the binary orbital-period and mass-ratio distribution at the onset of the relevant interaction, and the observable phase (if any) during which these progenitors should be detectable.

(b) Determine whether planetary-nebula formation proceeds through two physically distinct channels — gradual post-AGB evolution and common-envelope evolution — or through a single unified channel with a continuum of binary-interaction strengths. Quantify the relative birthrate, the fraction of all PNe produced by each channel, and predict observable diagnostics (morphology, expansion velocity field, central-star binary fraction, nebular abundances) that distinguish the channels.

In the spectroscopic analysis of an ionized gaseous nebula surrounding a hot central star (a planetary nebula), one can derive ionic abundances of heavy elements (e.g., O²⁺, N²⁺, C²⁺) by two independent methods:

(i) From collisionally excited "forbidden" lines (CELs), whose emissivities depend exponentially on the electron temperature T_e through factors of the form exp(−ΔE/kT_e), making them strongly temperature-sensitive; and

(ii) From optical recombination lines (ORLs), whose emissivities have only a weak (power-law) dependence on T_e.

For a given ion X^{i+}, define the abundance discrepancy factor

   ADF(X^{i+}) = (X^{i+}/H⁺)_ORL / (X^{i+}/H⁺)_CEL.

Observations show ADF > 1 systematically, with typical values 2–3, but a subset of planetary nebulae exhibit extreme values ADF ≳ 10–100, and many of these host a close-binary central star that has experienced common-envelope evolution.

Address the following:

(a) Identify the physical origin of the systematic discrepancy ADF > 1 between recombination-line and forbidden-line abundance determinations.

(b) Under the hypothesis that the discrepancy arises from a cool, hydrogen-deficient (metal-rich) plasma component coexisting with the main warm ionized gas, determine the spatial location, geometry, mass, and physical conditions (electron temperature, density, chemical composition) of this component within the nebula.

(c) Provide a quantitative mechanism by which close-binary or common-envelope evolution of the central star system can produce, eject, and preserve such a hydrogen-poor component so as to generate the extreme ADF values (ADF ≫ 10) observed in those systems.

Define the Zimin words over an infinite alphabet of variables x_1, x_2, ... recursively by Z_1 = x_1 and Z_{k+1} = Z_k x_{k+1} Z_k for k >= 1. A pattern is a nonempty word p = p_1 p_2 ... p_m over a finite set of variables. For a finite word w over some alphabet Σ, write |w|_a for the number of occurrences of letter a in w, and call two words u, v abelian-equivalent (u ~_ab v) if they have the same length and |u|_a = |v|_a for every letter a.

Say that a word w encounters the pattern p in the abelian sense if w has a factor of the form w = u · f(p_1) f(p_2) ... f(p_m) · v, where f is a map sending each variable of p to a nonempty word over Σ, such that whenever p_i and p_j denote the same variable, the words f(p_i) and f(p_j) are abelian-equivalent (in particular have the same length).

Question: Determine the computational complexity of the following decision problem. Given as input a pattern p (encoded as a word over a variable alphabet) and a positive integer n (encoded in unary or binary), decide whether the Zimin word Z_n encounters p in the abelian sense.

Let $\mathbb{T}^2 = (\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^2$ with coordinates $(x,y)$, and consider the advection–diffusion equation
$$\partial_t \rho(t,x,y) + U(t,y)\,\partial_x \rho(t,x,y) = \Delta \rho(t,x,y), \qquad t>0,\ (x,y)\in\mathbb{T}^2,$$
where the shear velocity $U:[0,\infty)\times\mathbb{T}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfies $\|U\|_{L^\infty_t L^2_y} := \operatorname{ess\,sup}_{t\geq 0}\Big(\int_{\mathbb{T}} |U(t,y)|^2\,dy\Big)^{1/2} < \infty$. Suppose the initial datum $\rho(0,\cdot)\in L^2(\mathbb{T}^2)$ is nonzero and has zero mean, i.e. $\int_{\mathbb{T}^2}\rho(0,x,y)\,dx\,dy = 0$.

For a function $f\in L^2(\mathbb{T}^2)$ with zero mean, define the homogeneous Sobolev norm
$$\|f\|_{\dot H^{-1}(\mathbb{T}^2)} = \Big(\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^2\setminus\{0\}} |k|^{-2}\,|\hat f(k)|^2\Big)^{1/2}.$$

Let $\rho$ be the weak solution of the equation above. Determine whether one must have
$$\liminf_{t\to\infty} \frac{\|\rho(t,\cdot)\|_{\dot H^{-1}(\mathbb{T}^2)}}{\|\rho(t,\cdot)\|_{L^2(\mathbb{T}^2)}} > 0.$$

\[
\begin{aligned}
\partial_t c + A(y+u)\partial_x c + v\,\partial_y c &= -(c^3 - c - \Delta c),\\
\partial_t u + Ay\,\partial_x u + u\,\partial_x u + v\,\partial_y u + Av &= -\partial_x p + (c^3 - c - \Delta c)\partial_x c + \Delta u,\\

\partial_x u + \partial_y v &= 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
with all functions $2\pi$-periodic in $x$. For an integrable function $f(x,y)$, define the $x$-average and zero-mean projection
\[
\langle f\rangle(y) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{T}} f(x,y)\,dx, \qquad f_{\neq}(x,y) = f(x,y) - \langle f\rangle(y).

\]

Let $D$ be a region in the complex plane bounded by an analytic Jordan curve $C$, and let $\bar D$ denote its closure. For $R>1$, let $E_R$ denote the level region associated with $C$ obtained from the conformal map of the exterior of $\bar D$ onto the exterior of the unit disk (i.e., $E_R$ is the interior of the level curve $C_R$ on which the mapping function has modulus $R$, so that $E_1 = D$).

Suppose $f$ is meromorphic in $E_R$ with infinitely many poles in $E_R \setminus \bar D$, analytic in $D$, and continuous on $\bar D$. Assume further that the $p$-th derivative $f^{(p)}$ exists on $C$ and satisfies a Lipschitz condition of order $\alpha$ on $C$, with $0<\alpha<1$ and $p$ a non-negative integer. For each $n\geq 1$, let $r_n$ denote a best uniform approximation to $f$ on $\bar D$ from the class of rational functions of degree at most $n$ (numerator and denominator each of degree at most $n$), and set
$$E_n(f) = \|f - r_n\|_{\bar D} = \sup_{z\in\bar D} |f(z)-r_n(z)|.$$

The classical polynomial Jackson-type theorem under the same smoothness hypothesis on $f$ gives, for the best polynomial approximations $p_n$ of degree $n$,
$$\|f - p_n\|_{\bar D} \leq \frac{A}{n^{p+\alpha}}$$
for some constant $A$ independent of $n$. The analogous estimate
$$E_n(f) \leq \frac{A}{R^n\, n^{p+\alpha}}$$
(or an appropriate Jackson-type analogue reflecting both the smoothness order $p+\alpha$ and the meromorphy in $E_R$) is known when $f$ is meromorphic in $E_R$ with only finitely many poles.

Question: Does the analogous Jackson-type estimate for best rational approximations $r_n$ remain valid when $f$ is meromorphic in $E_R$ with infinitely many poles?

Let R be an associative (not necessarily unital) ring. Recall that R is called nil if every element of R is nilpotent, i.e., for each r ∈ R there exists a positive integer n (depending on r) with r^n = 0. The Jacobson radical J(S) of a ring S is the intersection of the annihilators of all simple right S-modules; equivalently (for rings without unit, using the quasi-regular formulation) J(S) consists of those s ∈ S such that for every t ∈ S the element s + t + st (and t + s + ts) has a quasi-inverse. A ring S is said to be Jacobson radical (or "radical in Jacobson's sense") if S = J(S), i.e., every element of S is quasi-regular.

Form the polynomial ring R[x] in one commuting indeterminate x over R.

Question: Must R[x] be Jacobson radical whenever R is a nil ring?

Form the polynomial ring R[x] in one commuting indeterminate x over R.

Question: Must R[x] be Jacobson radical whenever R is a nil ring?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

By a theorem of Krempa, the statement "for every nil ring R the polynomial ring R[x] is Jacobson radical" is equivalent to Köthe's conjecture, which remains open as of 2026. Smoktunowicz (2000) constructed a nil ring R for which R[x] is not nil, refuting a stronger conjecture of Amitsur, but this does not settle whether R[x] must be Jacobson radical when R is nil.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

This question is a well-known equivalent formulation of Köthe's conjecture (1930): nilness of $M_n(R)$ for all nil $R$ is equivalent to the standard Köthe conjecture. Despite partial results (true for PI rings, right Noetherian rings, etc.) and a related counterexample by Smoktunowicz disproving Amitsur's stronger conjecture on $J[x]$, the matrix-ring version of Köthe's conjecture remains open.

A ring $R$ (not assumed to have a unit) is called *nil* if every element of $R$ is nilpotent, i.e., for each $r \in R$ there exists a positive integer $k$ (depending on $r$) such that $r^k = 0$. Call a ring $R$ *absolutely nil* if for every integer $n \geq 0$ the polynomial ring $R[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ in $n$ commuting indeterminates over $R$ is again a nil ring (so in particular, taking $n=0$, $R$ itself is nil).

Question: Is every nil ring absolutely nil? Equivalently, does there exist a nil ring $R$ and an integer $n \geq 1$ such that the polynomial ring $R[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ contains a non-nilpotent element?

A ring $R$ (not assumed to have a unit) is called *nil* if every element of $R$ is nilpotent, i.e., for each $r \in R$ there exists a positive integer $k$ (depending on $r$) such that $r^k = 0$. Call a ring $R$ *absolutely nil* if for every integer $n \geq 0$ the polynomial ring $R[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ in $n$ commuting indeterminates over $R$ is again a nil ring (so in particular, taking $n=0$, $R$ itself is nil).

Question: Is every nil ring absolutely nil? Equivalently, does there exist a nil ring $R$ and an integer $n \geq 1$ such that the polynomial ring $R[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ contains a non-nilpotent element?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question is equivalent to Amitsur's problem on whether the polynomial ring R[x] over a nil ring R must be nil. It was solved negatively by A. Smoktunowicz (2000), who constructed a nil algebra R over any countable field such that R[x] is not nil. Hence not every nil ring is absolutely nil.

[{"title": "Polynomial Rings over Nil Rings Need Not Be Nil", "url": "https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021869300984515", "snippet": "Smoktunowicz constructed a nil algebra over a countable field such that the polynomial ring over the algebra is not nil.", "claim": "There exists a nil ring R for which R[x] is not nil, so nil does not imply absolutely nil."}, {"title": "A polynomial ring that is Jacobson radical and not nil", "url": "https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02772627", "snippet": "Smoktunowicz: a polynomial ring that is Jacobson radical and not nil, answering a question of Amitsur.", "claim": "Related construction confirming negative answer to Amitsur-type questions about nil polynomial rings."}]

Let $R$ be an associative ring (not necessarily commutative and not necessarily with unit) that is finitely generated as a ring; that is, there exist finitely many elements $r_1,\dots,r_n \in R$ such that $R$ is the smallest subring of itself containing $r_1,\dots,r_n$. Let $J(R)$ denote the Jacobson radical of $R$, and recall that an ideal $I \trianglelefteq R$ is called nil if every element of $I$ is nilpotent.

Question: Must $J(R)$ be a nil ideal of $R$ for every finitely generated ring $R$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question (often attributed to Amitsur) of whether the Jacobson radical of a finitely generated ring/algebra must be nil is a long-standing open problem connected to Köthe's conjecture. Smoktunowicz constructed a nil algebra whose polynomial ring is Jacobson radical but not nil, refuting a related Amitsur conjecture, but the present question for finitely generated rings is not known to be resolved. No source found that settles it.

Let X be a locally ringed topos, and let D(X) denote the derived category of O_X-modules. Recall that a complex in D^-(X) is pseudo-coherent if it is locally quasi-isomorphic to a bounded-above complex of finitely generated free O_X-modules, and is perfect if it is locally quasi-isomorphic to a bounded complex of finitely generated free O_X-modules. Let K'(X) denote the Grothendieck group of perfect complexes on X (the free abelian group on quasi-isomorphism classes modulo the relations [B] = [A] + [C] for every distinguished triangle A → B → C → A[1]), with ring structure induced by derived tensor product, and let K'_naif(X) denote the Grothendieck ring of locally free O_X-modules of finite rank.

Question: Does there exist, functorially in X, a family of exterior-power operations Λ^i (i ≥ 0) defined on the derived category D(X) such that:

(1) Λ^i sends pseudo-coherent complexes to pseudo-coherent complexes and perfect complexes to perfect complexes;

(2) Λ^i is compatible with distinguished triangles and with the translation functor L → L[1] in a manner that induces well-defined operations on the Grothendieck group;

(3) the induced operations endow K'(X) with the structure of a λ-ring; and

(4) the canonical map K'_naif(X) → K'(X) is a homomorphism of λ-rings?

In particular, can a known construction (in the case where the structure sheaf O_X satisfies a restrictive hypothesis, such as containing Q or being suitably flat) be refined so as to remove all hypotheses on O_X?

Let f : X → Y be a proper morphism of ringed spaces (or, more generally, of ringed topoi). Recall that an object L of the derived category D(O_X) is said to be pseudo-coherent relative to Y if, locally on X, it is quasi-isomorphic to a bounded-above complex of finitely generated free O_X-modules whose formation is compatible with base change on Y (equivalently, L is m-pseudo-coherent relative to Y for every integer m). Let Rf_* : D(O_X) → D(O_Y) denote the total derived direct image functor.

(a) Suppose L on X is pseudo-coherent relative to Y. Is the derived direct image Rf_*(L) pseudo-coherent on Y?

(b) Can such an algebraic finiteness statement be used to prove a Grauert-type coherence theorem (the higher direct images of a coherent analytic sheaf under a proper holomorphic map of complex spaces are coherent) under substantially more general hypotheses, in particular for topologically ringed base spaces, or for topoi over complex algebras?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The algebraic version of the conjecture has been established in increasing generality: for proper morphisms of Noetherian schemes (SGA 6 / Stacks Project), and recent work on relative perfect/pseudo-coherent complexes extends finiteness of Rf_* for relatively pseudo-coherent complexes to quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes and beyond. The full conjecture in the topos-theoretic / topologically ringed setting, and its use to deduce Grauert's theorem under substantially more general hypotheses, does not appear fully resolved; a 2025 differential-geometric proof of Grauert's theorem and ongoing work on almost-coherence of higher direct images suggest the broader program remains active.

representations.normalized:
Let $X$ be a Noetherian scheme admitting an ample invertible sheaf, and let $f \colon Y \hookrightarrow X$ be a regular closed immersion of codimension $d$ with conormal sheaf $\mathcal{N} = \mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2$, where $\mathcal{I}$ is the sheaf of ideals defining $Y$. Let $K'(Y)$ denote the Grothendieck group of coherent sheaves on $Y$, $K(X)$ the Grothendieck group of locally free sheaves on $X$, and $A(X) = \bigoplus_i A^i(X)$ the Chow ring of $X$ for rational equivalence. The proper pushforward $f_* \colon K'(Y) \to K(X)$ is defined since $X$ has an ample invertible sheaf.

The classical Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch theorem expresses the Chern character of $f_*(y)$, for $y \in K'(Y)$, in $A(X) \otimes \mathbb{Q}$ as
$$\mathrm{ch}(f_*(y)) = f_*\bigl(\mathrm{ch}(y) \cdot \mathrm{td}(\mathcal{N}^{\vee})^{-1}\bigr),$$
which a priori requires inverting the integers because of the Todd class.

Question. Prove (or disprove) the following denominator-free Riemann–Roch formula: for every $i \ge 0$ and every $y \in K'(Y)$, there is a universal polynomial expression $P_{d,i}$ with integer coefficients in the Chern classes of $\mathcal{N}$ and of a representative of $y$ such that the Chern class $c_i(f_*(y)) \in A(X)$ (with rational, not merely algebraic, equivalence) is given by
$$c_i(f_*(y)) = f_*\bigl(P_{d,i}(c_*(\mathcal{N}), c_*(y))\bigr),$$
i.e., an integral identity in $A(X)$ that does not require tensoring with $\mathbb{Q}$ nor passing to a coarser equivalence relation. In particular, establish this in the first nontrivial case $i = d = 2$.

A denominator-free Riemann–Roch formula for regular closed immersions was proved by P. Jouanolou in November 1969 and subsequently developed in SGA 6 (Exposé XIV by Jouanolou), giving an integral formula for the Chern classes of $f_*(y)$ in the Chow ring. The result is therefore considered solved.

Let $k$ be a field and let $f\colon Y\hookrightarrow X$ be a closed immersion of smooth quasi-projective $k$-schemes, of pure codimension $d$. Let $N=N_{Y/X}$ denote the conormal sheaf of $Y$ in $X$ (a locally free $\mathcal O_Y$-module of rank $d$), and write $c_d(N)\in A^d(Y)$ for its top Chern class in the Chow ring $A^\bullet(Y)$ of $Y$. Let $f_*\colon A^\bullet(Y)\to A^{\bullet+d}(X)$ and $f^*\colon A^\bullet(X)\to A^\bullet(Y)$ be the proper pushforward and the (Gysin) pullback, and let $[Y]=\mathrm{cl}(Y)\in A^d(X)$ denote the cycle class of $Y$.

(a) (Self-intersection formula in the Chow ring.) Prove that
$$f^*\,\mathrm{cl}(Y) \;=\; c_d(N) \quad \text{in } A^d(Y).$$

(b) (Excess-intersection / projection-type formula.) Prove that for every $y\in A^\bullet(Y)$,
$$f^*f_*(y) \;=\; y\cdot c_d(N) \quad \text{in } A^\bullet(Y).$$

(c) (Blow-up formula.) Let $\pi\colon X'\to X$ be the blow-up of $X$ along $Y$, with exceptional divisor $E=\mathbb P(N)\to Y$. Determine the Chow ring $A^\bullet(X')$: prove that there is a natural isomorphism
$$A^\bullet(X')\;\cong\; A^\bullet(X)\oplus \bigoplus_{i=1}^{d-1} A^{\bullet-i}(Y)\,\xi^{\,i-1}\!,$$
compatible with the analogous decomposition for $E$, where $\xi$ is the first Chern class of the tautological line bundle on $\mathbb P(N)$, and describe explicitly the multiplicative structure.

(d) Establish the analogous formulas in $\ell$-adic étale cohomology $H^\bullet(\,\cdot\,,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (and, when applicable, with $\mathbb Z_\ell$-coefficients including torsion): namely the corresponding self-intersection, excess-intersection, and blow-up formulas.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The self-intersection and excess-intersection formulas in the Chow ring, as well as the Chow ring of a blow-up along a smooth center, are now standard theorems, established by Mumford, Jouanolou, Verdier, and exposed in Fulton's "Intersection Theory" (1984), with the blow-up formula in Chapter 6 and the self-intersection formula (Cor. 6.3) holding integrally. The corresponding $\ell$-adic cohomological formulas follow from SGA 5/SGA 6 and are also standard.

Let X be an arbitrary scheme and ℓ a prime number invertible on X (i.e. distinct from all residue characteristics of X). Let K'(X) denote the Grothendieck group of coherent sheaves on X (or, equivalently for regular X, the K-theory of locally free sheaves), equipped with the λ-operations and the associated γ-filtration. Denote by Gr'(X) the graded ring associated with this λ-(γ-)filtration on K'(X). Let H^{2*}(X, ℤ_ℓ(*)) = ⊕_{i ≥ 0} H^{2i}(X, ℤ_ℓ(i)) be the integral ℓ-adic cohomology ring of X (in the sense of SGA 5), and let c_i^{ét}(E) ∈ H^{2i}(X, ℤ_ℓ(i)) denote the ℓ-adic Chern classes of a locally free sheaf E.

Question: Does there exist a graded ring homomorphism
   g^* : Gr'(X) ⟶ H^{2*}(X, ℤ_ℓ(*))
such that, for every locally free module E on X and every i ≥ 0, the component g^i sends the class in Gr^i'(X) of the Chern class c_i(E) (defined via λ-operations) to the ℓ-adic cohomological Chern class c_i^{ét}(E)?

In particular: can the third graded component g^3 be constructed integrally? It is known a priori only that 2·g^3 can be defined (via the Adams operation ψ^3); the question is whether g^3 itself exists as an integral map without inverting 2 or any other torsion.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $h:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ be a primitive morphism, i.e. a monoid homomorphism whose incidence (composition) matrix $M_h\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{\Sigma\times\Sigma}$, defined by $(M_h)_{a,b}=|h(b)|_a$ (the number of occurrences of letter $a$ in $h(b)$), is primitive (some power has all entries strictly positive). Suppose $a\in\Sigma$ satisfies $h(a)=au$ for some non-empty $u$, so that $h$ admits the infinite fixed point $h^\infty(a)=\lim_{n\to\infty}h^n(a)\in\Sigma^\omega$.

A template $t$ over $\Sigma$ is, in the standard sense of abelian pattern realization, a finite combinatorial object specifying constraints on the Parikh vectors of factors of an infinite word; one says that $h^\infty(a)$ realizes $t$ if there exists a factorization of some factor of $h^\infty(a)$ whose Parikh vectors satisfy the linear/affine constraints encoded by $t$ (this captures abelian repetitions, abelian-$k$-powers, additive powers, and similar abelian patterns).

It is known that whenever every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $M_h$ satisfies $|\lambda|\neq 1$, there is an algorithm that, given $h$ and any template $t$, decides whether $h^\infty(a)$ realizes $t$.

Question: Is there an algorithm which, on input a primitive morphism $h$ (with a fixed point $h^\infty(a)$) whose matrix $M_h$ is allowed to have eigenvalues of complex norm $1$, together with a template $t$, decides whether $h^\infty(a)$ realizes $t$? Equivalently, can the hypothesis "$M_h$ has no eigenvalue of norm $1$" be removed from the above decidability result?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question appears as an explicitly listed open problem in the WORDS-conference open-problems compilation (arXiv:1705.04055 / hal-02355621). The underlying decidability result of Rao and Rosenfeld (2015) requires the no-eigenvalue-of-norm-1 hypothesis, and recent surveys on abelian combinatorics on words still list the eigenvalue-of-norm-1 case as unresolved. No source verifying a resolution was found.

Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a proper local complete intersection morphism of (Noetherian) schemes of virtual relative dimension $d$, and let $\ell$ be a prime invertible on the base. Write $H^n(-,\mathbb{Q}_\ell(j))$ for $\ell$-adic étale cohomology with Tate twists, $\mathrm{Gr}^{\bullet}(-)_{\mathbb{Q}}$ for the rationalized graded $K$-theory associated with the $\gamma$-filtration on $K_0$ (or its analogue $K'_0$ for coherent sheaves), $\mathrm{ch}\colon \mathrm{Gr}^{\bullet}(-)_{\mathbb{Q}}\to H^{2\bullet}(-,\mathbb{Q}_\ell(\bullet))$ for the $\ell$-adic Chern character, and $\mathrm{Td}(f)$ for the Todd class of the virtual relative tangent complex of $f$.

(a) Construct a cohomological Gysin homomorphism
$$f_*\colon H^n(X,\mathbb{Q}_\ell(j))\longrightarrow H^{n-2d}(Y,\mathbb{Q}_\ell(j-d))$$
attached to such an $f$, satisfying the expected functorial properties (covariance under composition, compatibility with proper base change, projection formula, and agreement with the known constructions in the smooth-proper and regular-closed-immersion cases).

(b) Establish the cohomological Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch formula by proving that the diagram
$$
\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathrm{Gr}^{\bullet}(X)_{\mathbb{Q}} & \xrightarrow{\mathrm{ch}(-)\cdot \mathrm{Td}(f)} & H^{2\bullet}(X,\mathbb{Q}_\ell(\bullet)) \\
\big\downarrow f_* & & \big\downarrow f_* \\
\mathrm{Gr}^{\bullet}(Y)_{\mathbb{Q}} & \xrightarrow{\mathrm{ch}} & H^{2\bullet}(Y,\mathbb{Q}_\ell(\bullet))
\end{array}
$$
commutes.

(c) More generally, show that whenever such a cohomological Gysin map $f_*$ has been defined (in any partial setting), the analogous square commutes.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Constructions of ℓ-adic / étale cohomological Gysin maps for local complete intersection morphisms have been carried out (e.g., via Gabber's localized cycle classes, and in the motivic/étale framework by Déglise, Jin, Khan and others), and cohomological Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch–type statements have been proven in increasing generality, including for projective lci morphisms between finite-dimensional Noetherian schemes (Navarro; Hoyois; Khan). Thus the question has been substantially answered in many settings, though a fully general unified treatment matching the original formulation continues to be developed.

Let $\ell$ be a prime and let $Y$ be a Noetherian scheme on which $\ell$ is invertible (or, in the second part, a projective scheme over $\mathbb{C}$). Let $X \subset Y$ be a closed local complete intersection of pure codimension $i$. For a coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ on $Y$, let $c_j(\mathcal{F}) \in H^{2j}(Y,\mathbb{Z}_\ell(j))$ denote its $\ell$-adic Chern classes.

(a) Does there exist an integral cohomology class $\gamma(X) \in H^{2i}(Y,\mathbb{Z}_\ell(i))$, functorial in the pair $(X,Y)$, with the property that for two local complete intersections $X_1, X_2 \subset Y$ meeting properly (i.e., with no excess components), the class of their scheme-theoretic intersection satisfies
$$\gamma(X_1 \cap X_2) = \gamma(X_1) \smile \gamma(X_2)?$$

(b) Equivalently, is the Chern class $c_i(\mathcal{O}_X) \in H^{2i}(Y,\mathbb{Z}_\ell(i))$ always divisible by $(i-1)!$?

(c) As the simplest nontrivial test case, let $Y$ be a projective three-dimensional scheme over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $X$ consist of a single (possibly singular) closed point of $Y$. Is $c_3(\mathcal{O}_X) \in H^6(Y,\mathbb{Z}_2(3))$ divisible by $2$, and in particular is its reduction in $H^6(Y,\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})$ equal to zero?

Let X be a scheme and let L^· be a perfect complex of O_X-modules (i.e., a complex Zariski-locally quasi-isomorphic to a bounded complex of locally free O_X-modules of finite rank). For a prime ℓ invertible on X, one has the ℓ-adic cohomology groups H^{2i}(X, Z_ℓ(i)). For a locally free O_X-module of finite rank, classical Chern classes c_i ∈ H^{2i}(X, Z_ℓ(i)) are defined (e.g. via the projective bundle formula).

(a) Construct, for every perfect complex L^· on X, Chern classes c_i(L^·) ∈ H^{2i}(X, Z_ℓ(i)) for i ≥ 0, in a way that:
   (i) when L^· is concentrated in degree 0 and is a locally free O_X-module of finite rank, c_i(L^·) coincides with the classical Chern classes;
   (ii) the construction is functorial under pullback along morphisms of schemes;
   (iii) it is additive on distinguished triangles in the sense of the Whitney sum formula: c(L^·) = c(L'^·) · c(L''^·) in the total Chern class for any distinguished triangle L'^· → L^· → L''^· → L'^·[1].

(b) Carry out an analogous construction for perfect complexes on a general locally ringed topos, with values in a suitable cohomology theory.

(c) In the topological setting, let X be a paracompact topological space ringed by the sheaf of continuous complex-valued functions, and let L^· be a perfect complex of modules over this sheaf of rings. Define Chern classes c_i(L^·) ∈ H^{2i}(X, Z) in ordinary integral singular cohomology, generalizing the classical topological Chern classes of complex vector bundles, satisfying functoriality and the Whitney sum formula on distinguished triangles.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem of defining Chern classes for perfect complexes was resolved by L. Illusie in the framework of Hodge cohomology, and subsequent work (e.g. Gillet's "Riemann-Roch theorems for higher algebraic K-theory", and later constructions via K-theory and motivic cohomology) provides Chern classes of perfect complexes in ℓ-adic and other cohomology theories. The topological analogue is also handled via topological K-theory of perfect complexes. The problem is therefore considered (at least partially) solved.
