Let $\mathbb{C}^* = \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}$. A polynomial $p \in \mathbb{C}[x,y]$ is called primitive if it cannot be written in the form $p = q \circ r$ for some polynomials $r \in \mathbb{C}[x,y]$ and $q \in \mathbb{C}[t]$ with $\deg q \geq 2$; equivalently, the generic fiber of the map $p \colon \mathbb{C}^2 	o \mathbb{C}$ is irreducible. For $c \in \mathbb{C}$, the fiber of $p$ at $c$ is the affine algebraic curve $p^{-1}(c) = \{(x,y) \in \mathbb{C}^2 : p(x,y) = c\}$.

Declare two polynomials $p, p' \in \mathbb{C}[x,y]$ equivalent if there exist a polynomial automorphism $\Phi$ of $\mathbb{C}^2$ (an element of the affine Cremona group, i.e., a polynomial map $\mathbb{C}^2 	o \mathbb{C}^2$ with polynomial inverse) and an affine automorphism $\alpha(t) = at + b$ of $\mathbb{C}$ (with $a \in \mathbb{C}^*$, $b \in \mathbb{C}$) such that
$$p'(x,y) = \alpha igl(p(\Phi(x,y)) igr).$$

Problem. Produce an explicit list $\mathcal{L}$ of pairwise non-equivalent primitive polynomials in $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ such that every primitive polynomial $p \in \mathbb{C}[x,y]$ admitting at least one fiber $p^{-1}(c)$ isomorphic (as an affine algebraic variety) to $\mathbb{C}^*$ is equivalent, in the above sense, to exactly one polynomial of $\mathcal{L}$.

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth four-dimensional Lorentzian manifold satisfying the vacuum Einstein equations $\mathrm{Ric}(g)=0$. A Regge spacetime is a four-dimensional piecewise linear manifold $(K,\ell)$ obtained by gluing flat Lorentzian 4-simplices along their tetrahedral faces, where the geometry is specified entirely by the assignment $\ell$ of squared edge lengths to the 1-simplices of $K$; curvature is concentrated as conical defects (deficit angles) on the 2-simplices ("bones"), and the Regge equations of motion are obtained by varying the Regge action $S_R(K,\ell)=\tfrac{1}{8\pi G}\sum_{\sigma^2}A(\sigma^2)\,\varepsilon(\sigma^2)$, where $A(\sigma^2)$ is the area of the bone $\sigma^2$ and $\varepsilon(\sigma^2)$ its deficit angle.

(a) Formulate and prove a precise sense in which a sequence $\{(K_n,\ell_n)\}_{n\ge 1}$ of Regge spacetimes satisfying the Regge equations of motion converges, as the simplicial refinement is increased (e.g., the maximal edge length tends to zero, subject to suitable non-degeneracy/fatness conditions on the simplices), to a smooth solution $(M,g)$ of the vacuum Einstein equations. Specify in what topology or measure-theoretic sense the discrete metric data $\ell_n$, the associated curvature distributions, and the Regge action approximate $g$, the Riemann/Ricci tensor of $g$, and the Einstein–Hilbert action of $g$.

(b) Formulate and prove an analogous convergence statement for spacetimes produced by numerical relativity: given a convergent family of numerical solutions to a well-posed formulation of the Einstein evolution equations on a sequence of grids with resolution tending to zero, identify the appropriate function-space topology and norms in which the numerical spacetimes approach a smooth (or suitably regular) vacuum solution, together with explicit convergence rates.

Several partial results are known: Cheeger–Müller–Schrader proved that the Regge action and curvature converge in the sense of measures to their continuum counterparts under fatness conditions on the simplices; Barrett established a convergence criterion in the linearized regime; and more recent works (e.g., on the definition of curvature in Regge calculus, 2024) refine these. representations.normalized:
Setup. Let $b:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded Borel vector field with bounded distributional divergence. A regular Lagrangian flow associated to $b$ is a Borel map $X:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ such that:
(i) for $\mathcal{L}^d$-a.e. $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$, the curve $t\mapsto X(t,x)$ is absolutely continuous and solves $\dot X(t,x)=b(t,X(t,x))$ with $X(0,x)=x$;
(ii) there exists $L\geq 0$ such that $X(t,\cdot)_\#\mathcal{L}^d\leq L\,\mathcal{L}^d$ for every $t\in[0,T]$.

Differentiability in measure. Say that $X(t,\cdot)$ is differentiable in measure at scale $r\to 0$ if there exists a measurable map $W(t,\cdot):\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ such that, for every $t\in[0,T]$, the difference quotients
$$\frac{X(t,x+rh)-X(t,x)}{r}\longrightarrow W(t,x)\,h\qquad(r\to 0)$$
converge locally in measure on $\mathbb{R}^d$, uniformly with respect to $h$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}^d$.

Approximate differentiability. The map $X(t,\cdot)$ is approximately differentiable at $x$ if there exists a linear map $L_x:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ such that the set $\{y:|X(t,y)-X(t,x)-L_x(y-x)|\leq \varepsilon |y-x|\}$ has density $1$ at $x$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

Assumption. It is known that when $b\in L^1_t(W^{1,p}_{x,\mathrm{loc}})$ with $p>1$ (the Sobolev case), the regular Lagrangian flow $X(t,\cdot)$ is differentiable in measure in the above sense.

Problem. Determine the precise relationship between differentiability in measure of the regular Lagrangian flow $X(t,\cdot)$ and other weak differentiability notions for $X(t,\cdot)$, in particular approximate differentiability. Specifically: does differentiability in measure of $X(t,\cdot)$ imply approximate differentiability $\mathcal{L}^d$-almost everywhere, or conversely, and under what additional hypotheses on $b$?

Subsequent work has obtained approximate differentiability of regular Lagrangian flows in several settings (e.g. Sobolev and BV cases, including 2D autonomous vector fields and nearly incompressible BV fields), and clarified that classical approximate differentiability is strictly stronger than differentiability in measure. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$, and let $A$ be an Artin local $k$-algebra that is finite-dimensional as a $k$-vector space. Write $\ell(M)$ for the length of a finitely generated $A$-module $M$, and let $\Omega^{1}_{A/k}$ denote the module of Kähler differentials of $A$ over $k$. Determine whether the following two statements hold:

(a) $\ell(\Omega^{1}_{A/k}) \ge \ell(A) - 1$.

(b) Equality $\ell(\Omega^{1}_{A/k}) = \ell(A) - 1$ holds if and only if $A$ is isomorphic, as a $k$-algebra, to $k[x]/(x^{n})$ for some integer $n \ge 1$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

This is the Artinian form of Berger's conjecture (the "Artin–Berger conjecture") studied by Cortiñas, Geller, and Weibel; they established it in a number of cases, but the general statement (and the original Berger conjecture for one-dimensional local rings, which it would imply in characteristic 0) remains open. Recent work (e.g., Huneke–Iyengar et al., 2022) continues to extend known cases but does not resolve the full conjecture.

Let $(M,g)$ be a globally hyperbolic spacetime, i.e., a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian manifold admitting a Cauchy hypersurface. A spacelike Cauchy hypersurface $\Sigma \subset M$ is called maximal if its mean curvature with respect to the future-directed timelike unit normal vanishes identically. Assume that the stress-energy tensor $T_{ab}$ of $(M,g)$ (via the Einstein equations $G_{ab} = 8\pi T_{ab}$, or directly as a symmetric 2-tensor) satisfies the dominant energy condition: for every future-directed causal vector $v^a$, the vector $-T^a{}_b v^b$ is future-directed causal.

Prove (or disprove) the following uniqueness statement: under the dominant energy condition alone — without assuming the timelike convergence condition ($\mathrm{Ric}(v,v) \geq 0$ for all timelike $v$) and without assuming the existence of a timelike Killing vector field on $(M,g)$ — any two maximal Cauchy hypersurfaces in $(M,g)$ must coincide (or, more generally, characterize the situations in which uniqueness fails).

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Classical uniqueness results for maximal Cauchy hypersurfaces (e.g., Brill–Flaherty, Marsden–Tipler) require the timelike convergence condition or a timelike Killing field. Recent work on initial data rigidity under the dominant energy condition (e.g., Hirsch–Kazaras–Khuri–Zhang and related results) addresses rigidity aspects of DEC, but a general uniqueness theorem for maximal Cauchy hypersurfaces under DEC alone does not appear to be established in the literature found. Status remains unclear.

Let $b: [0,T]\times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ be a (possibly time-dependent) vector field with bounded divergence (or, more generally, nearly incompressible), and let $X(t,\cdot)$ denote the associated regular Lagrangian flow, i.e. a Borel map satisfying $\partial_t X(t,y) = b(t,X(t,y))$ for a.e. $y$, with $X(0,y)=y$, and such that $X(t,\cdot)_\# \mathcal{L}^d \le C \mathcal{L}^d$ uniformly in $t$.

For Sobolev vector fields $b(t,\cdot) \in W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with $p>1$, the regular Lagrangian flow is known to enjoy several regularity properties, in particular approximate differentiability and differentiability in measure in the sense of Ambrosio–Malý: there exists a measurable matrix-valued map $W(t,y)$ such that
$$\frac{X(t,y+rz)-X(t,y)}{r} \;\longrightarrow\; W(t,y)\,z \qquad \text{in measure as } r\to 0.$$

Question: Do these differentiability-in-measure and related regularity properties of the regular Lagrangian flow continue to hold in the borderline cases $b(t,\cdot) \in W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ or $b(t,\cdot) \in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ (with bounded divergence, or nearly incompressible)?

A 2022/2023 result (Bohun–Bouchut–Crippa style line, and notably Bianchini–Bonicatto and collaborators) established differentiability in measure of the flow associated with a nearly incompressible BV vector field, in the sense of Ambrosio–Malý, with a BV derivative. This resolves the BV borderline case for differentiability in measure under the nearly incompressible assumption. Quantitative estimates and partial regularity results for BV vector fields with bounded divergence have also been obtained. The W^{1,1} borderline case and full extension of all related regularity results remain only partially addressed.

Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero, and let $R$ be a finitely generated factorial (i.e., unique factorization) $K$-domain. Let $L = Q(R)$ denote the field of fractions of $R$, and let $\delta\colon R \to R$ be a $K$-derivation, extended uniquely to a $K$-derivation of $L$, still denoted $\delta$.

A nonzero element $f \in R$ is called a $\delta$-integral factor (in $R$) if there exists $g \in R$ with $\delta(f) = g f$; equivalently, the logarithmic derivative $\delta(f)/f$ lies in $R$. A nonzero element $h \in L$ is called a $\delta$-integral factor in $L$ if $\delta(h)/h \in R$. The set $X_\delta$ of $\delta$-integral factors in $R$, taken modulo units of $R$, forms a commutative monoid under multiplication, and the set $\widetilde{X}_\delta$ of $\delta$-integral factors in $L$, taken modulo units of $R$, forms an abelian group under multiplication (its elements being represented by quotients $f_1/f_2$ of $\delta$-integral factors $f_1, f_2 \in R$).

Question: Must $\widetilde{X}_\delta$ be a finitely generated abelian group?

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth, time-oriented, globally hyperbolic, asymptotically flat spacetime of dimension $3+1$ satisfying the dominant energy condition. Recall that a Cauchy hypersurface $\Sigma \subset M$ is a smooth spacelike hypersurface that is met exactly once by every inextendible causal curve in $M$. The hypersurface $\Sigma$ is said to be "without horizons" if it contains no apparent horizons, i.e., no compact two-surface in $\Sigma$ on which the outgoing null expansion vanishes (so $\Sigma$ contains no trapped or marginally trapped surfaces). A Cauchy hypersurface $\Sigma$ is called maximal if its mean curvature (with respect to the future-pointing unit normal in $M$) vanishes identically, and $\Sigma$ is asymptotic at spatial infinity to a hyperplane of constant time in the asymptotic Minkowski coordinates.

Question: If $(M,g)$ admits a Cauchy hypersurface without horizons (in the sense above), must $(M,g)$ contain a maximal Cauchy hypersurface?

Let $M$ be a closed orientable hyperbolic 3-manifold. Say that $M$ admits a prime $p$ as a branching order if there exists a knot $K \subset S^3$ such that $M$ is the $p$-fold cyclic branched covering of $S^3$ branched along $K$. Investigate the following:

(a) For how many distinct primes $p$ can $M$ admit $p$ as a branching order?

(b) Is there a universal upper bound (independent of $M$) on the number of such primes?

(c) When $M$ admits several such primes $p_1, p_2, \dots$ with corresponding knots $K_1, K_2, \dots \subset S^3$, describe the possible relationships among the knots $K_i$.

(d) Determine which finite groups can arise as the full isometry group $\mathrm{Isom}(M)$ of a closed hyperbolic 3-manifold $M$ that is a $p$-fold cyclic branched covering of a knot in $S^3$ for some prime $p$.

(c) When $M$ admits several such primes $p_1, p_2, \dots$ with corresponding knots $K_1, K_2, \dots \subset S^3$, describe the possible relationships among the knots $K_i$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Substantial progress is known: results of Boileau–Paoluzzi, Reni–Zimmermann and others establish that a closed irreducible 3-manifold (not S^3) can be a p-fold cyclic branched covering of a knot in S^3 for at most six distinct odd primes p, and a hyperbolic 3-manifold can be a cyclic branched cover of at most fifteen inequivalent knots in S^3. Examples realizing three distinct odd primes are known. However, the sharp bounds, the exact list of possible isometry groups, and a complete description of how the knots are related remain open in general, so the problem is partially solved.

Does there exist a Lorentzian manifold (M, g) of dimension at least 4 with the following properties simultaneously?

(i) (M, g) is time-oriented and inextendible (there is no isometric embedding of (M, g) as a proper open subset into a strictly larger connected time-oriented Lorentzian manifold of the same dimension).

(ii) (M, g) is timelike geodesically complete, i.e. every affinely parametrized timelike geodesic extends to all values of its affine parameter in R.

(iii) (M, g) satisfies a (non-trivial) energy condition such as the null energy condition Ric(v,v) ≥ 0 for all null vectors v, or the strong energy condition Ric(v,v) ≥ 0 for all timelike vectors v.

(iv) (M, g) contains an acausal, edgeless spacelike hypersurface Σ (a partial Cauchy surface).

(v) Σ contains a closed (compact without boundary) spacelike submanifold S of codimension 2 that is a trapped surface, meaning that both families of future-directed null geodesics issuing orthogonally from S have everywhere negative mean curvature (i.e., both null mean curvatures of S are everywhere negative).

Equivalently, does there exist an example showing that one cannot drop the global hyperbolicity hypothesis from Penrose-type singularity theorems while keeping inextendibility, an energy condition, a partial Cauchy surface, and a trapped surface, and still force timelike geodesic incompleteness?

Penrose-type singularity theorems show that a globally hyperbolic spacetime satisfying an energy condition and containing a noncompact Cauchy surface together with a trapped surface must be timelike geodesically incomplete. Without global hyperbolicity (only assuming a partial Cauchy surface) and with inextendibility imposed, the existence/nonexistence of such a complete example remains a recognized open question in mathematical relativity; recent surveys and rigidity results (e.g., on rigid singularity theorems and trapped sets in globally hyperbolic spacetimes) do not appear to resolve this version. No source found that explicitly closes the problem.

Specifically, determine for each degree $d \geq 1$ and each prescribed collection of topological types of cusp singularities whether there exists such a curve $C \subset \mathbb{P}^2$ of degree $d$ with geometric genus $0$ (respectively $1$) realizing the prescribed cusps, and describe all such curves up to projective equivalence.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The full classification remains open. Substantial progress has been made: Koras and Palka proved that every rational cuspidal plane curve has at most four cusps via the almost minimal model program; complete classifications exist in special cases (e.g., rational unicuspidal curves with one Puiseux pair, by Fernández de Bobadilla–Luengo–Melle-Hernández–Némethi). However, a complete classification of rational (and elliptic) cuspidal plane curves of arbitrary degree and singularity type is still not achieved and is widely regarded as a difficult open problem.

Let $(M^{n+1}, g)$ be a cosmological spacetime, that is, a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold admitting a compact Cauchy hypersurface. Assume that $(M,g)$ satisfies the timelike convergence condition, $\mathrm{Ric}(X,X) \ge 0$ for every timelike vector $X$.

Recall the following notions:
- (Condition G) Every inextendible timelike geodesic in $(M,g)$ has both past and future endpoints on the "cosmological boundary" in the sense that no incomplete timelike geodesic ray escapes to a "hidden" portion of the spacetime; equivalently, the spacetime contains no timelike line confined to a region invisible from any Cauchy surface (a "hidden infinity").
- A hidden infinity is a region of $(M,g)$ where future or past inextendible causal geodesics fail to be captured by the family of Cauchy surfaces, allowing observers/geodesics to "escape" without completing.
- A trapped surface is a compact spacelike codimension-2 submanifold $\Sigma \subset M$ whose two future-directed null mean curvature vectors are both past-directed timelike (i.e., both null expansions are negative).

Prove the following:

(a) If condition (G) fails, or if $(M,g)$ contains a hidden infinity, then $(M,g)$ contains a trapped surface.

(b) Consequently, any cosmological spacetime satisfying the timelike convergence condition is either timelike geodesically incomplete, or it splits isometrically as a metric product $(\mathbb{R} \times N, -dt^2 \oplus h)$ for some compact Riemannian manifold $(N,h)$ and is static.

Let $M$ be a closed orientable hyperbolic 3-manifold. A hyperelliptic isometry of $M$ is an orientation-preserving isometry $\varphi : M \to M$ of finite order such that the quotient orbifold $M/\langle \varphi \rangle$ has underlying space the 3-sphere $S^3$ (so that $\varphi$ exhibits $M$ as a cyclic branched covering of $S^3$ along the branching link).

(a) Determine which prime numbers can occur as orders of hyperelliptic isometries of some closed hyperbolic 3-manifold $M$, and, for a fixed $M$, bound the number of distinct primes $p$ such that $M$ admits a hyperelliptic isometry of order $p$.

(b) Decide whether there exists a uniform constant $N$, independent of $M$, such that the number of distinct primes occurring as orders of hyperelliptic isometries of any closed hyperbolic 3-manifold $M$ is at most $N$.

(c) Classify the non-solvable finite groups that can arise as the full orientation-preserving isometry group $\mathrm{Isom}^+(M)$ of a closed hyperbolic 3-manifold $M$ admitting at least one hyperelliptic isometry.

Determine $N$: what is the maximal possible number of cusps on a rational cuspidal plane curve?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The exact maximum is not known. Tono proved that a rational cuspidal plane curve has at most 8 cusps, and Orevkov (2017) gave a remark/improvement on Tono's theorem. The largest number of cusps realized by known examples is 4, and it is widely conjectured (Piontkowski and others) that 4 is the true maximum, but this remains unproven. Hence the problem is partially solved with an upper bound of 8 and conjectural value 4.

The two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture asserts that if $f,g\in\mathbb{C}[X,Y]$ satisfy $\det\begin{pmatrix}f_X & f_Y\\ g_X & g_Y\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{C}^{*}$, then the map $(X,Y)\mapsto(f(X,Y),g(X,Y))$ is a polynomial automorphism of $\mathbb{C}^2$ (equivalently, $\mathbb{C}[f,g]=\mathbb{C}[X,Y]$). A counterexample would be a pair $(f,g)\in\mathbb{C}[X,Y]^2$ with nonzero constant Jacobian for which $\mathbb{C}[f,g]\subsetneq\mathbb{C}[X,Y]$.

Let $R\subset\mathbb{C}[X,Y]$ denote the $\mathbb{C}$-subalgebra
$$R=\mathbb{C}[\,Y,\;XY,\;X^{2}Y,\;X^{3}Y-X\,].$$

Prove that there does not exist a counterexample $(f,g)$ to the two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture with $f\in R$ and $g\in R$. That is, show that any pair $f,g\in R$ whose Jacobian determinant is a nonzero constant must satisfy $\mathbb{C}[f,g]=\mathbb{C}[X,Y]$.

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth manifold $M$ equipped with a Lorentzian metric $g$ of low regularity — either continuous ($C^0$) or Hölder-continuous ($C^{0,\alpha}$ for some $0<\alpha<1$) — and assume that $(M,g)$ is time-oriented and globally hyperbolic so that, between causally related points $p \le q$, length-maximizing causal curves exist.

A locally Lipschitz curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ is called timelike if its tangent vector is timelike almost everywhere, and length-maximizing between its endpoints if its Lorentzian length $L(\gamma)=\int_a^b \sqrt{-g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)}\,dt$ equals the time-separation $\tau(\gamma(a),\gamma(b))=\sup\{L(\sigma):\sigma\text{ future-directed causal from }\gamma(a)\text{ to }\gamma(b)\}$.

Address the following:

(a) For Lorentzian metrics $g$ of regularity $C^0$ or $C^{0,\alpha}$ ($0<\alpha<1$), determine whether the length-maximizing timelike geodesic between two chronologically related points $p\ll q$ is unique. That is, decide whether there can exist two distinct (up to reparametrization) length-maximizing future-directed timelike curves from $p$ to $q$, and characterize the regularity threshold at which uniqueness fails.

(b) Analogously, study the timelike geodesic initial-value problem: given a point $p\in M$ and a future-directed timelike vector $v\in T_pM$, decide whether there exists a unique inextendible locally length-maximizing timelike geodesic with initial data $(p,v)$ in the low-regularity setting.

(c) Provide a physical interpretation of nonuniqueness phenomena from (a) and (b) in the context of general relativity, and determine whether such nonuniqueness of geodesics (timelike worldlines of freely falling observers) should be regarded as a singularity of the spacetime $(M,g)$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Partial results exist. For globally hyperbolic continuous Lorentzian metrics, length-maximizing causal curves between causally related points are known to exist (Sämann and others). For metrics of Hölder class $C^{0,\alpha}$ or $C^{1,\alpha}$ with $\alpha<1$, solutions of the geodesic equation may fail to be local maximizers and the initial-value problem need not have unique solutions, so nonuniqueness phenomena are known to occur. However, a complete classification of uniqueness/nonuniqueness across all low-regularity classes, and the physical interpretation as singularities, remain active questions in low-regularity Lorentzian geometry and Lorentzian length space theory.

Let $K$ be a field. A $K$-algebra $A$ is called finitely presented if there exist a finite integer $n$ and a finite set of elements $r_1,\dots,r_m$ in the free associative $K$-algebra $K\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle$ such that $A \cong K\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle/(r_1,\dots,r_m)$, where $(r_1,\dots,r_m)$ denotes the two-sided ideal generated by the $r_i$. The algebra $A$ is called algebraic over $K$ if for every $a\in A$ there exists a nonzero polynomial $f_a(t)\in K[t]$ with $f_a(a)=0$; it is called nil if for every $a\in A$ there exists a positive integer $n_a$ with $a^{n_a}=0$ (equivalently, $f_a(t)$ may be taken to be a power of $t$).

Question: Must every finitely presented algebraic $K$-algebra be finite-dimensional over $K$? In particular, must every finitely presented nil $K$-algebra be finite-dimensional over $K$?

While Golod–Shafarevich (1964) gave finitely generated infinite-dimensional nil algebras, refuting the general Kurosh problem, the finitely presented version remains a well-known open problem: it is not known whether every finitely presented nil (or algebraic) algebra over a field is finite-dimensional. Recent work (e.g., the Quantitative Kurosh Problem and related papers) discusses the question without resolving the finitely presented case.

representations.normalized:
Consider the Einstein vacuum equations $\mathrm{Ric}(g)=0$ on a four-dimensional manifold, with Cauchy initial data $(\Sigma, h, K)$ where $\Sigma$ is a smooth three-manifold, $h$ is a Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, and $K$ is a symmetric (0,2)-tensor on $\Sigma$ satisfying the Hamiltonian and momentum constraint equations. Assume the data are asymptotically flat: there is a compact set $\mathcal{K}\subset\Sigma$ such that $\Sigma\setminus\mathcal{K}$ is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus B$ and, in the corresponding asymptotic coordinates $(x^i)$ with $r=|x|$,
$$h_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+O(r^{-1}),\qquad K_{ij}=O(r^{-2}),$$
together with appropriate decay of derivatives.

Let $(M,g)$ denote the maximal globally hyperbolic vacuum development of $(\Sigma,h,K)$. Penrose's conformal compactification consists of finding a conformal factor $\Omega>0$ on $M$, with $\Omega\to 0$ suitably at infinity, so that $\tilde g=\Omega^{2}g$ extends to a manifold-with-boundary $\widetilde M=M\cup\mathscr{I}$ whose boundary $\mathscr{I}=\mathscr{I}^{+}\cup\mathscr{I}^{-}$ (future and past null infinity) carries a regular conformal metric. The peeling property asserts that, along outgoing null geodesics parametrized by an affine parameter $r$, the Weyl tensor components $\Psi_k$ ($k=0,1,2,3,4$) of the physical metric $g$ decay as $\Psi_k = O(r^{k-5})$ as $r\to\infty$ towards $\mathscr{I}^{+}$.

Problem. Determine explicit conditions on the asymptotically flat initial data $(\Sigma,h,K)$ which are sufficient (and, ideally, necessary) to guarantee that the maximal vacuum development $(M,g)$ admits a Penrose conformal extension $(\widetilde M,\tilde g)$ in which the extended metric $\tilde g$ is at least of class $C^{3}$ across $\mathscr{I}^{+}$, and in which the peeling decay of the Weyl tensor holds.

The problem has been actively studied with substantial partial progress: Friedrich, Christodoulou–Klainerman, Chruściel–Delay, and others have given sufficient conditions on initial data (often involving conformally flat or symmetry conditions near spatial infinity, or specific decay/asymptotic-expansion hypotheses) yielding regular null infinity and peeling. A 2025 work ("From spatial to null infinity: Connecting initial data to peeling") gives further conditions on initial data ensuring peeling. Nevertheless, a complete characterization of the necessary and sufficient asymptotic conditions on general asymptotically flat data ensuring a $C^3$ Penrose extension and full peeling remains open.

Let K be a field. A K-algebra A (associative, not necessarily unital) is called nil if every element a ∈ A satisfies a^n = 0 for some positive integer n (depending on a). Suppose A is finitely generated over K, and let S ⊂ A be a finite-dimensional K-subspace generating A as a K-algebra. For each integer n ≥ 1, let S^n denote the K-linear span of all products a_1 a_2 ⋯ a_k with 1 ≤ k ≤ n and each a_i ∈ S. The algebra A is said to have finite Gelfand–Kirillov dimension (equivalently, polynomial growth) if there exists a polynomial f(t) ∈ R[t] such that dim_K S^n ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ 1 (this property is independent of the choice of finite-dimensional generating subspace S).

Question: Does there exist a finitely generated, infinite-dimensional, nil associative K-algebra A having finite Gelfand–Kirillov dimension?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Small's problem was answered affirmatively by T. H. Lenagan and A. Smoktunowicz (J. Amer. Math. Soc., 2007), who constructed a finitely generated infinite-dimensional nil associative algebra over any countable field having finite Gelfand–Kirillov dimension (in fact GK-dimension at most 3). Subsequent work has extended the range of possible GK-dimensions for such nil algebras.

Let $X$ be a smooth complex algebraic surface that is $\mathbb{Q}$-acyclic, meaning $H_i(X;\mathbb{Q}) = 0$ for all $i > 0$. Fix a smooth projective compactification $\overline{X}$ of $X$ such that the boundary $D = \overline{X}\setminus X$ is a simple normal crossing divisor, and let $K_{\overline{X}}$ denote the canonical divisor of $\overline{X}$. Say that $X$ is of log-general type if the logarithmic Kodaira dimension $\overline{\kappa}(X) := \kappa(\overline{X}, K_{\overline{X}}+D)$ equals $2$. Say that the pair $(\overline{X}, D)$ is rigid if it admits no non-trivial equisingular logarithmic deformations, i.e. $H^1(\overline{X}, T_{\overline{X}}(-\log D)) = 0$, where $T_{\overline{X}}(-\log D)$ is the logarithmic tangent sheaf.

Prove or disprove: every smooth $\mathbb{Q}$-acyclic surface $X$ of log-general type is rigid in the sense above.

Let $(M,g)$ be a four-dimensional Lorentzian manifold. Consider the vacuum Einstein equations $\mathrm{Ric}(g)=0$ in their weakest possible sense. Concretely, address the following:

(1) Identify the minimal regularity class for a Lorentzian metric $g$ under which the Ricci tensor $\mathrm{Ric}(g)$ can be defined as a tensor distribution and the equation $\mathrm{Ric}(g)=0$ makes rigorous distributional sense. In particular, investigate the borderline case in which both $g$ and its inverse $g^{-1}$ lie in $L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}(M)$ while the first partial derivatives of $g$ lie in $L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(M)$, so that the nonlinear terms $g^{-1}(\partial g)(\partial g)$ appearing in the curvature can be interpreted via products of an $L^{\infty}$ function with $L^{2}$ functions.

(2) Determine the optimal choice of coordinates (e.g.\ wave/harmonic coordinates, Coulomb-type gauges, geodesic normal coordinates) and of underlying differentiable structure on $M$ that realises this minimal regularity, i.e.\ such that, after a suitable change of $C^{k}$-atlas, the metric attains the lowest possible regularity threshold for which the vacuum equations are well defined and for which a meaningful Cauchy problem and well-posedness theory can be developed.

State and prove (or disprove) a theorem giving such an optimal regularity class together with the corresponding coordinate/atlas selection, or show obstructions ruling out any further weakening.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question is a long-standing program rather than a single theorem. Major progress has been made: the bounded $L^2$ curvature theorem of Klainerman–Rodnianski–Szeftel (Invent. Math. 2015) establishes well-posedness of the vacuum Einstein equations assuming only an $L^2$ bound on the curvature, which corresponds essentially to $H^2$ regularity of the metric and is critical with respect to the causal geometry. Subsequent work (e.g. the localised bounded $L^2$-curvature theorem, and the spacelike-characteristic Cauchy problem in low regularity, 2022) has extended the theory. However, the genuinely distributional regime in which $g, g^{-1}\in L^\infty$ and $\partial g\in L^2$, and the determination of an optimal coordinate/differentiable structure achieving the weakest possible regularity, remain not fully resolved. The problem is therefore partially solved.

Let $(V,D)$ be a minimal smooth simple-normal-crossings completion of $X$, so that $V$ is a smooth projective surface, $D\subset V$ is a reduced simple normal crossings divisor, $X=V\setminus D$, and $(V,D)$ is minimal in the sense that no $(-1)$-curve in $V$ meets $D$ in at most one point transversally (so it cannot be contracted while preserving the SNC property). Let $K_V$ denote a canonical divisor of $V$.

Prove or disprove: under these hypotheses, the intersection number

Background and setup. Let $X$ be a smooth complex algebraic surface that is contractible (resp. acyclic, i.e. has the integral homology of a point; resp. $\mathbb{Q}$-acyclic, i.e. $H_i(X;\mathbb{Q})=0$ for $i>0$). A smooth SNC-completion of $X$ is a pair $(V,D)$ where $V$ is a smooth projective surface, $D\subset V$ is a reduced simple normal crossing divisor (each component is smooth and components meet transversally with at most double points), and $V\setminus D\cong X$. Such a completion $(V,D)$ is called minimal if no irreducible component of $D$ is a $(-1)$-curve that can be smoothly contracted while preserving the SNC property.

Assume that $X$ is of log-general type, i.e. the logarithmic Kodaira dimension $\bar\kappa(X)$ equals $2$.

To the boundary divisor $D$ of a minimal smooth SNC-completion one associates its Eisenbud–Neumann splice diagram $\check{\Gamma}_D$: the weighted graph encoding the dual graph of $D$ together with the genera of components and self-intersection numbers (equivalently, the splice diagram describing the link of the singularity at infinity of $X$ as a graph manifold).

Question. Is the set
$$\{\,\check{\Gamma}_D : (V,D) \text{ is a minimal smooth SNC-completion of some smooth complex surface } X\}$$
finite, when $X$ ranges over all smooth contractible (resp. acyclic, resp. $\mathbb{Q}$-acyclic) complex algebraic surfaces of log-general type?

Let $(M, g)$ be a globally hyperbolic vacuum spacetime of dimension $3+1$ (i.e., $\mathrm{Ric}(g) = 0$) admitting a compact Cauchy surface $\Sigma_0$, and assume $(M,g)$ is cosmological in the sense that it possesses a Cauchy surface of constant mean curvature. A constant-mean-curvature (CMC) time function is a smooth function $\tau : M \to I \subset \mathbb{R}$ whose level sets $\Sigma_\tau = \tau^{-1}(\tau)$ are spacelike Cauchy hypersurfaces of constant mean curvature equal to $\tau$. In CMC slicing gauge, the Einstein vacuum equations reduce to a constrained evolution system for the induced metric and second fundamental form on $\Sigma_\tau$ together with lapse and shift determined by elliptic equations.

Prove that for every such cosmological vacuum spacetime $(M,g)$ with compact Cauchy surfaces, the maximal CMC time interval $I$ of existence is the entire range allowed by the topology of $\Sigma_0$; that is, establish long-time existence of the CMC-gauge Cauchy problem for vacuum Einstein equations with compact Cauchy data, showing in particular that the mean curvature $\tau$ exhausts $(-\infty, 0)$ in the expanding direction (or the appropriate maximal interval depending on the Yamabe type of $\Sigma_0$).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The long-time existence problem for CMC slicing in vacuum cosmological spacetimes with compact Cauchy surfaces remains a major open problem in mathematical relativity. Partial results are known under symmetry assumptions (e.g., U(1) symmetry, T^2 symmetry, surface symmetry) and for small perturbations of specific backgrounds, but the general conjecture has not been resolved. Related results address the existence of an initial CMC surface (Bartnik's conjecture), with both positive results under curvature assumptions and counterexamples (cosmological spacetimes without any CMC Cauchy surface) constructed for various spatial topologies.

Let $k$ be a field. By a division algebra over $k$ we mean an associative (not necessarily commutative) $k$-algebra $D$ with unit such that every nonzero element of $D$ has a two-sided multiplicative inverse in $D$. We say that $D$ is finitely generated (as a $k$-algebra) if there exist finitely many elements $d_1,\dots,d_n \in D$ such that $D$ is the smallest $k$-subalgebra of $D$ containing $d_1,\dots,d_n$ (note: closure under inverses is not assumed in the generation, only ring/algebra operations). The dimension of $D$ is its dimension as a $k$-vector space.

Question: Does there exist a field $k$ and a $k$-algebra $D$ which is simultaneously a division algebra, finitely generated as a $k$-algebra, and infinite-dimensional over $k$? (No assumption is made that $D$ be algebraic over $k$.)

The general Kurosh problem for division rings — whether a finitely generated algebraic division algebra must be finite-dimensional over its center — is widely reported to remain open since 1941. The weaker version asked here, dropping the algebraicity hypothesis and merely asking for the existence of any finitely generated infinite-dimensional division algebra, is also reported as open in the literature on infinite-dimensional algebras and survey treatments of the Kurosh problem. No construction or non-existence proof was found.

Let $n>3$ be an integer. A smooth hypersurface $X \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ is the zero locus of a polynomial $f \in \mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]$ such that $df$ does not vanish on $X$. We say that $X$ is contractible if it is contractible as a topological space. The logarithmic Kodaira dimension $\bar{\kappa}(X)$ of a smooth quasi-projective variety $X$ is defined as follows: choose a smooth projective compactification $\bar X$ of $X$ such that $D = \bar X \setminus X$ is a simple normal crossings divisor, and set
$$\bar\kappa(X) = \limsup_{m\to\infty} \frac{\log \dim H^0(\bar X, m(K_{\bar X}+D))}{\log m},$$
with the convention $\bar\kappa(X) = -\infty$ if $H^0(\bar X, m(K_{\bar X}+D)) = 0$ for all $m\geq 1$. The variety $X$ is said to be of log-general type if $\bar\kappa(X) = \dim X = n-1$.

Question: For $n>3$, does there exist a smooth contractible hypersurface $X \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ that is of log-general type?

Consider the class of smooth (3+1)-dimensional globally hyperbolic spacetimes (M, g) arising as maximal globally hyperbolic developments of smooth initial data (Σ, h, K) for the vacuum Einstein equations Ric(g) = 0 (or, more generally, for a reasonable Einstein–matter system). Some such developments possess a Cauchy horizon across which the metric g admits a nontrivial extension as a Lorentzian metric — either smoothly (C^∞) or in a distributional sense (e.g. as a C^0 Lorentzian metric with locally square-integrable Christoffel symbols, so that the Einstein equations make sense weakly).

Equip the space of admissible initial data sets (Σ, h, K) with a suitable topology and a notion of "generic" or "measure-zero" subset (for instance, a Baire-generic, prevalent, or measure-theoretic notion on an appropriate infinite-dimensional space of initial data).

Prove that the set of initial data whose maximal globally hyperbolic development admits a smooth, or even a distributional, Lorentzian extension across a Cauchy horizon forms a measure-zero (negligible / non-generic) subset of all admissible initial data, in an appropriate precise sense to be formulated.

Definitions. Let K be a field. A residually finite associative K-algebra A is one such that for every nonzero a ∈ A there is a finite-dimensional A-module on which a acts nontrivially; equivalently, the intersection of all cofinite-dimensional two-sided ideals of A is zero. An A-module V is residually finite if every nonzero v ∈ V is not annihilated by some finite-codimensional submodule (equivalently, the intersection of finite-codimensional submodules of V is zero). Suppose A is generated as a K-algebra by a finite-dimensional subspace S ⊆ A containing 1. We say A has algebraic property τ if there exists ε > 0 such that for every infinite-dimensional residually finite A-module V which has no nonzero finite-dimensional submodule, and for every finite-dimensional K-subspace W ⊆ V, one has
   dim(W + S·W) > (1 + ε) · dim W.

Setup. Let p and q be distinct prime numbers, and write K_p = Z/pZ, K_q = Z/qZ. For an integer n > 3, let SL_1(n, K_p[t]) denote the first congruence subgroup of SL(n, K_p[t]) with respect to the augmentation ideal (t) ⊂ K_p[t], that is, the kernel of the reduction homomorphism SL(n, K_p[t]) → SL(n, K_p) obtained by setting t = 0. Consider the group algebra K_q[SL_1(n, K_p[t])] over K_q, generated as an algebra by the K_q-span of any chosen finite generating set of SL_1(n, K_p[t]) (together with 1).

Question. Does K_q[SL_1(n, K_p[t])] satisfy algebraic property τ in the sense above?

Background. Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Lorentzian spacetime satisfying the Einstein equations (in vacuum or coupled to suitable matter) and possessing a cosmological singularity, e.g. a crushing singularity along which the mean curvature of a foliation by spacelike hypersurfaces blows up. In a neighborhood of such a singularity choose a Gaussian (or constant-mean-curvature) foliation with time coordinate $t\to 0^+$, induced spatial metric $g_{ij}(t,x)$ and second fundamental form $K_{ij}(t,x)$. The Einstein evolution equations on this foliation take the schematic form
$$\partial_t g_{ij} = -2 K_{ij},\qquad \partial_t K^i{}_j = (\text{spatial-curvature terms}) + (\text{velocity terms involving }K)+\text{matter}.$$
The associated "velocity-dominated system" is obtained by deleting all spatial-derivative (curvature) terms from the Einstein equations, leaving an ODE in $t$ at each spatial point $x$. A solution $(g,K)$ is said to be asymptotically velocity dominated (AVD) near the singularity if there exists a solution $(\tilde g,\tilde K)$ of the velocity-dominated system on the same spatial manifold such that, as $t\to 0^+$, suitable rescaled differences $g_{ij}-\tilde g_{ij}$, $K^i{}_j-\tilde K^i{}_j$ (and analogous matter quantities) tend to zero in an appropriate norm, with errors decaying faster than the leading velocity-dominated behavior.

Problem. Give an intrinsic characterization of the class of spacetimes that are asymptotically velocity dominated near a cosmological singularity in this sense. Specifically:

(a) Formulate a precise, geometrically invariant definition of "asymptotically velocity dominated singularity" valid for general (not necessarily symmetric) spacetimes.

(b) Identify necessary and sufficient conditions on the initial data, matter model, and symmetry/structure of the spacetime under which AVD behavior holds at the singularity.

(c) Describe the maximal class of spacetimes within vacuum general relativity, and within Einstein-matter systems (scalar field, stiff fluid, electromagnetic, etc.), whose generic singularities are AVD, distinguishing them from spacetimes exhibiting oscillatory (Mixmaster/BKL) behavior.

Let $G$ be a group with a fixed finite symmetric generating set $S$. Say that $G$ has property $(\tau)$ if there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for every surjective homomorphism $\pi : G \to G_0$ onto a finite group $G_0$, the Cayley graph $\mathrm{Cay}(G_0, \pi(S))$ is an $\varepsilon$-expander; equivalently, the smallest nonzero eigenvalue of the combinatorial Laplacian of $\mathrm{Cay}(G_0, \pi(S))$ is bounded below by $\varepsilon$, uniformly over all finite quotients. (This property is independent of the choice of finite generating set.)

A lattice in $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})$ is a discrete subgroup $\Gamma \le \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})$ such that the quotient $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})/\Gamma$ has finite Haar measure.

Prove or disprove: every lattice $\Gamma$ in $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})$ fails to have property $(\tau)$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The Lubotzky–Sarnak conjecture predicts that lattices in SL(2,ℂ) (equivalently, fundamental groups of finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifolds) do not have property (τ). Lackenby–Long–Reid showed that LERF (subgroup separability) of such a lattice implies the failure of property (τ). Agol's 2012 proof of the virtual Haken conjecture, together with the work of Wise on virtually special cube complexes, established that fundamental groups of closed hyperbolic 3-manifolds are LERF, and the analogous result holds for cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds. Together these results confirm the Lubotzky–Sarnak conjecture for all lattices in SL(2,ℂ), so the conjecture is now considered solved.

Let $k$ be a field of positive characteristic, and let $\mathbb{A}^n_k = \operatorname{Spec} k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ denote affine $n$-space over $k$. A regular injection (closed embedding) of the affine line into the affine plane is a morphism $\varphi : \mathbb{A}^1_k \to \mathbb{A}^2_k$ of $k$-schemes given by $t \mapsto (f(t), g(t))$ with $f,g \in k[t]$, such that $\varphi$ induces an isomorphism of $\mathbb{A}^1_k$ onto its scheme-theoretic image (equivalently, the induced ring homomorphism $k[x,y] \to k[t]$, $x \mapsto f$, $y \mapsto g$, is surjective). Two such embeddings $\varphi_1,\varphi_2$ are called equivalent if there exists a $k$-algebra automorphism $\Phi$ of $k[x,y]$ such that $\varphi_2 = \Phi \circ \varphi_1$.

In characteristic zero, the Abhyankar–Moh–Suzuki theorem asserts that every such embedding is equivalent to the standard embedding $t \mapsto (t,0)$. In positive characteristic this fails: there exist embeddings (for instance certain ones involving Frobenius-type polynomials) that are inequivalent to the standard one.

Problem: Give a complete classification, up to the above equivalence by polynomial automorphisms of $\mathbb{A}^2_k$, of all regular injections $\mathbb{A}^1_k \hookrightarrow \mathbb{A}^2_k$ when $k$ is a field of positive characteristic.

Let $(S_k)_{k\ge 0}$ be a simple symmetric random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ starting at the origin: $S_0=0$ and at each step the walker moves to one of its four nearest neighbors, each chosen independently with probability $1/4$. For each integer $n\ge 1$, let
$$T_n \;=\; \inf\bigl\{\,k\ge 0 \,:\, \{x\in\mathbb{Z}^2:\ |x|<n\}\subseteq\{S_0,S_1,\dots,S_k\}\,\bigr\}$$
be the first time at which the walk has visited every lattice point in the open Euclidean disk of radius $n$ about the origin.

Characterize the class of functions $f:\mathbb{N}\to(0,\infty)$ for which
$$\mathbb{P}\bigl(\,T_n \le f(n)\ \text{for all sufficiently large } n\,\bigr)\;=\;1,$$
i.e.\ give necessary and sufficient growth conditions on $f(n)$ under which, almost surely, by time $f(n)$ the walk has visited every lattice point within Euclidean distance $n$ of the origin for all sufficiently large $n$.

The Kesten–Révész conjecture on the asymptotics of the time needed for a planar simple random walk to cover the disk of radius n was resolved by Dembo, Peres, Rosen, and Zeitouni (Annals of Mathematics, 2004), who proved that T_n / (n^2 (log n)^2) → 4/π almost surely. A finitely presented graded algebra $A = F/I$, where $I$ is a two-sided ideal generated by homogeneous elements $r_1, r_2, \dots$ of degrees $2 \le n_1 \le n_2 \le \cdots$, is called a Golod–Shafarevich algebra (a GS-algebra) if there exists a real number $t_0 \in (0,1)$ such that
$$1 - d\,t_0 + \sum_{i\ge 1} t_0^{n_i} < 0.$$

For a finitely generated associative $K$-algebra $A$ with a fixed finite generating set $S = \{a_1,\dots,a_d\}$, one defines an algebraic analogue of property $(\tau)$ as follows. Consider the family $\mathcal F$ of all finite-dimensional $A$-modules $V$, and for each such $V$ define the Cayley-type expansion constant
$$h(V; S) = \min_{0 \ne W \subsetneq V}\; \frac{\dim\!\bigl(W + \sum_{i=1}^d a_i W\bigr) - \dim W}{\dim W}.$$
The algebra $A$ is said to have algebraic property $(\tau)$ if there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $h(V;S) \ge \varepsilon$ for every nonzero finite-dimensional $A$-module $V$ in some prescribed class (for instance, all finite-dimensional quotients of $A$, viewed as left $A$-modules). This property does not depend on the choice of finite generating set.

Question: Does every Golod–Shafarevich algebra fail to have algebraic property $(\tau)$? Equivalently, prove or disprove: for every GS-algebra $A$ there is no positive lower bound $\varepsilon > 0$ on the expansion constants $h(V;S)$ over the relevant family of finite-dimensional $A$-modules.

Call a smooth complex affine algebraic variety $X$ of dimension $n$ an exotic $\mathbb{C}^n$ if $X$ is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ but not algebraically isomorphic to the affine space $\mathbb{C}^n$.

(a) Do there exist two exotic $\mathbb{C}^n$'s $X$ and $Y$ that are biholomorphic as complex analytic varieties but not isomorphic as algebraic varieties?

(b) Does there exist a nontrivial algebraic deformation family $\{X_t\}_{t\in T}$ of exotic $\mathbb{C}^n$'s (a smooth morphism $\mathcal{X}\to T$ with positive-dimensional base $T$ whose fibers are exotic $\mathbb{C}^n$'s) such that all fibers $X_t$ share the same underlying complex analytic structure (i.e., are pairwise biholomorphic) while not all being algebraically isomorphic?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Part (a) has been answered affirmatively in dimension 3: Dubouloz constructed pairs of non-isomorphic contractible affine threefolds (with isomorphic cylinders) that are biholomorphic as complex analytic varieties, giving examples of biholomorphic but non-algebraically-isomorphic exotic affine 3-spaces. Subsequent work by Dubouloz–Fasel produced positive-dimensional families of pairwise non-isomorphic $\mathbb{A}^1$-contractible affine threefolds. The full question (existence in all dimensions and for the strict diffeomorphism-to-$\mathbb{C}^n$ class, plus the deformation-family form) does not appear to be definitively settled in the general form posed.

Let $(S_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be the simple symmetric random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with $d \ge 3$, started at the origin, and let $|S_n|$ denote its Euclidean distance from the origin. Define the eventual escape radius
$$c(n) = \inf_{k \ge n} |S_k|,$$
i.e. the smallest distance from the origin attained by the walk at any time from $n$ onward. For a positive nondecreasing function $\varphi: \mathbb{N} \to (0, \infty)$, say that $\varphi$ is an "upper bound" for $c$ if
$$\mathbb{P}\bigl(c(n) \le \varphi(n) \text{ for all sufficiently large } n\bigr) = 1,$$
and a "non-upper bound" otherwise.

Determine an integral (or series) test giving necessary and sufficient conditions on $\varphi$ so that $\varphi$ is an upper bound for $c(n)$, in a form analogous to the Kolmogorov–Erdős–Feller integral test that provides necessary and sufficient conditions for upper functions in the law of the iterated logarithm.

Dvoretzky and Erdős (1951) established the basic almost-sure escape rate $|S_n| \gtrsim \sqrt{n}/(\log n)^{1/(d-2)+\varepsilon}$ for transient simple random walks in $\mathbb{Z}^d$, $d\ge 3$, providing upper-bound-type results but not a complete necessary-and-sufficient integral test in the spirit of the Kolmogorov–Erdős–Feller test for the LIL. A web search did not surface a definitive reference establishing such a sharp integral test characterizing all upper bounds of $c(n) = \inf_{k\ge n}|S_k|$, so the precise status of the originally posed problem could not be conclusively verified.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is a well-known conjecture on the analytic characterization of affine space. For n=1 it is classical; for n=2 it follows from results of Ramanujam and Miyanishi-Sugie characterizing the affine plane (a smooth contractible affine surface biholomorphic to C^2 is algebraically C^2). For n≥3 it is generally regarded as open, and no proof or counterexample appears in the literature. The closely related (without the diffeomorphism hypothesis) Ramanujam-style examples show topological hypotheses cannot be dropped, but the stated conjecture with both diffeomorphism and biholomorphism to C^n remains an open problem.

Let $(S_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be a simple symmetric random walk on the two-dimensional integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$ starting at the origin (at each step the walker moves to one of the four nearest neighbours with equal probability $1/4$, independently of the past). For each integer $n\ge 1$ and each $x\in\mathbb{Z}^2$, let
\[ L_n(x) \;=\; \#\{\,0\le k\le n : S_k = x\,\} \]
denote the number of visits of the walk to the site $x$ during the first $n$ steps, and define the maximum multiplicity
\[ T_2(n) \;=\; \max_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^2} L_n(x). \]
Determine the exact almost-sure asymptotic behaviour of $T_2(n)$ as $n\to\infty$. In particular, prove or disprove that
\[ \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{T_2(n)}{(\log n)^2} \;=\; \frac{1}{\pi} \qquad \text{almost surely.} \]

denote the number of visits of the walk to the site $x$ during the first $n$ steps, and define the maximum multiplicity

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

This is the Erdős–Taylor conjecture (1960) for planar simple random walk. It was resolved by Dembo, Peres, Rosen and Zeitouni, who proved that $T_2(n)/(\log n)^2 \to 1/\pi$ almost surely, via a multiscale second-moment analysis and the theory of thick points of planar Brownian motion. Subsequent works (e.g., Rosen's random-walk proof and a multivariate extension by Louidor and collaborators) have refined and extended the result.

Find a notion of quasi-local mass m_QL(Ω) assigned to bounded 3-dimensional spacelike regions Ω (with appropriate induced geometric data: a Riemannian metric, a second fundamental form, and matter fields satisfying the dominant energy condition) in 3+1-dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes solving the Einstein equations, with the following property. There should exist a function M_0(V, …) of the volume V = Vol(Ω) (and possibly of other geometric quantities of Ω such as diameter or boundary geometry) such that the following theorem holds:

If Ω is any such 3-dimensional region with Vol(Ω) = V and m_QL(Ω) > M_0(V, …), then every globally hyperbolic spacetime (M, g) satisfying the Einstein equations with dominant energy condition that contains Ω as a spacelike region must contain a closed trapped surface (a closed spacelike 2-surface in M whose two null mean curvatures are both negative), and hence, by the Penrose singularity theorem, must be future causally incomplete (contain a "black hole").

Problem: Construct such a quasi-local mass m_QL and prove a nontrivial trapped-surface-formation theorem of the above type, with an explicit threshold function M_0(V, …).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

No definitive notion of quasi-local mass currently appears in a theorem of the stated "volume + mass threshold ⇒ trapped surface" form. Existing results (e.g., Schoen–Yau hoop-type theorems, Khuri's inequalities, and Wang–Yau quasilocal mass studies) give related but partial trapped-surface formation criteria, typically involving concentration of matter or initial-data conditions rather than a clean quasi-local-mass threshold. Recent work on Einstein–Vlasov trapped-surface formation (2025) and quasilocal mass at marginally trapped surfaces shows continued activity but no resolution of the general problem.

Let X ⊂ ℂ⁴ be the smooth affine complex hypersurface defined by
    X = { (x, y, z, t) ∈ ℂ⁴ : x + x²y + z³ + t² = 0 }.
It is known that X is diffeomorphic to ℝ⁶ and is not algebraically isomorphic to ℂ³ (it carries fewer algebraic 𝔾ₐ-actions than ℂ³; equivalently, its Makar–Limanov invariant is nontrivial), so X is an "exotic" affine 3-space.

Prove that X is not biholomorphic to ℂ³, i.e. that there is no biholomorphism between X (with its complex-analytic structure inherited from ℂ⁴) and the complex affine space ℂ³.

More generally, for the known families of smooth affine hypersurfaces Y ⊂ ℂⁿ that are diffeomorphic but not algebraically isomorphic to ℂⁿ⁻¹ (exotic ℂⁿ⁻¹'s), prove that no such Y is biholomorphic to ℂⁿ⁻¹.

The algebraic version of the problem was resolved by Makar-Limanov (1996), who showed that the Koras–Russell cubic threefold X = {x + x²y + z³ + t² = 0} is not algebraically isomorphic to ℂ³. The holomorphic (biholomorphic) version, however, remains an open problem: standard algebraic invariants such as the Makar-Limanov invariant are not holomorphic invariants, and recent work (e.g., A¹-contractibility results of Hoyois–Krishna–Østvær, 2014, and the trivial Makar-Limanov invariant of the cylinder X × ℂ shown by Dubouloz, 2009) underscores that the biholomorphic classification of these exotic affine threefolds is not settled.

Let $A$ be a $C^*$-algebra. A linear map $\delta: A \to A$ is called a derivation if it satisfies the Leibniz rule $\delta(ab) = \delta(a) b + a\, \delta(b)$ for all $a, b \in A$; no continuity assumption is imposed on $\delta$. An element $x \in A$ is called normal if $x^* x = x x^*$.

Prove or disprove: for every $C^*$-algebra $A$, every (not necessarily continuous) derivation $\delta: A \to A$, and every normal element $x \in A$ satisfying $x\,\delta(x) = \delta(x)\, x$, one has $\delta(x) = 0$.
representations.original:
Let $A$ be a $C^*$-algebra. A linear map $\delta: A \to A$ is called a derivation if it satisfies the Leibniz rule $\delta(ab) = \delta(a) b + a\, \delta(b)$ for all $a, b \in A$; no continuity assumption is imposed on $\delta$. An element $x \in A$ is called normal if $x^* x = x x^*$. 

Prove or disprove: for every $C^*$-algebra $A$, every (not necessarily continuous) derivation $\delta: A \to A$, and every normal element $x \in A$ satisfying $x\,\delta(x) = \delta(x)\, x$, one has $\delta(x) = 0$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

By Sakai's automatic-continuity theorem, every derivation of a C*-algebra into itself is norm-continuous, so the continuity hypothesis can always be dropped. Combined with the known result for continuous derivations (a normal element commuting with its image under a continuous derivation lies in the kernel of the derivation), the statement holds: δ(x)=0.

Call a smooth complex affine algebraic variety $X$ of dimension $n$ an exotic $\mathbb{C}^n$ if $X$ is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ (equivalently, $X$ is contractible and, for $n\ge 3$, has the underlying smooth manifold structure of $\mathbb{C}^n$) but $X$ is not isomorphic, as an algebraic variety, to the affine space $\mathbb{C}^n$. Recall that $X$ is rational if its function field $\mathbb{C}(X)$ is purely transcendental over $\mathbb{C}$, i.e. isomorphic to $\mathbb{C}(t_1,\dots,t_n)$.

Question: Does there exist an integer $n\ge 1$ and an exotic $\mathbb{C}^n$ that is not rational?

Let $H$ be an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, and let $B = B(H)$ denote the C*-algebra of all bounded linear operators on $H$. A state on $B$ is a positive linear functional $\varphi : B \to \mathbb{C}$ with $\varphi(I)=1$; the state space $S(B)$ is convex, and its extreme points are called pure states. Equip the dual $B^*$ with the weak-* topology $\sigma(B^*,B)$, and consider the pure state space $P(B) \subset B^*$ with the induced topology.

For a commutative unital C*-algebra $C(X)$ (with $X$ compact Hausdorff), the pure state space is homeomorphic to $X$ and hence weak-* compact. Determine whether the pure state space $P(B)$ of $B(H)$ is weak-* compact in this noncommutative setting.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

It is a classical fact that for $B = B(H)$ with $H$ infinite-dimensional, the pure state space is not weak-* compact: the weak-* closure of the pure states contains non-pure states (e.g., one can approximate singular states by vector states). The parsed metadata also marks this question as solved (negatively).

Let $(M,g)$ be a complete, asymptotically flat Riemannian 3-manifold of nonnegative scalar curvature satisfying the hypotheses of the positive mass theorem (so that the ADM mass is well-defined and nonnegative). Let $\Omega \subset M$ be a bounded domain with connected smooth boundary $\Sigma = \partial\Omega$.

A static extension of $\Omega$ is a complete, asymptotically flat Riemannian 3-manifold $(N,h)$ of nonnegative scalar curvature together with an isometric embedding $\Omega \hookrightarrow N$ such that $N \setminus \Omega$ is a static vacuum manifold, i.e. there exists a positive function $V$ on $N\setminus\Omega$ (tending to $1$ at infinity) satisfying
$$V \mathrm{Ric}(h) = \nabla^2 V, \qquad \Delta V = 0$$
on $N\setminus\Omega$, with matching of the induced metric and mean curvature of $\Sigma$ from the two sides.

(a) Prove that for every such $\Omega \subset M$ there exists a static extension $(N,h)$ as above.

(b) Among all asymptotically flat extensions of $\Omega$ with nonnegative scalar curvature whose exterior region $N\setminus\Omega$ contains no closed minimal surfaces (horizon-free), determine whether the static extension realizes the infimum of the ADM mass.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Bartnik's static metric extension conjecture remains open in full generality. Substantial partial progress has been made: local well-posedness of the static vacuum extension problem near a Euclidean ball and near general static vacuum metrics (Anderson–Khuri, An, and others, 2003–2025), axisymmetric flow approaches (2019), and recent local well-posedness for the stationary version near Schwarzschild spheres (2025). None of these resolve the global existence and the minimization property of the ADM mass among horizon-free extensions.

Let $\mathbb{F}$ be a finite field. A matroid $M$ on a finite ground set $E$ is said to be $\mathbb{F}$-representable if there exists a matrix $A$ with entries in $\mathbb{F}$ whose columns are indexed by $E$ such that a subset $X \subseteq E$ is independent in $M$ if and only if the corresponding columns of $A$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}$. An $\mathbb{F}$-represented matroid is such a matroid given together with an explicit representing matrix $A$ over $\mathbb{F}$. A minor of $M$ is any matroid obtained from $M$ by a sequence of deletions and contractions of elements; for a fixed matroid $N$, we say $M$ has an $N$-minor if some minor of $M$ is isomorphic to $N$.

Fix a finite field $\mathbb{F}$ and a fixed $\mathbb{F}$-representable matroid $N$. Question: Does there exist an algorithm which, given as input an $\mathbb{F}$-represented matroid $M$ (specified by a matrix over $\mathbb{F}$ with $n$ columns), decides in time bounded by a polynomial in $n$ whether $M$ has $N$ as a minor?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The Minor-Testing Conjecture for matroids representable over a finite field appears to remain open in general. Although Geelen, Gerards, and Whittle's Matroid Minors Project has produced major structural results (including a proof of Rota's conjecture and finite excluded-minor characterizations), no general polynomial-time minor-testing algorithm for arbitrary fixed N over arbitrary finite fields has been published. Partial results exist (e.g., for specific minors and small fields), but the general conjecture is still listed as open in the matroid theory literature.

Question: If X is an elliptically connected complete Kähler manifold, must its fundamental group π₁(X) be almost abelian? In the weaker form, must π₁(X) be at least almost nilpotent?

Let (M, g, K) be an asymptotically flat initial data set for the Einstein equations consisting of a 3-manifold M with Riemannian metric g and symmetric (0,2)-tensor K representing the second fundamental form, satisfying the dominant energy condition. For a bounded domain Ω ⊂ M with smooth boundary Σ = ∂Ω, the Bartnik quasi-local mass m_B(Ω) is defined as

  m_B(Ω) = inf { m_ADM(M̃, g̃, K̃) },

where the infimum is taken over all admissible asymptotically flat extensions (M̃, g̃, K̃) of (Ω, g|_Ω, K|_Ω) that contain no horizons enclosing Ω and satisfy the dominant energy condition. Call the data on Ω "non-flat" if (Ω, g|_Ω, K|_Ω) is not locally isometric to a region in Minkowski initial data.

Similarly, for a closed spacelike 2-surface Σ bounding a region in a spacetime satisfying the dominant energy condition, let m_P(Σ) denote the Penrose quasi-local mass associated with Σ (defined via the area and properties of trapped/marginally trapped surfaces enclosed by Σ).

Prove the following two assertions:
(a) For every bounded domain Ω with non-flat initial data, m_B(Ω) > 0.
(b) For every closed 2-surface Σ arising as the boundary of a region in physically reasonable initial data (satisfying the dominant energy condition with no naked singularities enclosed), m_P(Σ) ≥ 0.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Partial results exist: Huisken–Ilmanen type results show that vanishing Bartnik mass forces local flatness in the time-symmetric (Riemannian) case, and the Riemannian Penrose inequality (Huisken–Ilmanen, Bray) gives nonnegativity in the time-symmetric setting. However, the full strict positivity of Bartnik mass for general non-flat (non time-symmetric) data and nonnegativity of the Penrose quasi-local mass on general reasonable spacetime data remain open in full generality.

A matroid is a pair $M=(E,\mathcal{I})$ where $E$ is a finite ground set and $\mathcal{I}\subseteq 2^E$ is a nonempty family of "independent" subsets closed under taking subsets and satisfying the augmentation axiom: if $I,J\in\mathcal{I}$ with $|I|<|J|$, then there exists $e\in J\setminus I$ with $I\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal{I}$. Given a finite field $\mathbb{F}$ and a matrix $A$ over $\mathbb{F}$ whose columns are indexed by a finite set $E$, the matrix $A$ represents a matroid $M(A)$ on $E$ whose independent sets are exactly those $S\subseteq E$ for which the columns of $A$ indexed by $S$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}$.

Question: Fix a finite field $\mathbb{F}$. Does there exist an algorithm that, given as input two matrices $A_1$ and $A_2$ over $\mathbb{F}$ sharing the same column-index set $E$, decides in time polynomial in the total bit-length of the input whether $M(A_1)=M(A_2)$ (i.e., whether the two matrices represent the same matroid on $E$)?

Let $X$ be a compact Riemann surface of genus $g \geq 2$, and let $\mathrm{SU}_X(r)$ denote the moduli space of semistable rank-$r$ vector bundles on $X$ with trivial determinant. The Picard group of $\mathrm{SU}_X(r)$ is infinite cyclic, generated by an ample line bundle $\mathcal{L}$ called the determinant line bundle: it is characterized (up to isomorphism) by the property that for any line bundle $M$ of degree $g-1$ on $X$, the divisor
$$\Theta_M = \{E \in \mathrm{SU}_X(r) : h^0(X, E \otimes M) \neq 0\}$$
is a divisor in the linear system $|\mathcal{L}|$.

Determine whether the linear system $|\mathcal{L}^{\otimes 2}|$ associated to the second tensor power of the determinant line bundle is base-point free; that is, whether for every semistable rank-$r$ vector bundle $E$ on $X$ with trivial determinant there exists a global section $s \in H^0(\mathrm{SU}_X(r), \mathcal{L}^{\otimes 2})$ which does not vanish at the point $[E] \in \mathrm{SU}_X(r)$.

Effective base-point-freeness of powers $|\mathcal{L}^{k}|$ on $\mathrm{SU}_X(r)$ has been studied extensively (Le Potier, Hein, Popa, Pauly), giving explicit bounds on $k$ depending on $r$ and $g$ for which $|\mathcal{L}^k|$ is base-point free, but these bounds are far from $k=2$ in general. Let $X$ be a compact Riemann surface of genus $g \ge 2$. Denote by $\mathrm{SU}_X(r)$ the moduli space of S-equivalence classes of semistable rank-$r$ holomorphic vector bundles on $X$ with trivial determinant. For a smooth projective curve $Y$, let $J^{g_Y-1}(Y)$ denote the component of the Picard variety of $Y$ parametrizing line bundles of degree $g_Y-1$, where $g_Y$ is the genus of $Y$. For a semistable vector bundle $F$ of rank $r$ and trivial determinant on $Y$, define the (set-theoretic) theta locus
$$\theta(F) := \{\, L \in J^{g_Y-1}(Y) \;:\; h^0(Y, F\otimes L) \neq 0 \,\}.$$
It is known that $\theta(F)$ is either a divisor in $J^{g_Y-1}(Y)$ or all of $J^{g_Y-1}(Y)$.

Question: For every $E \in \mathrm{SU}_X(r)$, does there exist a finite étale covering $\pi : Y \to X$ from a smooth projective curve $Y$ such that
$$\theta(\pi^* E) \neq J^{g_Y-1}(Y),$$
i.e., such that $\theta(\pi^* E)$ is a proper divisor of $J^{g_Y-1}(Y)$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Searches in surveys on generalized theta divisors (Popa, Beauville) do not reveal a definitive resolution of the question whether every semistable bundle with trivial determinant admits an étale cover on which the pullback has a proper theta divisor. Examples of bundles whose theta divisor equals all of $J^{g-1}$ are known (e.g., Raynaud's examples and constructions by Pauly, Schneider, and others), but whether such bundles always become "theta-proper" after some étale pullback is not clearly settled in the accessible literature. Status appears unknown / likely still open.

Let $X$ be a smooth, complex, non-hyperelliptic compact Riemann surface (equivalently, smooth projective curve) of genus $g \ge 3$. Let $SU_X(2)$ denote the moduli space of S-equivalence classes of semistable rank-$2$ holomorphic vector bundles on $X$ with trivial determinant. Let $\Theta \subset \mathrm{Pic}^{g-1}(X)$ denote the canonical theta divisor consisting of line bundles of degree $g-1$ admitting a nonzero global section, and let $|2\Theta|$ be the linear system of divisors on $\mathrm{Pic}^{g-1}(X)$ algebraically equivalent to $2\Theta$. There is a natural morphism (the rank-$2$ theta map)
$$\theta : SU_X(2) \longrightarrow |2\Theta|, \qquad E \longmapsto \Theta_E := \{L \in \mathrm{Pic}^{g-1}(X) : h^0(X, E \otimes L) > 0\},$$
which is known to be a finite morphism of degree one onto its image when $X$ is non-hyperelliptic.

Question: Is $\theta$ a closed embedding for every non-hyperelliptic smooth projective curve $X$ of genus $g \ge 3$?

$$\theta : SU_X(2) \longrightarrow |2\Theta|, \qquad E \longmapsto \Theta_E := \{L \in \mathrm{Pic}^{g-1}(X) : h^0(X, E \otimes L) > 0\},$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The theta map $\theta: SU_X(2) \to |2\Theta|$ is known to be injective with injective differential at smooth points for every non-hyperelliptic curve (Brivio–Verra), and is known to be a closed embedding for $g=3$ and for generic curves of any genus $\ge 3$. However, no source found establishes that $\theta$ is an embedding for every non-hyperelliptic curve of genus $\ge 3$; the question continues to be cited as open in subsequent literature on generalized theta functions.

Provide a direct algebro-geometric proof of this formula by computing the Chern numbers of SU_X(r) (or of a suitable desingularization or modular cover) and applying the Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem to L^k on SU_X(r).

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The Verlinde formula now has several direct algebro-geometric/intersection-theoretic proofs. Jeffrey and Kirwan (Annals of Math., 1998) computed intersection pairings on the moduli space of rank-n bundles of fixed determinant on a Riemann surface and used them, via Riemann–Roch, to give a direct proof of the Verlinde formula. Further proofs along these lines have been given by Meinrenken, Bismut–Labourie, and others, including a finite-dimensional proof published in Science China Mathematics (2021).

$$\Theta_k = \{E \in \mathcal{U}^*_X(k) \mid h^0(X,E) \neq 0\}$$
is a divisor; let $\mathcal{M} = \mathcal{O}(\Theta_k)$ be the associated line bundle.

Consider the tensor product map
$$\tau_{k,r}: \mathcal{SU}_X(r) \times \mathcal{U}^*_X(k) \longrightarrow \mathcal{U}^*_X(kr), \qquad (F,E) \mapsto F \otimes E,$$

$$D_{k,r} = \{(F,E) \mid h^0(X, F \otimes E) \neq 0\} \subset \mathcal{SU}_X(r) \times \mathcal{U}^*_X(k)$$
is (when nonempty as a divisor) a divisor in the linear system $|\mathcal{L}^k \boxtimes \mathcal{M}^r|$, and so determines a section, hence (up to scalar) a linear map
$$\vartheta_{k,r}: H^0(\mathcal{SU}_X(r), \mathcal{L}^k) \longrightarrow H^0(\mathcal{U}^*_X(k), \mathcal{M}^r)^*.$$

The two spaces in question are known to have the same dimension. Prove or disprove: for every compact Riemann surface $X$ of genus $g \geq 2$ and all positive integers $k, r$, the map $\vartheta_{k,r}$ is an isomorphism.

A radio coloring (also known as an L(2,1)-labeling) of a simple finite undirected graph G=(V,E) is an assignment f: V → ℤ_{>0} of positive integers to the vertices such that:
  (i) |f(u) − f(v)| ≥ 2 whenever u and v are adjacent in G, and
  (ii) f(u) ≠ f(v) whenever u and v are at distance exactly 2 in G.
The span of f is max_{v ∈ V} f(v). The Radio Coloring problem (RC) asks, given a graph G and a positive integer k, whether G admits a radio coloring of span at most k.

A graph has treewidth at most 2 if it is a subgraph of a series-parallel graph (equivalently, it contains no K_4 minor).

Determine the computational complexity of the Radio Coloring problem RC restricted to the class of graphs of treewidth at most 2: is it polynomial-time solvable or NP-hard?

Background. A matroid $M$ on a finite ground set $E$ is determined by its rank function $r:2^E\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, which is integer-valued, monotone, submodular, and satisfies $0\le r(X)\le|X|$. Access to $M$ is via a rank oracle that, given $X\subseteq E$, returns $r(X)$ in unit time. The matroid $M$ is said to be representable over a field $\mathbb{F}$ (in particular over $\mathbb{R}$) if there exist vectors $\{v_e:e\in E\}$ in some $\mathbb{F}$-vector space such that for every $X\subseteq E$, $r(X)$ equals the dimension of the $\mathbb{F}$-linear span of $\{v_e:e\in X\}$.

The branch-width of $M$ is defined as follows. A branch-decomposition of $M$ is a pair $(T,\mu)$ where $T$ is a cubic tree and $\mu$ is a bijection from $E$ to the set of leaves of $T$. Each edge $e$ of $T$ partitions $E$ into two sets $A_e, B_e$ corresponding to the leaves of the two components of $T-e$, and the width of $e$ is $r(A_e)+r(B_e)-r(E)+1$. The width of $(T,\mu)$ is the maximum width over edges of $T$, and the branch-width of $M$ is the minimum width over all branch-decompositions (with branch-width $1$ if $|E|\le 1$).

A certificate for non-$\mathbb{R}$-representability of $M$ accessed via a rank oracle is a sequence of subsets $X_1,\dots,X_t\subseteq E$ together with the values $r(X_1),\dots,r(X_t)$, such that no matroid on $E$ with this rank data on these sets is representable over $\mathbb{R}$. The length of the certificate is $t$.

Question. Fix a positive integer $k$. Does there exist a polynomial $p_k$ such that every matroid $M$ on $n$ elements with branch-width at most $k$ that is not representable over $\mathbb{R}$ admits a certificate of non-$\mathbb{R}$-representability of length at most $p_k(n)$ using only rank evaluations?

Let $X$ be a smooth complex projective curve of genus $g\ge 2$, and let $\mathrm{SU}_X(r)$ denote the moduli space of semistable rank-$r$ vector bundles on $X$ with trivial determinant. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the ample generator of $\mathrm{Pic}(\mathrm{SU}_X(r))\cong\mathbb{Z}$ (the determinant line bundle). For each integer $k\ge 1$, consider the finite-dimensional vector space of generalized theta functions
$$V_{r,k}(X) := H^0(\mathrm{SU}_X(r),\mathcal{L}^{\otimes k}).$$

As $X$ varies over the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_g$ of smooth genus-$g$ curves, the spaces $V_{r,k}(X)$ assemble into a holomorphic vector bundle on $\mathcal{M}_g$ (or on Teichmüller space $\mathcal{T}_g$) that carries a canonical projectively flat connection (the Hitchin connection). Projectivizing the resulting monodromy yields a projective representation of the mapping class group $\Gamma_g = \pi_1(\mathcal{M}_g, X)$:
$$\rho_{r,k}: \Gamma_g \longrightarrow \mathrm{PGL}(V_{r,k}(X)).$$

Identify the projective representation $\rho_{r,k}$. More precisely, give an intrinsic topological/algebraic description of $\rho_{r,k}$ (for example, in terms of a known modular functor or topological quantum field theory), and describe its image, kernel, and characters.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The representation $\rho_{r,k}$ has been identified, via the Hitchin connection and its identification with the WZW/TUY connection on conformal blocks, with the $\mathrm{SU}(r)$ Reshetikhin–Turaev (Witten) TQFT projective representation of the mapping class group. This identification was completed by Laszlo (matching Hitchin and TUY connections) and by Andersen–Ueno (equivalence of the conformal-blocks modular functor with the skein/Reshetikhin–Turaev modular functor for $\mathrm{SU}(n)$). However, finer structural questions about $\rho_{r,k}$ — its kernel (asymptotic faithfulness is known, by Andersen, but the precise kernel for fixed $k$ is not), the image, irreducibility, and a complete intrinsic character formula — remain only partially understood.

An interval graph is the intersection graph of a family of intervals on the real line: each vertex corresponds to an interval, and two vertices are adjacent if and only if the corresponding intervals intersect.

A radio labeling of a graph G=(V,E) is an injective function f: V → ℤ_{>0} assigning distinct positive integers to the vertices such that |f(u) − f(v)| ≥ 2 whenever uv ∈ E. The span of f is max_{v∈V} f(v). The Radio Labeling problem (RL) asks for a radio labeling of G of minimum span.

Two pre-labeled variants are considered:
• p-RL(l): for a fixed positive integer l (not part of the input), the input consists of a graph G, a set S ⊆ V with |S| = l, and an assignment g: S → ℤ_{>0}; the task is to determine a radio labeling f of G of minimum span such that f(v) = g(v) for all v ∈ S.
• p-RL(*): the same task as p-RL(l), except that the size of the pre-labeled set S is part of the input.

Problem: Determine the computational complexity of RL, p-RL(l), and p-RL(*) when the input graph G is restricted to the class of interval graphs.

A literature search finds general complexity results for radio labeling variants — p-RL(*) is NP-hard on cographs and on k-colorable graphs (k≥3) with a given coloring, while polynomial-time algorithms exist for bounded-degree graphs and for p-RL(l) on k-colored graphs — but no source was found establishing the complexity of RL, p-RL(l), or p-RL(*) specifically on interval graphs. The difference body of $K$ is $D_K = \{x - y : x, y \in K\}$, and $\mathrm{bd}\, D_K$ denotes its topological boundary. Let $o$ denote the origin. For a closed set $X \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, say that condition $\mathrm{GC}(X)$ holds if $g_K(x) = g_H(x)$ for all $x$ in some open neighbourhood of $X$.

A local symmetry of a planar convex body $K$ is a pair $(\alpha, \beta)$ of closed boundary arcs of $K$ such that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are reflections of each other in some point, have disjoint and nonempty relative interiors, and are not properly contained in any larger pair of arcs with these same properties. The body $K$ is said to be globally non-symmetric if it admits no local symmetry.

Assume that $K$ is strictly convex and globally non-symmetric, and assume $\mathrm{GC}(X)$ holds where $X$ is either $\{o\}$ or $\mathrm{bd}\, D_K$. Without imposing any further regularity on $\partial K$ (in particular, without assuming that $\partial K$ is of class $C^2$ with everywhere nonzero principal curvature), must $K$ and $H$ coincide up to translations and point reflections?

The covariogram problem in the plane was settled affirmatively by Averkov and Bianchi (2009), who proved Matheron's conjecture for all planar convex bodies, removing earlier C^2-type regularity hypotheses. Consequently the local-versus-global determination results (including the variant asked here for strictly convex globally non-symmetric planar bodies without C^2 boundary) follow from this more general resolution. The status is therefore solved.

A matroid $M$ is called an intertwine of two matroids $N_1$ and $N_2$ if $M$ has both an $N_1$-minor and an $N_2$-minor, but no proper minor of $M$ has both an $N_1$-minor and an $N_2$-minor. For positive integers $r \le n$, $U_{r,n}$ denotes the uniform matroid of rank $r$ on $n$ elements. The branch-width of a matroid is defined in the standard way via branch-decompositions of its connectivity function.

Prove or disprove the following: for every pair of matroids $N_1$ and $N_2$ and every positive integer $k$, there exists an integer $n$ (depending on $N_1$, $N_2$, and $k$) such that every intertwine $M$ of $N_1$ and $N_2$ with no $U_{k,2k}$-minor satisfies $\mathrm{bw}(M) \le n$.
